Accumulate-repeat-accumulate (ARA) code › p. 178 

A generalization of the RA code in which the outer repetition-code encoding step is augmented with an accumulator acting on a fraction of the incoming bits. In addition, the code may be punctured after the final accumulating step. Affine-permutation-matrix LDPC (APM-LDPC) code 

> › p. 178

LDPC code whose parity-check matrix can be put into the form of a block matrix consisting of permutation submatrices representing the affine permutation group or the zero submatrix. Given a cyclic group Z𝑟 , the affine permutation group is Z𝑟 ⋊ Z ×

𝑟 , where Z×

𝑟 is the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑟 . Such codes are often constructed by lifting › p. 211 certain protographs into such block matrices [40]. Algebraic LDPC code › p. 178 

LDPC code whose parity check matrix is constructed explicitly (i.e., non-randomly) from a particular graph [ 41 , 42 ] or an algebraic structure such as a combinatorial design [ 43 –45 ], balanced incomplete block design [ 46 ], a partial geometry [ 47 ], a generalized polygon [ 48 , 49 ], or a Latin square [ 50 –52 ]. The extra structure and/or symmetry [ 53 ] of these codes can often be used to gain a better understanding of their properties. Array-based LDPC (AB-LDPC) code 

> › p. 178

QC-LDPC code constructed deterministically from a disk array code known as a B-code. Its parity-check matrix admits a compact representation [56] and is related to RS codes. Block LDPC (B-LDPC) code › p. 181 

Member of a particular class of irregular QC-LDPC codes with efficient encoders. Cycle LDPC code 

> › p. 184

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix forms the incidence matrix of a graph, i.e., has weight-two columns. Difference-set cyclic (DSC) code › p. 185 

Cyclic LDPC code constructed deterministically from a difference set. Certain DSC codes satisfy more redundant constraints than Gallager codes and thus can outperform them [62]. Expander code › p. 186 LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is derived from the adjacency matrix of a bipartite expander graph [ 64 ] such as a Ramanujan graph or a Cayley graph of a projective special linear group over a finite field [ 65 , 66 ]. Expander codes admit efficient encoding and decoding algorithms and yield an explicit (i.e., non-random) asymptotically good LDPC code family. Extended IRA (eIRA) code › p. 186 

A generalization of the IRA code in which the outer LDGM code is replaced by a random sparse matrix containing no weight-two columns. Finite-geometry LDPC (FG-LDPC) code › p. 186 

LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is the incidence matrix of points and hyperplanes in either a Euclidean or a projective geometry. Such codes are called Euclidean-geometry LDPC (EG-LDPC) and projective-geometry LDPC (PG-LDPC) , respectively. Such constructions have been generalized to incidence matrices of hyperplanes of different dimensions [67]. Gallager (GL) code 

> › p. 187

The first LDPC code. The rows of the parity-check matrix of this regular code are divided into equal subsets, and columns in the first subset are randomly permuted to yield the corresponding rows in subsequent subsets. 36 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Hsu-Anastasopoulos LDPC (HA-LDPC) code › p. 189 

A regular LDPC code obtained from a concatenation of a certain random regular LDPC code and a certain random LDGM code. An (𝑙, 𝑟 , 𝑔 )-HA-LDPC code can be written using punctured LDPC and LDGM parts, and it is dual to the corresponding (𝑟 , 𝑙, 𝑔 )-MN-LDPC code [ 73 ]. Using rate-one LDGM codes eliminates high-weight codewords while admitting an amount of low-weight codewords that asymptotically vanishes, allowing code families to achieve the GV bound › p. 209 with high probability. Irregular LDPC code 

> › p. 190

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix has a variable number of entries in each row or column. Irregular repeat-accumulate (IRA) code › p. 190 

A generalization of the RA code in which the outer 1-in-3 repetition encoding step is replaced by an LDGM code. A simple version is when different bits in the RA block are repeated a different number of times. Lazebnik-Ustimenko (LU) code › p. 192 

LDPC code whose Tanner graph comes from a particular family of 𝑞 -regular graphs [ 75 ] of known girth and relatively large stopping sets. Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 

A binary linear code with a sparse parity-check matrix. Often a member of an infinite family of [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] codes for which the numbers of nonzero entries in each row and in each column of the parity-check matrix are both bounded above by a constant as 

𝑛 → ∞ .MacKay-Neal LDPC (MN-LDPC) code 

> › p. 195

A code whose parity-check matrix is constructed non-deterministically via the MacKay-Neal prescription. Margulis LDPC code 

> › p. 196

Member of a class of LDPC codes deterministically constructed from explicit sparse regular expander graphs. The underlying Margulis-Gabber-Galil graph family provides explicit expanders [ 41 , 78 ], yielding deterministic sparse parity-check matrices. Related explicit LDPC constructions [79] utilize Ramanujan graphs [65, 66]. Multi-edge LDPC code › p. 196 

Irregular LDPC code whose construction generalizes those of the original examples of irregular LDPC as well as RA codes. Pinwheel code › p. 232 A geometrically local binary LDPC code defined on planar graphs obtained from the pinwheel tiling [ 81 ]. Both bits and checks live on vertices of the graph. If 𝐿 𝑁 is the graph Laplacian at generation 𝑁 , the undepleted check matrix is ˜𝐻 𝑁 = (𝐿 𝑁 − I) mod 2, and the actual parity-check matrix 𝐻 𝑁 is obtained by removing an evenly spaced fraction of boundary checks. Protograph LDPC code › p. 198 

Binary version of a 𝑞 -ary protograph LDPC code. Its parity-check matrix can be written as a block matrix whose blocks are either sums of permutation matrices or the zero matrix. Quasi-cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) code 

> › p. 199

LDPC code that can be put into quasi-cyclic form. Its parity check matrix can be put into the form of a block matrix consisting of either circulant permutation sub-matrices or the zero sub-matrix. Such codes are often constructed by lifting › p. 211 certain protographs into such block matrices [ 40 ]. Their simple structure makes them useful for several wireless communication standards. Regular LDPC code 

> › p. 201

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix has a fixed number of ones in each row and each column. Such a code is called ( 𝑗, 𝑘 )-regular if each column has weight 𝑗 (variable-node degree) and each row has weight 𝑘 (check-node degree). If the parity-check matrix has 𝑛 columns and 𝑚 rows, then regularity implies 𝑛 𝑗 = 𝑚𝑘 .Repeat-accumulate (RA) code › p. 201 

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix has weight-two columns arranged in a step-like pattern for its last columns [82]. Repeat-accumulate-accumulate (RAA) code › p. 202 

Generalization of the RA code in which two accumulators and permutations are used. Spatially coupled LDPC (SC-LDPC) code › p. 203 

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is constructed by "spatially" coupling several copies of a regular LDPC parity-check matrix in chain-like fashion (or, more generally, in grid-like fashion) to yield a band matrix. A finite-length chain is then capped by imposing either open boundary conditions (yielding non-tail-biting SC-LDPC codes) or periodic boundary conditions (yielding 

tail-biting SC-LDPC codes); sometimes extra terminating vertices are added to the ends of the chain. Matrices corresponding to translationally invariant chains are called time-invariant , and otherwise are called time-varying . These codes can be constructed, e.g., using the lifting › p. 211 procedure or using edge-cutting vectors [ 83 ]. Spatial coupling can also be applied to MN-LDPC and HA-LDPC protographs, yielding bounded-density SC-MN and SC-HA families [73]. Tanner-Sridhara-Fuja (TSF) code 

> › p. 203

Array QC-LDPC code constructed from a cyclically shifted identity matrix; see [85, Exam. 21.6.5]. Tornado code › p. 203 Linear binary erasure code that is a precursor to fountain codes and is built from a multilayer cascade of sparse bipartite graphs. Its encoding and decoding operations involve only XOR gates [86, 87][88, Sec. 30.2]. 

[7, 3, 4] simplex code › p. 176 

Second-smallest nontrivial member of the simplex-code family. The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (2, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

Code Description 

Analog code › p. 256 Encodes states (codewords) into continuous coordinates in the 𝑛 -dimensional (real or complex) coordinate space ( R𝑛 or C𝑛 ). Important subclasses include sphere packings, tilings, and modulation constellations. The number of codewords may be infinite because the coordinate space is infinite, so various restricted versions have to be constructed in practice. Extended GRS code 

> › p. 221

A GRS code extended by one extra coordinate to form an [𝑛 + 1, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 2]𝑞 MDS code. In projective language, this corresponds to adding one more evaluation point, often interpreted as the point at infinity; in suitable equivalent descriptions, one may instead use an affine point such as 0. The case when 𝑛 = 𝑞 − 1, multipliers 𝑣 𝑖 = 1, and 𝛼 𝑖 are 𝑖 − 1st powers of a primitive 𝑛 th root of unity is an extended narrow-sense RS code .Generalized RM (GRM) code › p. 222 

Extensions of RM codes to 𝑞 -ary coordinates that can be described as multivariate polynomial evaluation codes over affine or projective space. Locally correctable code (LCC) › p. 166 

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LCC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of a codeword from at most 𝑟 

coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Locally decodable code (LDC) › p. 166 

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LDC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of the message from at most 

𝑟 coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Efficiency of the decoding is quantified by the code’s query complexity 𝑟 , and decoding is performed by sampling subsets of 𝑟 bits. Locally testable code (LTC) › p. 167 

Code for which one can efficiently check whether a given string is a codeword or is far from a codeword. Efficiency of the verification is quantified by the code’s query complexity 𝑢 , while effectiveness is quantified by the code’s soundness 𝑅 .Multiplicity code 

> › p. 230

A generalization of an 𝑚 -variate polynomial evaluation code based on evaluating polynomials together with their Hasse derivatives up to order 𝑠 − 1 at all points in F𝑚 𝑞 . Originally proposed for coding using the Rosenbloom-Tsfasman metric [ 164 ]. Univariate ( 𝑚 = 1)[164, 165] and multivariate ( 𝑚 > 1) [166] codes have been proposed. 38

The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (2, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

Affine-permutation-matrix LDPC (APM-LDPC) code 

› p. 178 

LDPC code whose parity-check matrix can be put into the form of a block matrix consisting of permutation submatrices representing the affine permutation group or the zero submatrix. Given a cyclic group Z𝑟 , the affine permutation group is Z𝑟 ⋊ Z ×

𝑟 , where Z×

𝑟 is the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑟 . Such codes are often constructed by lifting › p. 211 certain protographs into such block matrices [40]. Algebraic LDPC code › p. 178 

LDPC code whose parity check matrix is constructed explicitly (i.e., non-randomly) from a particular graph [ 41 , 42 ] or an algebraic structure such as a combinatorial design [ 43 –45 ], balanced incomplete block design [ 46 ], a partial geometry [ 47 ], a generalized polygon [ 48 , 49 ], or a Latin square [ 50 –52 ]. The extra structure and/or symmetry [ 53 ] of these codes can often be used to gain a better understanding of their properties. Array-based LDPC (AB-LDPC) code 

› p. 178 

QC-LDPC code constructed deterministically from a disk array code known as a B-code. Its parity-check matrix admits a compact representation [56] and is related to RS codes. Availability code 

› p. 213 

A 𝑡 -availability parallel-recovery code is a code such that coordinates can be recovered in multiple ways. The availability of a locally recoverable code is the minimum, over all coordinates, of the number of recovery sets for that coordinate [ 21 , Def. 15.9.20]. That way, the code accommodates nodes that may be inaccessible during the recovery procedure. Barg-Tamo-Vladut code › p. 214 

Evaluation AG code on algebraic curves built from a Galois cover 𝜙 : 𝑌 → 𝑋 , where the recovery sets are fibres over rational points of 𝑋 that split completely in the cover [ 21 , Def. 15.9.10][ 21 , Thm. 15.9.14]. The Barg-Tamo-Vladut construction generalizes the Tamo-Barg construction from 𝑃𝐺 (1, 𝑞 ) to longer AG codes, and variants can be built with higher local distance or availability 2 via fibre products of curves [21, Thm. 15.9.19][21, Thm. 15.9.21]. Block LDPC (B-LDPC) code › p. 181 

Member of a particular class of irregular QC-LDPC codes with efficient encoders. Cycle LDPC code 

› p. 184 

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix forms the incidence matrix of a graph, i.e., has weight-two columns. Denniston code 

› p. 217 

Projective code that is part of a family of [2𝑎 +𝑖 + 2𝑖 − 2𝑎 , 3, 2𝑎 +𝑖 − 2𝑎 ]2𝑎 codes for 𝑖 < 𝑎 constructed using Denniston arcs [ 157 ,Sec. 19.7.3]. Difference-set cyclic (DSC) code › p. 185 

Cyclic LDPC code constructed deterministically from a difference set. Certain DSC codes satisfy more redundant constraints than Gallager codes and thus can outperform them [62]. Expander code › p. 186 LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is derived from the adjacency matrix of a bipartite expander graph [ 64 ] such as a Ramanujan graph or a Cayley graph of a projective special linear group over a finite field [ 65 , 66 ]. Expander codes admit efficient encoding and decoding algorithms and yield an explicit (i.e., non-random) asymptotically good LDPC code family. Extended GRS code 

› p. 221 

A GRS code extended by one extra coordinate to form an [𝑛 + 1, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 2]𝑞 MDS code. In projective language, this corresponds to adding one more evaluation point, often interpreted as the point at infinity; in suitable equivalent descriptions, one may instead use an affine point such as 0. The case when 𝑛 = 𝑞 − 1, multipliers 𝑣 𝑖 = 1, and 𝛼 𝑖 are 𝑖 − 1st powers of a primitive 𝑛 th root of unity is an extended narrow-sense RS code .Extended IRA (eIRA) code › p. 186 

A generalization of the IRA code in which the outer LDGM code is replaced by a random sparse matrix containing no weight-two columns. Finite-geometry LDPC (FG-LDPC) code › p. 186 

LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is the incidence matrix of points and hyperplanes in either a Euclidean or a projective geometry. Such codes are called Euclidean-geometry LDPC (EG-LDPC) and projective-geometry LDPC (PG-LDPC) , respectively. Such constructions have been generalized to incidence matrices of hyperplanes of different dimensions [67]. Gallager (GL) code 

› p. 187 

The first LDPC code. The rows of the parity-check matrix of this regular code are divided into equal subsets, and columns in the first subset are randomly permuted to yield the corresponding rows in subsequent subsets. 40

Generalized RM (GRM) code › p. 222 

Extensions of RM codes to 𝑞 -ary coordinates that can be described as multivariate polynomial evaluation codes over affine or projective space. Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 

An [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1]𝑞 MDS code that is a modification of the RS code where codeword polynomials are multiplied by additional prefactors [21, Def. 15.3.19]. Griesmer code › p. 224 A type of 𝑞 -ary code whose parameters satisfy the Griesmer bound with equality. Hirschfeld code 

> › p. 226

A [𝑞 + 1, 4, 𝑞 − 2]𝑞 projective geometry code for non-prime 𝑞 that is an example of an MDS code that is not an RS code; see [ 167 ,Exam. 7.6] for the generator matrix. Hsu-Anastasopoulos LDPC (HA-LDPC) code › p. 189 

A regular LDPC code obtained from a concatenation of a certain random regular LDPC code and a certain random LDGM code. An (𝑙, 𝑟 , 𝑔 )-HA-LDPC code can be written using punctured LDPC and LDGM parts, and it is dual to the corresponding (𝑟 , 𝑙, 𝑔 )-MN-LDPC code [ 73 ]. Using rate-one LDGM codes eliminates high-weight codewords while admitting an amount of low-weight codewords that asymptotically vanishes, allowing code families to achieve the GV bound › p. 209 with high probability. Irregular LDPC code 

> › p. 190

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix has a variable number of entries in each row or column. Irregular repeat-accumulate (IRA) code › p. 190 

A generalization of the RA code in which the outer 1-in-3 repetition encoding step is replaced by an LDGM code. A simple version is when different bits in the RA block are repeated a different number of times. Lazebnik-Ustimenko (LU) code › p. 192 

LDPC code whose Tanner graph comes from a particular family of 𝑞 -regular graphs [ 75 ] of known girth and relatively large stopping sets. Locally correctable code (LCC) › p. 166 

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LCC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of a codeword from at most 𝑟 

coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Locally recoverable code (LRC) › p. 167 

A block code for which one can recover any coordinate of a codeword from at most 𝑟 other coordinates of the codeword [ 21 , Def. 15.9.3]. Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 

A binary linear code with a sparse parity-check matrix. Often a member of an infinite family of [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] codes for which the numbers of nonzero entries in each row and in each column of the parity-check matrix are both bounded above by a constant as 

𝑛 → ∞ .MacKay-Neal LDPC (MN-LDPC) code 

> › p. 195

A code whose parity-check matrix is constructed non-deterministically via the MacKay-Neal prescription. Margulis LDPC code 

> › p. 196

Member of a class of LDPC codes deterministically constructed from explicit sparse regular expander graphs. A 𝑞 -ary linear code whose parameters satisfy the Singleton bound with equality. Multi-edge LDPC code › p. 196 

Irregular LDPC code whose construction generalizes those of the original examples of irregular LDPC as well as RA codes. Narrow-sense RS code › p. 230 

An [𝑞 − 1, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1]𝑞 RS code whose points 𝛼 𝑖 are all (𝑖 − 1)st powers of a primitive › p. 164 element 𝛼 of F𝑞 .Optimal LRC › p. 168 An LRC whose parameters saturate a generalized Singleton bound. Parallel-recovery code › p. 231 

A 𝑡 -erasure LRC whose coordinate erasures can be recovered in parallel. Pinwheel code › p. 232 A geometrically local binary LDPC code defined on planar graphs obtained from the pinwheel tiling [ 81 ]. Both bits and checks live on vertices of the graph. If 𝐿 𝑁 is the graph Laplacian at generation 𝑁 , the undepleted check matrix is ˜𝐻 𝑁 = (𝐿 𝑁 − I) mod 2, and the actual parity-check matrix 𝐻 𝑁 is obtained by removing an evenly spaced fraction of boundary checks. Projective RM (PRM) code › p. 234 

Evaluation code obtained by evaluating homogeneous polynomials on the points of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (𝑚, 𝑞 ), equivalently on representatives of the nonzero vectors in F𝑚 +1 

> 𝑞

whose leftmost nonzero coordinate is one. Protograph LDPC code › p. 198 

Binary version of a 𝑞 -ary protograph LDPC code. Its parity-check matrix can be written as a block matrix whose blocks are either sums of permutation matrices or the zero matrix. Pyramid code › p. 235 An LRC whose generator matrix is that of an RS code in standard form, but some of whose columns are split into multiple columns; see [168, Sec. 31.3.1.1] for an example. Quasi-cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) code 

> › p. 199

LDPC code that can be put into quasi-cyclic form. Its parity check matrix can be put into the form of a block matrix consisting of either circulant permutation sub-matrices or the zero sub-matrix. Such codes are often constructed by lifting › p. 211 certain protographs into such block matrices [ 40 ]. Their simple structure makes them useful for several wireless communication standards. 41

> › p. 202

[𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ] binary linear code encoding one bit of information into an 𝑛 -bit string. Majority decoding requires 𝑛 to be odd in order to avoid ties. The idea is to increase the code distance by repeating the logical information several times. It is a (𝑛, 1)-Hamming code. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .Roth-Lempel code 

> › p. 238

A 𝑡 -erasure LRC whose erased coordinates are recovered sequentially. Spatially coupled LDPC (SC-LDPC) code › p. 203 

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is constructed by "spatially" coupling several copies of a regular LDPC parity-check matrix in chain-like fashion (or, more generally, in grid-like fashion) to yield a band matrix. A finite-length chain is then capped by imposing either open boundary conditions (yielding non-tail-biting SC-LDPC codes) or periodic boundary conditions (yielding 

tail-biting SC-LDPC codes); sometimes extra terminating vertices are added to the ends of the chain. Matrices corresponding to translationally invariant chains are called time-invariant , and otherwise are called time-varying . These codes can be constructed, e.g., using the lifting › p. 211 procedure or using edge-cutting vectors [ 83 ]. Spatial coupling can also be applied to MN-LDPC and HA-LDPC protographs, yielding bounded-density SC-MN and SC-HA families [73]. Tamo-Barg code

> › p. 203

Tornado code › p. 203 Linear binary erasure code that is a precursor to fountain codes and is built from a multilayer cascade of sparse bipartite graphs. Its encoding and decoding operations involve only XOR gates [86, 87][88, Sec. 30.2].

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or parity bit 

such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .

Cyclic linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 216 

A 𝑞 -ary code of length 𝑛 is cyclic if, for each codeword 𝑐 1 𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the cyclically shifted string 𝑐 𝑛 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 −1 is also a codeword. A cyclic code is called primitive when 𝑛 = 𝑞 𝑟 − 1 for some 𝑟 ≥ 2. A shortened cyclic code is obtained from a cyclic code by taking only codewords with the first 𝑗 zero entries, and deleting those zeroes. Cyclic linear binary code › p. 184 

A binary code of length 𝑛 is cyclic if, for each codeword 𝑐 1 𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the cyclically shifted string 𝑐 𝑛 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 −1 is also a codeword. Kopparty-Meir-Ron-Zewi-Saraf (KMRS) code › p. 192 

Member of a family of locally testable binary linear codes with constant rate, constant relative distance, and subpolynomial query complexity 𝑢 = (log 𝑛 )𝑂 (log log 𝑛 ) . Later work by Gopi, Kopparty, Oliveira, Ron-Zewi, and Saraf [ 74 ] showed that related concatenated codes achieve the GV bound › p. 209 .Left-right Cayley complex code › p. 192 

Binary code constructed on a left-right Cayley complex using a pair of base codes 𝐶 𝐴 , 𝐶 𝐵 and an expander graph [ 64 ]. Bits live on the squares of the complex, while local constraints are imposed on edges; for a fixed graph vertex, the incident symbols form a codeword of the tensor code 𝐶 𝐴 ⊗ 𝐶 𝐵 . A family of such codes is one of the first 𝑐 3-LTCs [76]. Locally correctable code (LCC) › p. 166 

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LCC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of a codeword from at most 𝑟 

coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Locally decodable code (LDC) › p. 166 

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LDC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of the message from at most 

𝑟 coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Efficiency of the decoding is quantified by the code’s query complexity 𝑟 , and decoding is performed by sampling subsets of 𝑟 bits. Locally testable code (LTC) › p. 167 

Code for which one can efficiently check whether a given string is a codeword or is far from a codeword. Efficiency of the verification is quantified by the code’s query complexity 𝑢 , while effectiveness is quantified by the code’s soundness 𝑅 .Long code › p. 194 Nonlinear locally testable code of extremely large length that is not practical, but is useful for certain probabilistically checkable proof (PCP) constructions [77]. Lossless expander balanced-product code › p. 415 

QLDPC code constructed by taking the balanced product of lossless expander graphs. Using one part of a quantum-code chain com-plex constructed with one-sided loss expanders [ 170 ] yields a 𝑐 3-LTC [ 171 ]. Using two-sided expanders [ 172 ] yields an asymptotically good QLDPC code family [173]. Meir code › p. 230 Locally testable [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 code with query complexity poly (log 𝑘 ) and rejection ratio 𝑅 /𝑛 = 1/poly (log 𝑘 ). The code construction is probabilistic and combinatorial. > › p. 230

A generalization of an 𝑚 -variate polynomial evaluation code based on evaluating polynomials together with their Hasse derivatives up to order 𝑠 − 1 at all points in F𝑚 𝑞 . Repetition code 

> › p. 202

[𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ] binary linear code encoding one bit of information into an 𝑛 -bit string. Majority decoding requires 𝑛 to be odd in order to avoid ties. [7, 3, 4] simplex code › p. 176 

Second-smallest nontrivial member of the simplex-code family. The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (2, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or parity bit 

such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 𝑞 -ary parity-check code 

> › p. 208

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 linear 𝑞 -ary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check or zero-sum check digit such that the sum over all coordinates of each codeword is zero.

An IRS code constructed from two shortened RS codes and two forms of interleaving. In a 2D array visualization, one component code runs vertically and the other diagonally [174]. Cyclic linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 216 

A 𝑞 -ary code of length 𝑛 is cyclic if, for each codeword 𝑐 1 𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the cyclically shifted string 𝑐 𝑛 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 −1 is also a codeword. A cyclic code is called primitive when 𝑛 = 𝑞 𝑟 − 1 for some 𝑟 ≥ 2. A shortened cyclic code is obtained from a cyclic code by taking only codewords with the first 𝑗 zero entries, and deleting those zeroes. Deligne-Lusztig code › p. 217

Divisible code › p. 217 A linear 𝑞 -ary block code is Δ-divisible if the Hamming weight of each of its codewords is divisible by divisor Δ. A 2-divisible (4-divisible, 8-divisible) code is called even (doubly even , triply even ) [ 32 , 155 ]. A code is called singly even if all codewords are even and at least one has weight equal to 2 modulo 4. More generally, a code is 𝑚 -even if it is 2𝑚 -divisible. Dual linear code 

> › p. 218

For any [𝑛, 𝑘 ]𝑞 linear code 𝐶 , the dual code is the set of 𝑞 -ary strings that are orthogonal to the codewords of 𝐶 under a particular inner product. Elliptic code › p. 219 Evaluation AG code of rational functions evaluated on points lying on an elliptic curve, i.e., a curve of genus one. Evaluation AG code 

> › p. 219

> › p. 221

A GRS code extended by one extra coordinate to form an [𝑛 + 1, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 2]𝑞 MDS code. The case when 𝑛 = 𝑞 − 1, multipliers 𝑣 𝑖 = 1, and 𝛼 𝑖 are 𝑖 − 1st powers of a primitive 𝑛 th root of unity is an extended narrow-sense RS code .Flag-variety code

A code obtained from an RS code by bundling consecutive symbols into larger alphabet symbols. Goppa code › p. 223 A linear 𝑞 -ary code defined from a polynomial 𝐺 ( 𝑥 ) over an extension field and a set of evaluation points 𝐿 avoiding the roots of 

𝐺 . Goppa codes form a central family of alternant codes, admit efficient algebraic decoding algorithms, and include the binary Goppa codes used in the McEliece cryptosystem. [24 , 12 , 8] Extended Golay code › p. 175

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or parity bit such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 𝑞 -ary parity-check code 

> › p. 208

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 linear 𝑞 -ary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check or zero-sum check digit such that the sum over all coordinates of each codeword is zero.

An [𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ]𝑞 code consisting of codewords ( 𝑗, 𝑗, · · · , 𝑗 ) for 𝑗 ∈ F𝑞 .

A projective code whose generator matrix is the incidence matrix of points and hyperplanes in a projective space. Laplacian code › p. 192 A binary linear code whose parity-check matrix is the graph Laplacian reduced mod 2. > › p. 196

Member of a class of LDPC codes deterministically constructed from explicit sparse regular expander graphs. The underlying Margulis-Gabber-Galil graph family provides explicit expanders [ 41 , 78 ], yielding deterministic sparse parity-check matrices. Related explicit LDPC constructions [79] utilize Ramanujan graphs [65, 66]. Ovoid code › p. 231 Member of a [𝑞 2 + 1, 4, 𝑞 2 − 𝑞 ]𝑞 projective two-weight code family obtained from ovoids in PG (3, 𝑞 ). If the columns of a generator matrix are the 𝑞 2 + 1 points of an ovoid, then every hyperplane meets the ovoid in either 1 or 𝑞 + 1 points, yielding the two nonzero weights 𝑞 2 and 𝑞 2 − 𝑞 . See [188, pg. 107][54, pg. 192] for further details. Projective geometry code › p. 233 

Linear 𝑞 -ary [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code whose generator matrix 𝐺 does not contain any repeated columns or the zero column. That way, each column corresponds to a distinct point in the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (𝑘 − 1, 𝑞 ) arising from a 𝑘 -dimensional vector space over F𝑞 . A choice of 𝑘 linearly independent columns determines an information set . Columns of a code’s parity-check matrix can similarly correspond to points in projective space. This formulation yields connections to projective geometry, which can be applied to determine code properties. Projective two-weight code 

> › p. 234

A projective code whose codewords all have one of two possible nonzero Hamming weights.

Second-smallest nontrivial member of the simplex-code family. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

Classical fractal liquid code › p. 215 

Member of a family of [ 𝐿 𝐷 , 𝑂 (𝐿 𝐷 −1 ), 𝑂 (𝐿 𝐷 − 𝜖 ) ] 𝑝 linear codes on 𝐷 -dimensional square lattices of side length 𝐿 and for prime 

𝑝 and 𝜖 > 0 that is based on 𝑝 -ary generalizations of the Sierpinski triangle. Classical topological code › p. 181 

Classical code defined on a two-dimensional lattice and inspired by geometrically local topological quantum codes, such as the surface code or color code. Cycle code › p. 184 A code whose parity-check matrix is obtained from the incidence matrix of a graph over F2. This code’s properties are derived from the size two chain complex associated with the graph. Not every binary linear code is homological, but there exist homological families that asymptotically saturate the Hamming bound [61]. Fibonacci code › p. 186 Quantum-inspired binary linear code defined on an 𝐿 × 𝐿 /2 lattice with one bit on each site, where 𝐿 = 2𝑁 for an integer 𝑁 ≥ 2.The codewords are defined to satisfy the condition that, for each lattice site ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ), the bits on ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ), ( 𝑥 + 1, 𝑦 ), ( 𝑥 − 1, 𝑦 ) and 

( 𝑥, 𝑦 + 1) (where the lattice is taken to be periodic in both directions) contain an even number of 1’s. Gauss’ law code 

> › p. 187

An [𝑚 + 𝐷𝑚, 𝐷𝑚, 3] linear binary code for 𝑚 ≥ 3𝐷 , defined by the Gauss’ law constraint of a 𝐷 -dimensional fermionic Z2 gauge theory [ 68 , Thm. 1]. The code can be rephrased as a distance-one stabilizer code whose stabilizers consist of gauge-group elements. It can be concatenated to form a stabilizer code for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of the underlying gauge theory [68, 69]. Laplacian code › p. 192 A binary linear code whose parity-check matrix is the graph Laplacian reduced mod 2. For an undirected graph Γ with degree matrix 𝐷 and adjacency matrix 𝐴 , the parity-check matrix is the symmetric matrix 𝐻 = (𝐷 − 𝐴 ) mod 2 .Newman-Moore code › p. 196 

Member of a family of [ 𝐿 2 , 𝑂 (𝐿 ), 𝑂 (𝐿 log 3 log 2 ) ] binary linear codes on 𝐿 × 𝐿 square lattices that form the ground-state subspace of a class of exactly solvable spin-glass models with three-body interactions. The codewords resemble the Sierpinski triangle on a square lattice, which can be generated by a cellular automaton [80]. Pinwheel code › p. 232 A geometrically local binary LDPC code defined on planar graphs obtained from the pinwheel tiling [ 81 ]. Both bits and checks live on vertices of the graph. If 𝐿 𝑁 is the graph Laplacian at generation 𝑁 , the undepleted check matrix is ˜𝐻 𝑁 = (𝐿 𝑁 − I) mod 2, and the actual parity-check matrix 𝐻 𝑁 is obtained by removing an evenly spaced fraction of boundary checks. Plaquette Ising code 

> › p. 197

Classical code defined on a cubic lattice in usually two or three dimensions whose parity checks are applied on the four vertices of each square. Quantum-inspired classical block code 

> › p. 235

A 𝑞 -ary linear code whose construction was inspired by a quantum code. X-cube model code 

> › p. 468

A foliated type-I fracton CSS code on a cubic lattice with qubits on edges, cube stabilizers, and three cross-shaped vertex stabilizers for each vertex [216]. It supports a subextensive number of logical qubits.

[11 , 6, 5]3 Ternary Golay code › p. 205 

A [11 , 6, 5]3 perfect ternary linear code with connections to various areas of mathematics, e.g., lattices [ 32 ] and sporadic simple groups [ 34 ]. [7, 3, 4] simplex code › p. 176 

Second-smallest nontrivial member of the simplex-code family. The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (2, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

[7, 4, 3] Hamming code › p. 176 

Second-smallest member of the Hamming code family.

> › p. 208

Extension of the [7, 4, 3] Hamming code by a parity-check bit. The smallest doubly even self-dual code, and the unique Type II code of length 8 [33, Rem. 4.3.10]. 

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or parity bit 

such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .

> › p. 202

[𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ] binary linear code encoding one bit of information into an 𝑛 -bit string. Majority decoding requires 𝑛 to be odd in order to avoid ties. > › p. 290

A code 𝑊 in a compact connected two-point homogeneous space with 𝑚 = 𝑙 (𝑊 ) distinct distances such that either 𝑟 (𝑊 ) ≥ 2𝑚 − 1,or 𝑟 (𝑊 ) = 2𝑚 − 2 > 0 and 𝑊 is diametrical [156]. Simplex spherical code › p. 276 

Spherical (𝑛, 𝑛 + 1, 2 + 2/𝑛 ) code whose codewords are all permutations of the 𝑛 + 1-dimensional vector (1, 1, · · · , 1, −𝑛 ), up to normalization, forming an 𝑛 -simplex. Member of an infinite family of perfect linear codes with parameters [2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3] for 𝑟 ≥ 2. Their 𝑟 × ( 2𝑟 − 1) parity-check matrix 𝐻 has all possible nonzero 𝑟 -bit strings as its columns. Adding a parity check yields the [2𝑟 , 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 4] extended Hamming code.

[7, 3, 4] simplex code › p. 176 

Second-smallest nontrivial member of the simplex-code family. The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (2, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. The codewords form a (8, 9) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . As a simplex code, it is equidistant: every nonzero codeword has Hamming weight 4.

[7, 4, 3] Hamming code › p. 176 

Second-smallest member of the Hamming code family. 

[78 , 6, 56 ]4 Hill-cap code › p. 208 

Projective two-weight quaternary code based on a cap that corresponds to a strongly regular graph [190, Table 7.1]. 

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or parity bit 

such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 .

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 𝑞 -ary parity-check code 

> › p. 208

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 linear 𝑞 -ary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check or zero-sum check digit such that the sum over all coordinates of each codeword is zero. 

Λ24 Leech lattice 

> › p. 253

Even unimodular lattice in 24 dimensions that exhibits optimal packing. Its automorphism group is the Conway group Co 0.

An [𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ]𝑞 code consisting of codewords ( 𝑗, 𝑗, · · · , 𝑗 ) for 𝑗 ∈ F𝑞 .

𝑞 -ary sharp configuration › p. 212 

A 𝑞 -ary code that admits 𝑚 different distances between distinct codewords and forms a design of strength 2𝑚 − 1 or greater.

> › p. 212

FIG. 21: 1D stabilizer codes (view online). Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Quantum convolutional code 

> › p. 424

1D translationally invariant qubit stabilizer code whose stabilizer group can be partitioned into constant-size subsets of constant support and of constant overlap between neighboring sets. Initially formulated as a quantum analogue of convolutional codes, which were designed to protect a continuous and never-ending stream of information. Precise formulations sometimes begin with a finite-dimensional lattice, with the intent to take the thermodynamic limit; logical dimension can be infinite as well. Quantum irregular convolutional code (QIRCC) › p. 426 

Quantum convolutional code whose stabilizer group consists of different constant-size subsets. Quantum repetition code › p. 429 

Encodes 1 qubit into 𝑛 qubits according to |0⟩ → | 𝜙 0 ⟩⊗𝑛 and |1⟩ → | 𝜙 1 ⟩⊗𝑛 . The code is called a bit-flip code when | 𝜙 𝑖 ⟩ = |𝑖 ⟩,and a phase-flip code when | 𝜙 0 ⟩ = |+⟩ and | 𝜙 1 ⟩ = | −⟩ . This repetition-style encoding does not clone an arbitrary quantum state; instead, it extends the copying of computational-basis states linearly to entangled codewords [381, Ch. 2]. Quantum turbo code › p. 432 

A quantum version of the turbo code, obtained from an interleaved serial quantum concatenation [ 382 , Def. 30] of quantum convolutional codes. The interleaver induces long-range entanglement and can increase the minimum distance relative to the constituent convolutional codes [383]. Tetron code › p. 460 A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) code › p. 462 

A 1D translationally invariant stabilizer code whose encoding is a constant-depth circuit of nearest-neighbor gates on alternating even and odd bonds that consist of transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian interactions. The code allows for perfect state transfer of arbitrary distance using local operations and classical communications (LOCC). 

(5, 1, 2)-convolutional code 

> › p. 331

Family of quantum convolutional codes that are 1D lattice generalizations of the five-qubit perfect code, with the former’s lattice-translation symmetry being the extension of the latter’s cyclic permutation symmetry. 

⟦5, 1, 3⟧ Five-qubit perfect code › p. 348 

Five-qubit cyclic stabilizer code that is the smallest qubit stabilizer code to correct a single-qubit error.

2D bosonization code › p. 361 

A mapping between a 2D lattice quadratic Hamiltonian of Majorana modes and a 2D lattice of qubits. The original exact 2D bosonization code [ 386 ] is a stabilizer code whose generators are products of plaquettes and stars of the surface code, with gauge constraints that project onto a toric-code-like subspace with emergent fermions [ 386 , 387 ]. Finite-depth generalized local unitary Clifford circuits generate a family of equivalent local encodings with qubit-to-fermion ratio 𝑟 = 1 + 12𝑘 for any positive integer 𝑘 ; the square-lattice compact encoding with 𝑟 = 1.5 and the super-compact encoding with 𝑟 = 1.25 are explicit examples [387]. 2D color code › p. 362 Color code defined on a graph embedded in a two-dimensional surface. Each face hosts two stabilizer generators, a Pauli-𝑋 and a Pauli-𝑍 string acting on all the qubits of the face. 2D lattice stabilizer code › p. 543 

Lattice stabilizer code in two Euclidean dimensions, using either the ordinary block notion of locality or the fermionic/Majorana notion of locality. Abelian TQD stabilizer code › p. 475 

Modular-qudit stabilizer code whose codewords realize a 2D Abelian twisted-quantum-double topological order on composite-dimensional qudits. For every finite Abelian group 𝐺 = Î𝑖 Z𝑁 𝑖 and every product of Type-I and Type-II cocycles, there is a Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonian realizing the corresponding Abelian TQD [ 388 ]. Equivalently, these codes exhaust the 2D Abelian topological orders that admit gapped boundaries [388, 389]. Abelian quantum-double stabilizer code › p. 474 

Modular-qudit stabilizer code whose codewords realize 2D modular gapped Abelian topological order with trivial cocycle. The corresponding anyon theory is defined by an Abelian group. The 𝐺 = Z2 instance on a torus is the toric code, and cyclic-group instances reduce to modular-qudit surface codes. All such codes can be realized by a stack of modular-qudit surface codes because all finite Abelian groups are direct products of cyclic groups. Analog surface code 

› p. 511 

An analog CSS version of the Kitaev surface code realizing a phase of 2D R gauge theory. BB5 code › p. 369 A BB code with weight-five stabilizer generators (contrasting with the weight-six checks of standard BB codes), designed and benchmarked for long chains of trapped ions [390]. Ball-Verstraete-Cirac (BVC) code 

› p. 369 

A 2D fermion-into-qubit encoding that builds upon the JW transformation by eliminating the weight-𝑂 (𝑛 ) non-local 𝑍 -type string at the expense of introducing an auxiliary qubit per site and local gauge constraints. See [387, Sec. IV.B] for details. Bivariate bicycle (BB) code › p. 370 

One of several Abelian 2BGA codes which admit time-optimal syndrome measurement circuits that can be implemented in a two-layer architecture, a generalization of the square-lattice architecture optimal for the surface codes. Codes can be classified by the weight of their checks, e.g., by BB 𝑤 where 𝑤 is the check weight. Bravyi-Kitaev superfast (BKSF) code › p. 372 

A single-error-detecting fermion-into-qubit encoding defined on a 2D qubit lattice whose stabilizers are associated with loops in the lattice. For the square-lattice edge ordering used in Ref. [ 387 ], the BKSF logical operators coincide with exact 2D bosonization on the dual lattice after relabeling 𝑋 and 𝑌 . The code can be generalized to a single error-correcting code (i.e., with distance three) on graphs of degree ≥ 6 [391]. Clifford-deformed surface code (CDSC) 

› p. 375 

A generally non-CSS derivative of the surface code defined by applying a translationally invariant constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 

to the original (CSS) surface code. Unlike the surface code, CDSCs include codes whose thresholds and subthreshold performance are enhanced under noise biased towards dephasing. Examples of CDSCs include the XY code, XZZX code, and random CDSCs. 72 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Compactified R

gauge theory code 

> › p. 518

An integer-homology bosonic CSS code realizing 2D 𝑈 (1) gauge theory on bosonic modes. The code can be obtained from the analog surface code by condensing › p. 559 certain anyons [ 392 ]. This results in a pinning of each mode to the space of periodic functions, which is the Hilbert space of a physical rotor, and can be thought of as compactification of the 2D R gauge theory phase realized by the analog surface code. Derby-Klassen (DK) code › p. 384 

A fermion-into-qubit code defined on regular tilings with maximum degree 4 whose stabilizers are associated with loops in the tiling. The code outperforms several other encodings in terms of encoding rate [ 393 , Table I]. It has been extended for models with several modes per site [394]. Double-semion stabilizer code › p. 476 

A 2D lattice modular-qudit stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 that realizes the 2D double semion topological phase. The code can be obtained from a Z4 toric-code ground state by condensing › p. 559 the emergent boson 𝑒 2 𝑚 2; in the stabilizer construction this condensation is implemented by two-body measurements [ 388 , 395 ]. Its ground-state subspace can be mapped to that of the double-semion string-net model by a finite-depth quantum circuit with ancillas [388]. GKP-surface code 

> › p. 522

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code and whose inner code is a surface code, including toric surface-code variants [396, 397], rotated surface codes [398–401], and XZZX surface codes [402]. Galois-qudit color code › p. 493 

Extension of the color code to 2D lattices of Galois qudits. Galois-qudit surface code › p. 498 

Extension of the surface code to 2D lattices of Galois qudits. Honeycomb (6.6.6) color code › p. 402 

2D color code defined on a (typically triangular) patch of the 6.6.6 (honeycomb) tiling. The usual triangular patch has three differently colored boundaries, encodes one logical qubit, and is local-Clifford equivalent to a folded surface/toric code with two smooth and two rough boundaries [403]. Kitaev surface code 

> › p. 410

A family of Abelian topological CSS stabilizer › p. 544 codes whose generators are few-body 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type Pauli strings associated to the stars and plaquettes, respectively, of a cellulation of a two-dimensional surface (with a qubit located at each edge of the cellulation). Codewords correspond to ground states of the surface code Hamiltonian, and error operators create or annihilate pairs of anyonic charges or vortices. Klein-bottle surface code › p. 414 

A family of Kitaev surface codes on the non-orientable Klein bottle. Majorana color code 

> › p. 416

A fermionic analogue of a 2D color code. Majorana loop stabilizer code (MLSC) › p. 417 

A single-error-correcting fermion-into-qubit encoding defined on a 2D qubit lattice whose stabilizers are associated with loops in the lattice. Majorana surface code › p. 418 

Fermionic analogue of the surface code defined on a three-colorable 2D tiling whose face operators are non-overlapping even-Majorana stabilizers. Open patches with four or six alternating colored boundaries encode logical tetrons or hexons. The uniform 4.8.8, 6.6.6, and 4.6.12 tilings yield families with tetron, hexon, or dodecon building blocks and with twist-based lattice surgery supporting minimal-overhead logical Clifford gates [385]. Matching code › p. 419 Member of a class of qubit stabilizer codes based on the Abelian phase of the Kitaev honeycomb model. Modular-qudit surface code › p. 482 

Extension of the surface code to prime-dimensional [ 404 , 405 ] and more general modular qudits. Stabilizer generators are few-body 

𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type Pauli strings associated to the stars and plaquettes, respectively, of a tessellation of a two-dimensional surface. Since qudits have more than one 𝑋 and 𝑍 -type operator, various sets of stabilizer generators can be defined. Projective-plane surface code › p. 423 

A family of Kitaev surface codes on the non-orientable 2-dimensional compact manifold R𝑃 2 (in contrast to a genus-𝑔 surface). Whereas genus-𝑔 surface codes require 2𝑔 logical qubits, qubit codes on R𝑃 2 are made from a single logical qubit. Rotated surface code › p. 448 

Variant of the surface code obtained by taking the medial graph of the surface code lattice (treated as a graph) and applying a procedure to construct the check operators [ 406 , 407 ][ 408 , Fig. 8]. On a square lattice, this amounts to a rotation by 45 degrees such that qubits are on vertices, and both 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type check operators occupy plaquettes in an alternating checkerboard pattern. Square-lattice cluster-state code 

> › p. 452

A code based on the cluster state on a square lattice that was used in the first proposal for MBQC [ 409 , 410 ]. In the one-way model, the pre-entangled square-lattice cluster is a universal resource, and the computation is carried out entirely by adaptive single-qubit measurements. Square-octagon (4.8.8) color code 

> › p. 452

2D color code defined on a patch of the 4.8.8 (square-octagon) tiling, which itself is obtained by applying a fattening procedure to the square lattice [ 411 ]. An equivalent description uses the Tetrakis square tiling (a.k.a. the Union Jack lattice), which is dual to the 4.8.8 lattice [ 412 ]. Among the three semiregular triangular 2D color-code families, the 4.8.8 family uses the fewest physical qubits for a given distance and is the only one of the three with transversal implementations of the full Clifford group [413]. Stellated color code 

> › p. 453

A non-CSS color-code family on a lattice patch with a single central puncture that hosts a twist defect connected to the boundary by a domain wall. Stellated surface code › p. 453 

A twist-defect surface-code family parameterized by a rotational symmetry order 𝑠 , with a central toric-code twist connected to the boundary by a domain wall. The 𝑠 = 3 member is the triangular surface code [414]. Super-compact fermion-to-qubit code › p. 459 

A 2D fermion-into-qubit encoding on the square lattice obtained from exact 2D bosonization by a finite-depth generalized local unitary Clifford circuit, followed by re-pairing of Majorana modes and a slight lattice deformation. The code uses 1.25 qubits per fermion, improving on the square-lattice compact encoding with ratio 𝑟 = 1.5. Its fermion-parity, hopping, and stabilizer operators have weights 1-2, 2-6, and 12 , respectively [387, Table I]. 73 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Toric code › p. 461 Version of the Kitaev surface code on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions, encoding two logical qubits. Being the first manifestation of the surface code, "toric code" is often an alternative name for the general construction. Twisted toric code [ 415 , Fig. 8] refers to the construction on a torus with twisted (a.k.a. shifted) boundary conditions. In the original Hamiltonian construction, open Pauli-𝑍 and Pauli-𝑋 strings create pairs of electric charges and magnetic vortices, and braiding one type around the other yields the nontrivial Abelian anyonic phase [404]. Triangular surface code › p. 463 

A member of a twist-defect surface code family with a single central twist whose planar layout fits within a triangle. Triangle codes can be viewed as three conjoined surface-code patches projected into two dimensions, with weight-four plaquette stabilizers and weight-two edge stabilizers [ 414 ]. Symmetric distance-𝑑 triangle codes use 3𝑑 2/4 + 1/4 data qubits, i.e., about 25% fewer than the rotated surface code for a given odd distance. Logical 𝑋 , 𝑌 , and 𝑍 operators can be supported on the three sides of the triangle, enabling initialization and measurement in any Pauli basis. Truncated trihexagonal (4.6.12) color code › p. 465 

2D color code defined on a (typically triangular) patch of the 4.6.12 (truncated trihexagonal or square-hexagon-dodecagon) tiling. Twist-defect color code › p. 465 

A non-CSS extension of the 2D color code whose non-CSS stabilizer generators are associated with twist defects of the associated lattice. These twists terminate domain walls that permute color labels, Pauli labels, or interchange the two. Twist-defect surface code › p. 465

> › p. 469

A variant of the surface code whose generators are 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋 and 𝑌𝑌𝑌𝑌 , obtained by mapping 𝑍 → 𝑌 in the surface code. Chern-Simons GKP code › p. 508 

A non-CSS multimode GKP code defined on a 2D mode lattice that encodes a qudit logical space and whose excitations are characterized by the 𝑈 (1)2𝑛 × 𝑈 (1)−2𝑚 Chern-Simons theory. The code can be obtained from the analog surface code by condensing › p. 559 certain anyons [392]. 

⟦10 , 2, 3⟧ rotated toric code › p. 332 

Rotated toric code that is the CSS form of the twisted XZZX toric code with parameters 𝑎 = 1, 𝑏 = 3 [408 , 418 ], related to the XZZX form by Hadamard on the 𝐵 -sublattice. It is also the symplectic double › p. 485 (a.k.a. genus-one double cover) of the ⟦5, 1, 3⟧

five-qubit perfect code [416, 419], the symplectic double › p. 485 of the ⟦5, 1, 2⟧ rotated surface code [416], and a BCC code [420]. 

⟦108 , 8, 10 ⟧ BB6 code › p. 332 

A bivariate bicycle (BB) code with parameters ⟦108 , 8, 10 ⟧ and weight-six stabilizer generators [421]. 

⟦13 , 1, 5⟧ twisted toric code › p. 334 

Thirteen-qubit twisted toric code whose stabilizer tableau consists of cyclic permutations of the 𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝑋 -type Pauli string 

𝑋𝐼 𝑍 𝑍 𝐼 𝑋𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 . The code can be thought of as a small twisted XZZX code [418, Exam. 11 and Fig. 3]. 

⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ Rhombic dodecahedron surface code › p. 335 

A ⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ twist-defect surface code whose qubits lie on the vertices of a rhombic dodecahedron. Its non-CSS nature is due to twist defects [ 422 ] stemming from the geometry of the polytope. A local-Clifford-equivalent clean realization has only 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type operators on its four-valent vertices, and its symplectic double is a ⟦28 , 6, 3⟧ genus-three code [416]. 

⟦144 , 12 , 12 ⟧ gross code › p. 335 

A BB code which requires less physical and ancilla qubits (for syndrome extraction) than the surface code with the same number of logical qubits and distance. The gross code is equivalent to 8 copies of the surface code via a constant-depth Clifford circuit, and is an element of a larger family of 2D stabilizer codes [423]. The name stems from the fact that a gross is a dozen dozen. 

⟦17 , 1, 5⟧ 4.8.8 color code › p. 337 

Seventeen-qubit doubly even 2D color code that admits a transversal implementation of the logical Clifford group. The smallest distance-five CSS code has 𝑛 = 17 [ 424 ]. It is also a normal self-dual CSS code whose transversal Hadamard acts logically, making it suitable as an inner code for fifth-order magic-state distillation [89].

⟦4, 1, 2⟧ twist-defect code › p. 344 

A four-qubit non-CSS stabilizer code that can be interpreted as the smallest triangular color code with 𝑥 -, 𝑦 -, and 𝑧 -type Pauli boundaries [ 425 , Fig. 7], and equivalently as a small twist-defect surface code on a tetrahedron inscribed in a sphere [ 416 ]. ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ Four-qubit code › p. 345 

A four-qubit hyperbolic self-dual CSS stabilizer code that is the smallest two-logical-qubit stabilizer code to detect a single-qubit error. It is unique for its parameters [426, Thm. 8]. 

⟦5, 1, 2⟧ rotated surface code › p. 347 

A rotated surface code on one rung of a ladder, with one qubit on the rung, and four qubits surrounding it. This is the smallest code that implements a fault-tolerant logical 𝑆 gate using a diagonal depth-one Clifford circuit [427]. 

⟦5, 1, 3⟧ Five-qubit perfect code › p. 348 

Five-qubit cyclic stabilizer code that is the smallest qubit stabilizer code to correct a single-qubit error.

> › p. 350

Error-detecting normal self-dual CSS code on three qubit pairs that encodes a logical qubit pair and detects any error acting on one pair [428]. In Knill’s 𝐶 4/𝐶 6 architecture, this code is used at the second and higher concatenation levels.

error-detecting code 

> › p. 352

Self-complementary six-qubit code with rate 2/3 that is unique for its parameters, up to equivalence [ 429 , Tab. III]. Concatenations of this code with itself yield the ⟦6𝑟 , 4𝑟 , 2𝑟 ⟧ level-𝑟 many-hypercube code [430]. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ Steane code › p. 353 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ self-dual CSS code that is the smallest qubit CSS code to correct a single-qubit error [ 431 ]. The code is constructed using the classical binary [7, 4, 3] Hamming code for protecting against both 𝑋 and 𝑍 errors. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ XZZX cyclic code › p. 355 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ cyclic non-CSS code whose stabilizer generators are the seven cyclic shifts of the weight-four Pauli string 𝑋𝑍 𝐼 𝑍 𝑋𝐼 𝐼 , any six of which are independent. The non-identity support of this generator is 𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝑋 (at positions 0, 1, 3, 4), making this a member of the twisted XZZX code family. It is one of sixteen distinct indecomposable ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ codes [432]. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ twist-defect surface code › p. 355 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ code (different from the Steane code) that is a small example of a twist-defect surface code. 

⟦72 , 12 , 6⟧ BB6 code 

> › p. 356

A bivariate bicycle (BB) code with parameters ⟦72 , 12 , 6⟧ and weight-six stabilizer generators [421]. 

⟦8, 3, 2⟧ Surface code on a cube › p. 358 

An ⟦8, 3, 2⟧ twist-defect surface code whose qubits lie on the vertices of a cube. It is obtained by three-coloring the faces of a cube and placing 𝑋 , 𝑌 , and 𝑍 stabilizer generators on each pair of faces of the same color. Its non-CSS nature is due to twist defects [ 422 ]stemming from the geometry of the polytope. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Shor code 

> › p. 358

Nine-qubit CSS code › p. 544 that is the first quantum error-correcting code [ 433 , ID 8802]. Among indecomposable ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ CSS codes, the Shor code has the largest automorphism group [434]. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Surface-17 code › p. 359 

A ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ rotated surface code named for the sum of its 9 data qubits and 8 syndrome qubits. It is one of the four inequivalent CSS gauge fixings of the nine-qubit Bacon-Shor code [ 434 ]. It uses the smallest number of qubits to perform fault-tolerant error correction on a surface code with parallel syndrome extraction.

Binomial code › p. 511 Bosonic rotation codes designed to approximately protect against errors consisting of powers of raising and lowering operators up to some maximum power. A one-to-one mapping between basis states on 𝑛 prime-dimensional qudits (of dimension 𝑞 = 𝑝 ) and the subspace of the first 𝑝 𝑛 

single-mode Fock states. While this mapping offers a way to map qudits into a single mode, noise models for the two code families induce different notions of locality and thus qualitatively different physical interpretations [474]. Bosonic rotation code › p. 514 

A single-mode Fock-state bosonic code whose codespace is preserved by a phase-space rotation by a multiple of 2 𝜋 /𝑁 for some 𝑁 .The rotation symmetry ensures that encoded states have support only on every 𝑁 th Fock state. For example, single-mode Fock-state codes for 𝑁 = 2 encoding a qubit admit basis states that are, respectively, supported on Fock state sets { | 0⟩, |4⟩, |8⟩, · · · } and

Bosonic Fock-state code that encodes 𝑘 qubits into 𝑛 oscillators, with each oscillator restricted to having at most 𝑁 excitations. Codewords are superpositions of oscillator Fock states which have exactly 𝑁 total excitations, and are either uniform (i.e., balanced) superpositions or unbalanced superpositions. Dual-rail quantum code › p. 520 

Two-mode bosonic code encoding a logical qubit in Fock states with one excitation. The logical-zero state is represented by |10 ⟩,while the logical-one state is represented by |01 ⟩. This encoding is often realized in temporal or spatial modes, corresponding to a 

time-bin or frequency-bin encoding. Two different types of photon polarization can also be used. 79 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Fock-state bosonic code › p. 521 

Qudit-into-oscillator code whose protection against AD › p. 508 noise (i.e., photon loss) stems from the use of disjoint sets of Fock states for the construction of each code basis state. The simplest example is the dual-rail code, which has codewords consisting of single Fock states |10 ⟩ and |01 ⟩. This code can detect a single loss error since a loss operator in either mode maps one of the codewords to a different Fock state |00 ⟩. More involved codewords consist of several well-separated Fock states such that multiple loss events can be detected and corrected. Icosahedral Fock-state code 

> › p. 525

A constant-excitation Fock-state code designed to realize the 2𝐼 group of gates using Gaussian rotations. It is obtained from the corresponding icosahedral spin code via the simplex mapping › p. 313 between spin and constant-excitation Fock spaces [475]. Matrix-model code 

> › p. 525

Multimode Fock-state bosonic approximate code derived from a matrix model, i.e., a bosonic theory with a large non-Abelian gauge group. The model’s degrees of freedom are matrix-valued bosons 𝑎 , each consisting of 𝑁 2 harmonic oscillator modes and subject to an 𝑆𝑈 ( 𝑁 ) gauge symmetry. Number-phase code 

> › p. 526

This code is useful for encoding and performing operations on qudits in multiple modes [477–481]. Ouyang-Chao constant-excitation PI code › p. 528 

A constant-excitation PI Fock-state code whose construction is based on integer partitions. Pair-cat code › p. 528 Two- or higher-mode extension of cat codes whose codewords are right eigenstates of powers of products of the modes’ lowering operators. Many gadgets for cat codes have two-mode pair-cat analogues, with the advantage being that such gates can be done in parallel with a dissipative error-correction process. Squeezed-vacuum code › p. 532

> › p. 535

𝜒 (2) code › p. 507 A 3𝑛 -mode bosonic Fock-state code that requires only linear optics and the 𝜒 (2) optical nonlinear interaction for encoding, decoding, and logical gates. Codewords lie in Fock-state subspaces that are invariant under Hermitian combinations of the 𝜒 (2) nonlinearities 

𝑎𝑏𝑐 † and 𝑖𝑎𝑏𝑐 †, where 𝑎 , 𝑏 , and 𝑐 are lowering operators acting on one of the 𝑛 triples of modes on which the codes are defined. Codewords are also +1 eigenstates of stabilizer-like symmetry operators , and photon parities are error syndromes.

Analog cluster-state code › p. 509 

A code based on a continuous-variable (CV), or analog, cluster state. Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Analog stabilizer code › p. 510 

An oscillator-into-oscillator stabilizer code encoding logical oscillator modes into 𝑛 physical modes. If the code is defined by 𝑟 

independent nullifiers, then it is denoted by ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 𝑟 ⟧R and encodes 𝑘 = 𝑛 − 𝑟 logical modes [ 482 ]. Any analog stabilizer state can be thought of as a pure Gaussian state that has been infinitely squeezed on all modes [482]. Analog surface code 

> › p. 511

An analog CSS version of the Kitaev surface code realizing a phase of 2D R gauge theory. Bosonic CSS code 

> › p. 514

Bosonic stabilizer code admitting a set of stabilizer generators that are either position or momentum displacements. Bosonic stabilizer code › p. 515 

Bosonic code whose codespace is defined as the common +1 eigenspace of a group of mutually commuting displacement operators. Displacements form the stabilizers of the code, and have continuous eigenvalues, in contrast with the discrete set of eigenvalues of qubit stabilizers. As a result, exact codewords are non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Stabilizer groups are any locally compact Abelian subgroups of R𝑛 , can themselves contain discrete or continuous subgroups, and can admit logical qudit and/or oscillator logical subspaces. Compactified R

gauge theory code 

> › p. 518

An integer-homology bosonic CSS code realizing 2D 𝑈 (1) gauge theory on bosonic modes. The code can be obtained from the analog surface code by condensing › p. 559 certain anyons [ 392 ]. This results in a pinning of each mode to the space of periodic functions, which is the Hilbert space of a physical rotor, and can be thought of as compactification of the 2D R gauge theory phase realized by the analog surface code. Concatenated GKP code › p. 519 

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code. In other words, a bosonic code that can be thought of as a concatenation of an arbitrary inner code and another bosonic outer code. Most examples encode physical qubits of an inner stabilizer code into the square-lattice GKP code. GKP CV-cluster-state code › p. 521 

A cluster-state code that utilizes a generalized analog cluster state with some of its physical modes initialized in GKP (resource) states. Alternatively, it can be thought of as a multimode GKP code whose encoding consists of initializing 𝑘 modes in momentum states (or, in the normalizable case, squeezed vacua), 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes in (normalizable) GKP states, and applying a Gaussian circuit consisting of two-body gates 𝑒 𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 for some angles 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 . The code provides a way to perform fault-tolerant MBQC, with the required number 𝑛 − 𝑘 of GKP-encoded physical modes determined by the particular protocol [396, 483–485]. GKP-surface code 

> › p. 522

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code and whose inner code is a surface code, including toric surface-code variants [396, 397], rotated surface codes [398–401], and XZZX surface codes [402]. Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code 

> › p. 522

Quantum lattice code for a non-degenerate lattice, thereby admitting a finite-dimensional logical subspace. Codes on 𝑛 modes can be constructed from lattices with 2𝑛 -dimensional full-rank Gram matrices 𝐴 . Any GKP code can be generated from a Gram matrix in standard form via a Gaussian unitary transformation [486, Corr. 1]. Hayden-Nezami-Salton-Sanders bosonic code › p. 523 

An ⟦𝑛, 1⟧R analog CSS code defined using homological structures associated with an 𝑛 − 1 simplex. Relevant to the study of spacetime replication of quantum information [487]. Hexagonal GKP code › p. 524 

Single-mode GKP qudit-into-oscillator code based on the triangular lattice. Offers the best error correction against displacement noise in a single mode due to the optimal packing of the underlying lattice [488, Sec. VI]. Integer-homology bosonic CSS code 

> › p. 525

A bosonic stabilizer code whose physical modes have been restricted, via a single GKP stabilizer, from the space of functions on the real line to the space of periodic functions. This restriction effectively realizes a rotor on each physical mode, allowing one to construct homological rotor codes out of displacement stabilizer groups. The stabilizer group is continuous, but contains discrete components in the form of the single-mode GKP stabilizers. The homology group of the logical operators has a torsion component because the chain complexes are defined over the ring of integers, which yields codes with finite logical dimension. NTRU-GKP code 

> › p. 525

Multi-mode GKP code whose underlying lattice is utilized in variations of the NTRU cryptosystem [ 271 ]. Randomized constructions yield constant-rate GKP code families whose largest decodable displacement length scales as 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) with high probability. Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP code 

> › p. 527

Multimode GKP code with an infinite-dimensional logical space. Can be obtained by considering an 𝑛 -mode GKP code with a finite-dimensional logical space, removing stabilizers such that the logical space becomes infinite dimensional, and applying a Gaussian circuit. Quantum lattice code › p. 529 

Bosonic stabilizer code on 𝑛 bosonic modes whose stabilizer group is an infinite countable group of oscillator displacement operators which implement lattice translations in phase space. Square-lattice GKP code › p. 530 

Single-mode GKP qudit-into-oscillator CSS code based on the rectangular lattice. Its stabilizer generators are oscillator displacement operators ˆ𝑆 𝑞 (2𝛼 ) = 𝑒 −2𝑖 𝛼 ˆ𝑝 and ˆ𝑆 𝑝 (2𝛽 ) = 𝑒 2𝑖𝛽 ˆ𝑥 . To ensure ˆ𝑆 𝑞 (2𝛼 ) and ˆ𝑆 𝑝 (2𝛽 ) generate a stabilizer group that is Abelian, there is a constraint that 𝛼𝛽 = 2𝑞 𝜋 where 𝑞 is an integer denoting the logical dimension.

Concatenated quantum code › p. 299 

A combination of two quantum codes, an inner code 𝐶 in and an outer code 𝐶 out , where the physical subspace used for the inner code consists of the logical subspace of the outer code. In other words, one first encodes in the inner code, and then encodes each of its physical registers in the outer code. An inner 𝐶 in = (( 𝑛 1 , 𝐾 , 𝑑 1 )) 𝑞 1 and outer 𝐶 out = (( 𝑛 2 , 𝑞 1 , 𝑑 2 )) 𝑞 2 block quantum code yield an (( 𝑛 1 𝑛 2 , 𝐾 , 𝑑 ≥ 𝑑 1 𝑑 2 )) 𝑞 2 concatenated block quantum code [381]. Concatenated qubit code › p. 380 

A concatenated code whose outer code is a qubit code. In other words, a qubit code that can be thought of as a concatenation of an inner qubit code and an outer qubit code. An inner 𝐶 in = (( 𝑛 1 , 𝐾 , 𝑑 1 )) and outer 𝐶 out = (( 𝑛 2 , 2, 𝑑 2 )) qubit code yield an 

(( 𝑛 1 𝑛 2 , 𝐾 , 𝑑 ≥ 𝑑 1 𝑑 2 )) concatenated qubit code. GKP-surface code

> › p. 399

Member of a family of ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer codes resulting from a concatenation of a constant-rate QLDPC code › p. 439 with a rotated surface code › p. 448 . Concatenation allows for syndrome extraction to be performed on a 2D geometry while maintaining a threshold at the expense of a logarithmically vanishing rate. The growing syndrome extraction circuit depth allows known bounds in the literature to be weakened [495, 496]. Quantum parity code (QPC) › p. 427 

A ⟦𝑚 1 𝑚 2 , 1, min (𝑚 1 , 𝑚 2 )⟧ CSS code family obtained from concatenating an 𝑚 1-qubit bit-flip repetition code with an 𝑚 2-qubit phase-flip repetition code. Quantum repetition code › p. 429 

Encodes 1 qubit into 𝑛 qubits according to |0⟩ → | 𝜙 0 ⟩⊗𝑛 and |1⟩ → | 𝜙 1 ⟩⊗𝑛 . The code is called a bit-flip code when | 𝜙 𝑖 ⟩ = |𝑖 ⟩,and a phase-flip code when | 𝜙 0 ⟩ = |+⟩ and | 𝜙 1 ⟩ = | −⟩ . This repetition-style encoding does not clone an arbitrary quantum state; instead, it extends the copying of computational-basis states linearly to entangled codewords [381, Ch. 2]. Quantum turbo code › p. 432 

A quantum version of the turbo code, obtained from an interleaved serial quantum concatenation [ 382 , Def. 30] of quantum convolutional codes. The interleaver induces long-range entanglement and can increase the minimum distance relative to the constituent convolutional codes [383]. Tetron code › p. 460 A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Two-component cat code › p. 534 

Code whose codespace is spanned by two coherent states |± 𝛼 ⟩ for nonzero complex 𝛼 .XYZ 2 hexagonal stabilizer code › p. 470 

An instance of the matching code based on the Kitaev honeycomb model. It is described on a honeycomb tiling with 𝑋𝑌 𝑍 𝑋𝑌 𝑍 

stabilizers on each hexagonal plaquette. Each vertical pair of qubits has an 𝑋𝑋 , 𝑌𝑌 , or 𝑍 𝑍 link stabilizer depending on the orientation of the plaquette stabilizers. Yoked surface code 

> › p. 471

⟦12 , 1, 3⟧ CE CSS code › p. 333 

Twelve-qubit constant-excitation (CE) CSS code that encodes one logical qubit with distance three. It is the smallest CE CSS code that corrects a single-qubit error [ 498 ]. Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto (CLY) code › p. 517 

Bosonic Fock-state code that encodes 𝑘 qubits into 𝑛 oscillators, with each oscillator restricted to having at most 𝑁 excitations. Codewords are superpositions of oscillator Fock states which have exactly 𝑁 total excitations, and are either uniform (i.e., balanced) superpositions or unbalanced superpositions. Constant-excitation (CE) code › p. 300 

Code whose codewords lie in an eigenspace of fixed total energy or fixed total excitation number for the underlying quantum system. For qubit codes, such a Hamiltonian is often the total spin Hamiltonian , 𝐻 = Í𝑖 𝑍 𝑖 . For spin-𝑆 codes, this generalizes to 𝐻 = Í𝑖 𝐽 (𝑖 ) 

> 𝑧

, where 𝐽 𝑧 is the spin-𝑆 𝑍 -operator. For bosonic (and, similarly, for fermion) codes, such as Fock-state codes, codewords are often in an eigenspace with eigenvalue 𝑁 > 0 of the total excitation or energy Hamiltonian , 𝐻 = Í𝑖 ˆ𝑛 𝑖 .Dual-rail quantum code › p. 520

time-bin or frequency-bin encoding. Two different types of photon polarization can also be used. Icosahedral Fock-state code

Jump code › p. 408 A CE code designed to detect and correct AD › p. 508 errors. Codewords can be expressed as superpositions of Dicke states › p. 422 with coefficients given by square roots of polynomial coefficients, with the case of binomial coefficients reducing to the GNU PI codes. Tetron code › p. 460 A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Twisted XZZX toric code › p. 466 

A cyclic code that can be thought of as the XZZX toric code with shifted (a.k.a twisted) boundary conditions. Admits a set of stabilizer generators that are equivalent to cyclic shifts of a particular weight-four 𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝑋 Pauli string. Twisted 1-group code › p. 541 

Block group-representation code realizing particular irreps of particular groups such that a distance of two is automatically guaranteed. Groups which admit irreps with this property are called twisted (unitary) 1-groups and include the binary icosahedral group 2𝐼 , the Σ (360 𝜙 ) subgroup of 𝑆𝑈 (3), the family { 𝑃𝑆 𝑝 (2𝑏, 3), 𝑏 ≥ 1}, and the alternating groups 𝐴 5,6. Groups whose irreps are images of the appropriate irreps of twisted 1-groups also yield such properties, e.g., the binary tetrahedral group 2𝑇 or qutrit Pauli group Σ (72 𝜙 ).86
