3D subsystem color code › p. 365 

The 3D subsystem color code defined on the cube-truncated rhombic dodecahedral honeycomb, i.e., a tessellation of cubes and chamfered cubes (a.k.a. tetratruncated rhombic dodecahedra) [794, Fig. 1], is a single-shot code [794, 800]. 3D subsystem surface code › p. 366 

The 3D subsystem surface code is a single-shot code [801, 802]; see Ref. [803] for an alternative formulation. Campbell double homological product code › p. 373 

For a minimal input chain complex associated with a classical [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code, the Campbell double homological product code is a single-shot code with 𝑑 ss = ∞, (𝑑, 𝑓 )-soundness for 𝑓 ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑥 3/4, and check redundancy bounded by < 2 [644]. Generalized bicycle (GB) code › p. 498 

A qubit GB code ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧2 has 𝑘 non-trivial relations between the syndrome bits, which is expected to help with operation in a fault-tolerant regime (in the presence of syndrome measurement errors). See Ref. [ 804 ] for many examples of such codes. There is numerical evidence that a particular family is single shot [805]. Homological product code › p. 401 

It is conjectured that a particular class of codes called three-dimensional product codes is single shot [806]. Hyperbolic surface code › p. 405 

A 4D hyperbolic surface code can be decoded with the Hastings decoder [ 807 ] in time 𝑂 (𝑛 log 𝑛 ) and with a logical error scaling inverse polynomially with 𝑛 .Hypergraph product (HGP) code › p. 406 

Two-fold application of the hypergraph product to a pair of binary linear codes yields single-shot QLDPC codes that exploit redundancy in their stabilizer generators [644]. Quantum Tanner code › p. 431 

Certain quantum Tanner codes facilitate single-shot decoding [808]. Quantum data-syndrome (QDS) code › p. 424 

QDS codes are closely related to single-shot codes because both use redundant syndrome information to suppress measurement errors in a single round of syndrome extraction [644]. Quantum expander code › p. 426 

Quantum expander codes are single-shot [809]. Qubit QLDPC code 

> › p. 439

Qubit QLDPC codes satisfying linear confinement are single shot [ 806 ]. Any code that admits a local greedy decoder also satisfies linear confinement, and so is single shot [810]. Qubit stabilizer code 

> › p. 441

Any stabilizer code can be single shot if sufficiently non-local high-weight stabilizer generators are used for syndrome measurements. These can be obtained with a Gaussian elimination procedure [644]. Self-correcting quantum code › p. 319 

The presence of an energy barrier (i.e., confinement) is sufficient for a code to be single shot, and is also conjectured to be necessary for a code to be a self-correcting memory. Linear confinement of QLDPC (LDPC) codes implies (classical) self-correction [811]. Single-shot code 

> › p. 320

Subsystem Hypergraph Product Simplex (SHYPS) code › p. 455 

SHYPS codes exhibit practical single-shot signatures, including logical error-rate stability under small-window sliding-window decoding and constant single-shot distance 𝑑 ss = 3, which supports using one syndrome-extraction round between logical generators [749]. 

(2, 2) Loop toric code › p. 330 

Single-shot QEC has been realized using the ⟦33 , 1, 4⟧ loop toric code on the Quantinuum H2 device [812]. 142 Small-distance block code

35. SMALL-DISTANCE QUBIT STABILIZER CODES AND FRIENDS 

All descendants and cousins of Small-distance qubit stabilizer code › p. 451 .

See code graph in Fig. 47. 

Code Description 

Ball code › p. 369 A distance-two color code defined on a colorable 𝐷 -ball, equivalently on a 𝐷 -colex with boundary [ 655 , Appx. A]. In the morphing construction of Ref. [ 655 ], ball codes arise as the child codes associated with the morphed ball-like regions. This family includes hypercube codes (defined on balls constructed from hyperoctahedra) and 3D ball codes (defined on duals of certain Archimedean solids). Hyperbolic color code › p. 405 

An extension of the color code construction to hyperbolic manifolds. As opposed to there being only three types of uniform three-valent and three-colorable lattice tilings in the 2D Euclidean plane, there is an infinite number of admissible hyperbolic tilings in the 2D hyperbolic plane [ 798 ]. Certain double covers of hyperbolic tilings also yield admissible tilings [ 799 ]. Other admissible hyperbolic tilings can be obtained via a fattening procedure [ 411 ]; see also a construction based on the more general quantum pin codes [669]. Kitaev chain code 

› p. 409 

A Majorana stabilizer code obtained from the ground-state subspace of the Kitaev Majorana chain in its fermionic topological phase [ 531 ]. Its codespace is stabilized by nearest-neighbor Majorana bilinears, while two unpaired edge Majoranas furnish one logical fermionic mode. Under parity-preserving noise, it behaves as the Majorana analogue of the repetition code [532]. Majorana box qubit 

› p. 416 

A family of Majorana stabilizer codes obtained by fixing the total fermion parity of 𝑛 fermionic modes, equivalently 2𝑛 Majorana zero modes, within the ground-state subspace of 𝑛 Kitaev Majorana chain Hamiltonians. The resulting positive-parity subspace encodes 𝑛 − 1 logical qubits and has Majorana distance 2.Quantum multi-dimensional parity-check (QMDPC) code › p. 426 

High-rate low-distance CSS code whose qubits lie on a 𝐷 -dimensional rectangle, with 𝑋 -type stabilizer generators defined on each 

𝐷 − 1-dimensional rectangle. The 𝑍 -type stabilizer generators are defined via permutations in order to commute with the 𝑋 -type generators. 146 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

Quantum repetition code › p. 429 

Encodes 1 qubit into 𝑛 qubits according to |0⟩ → | 𝜙 0 ⟩⊗𝑛 and |1⟩ → | 𝜙 1 ⟩⊗𝑛 . The code is called a bit-flip code when | 𝜙 𝑖 ⟩ = |𝑖 ⟩,and a phase-flip code when | 𝜙 0 ⟩ = |+⟩ and | 𝜙 1 ⟩ = | −⟩ . This repetition-style encoding does not clone an arbitrary quantum state; instead, it extends the copying of computational-basis states linearly to entangled codewords [381, Ch. 2]. Reinforcement-learning quantum code › p. 447 

An approximate qubit code obtained from a numerical optimization involving a reinforcement learning agent. Small-distance qubit stabilizer code › p. 451 

A qubit stabilizer code that either detects or corrects errors on at most two subsystems, i.e., has distance ≤ 5.Tetron code › p. 460 A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) code › p. 462 

A 1D translationally invariant stabilizer code whose encoding is a constant-depth circuit of nearest-neighbor gates on alternating even and odd bonds that consist of transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian interactions. The code allows for perfect state transfer of arbitrary distance using local operations and classical communications (LOCC). Trapezoid subsystem code 

> › p. 463

A member of a family of BBS codes with weight-two (two-body) gauge generators designed to suppress errors in adiabatic quantum computation. 

⟦10 , 1, 2⟧

Vasmer-Kubica code 

> › p. 331

A stabilizer code obtained by morphing the ⟦15 , 1, 3⟧ quantum Reed-Muller code on a subset whose child code is the ⟦8, 3, 2⟧

smallest interesting color code [655]. It is the smallest known stabilizer code with a fault-tolerant logical 𝑇 gate, implemented via physical 𝑇 , 𝑇 †, and 𝐶𝐶 𝑍 gates [655]. 

⟦10 , 1, 3; 1 , 3, 4⟧

EAOA Hamming code › p. 332 

An EAOA qubit stabilizer code constructed from the dual of a [10 , 6, 3] code obtained by shortening the classical [15 , 11 , 3] Hamming code at five positions. In the notation of the parent entry, the example of Ref. [ 818 ] is a ⟦10 , 1, 3; 1 , 3, 4⟧ code: it encodes one logical qubit and four classical strings (equivalently, two classical bits), while retaining one gauge qubit and using three ebits. 

⟦10 , 2, 3⟧ binarized Galois-qudit code 

> › p. 332

CSS code obtained by binarizing a ⟦5, 1, 3⟧4 Galois-qudit CSS code in the self-dual normal basis { 𝜔, 𝜔 2 }.

⟦10 , 2, 3⟧ rotated toric code › p. 332 

Rotated toric code that is the CSS form of the twisted XZZX toric code with parameters 𝑎 = 1, 𝑏 = 3 [408 , 418 ], related to the XZZX form by Hadamard on the 𝐵 -sublattice. It is also the symplectic double › p. 485 (a.k.a. genus-one double cover) of the ⟦5, 1, 3⟧

five-qubit perfect code [416, 419], the symplectic double › p. 485 of the ⟦5, 1, 2⟧ rotated surface code [416], and a BCC code [420]. 

⟦11 , 1, 5⟧ quantum dodecacode › p. 333 

Eleven-qubit pure › p. 434 stabilizer code that is the smallest qubit stabilizer code to correct two-qubit errors. It can be obtained from the non-additive dodecacode by puncturing [429, Table IV]. 

⟦12 , 1, 3⟧ CE CSS code › p. 333 

Twelve-qubit constant-excitation (CE) CSS code that encodes one logical qubit with distance three. It is the smallest CE CSS code that corrects a single-qubit error [ 498 ]. Codewords lie in a fixed Hamming-weight subspace, making the code immune to coherent noise in the form of transversal 𝑍 -rotations. 

⟦12 , 2, 2⟧ CSS code 

> › p. 333

CSS code that admits a logical 𝐶𝑆 gate via application of physical 𝑇 and 𝑇 † gates. 

⟦12 , 2, 4⟧ carbon code › p. 334 

Twelve-qubit CSS code based on Knill’s 𝐶 4/𝐶 6 scheme [ 499 ]. Using the concatenation convention of the Zoo, the carbon code can be viewed as a block concatenation with inner code ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ and outer code 𝐶 6: three inner ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ blocks encode six intermediate qubits, which are then encoded into two logical qubits by the outer ⟦6, 2, 2⟧ code. 

⟦13 , 1, 5⟧ quantum QR code › p. 334 

Thirteen-qubit cyclic Hermitian qubit code derived from a quaternary quadratic-residue code using the Hermitian construction [ 780 ][ 781 , pg. 11]. The code admits a stabilizer tableau whose rows are cyclic permutations of the Pauli string 𝑋𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝐼 𝑍 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝑍 𝐼 𝑍 𝑍 

[745, ID 67067199e766ad364e845262]. 

⟦13 , 1, 5⟧ twisted toric code › p. 334 

Thirteen-qubit twisted toric code whose stabilizer tableau consists of cyclic permutations of the 𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝑋 -type Pauli string 

𝑋𝐼 𝑍 𝑍 𝐼 𝑋𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 𝐼 . The code can be thought of as a small twisted XZZX code [418, Exam. 11 and Fig. 3]. 

⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ CE phantom code › p. 334 

CSS phantom code obtained by concatenating the ⟦7, 3, (𝑑 𝑋 = 3, 𝑑 𝑍 = 2)⟧ punctured hypercube code with the two-qubit phase-flip repetition code. The code is equivalent to the ⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ constant-excitation (CE) CSS code obtained by applying dual-rail concatenation to the ⟦7, 3, 2⟧ punctured hypercube code, up to single-qubit Clifford gates, a physical-qubit permutation, and a Pauli frame [498]. 

⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ Rhombic dodecahedron surface code › p. 335 

A ⟦14 , 3, 3⟧ twist-defect surface code whose qubits lie on the vertices of a rhombic dodecahedron. Its non-CSS nature is due to twist defects [ 422 ] stemming from the geometry of the polytope. A local-Clifford-equivalent clean realization has only 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type operators on its four-valent vertices, and its symplectic double is a ⟦28 , 6, 3⟧ genus-three code [416]. 

⟦15 , 7, 3⟧ quantum Hamming code 

> › p. 335

Self-dual quantum Hamming code that admits permutation-based CZ logical gates. The code is constructed using the CSS construc-tion from the [15 , 11 , 3] Hamming code and its [15 , 4, 8] dual simplex code. 

⟦15 , 1, 3⟧ quantum RM code › p. 335 

A ⟦15 , 1, 3⟧ quantum Reed-Muller code that is most easily thought of as a tetrahedral 3D color code. It can be constructed as a CSS code from the [15 , 5, 8] punctured Reed-Muller code and its even subcode, which explains its transversal 𝑇 † gate [381]. 147 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

⟦16 , 4, 3⟧

dodecahedral code 

> › p. 336

A ⟦16 , 4, 3⟧ non-CSS qubit stabilizer code whose encoder-respecting form › p. 442 is the graph of vertices of a dodecahedron [819]. 

⟦16 , 6, 4⟧ Tesseract color code › p. 337 

A (hyperbolic self-dual CSS) 4D color code defined on a tesseract, with stabilizer generators of both types supported on each cube. A 

⟦16 , 4, 2, 4⟧ tesseract subsystem code can be obtained from this code by using two logical qubits as gauge qubits [463]. 

⟦17 , 1, 5⟧ 4.8.8 color code › p. 337 

Seventeen-qubit doubly even 2D color code that admits a transversal implementation of the logical Clifford group. The smallest distance-five CSS code has 𝑛 = 17 [ 424 ]. It is also a normal self-dual CSS code whose transversal Hadamard acts logically, making it suitable as an inner code for fifth-order magic-state distillation [89]. 

⟦18 , 2, 5⟧ BCC code 

> › p. 487

BCC code on 18 qubits encoding 2 logical qubits with distance 5, found by computer search [420]. 

⟦2(𝑚 + 1), 𝑚, 2⟧

single-loss AD code 

> › p. 337

A member of a class of ⟦2(𝑚 + 1), 𝑚, 2⟧ CSS codes for 𝑚 ≥ 1 that generalizes the ⟦4, 1, 2⟧ approximate amplitude-damping code of Ref. [ 820 ]. Its 𝑍 -type generators are 𝑚 + 1 pairwise products, with each qubit participating in only one check; the single 𝑋 -type generator is the all-𝑋 string. 

⟦23 , 1, 7⟧ Quantum Golay code › p. 341 

A ⟦23 , 1, 7⟧ self-dual CSS code with eleven stabilizer generators of each type, and with each generator being weight eight. 

⟦2𝐷 , 𝐷, 2⟧

hypercube quantum code › p. 338 

Member of a family of codes defined by placing qubits on a 𝐷 -dimensional hypercube, 𝑍 -stabilizers on all two-dimensional faces, and an 𝑋 -stabilizer on all vertices. These codes realize gates at the (𝐷 − 1)-st level of the Clifford hierarchy. The measured physical bit string can be post-processed into both a logical output string and stabilizer checks, enabling end-of-circuit error detection directly from classical samples [ 723 ]. Puncturing the ⟦2𝐷 , 𝐷, 2⟧ hypercube quantum code yields the ⟦2𝐷 − 1, 𝐷, 2⟧ punctured-hypercube family. 

⟦2𝑟 +𝑟 , 2𝑟 −𝑟 −2, 3⟧

Ring CPC code › p. 340 

A family of ⟦2𝑟 +𝑟 , 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 2, 3⟧ CPC codes for 𝑟 ≥ 3 whose matrices are based on the shortened version of the [2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3]

Hamming code. See [821, Thm. 4] for their stabilizer generator matrix. 

⟦2𝑟 + 𝑟 − 1, 1, 2⟧

morphed simplex code › p. 340 

A member of a family of codes obtained by morphing the ⟦2𝑟 +1 − 1, 1, 3⟧ simplex codes on a region whose child code is a ⟦2𝑟 , 𝑟 , 2⟧

hypercube code [ 655 , Appx. C]. The morphing process replaces a subset of qubits with their logical qubits, yielding a code with parameters ⟦2𝑟 + 𝑟 − 1, 1, 2⟧ that inherits a diagonal gate at the (𝑟 − 1)st level of the Clifford hierarchy from the parent code. 

⟦2𝑟 , 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 2, 3⟧

Gottesman code 

> › p. 340

A family of pure › p. 434 [429] non-CSS stabilizer codes of distance 3 that saturate the asymptotic quantum Hamming bound. 

⟦2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 2𝑟 −

1, 3⟧ quantum Hamming code 

> › p. 339

Member of a family of self-dual CSS codes constructed from [2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3] = 𝐶 𝑋 = 𝐶 𝑍 Hamming codes and their duals, the simplex codes. The code’s stabilizer generator matrix blocks 𝐻 𝑋 and 𝐻 𝑍 are both the generator matrix for a simplex code. The weight of each stabilizer generator is 2𝑟 −1.

⟦2𝑟 − 1, 1, 3⟧

simplex code › p. 339 

Member of a color-code family constructed from a punctured first-order RM (1, 𝑚 = 𝑟 ) code and its even subcode for 𝑟 ≥ 3. Each code transversally implements a diagonal gate at the (𝑟 − 1)st level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 [ 763 , 764 ]. Each code is a color code defined on a simplex in 𝑟 − 1 dimensions [ 455 , 794 ], where qubits are placed on the vertices, edges, and faces as well as on the simplex itself. 

⟦2𝑚 −1 , 2𝑚 −1 − 𝑚 −

1, 4⟧ 𝑓 Hamming Majorana code › p. 338 

A member of the ⟦2𝑚 −1 , 2𝑚 −1 − 𝑚 − 1, 4⟧ 𝑓 family of Majorana stabilizer codes for 𝑚 ≥ 3 constructed from a self-orthogonal first-order RM code (whose dual is the extended Hamming code). A shortened ⟦2𝑚 −1 − 1, 2𝑚 −1 − 𝑚 − 2, 3⟧ 𝑓 version can also be defined [ 537 , Prop. 2.5.1]. The logical subspace of the ⟦8, 3, 4⟧ 𝑓 Hamming Majorana code is a Cartan subspace of the 𝐸 8 Lie algebra [538]. 

⟦2𝑚, 2𝑚 − 2, 2⟧

error-detecting code 

> › p. 342

Self-complementary and self-dual CSS code for 𝑚 ≥ 2 with generators {𝑋𝑋 · · · 𝑋, 𝑍 𝑍 · · · 𝑍 } acting on all 2𝑚 physical qubits. The code is constructed via the CSS construction from an SPC code and a repetition code [ 737 , Sec. III]. This is the highest-rate distance-two code when an even number of qubits is used [429]. 

⟦3, 1, 3; 2 ⟧ EA code 

> › p. 343

Distance-three EA stabilizer code encoding one logical qubit and using two ebits. It is the smallest example of an EA code correcting an arbitrary single-qubit error. 

⟦30 , 8, 3⟧ Bring code › p. 343 

A ⟦30 , 8, 3⟧ hyperbolic surface code on a quotient of the {5, 5} hyperbolic tiling called Bring’s curve. Its qubits and stabilizer generators lie on the vertices of the small stellated dodecahedron. It admits a set of weight-five stabilizer generators. 

⟦3𝑘 + 8, 𝑘, 2⟧

triorthogonal code 

> › p. 343

Member of the ⟦3𝑘 + 8, 𝑘, 2⟧ family (for even 𝑘 ) of triorthogonal and quantum divisible codes that admit a transversal 𝑇 gate and are relevant for magic-state distillation [659][699, Sec. VI.C]. 

⟦4, 1, 1, 2⟧

Four-qubit subsystem code 

> › p. 343

Error-detecting four-qubit subsystem stabilizer code encoding one logical qubit and one gauge qubit. 

⟦4, 1, 2⟧

Leung-Nielsen-Chuang-Yamamoto (LNCY) code › p. 343 

A four-qubit CSS stabilizer code that is the only qubit CSS code with such parameters. 148 

Code (cont’d) Description (cont’d) 

⟦4, 1, 2⟧ twist-defect code › p. 344 

A four-qubit non-CSS stabilizer code that can be interpreted as the smallest triangular color code with 𝑥 -, 𝑦 -, and 𝑧 -type Pauli boundaries [ 425 , Fig. 7], and equivalently as a small twist-defect surface code on a tetrahedron inscribed in a sphere [ 416 ]. It is the only non-CSS qubit stabilizer code with parameters ⟦4, 1, 2⟧. The code admits weight-three stabilizer generators and weight-two logical Pauli 𝑋, 𝑌 , 𝑍 operators. 

⟦4, 2, 2⟧ Four-qubit code › p. 345 

A four-qubit hyperbolic self-dual CSS stabilizer code that is the smallest two-logical-qubit stabilizer code to detect a single-qubit error. It is unique for its parameters [426, Thm. 8]. 

⟦49 , 1, 5⟧

triorthogonal code 

> › p. 347

Triorthogonal and quantum divisible code which is the smallest distance-five stabilizer code to admit a transversal 𝑇 gate [ 631 ][ 659 ,Appx. B]. It is one example of a level-three generalized divisible code obtainable from the doubling transformation [ 699 , Sec. VI.D]. Its 𝑋 -type stabilizers form a triply even linear binary code in the symplectic representation › p. 442 .

⟦5, 1, 2⟧ rotated surface code › p. 347 

A rotated surface code on one rung of a ladder, with one qubit on the rung, and four qubits surrounding it. This is the smallest code that implements a fault-tolerant logical 𝑆 gate using a diagonal depth-one Clifford circuit [427]. 

⟦5, 1, 3⟧ Five-qubit perfect code › p. 348 

Five-qubit cyclic stabilizer code that is the smallest qubit stabilizer code to correct a single-qubit error. 

⟦54 , 6, 5⟧

five-covered icosahedral code 

> › p. 350

A ⟦54 , 6, 5⟧ qubit stabilizer code whose encoder-respecting form › p. 442 is the graph of a five-cover of the icosahedron [ 819 ]. The covering-space construction avoids the weight-three logical operators that occur for the bare icosahedral graph [819]. 

⟦6, 1, 2⟧

semi-self-dual CSS code › p. 350 

A six-qubit CSS stabilizer code that is an example of a semi-self-dual CSS code, i.e., a CSS code whose 𝑋 -type stabilizers are contained in the 𝑍 -type stabilizers [703]. 

⟦6, 1, 3⟧ Six-qubit stabilizer code › p. 350 

A degenerate, non-trivial ⟦6, 1, 3⟧ stabilizer code. It is one of two six-qubit distance-three codes that are unique up to equivalence [ 429 ], with the other code being decomposable and an extension of the five-qubit code [ 431 ][ 433 , ID 87]. The code admits fault-tolerant syndrome extraction using only one ancilla per stabilizer generator measurement. 

⟦6, 1, 3⟧ 𝑓 Vijay-Fu Majorana code › p. 350 

A Majorana stabilizer code encoding a logical fermion into six physical fermions. This code is the shortest code correcting single fermion-parity flips [539]. 

⟦6, 2, 2⟧ 𝐶 6 code 

> › p. 350

Error-detecting normal self-dual CSS code on three qubit pairs that encodes a logical qubit pair and detects any error acting on one pair [428]. In Knill’s 𝐶 4/𝐶 6 architecture, this code is used at the second and higher concatenation levels. 

⟦6, 2, 3, 2⟧ BBS code › p. 351 

Error-detecting six-qubit BBS subsystem code with parameters ⟦6, 2, 3, 2⟧ that can suppress errors in adiabatic quantum computa-tion [640]. 

⟦6, 4, 2⟧

error-detecting code 

> › p. 352

Self-complementary six-qubit code with rate 2/3 that is unique for its parameters, up to equivalence [ 429 , Tab. III]. Concatenations of this code with itself yield the ⟦6𝑟 , 4𝑟 , 2𝑟 ⟧ level-𝑟 many-hypercube code [430]. 

⟦6𝑘 + 2, 3𝑘, 2⟧

Campbell-Howard code › p. 352 

Family of ⟦6𝑘 + 2, 3𝑘, 2⟧ qubit stabilizer codes with quasi-transversal 𝐶𝐶 𝑍 ⊗𝑘 gates that are relevant to magic-state distillation. In the synthillation framework, these distance-two codes realize batches of logical 𝐶𝐶 𝑍 gates using physical 𝑇 gates followed by a Clifford correction. 

⟦6𝑟 , 2𝑟 , 2⟧ Ganti-Onunkwo-Young code › p. 352 

A member of the family of ⟦6𝑟 , 2𝑟 , 2⟧ CSS codes designed to suppress errors in adiabatic quantum computation. All but two of its stabilizer generators are weight-two (two-body), and the remaining two are weight-4𝑟 .

⟦7, 1 : 1 , 3⟧ hybrid stabilizer code › p. 353 

A distance-three seven-qubit hybrid stabilizer code storing one qubit and one classical bit. Admits a stabilizer generator set with a weight-two generator, which delineates the underlying classical code [641, Eq. (3)]. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ Steane code › p. 353 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ self-dual CSS code that is the smallest qubit CSS code to correct a single-qubit error [ 431 ]. The code is constructed using the classical binary [7, 4, 3] Hamming code for protecting against both 𝑋 and 𝑍 errors. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ XZZX cyclic code › p. 355 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ cyclic non-CSS code whose stabilizer generators are the seven cyclic shifts of the weight-four Pauli string 𝑋𝑍 𝐼 𝑍 𝑋𝐼 𝐼 , any six of which are independent. The non-identity support of this generator is 𝑋𝑍 𝑍 𝑋 (at positions 0, 1, 3, 4), making this a member of the twisted XZZX code family. It is one of sixteen distinct indecomposable ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ codes [432]. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ bare code 

> › p. 353

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ code that admits fault-tolerant syndrome extraction using only one ancilla per stabilizer generator measurement. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ twist-defect surface code › p. 355 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ code (different from the Steane code) that is a small example of a twist-defect surface code. 

⟦7, 2, 2⟧ HGP phantom code › p. 355 

Smallest member of a family of CSS phantom HGP codes obtained from the hypergraph product of a classical simplex code and a repetition code. 

⟦7, 2, 2⟧ QETC › p. 355 Seven-qubit pure › p. 434 QETC that transmutes all single-qubit Pauli errors to logical phase errors. 

⟦7, 3, 2⟧ punctured hypercube code 

> › p. 356

A seven-qubit pure › p. 434 CSS code that corrects a single 𝑋 or a single 𝑍 error, but not a single 𝑌 error. It is the punctured version of the ⟦8, 3, 2⟧ hypercube quantum code and is a phantom code [489]. 

⟦8, 2 : 1 , 3⟧ hybrid stabilizer code › p. 356 

A code obtained from the ⟦8, 3, 3⟧ Gottesman code by using one of its logical qubits as a classical bit. One can also use two logical qubits as classical bits, obtaining an ⟦8, 1 : 2 , 3⟧ hybrid stabilizer code. 149

⟦8, 3, 3⟧ Eight-qubit Gottesman code 

> › p. 356

Eight-qubit non-degenerate › p. 304 code that can be obtained from a modified CSS construction using the [8, 4, 4] extended Hamming code and a [8, 7, 2] even-weight code [822]. The modification introduces signs between the codewords. 

⟦8, 1, 2⟧

Shen-Wang-Cao code › p. 356 

A stabilizer code that admits a logical 𝑇 gate via application of physical 𝑇 gates and a 𝐶 𝑍 -like gate. 

⟦8, 2, 2⟧ hyperbolic color code › p. 357 

An ⟦8, 2, 2⟧ hyperbolic color code defined on the projective plane. It is a self-dual CSS code. 

⟦8, 2, 3⟧ Hermitian code › p. 357 

A non-CSS Hermitian eight-qubit stabilizer code that is the only Hermitian code and that has the largest automorphism group among the 20 inequivalent ⟦8, 2, 3⟧ codes [ 434 ]. The code has an exceptionally short fault-tolerant syndrome measurement sequence [434, 823]. 

⟦8, 3, 2⟧ Smallest interesting color code › p. 357 

Smallest 3D color code whose physical qubits lie on vertices of a cube and which admits a (weakly) transversal 𝐶𝐶 𝑍 gate. 

⟦8, 3, 2⟧ Surface code on a cube › p. 358 

An ⟦8, 3, 2⟧ twist-defect surface code whose qubits lie on the vertices of a cube. It is obtained by three-coloring the faces of a cube and placing 𝑋 , 𝑌 , and 𝑍 stabilizer generators on each pair of faces of the same color. Its non-CSS nature is due to twist defects [ 422 ]stemming from the geometry of the polytope. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Shor code 

> › p. 358

Nine-qubit CSS code › p. 544 that is the first quantum error-correcting code [ 433 , ID 8802]. Among indecomposable ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ CSS codes, the Shor code has the largest automorphism group [434]. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Surface-17 code › p. 359 

A ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ rotated surface code named for the sum of its 9 data qubits and 8 syndrome qubits. It is one of the four inequivalent CSS gauge fixings of the nine-qubit Bacon-Shor code [ 434 ]. It uses the smallest number of qubits to perform fault-tolerant error correction on a surface code with parallel syndrome extraction. 

⟦9, 1, 4, 3⟧

Nine-qubit Bacon-Shor code 

> › p. 359

Error-correcting nine-qubit subsystem stabilizer code encoding one logical qubit and four gauge qubits. There are exactly four inequivalent CSS gauge fixings of the code, including the Shor code › p. 358 and the surface-17 code › p. 359 [434]. 

⟦9, 3, 3⟧ Quadric code › p. 360 

Nine-qubit pure › p. 434 Hermitian qubit code constructed from the almost MDS [9, 3, 6]4 Hermitian self-orthogonal code. It is the only pure › p. 434 Hermitian code with its parameters and is the highest-distance qubit stabilizer code for its 𝑛 and 𝑘 .

⟦𝑘 + 4, 𝑘, 2⟧ H code 

> › p. 360

Family of ⟦𝑘 + 4, 𝑘, 2⟧ self-dual CSS codes (for even 𝑘 ) with transversal Hadamard gates that are relevant to magic state distillation. The four stabilizer generators are 𝑋 1 𝑋 2 𝑋 3 𝑋 4, 𝑍 1 𝑍 2 𝑍 3 𝑍 4, 𝑋 1 𝑋 2 𝑋 5 𝑋 6 ...𝑋 𝑘 +4, and 𝑍 1 𝑍 2 𝑍 5 𝑍 6 ...𝑍 𝑘 +4.

⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 2𝑘, 4⟧

Analog cluster-state code › p. 509 

A code based on a continuous-variable (CV), or analog, cluster state. Such a state can be used to perform MBQC of logical modes, which substitutes the temporal dimension necessary for decoding a conventional code with a spatial dimension. The exact analog cluster state is non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Analog stabilizer code › p. 510 

An oscillator-into-oscillator stabilizer code encoding logical oscillator modes into 𝑛 physical modes. If the code is defined by 𝑟 

independent nullifiers, then it is denoted by ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 𝑟 ⟧R and encodes 𝑘 = 𝑛 − 𝑟 logical modes [ 482 ]. Any analog stabilizer state can be thought of as a pure Gaussian state that has been infinitely squeezed on all modes [482]. Bosonic stabilizer code › p. 515 

Bosonic code whose codespace is defined as the common +1 eigenspace of a group of mutually commuting displacement operators. Displacements form the stabilizers of the code, and have continuous eigenvalues, in contrast with the discrete set of eigenvalues of qubit stabilizers. As a result, exact codewords are non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Stabilizer groups are any locally compact Abelian subgroups of R𝑛 , can themselves contain discrete or continuous subgroups, and can admit logical qudit and/or oscillator logical subspaces. Chiral semion Walker-Wang model code › p. 475 

A 3D lattice modular-qudit stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 whose low-energy excitations on boundaries realize the chiral semion topological order. The model admits 2D chiral semion topological order at one of its surfaces [ 451 , 452 ]. The corresponding phase can also be realized via a non-stabilizer Hamiltonian [453]. Concatenated GKP code › p. 519 

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code. In other words, a bosonic code that can be thought of as a concatenation of an arbitrary inner code and another bosonic outer code. Most examples encode physical qubits of an inner stabilizer code into the square-lattice GKP code. Double-semion stabilizer code › p. 476 

A 2D lattice modular-qudit stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 that realizes the 2D double semion topological phase. The code can be obtained from a Z4 toric-code ground state by condensing › p. 559 the emergent boson 𝑒 2 𝑚 2; in the stabilizer construction this condensation is implemented by two-body measurements [ 388 , 395 ]. Its ground-state subspace can be mapped to that of the double-semion string-net model by a finite-depth quantum circuit with ancillas [388]. Fracton stabilizer code › p. 476 

A 3D modular-qudit stabilizer code whose codewords make up the ground-state space of a Hamiltonian in a fracton phase. Unlike topological phases, whose excitations can move in any direction, fracton phases are characterized by excitations whose movement is restricted. Frobenius code 

› p. 477 

A cyclic prime-qudit stabilizer code whose length 𝑛 divides 𝑝 𝑡 + 1 for some positive integer 𝑡 .GKP CV-cluster-state code › p. 521 

A cluster-state code that utilizes a generalized analog cluster state with some of its physical modes initialized in GKP (resource) states. Alternatively, it can be thought of as a multimode GKP code whose encoding consists of initializing 𝑘 modes in momentum states (or, in the normalizable case, squeezed vacua), 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes in (normalizable) GKP states, and applying a Gaussian circuit consisting of two-body gates 𝑒 𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 for some angles 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 . The code provides a way to perform fault-tolerant MBQC, with the required number 𝑛 − 𝑘 of GKP-encoded physical modes determined by the particular protocol [396, 483–485]. GKP-surface code 

› p. 522 

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code and whose inner code is a surface code, including toric surface-code variants [396, 397], rotated surface codes [398–401], and XZZX surface codes [402]. Galois-qudit BCH code › p. 492 

True Galois-qudit stabilizer code constructed from BCH codes via either the Hermitian construction or the Galois-qudit CSS construction. Parameters can be improved by applying Steane enlargement › p. 437 [824], e.g., as in Ref. [825]. Galois-qudit GRS code › p. 495 

A true 𝑞 -Galois-qudit stabilizer code constructed from GRS codes via either the Hermitian construction [ 785 – 787 ] or the Galois-qudit CSS construction [788, 789]. 151

An (( 𝑛, 𝐾 , 𝑑 )) 𝑞 Galois-qudit code whose logical subspace is the joint eigenspace of commuting Galois-qudit Pauli operators forming the code’s stabilizer group S. Traditionally, the logical subspace is the joint +1 eigenspace, and the stabilizer group does not contain 

𝑒 𝑖 𝜙 𝐼 for any 𝜙 ≠ 0. The distance 𝑑 is the minimum weight of a Galois-qudit Pauli string that implements a nontrivial logical operation in the code. Generalized homological-product code › p. 546 

Stabilizer code whose properties are determined from an underlying chain complex, which often consists of some type of product of other chain complexes. Good QLDPC code 

> › p. 547

Also called asymptotically good QLDPC codes . A family of QLDPC codes ⟦𝑛 𝑖 , 𝑘 𝑖 , 𝑑 𝑖 ⟧ whose asymptotic rate lim 𝑖 →∞ 𝑘 𝑖 /𝑛 𝑖 and asymptotic distance lim 𝑖 →∞ 𝑑 𝑖 /𝑛 𝑖 are both positive. Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code 

> › p. 522

Quantum lattice code for a non-degenerate lattice, thereby admitting a finite-dimensional logical subspace. Codes on 𝑛 modes can be constructed from lattices with 2𝑛 -dimensional full-rank Gram matrices 𝐴 . Any GKP code can be generated from a Gram matrix in standard form via a Gaussian unitary transformation [486, Corr. 1]. Graph quantum code › p. 547 

A stabilizer code on tensor products of 𝐺 -valued qudits for Abelian 𝐺 whose encoding isometry is defined using a graph [ 826 , Eqs. (4-5)]. An analytical form of the codewords exists in terms of the adjacency matrix of the graph and bicharacters of the Abelian group [ 826 ]; see [ 827 , Eq. (1)]. A graph quantum code for 𝐺 = Z2 contains a cluster state as one of its codewords and reduces to a cluster state when its logical dimension is one [828]. Hermitian Galois-qudit code 

> › p. 500

An ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧𝑞 true Galois-qudit stabilizer code constructed from a Hermitian self-orthogonal linear code over F𝑞 2 using the one-to-one correspondence between the Galois-qudit Pauli matrices and elements of the Galois field F𝑞 2 .Hexagonal GKP code › p. 524 

Single-mode GKP qudit-into-oscillator code based on the triangular lattice. Offers the best error correction against displacement noise in a single mode due to the optimal packing of the underlying lattice [488, Sec. VI]. Lattice stabilizer code › p. 551 

A geometrically local stabilizer code with sites organized on a lattice modeled by the additive group Z𝐷 for spatial dimension 𝐷 ,using either the ordinary block notion of locality or the fermionic/Majorana notion of locality. On an infinite lattice, its stabilizer group is generated by few-site Pauli-type operators and their translations, in which case the code is called translationally invariant stabilizer code . Boundary conditions have to be imposed on the lattice in order to obtain finite-dimensional versions. Lattice defects and boundaries between different codes can also be introduced. Locally compact Abelian (LCA) stabilizer code › p. 553 

A mixed oscillator stabilizer code whose codewords are quantum lattice states defined on any number of qudits and a nonzero number of oscillators. Its stabilizers are countably infinite subgroups of the qudit Pauli and oscillator displacement groups. Codewords are entangled across the qudit-oscillator bipartition. Modular-qudit cluster-state code 

> › p. 477

A code based on a modular-qudit cluster state. Modular-qudit stabilizer code › p. 481 

An (( 𝑛, 𝐾 , 𝑑 )) 𝑞 modular-qudit code whose logical subspace is the joint eigenspace of commuting qudit Pauli operators forming the code’s stabilizer group S [701 , Sec. 3.6]. Traditionally, the logical subspace is the joint +1 eigenspace, and the stabilizer group does not contain 𝑒 𝑖 𝜙 𝐼 for any 𝜙 ≠ 0. The distance 𝑑 is the minimum weight of a qudit Pauli string that implements a nontrivial logical operation in the code. NTRU-GKP code 

> › p. 525

Multi-mode GKP code whose underlying lattice is utilized in variations of the NTRU cryptosystem [ 271 ]. Randomized constructions yield constant-rate GKP code families whose largest decodable displacement length scales as 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) with high probability. Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP code 

> › p. 527

Multimode GKP code with an infinite-dimensional logical space. Can be obtained by considering an 𝑛 -mode GKP code with a finite-dimensional logical space, removing stabilizers such that the logical space becomes infinite dimensional, and applying a Gaussian circuit. QLDPC code › p. 554 Member of a family of stabilizer codes for which the number of sites participating in each stabilizer generator and the number of stabilizer generators that each site participates in are both bounded by a constant as 𝑛 → ∞ . Sometimes, the two parameters are explicitly stated: each site of an (𝑙, 𝑤 )-regular QLDPC code is acted on by ≤ 𝑙 generators of weight ≤ 𝑤 .Quantum AG code

True Galois-qudit stabilizer code constructed from evaluation AG codes via the Galois-qudit Hermitian construction or the Galois-qudit CSS construction. Quantum Gabidulin code › p. 502 

A Galois-qudit stabilizer code over 𝑛 Galois qudits of dimension 𝑞 = 2𝑛 that is useful in protecting against faults in qubit Clifford circuits acting on stacked quantum memories. This code can be treated as a code on an 𝑛 × 𝑛 qubit stacked memory by decomposing each Galois qudit into a Kronecker product of 𝑛 qubits; see [381, 663–666][667, Sec. 5.3]. Quantum Hermitian AG code › p. 502 

Quantum AG code constructed from Hermitian AG codes via the Galois-qudit Hermitian construction or the Galois-qudit CSS construction. In parameter ranges where two-point Hermitian codes improve on one-point codes, the resulting quantum codes can also have improved parameters [830]. 152

An 𝑛 -qubit, modular-qudit, or Galois-qudit stabilizer code whose construction is non-deterministic. Since stabilizer encoders are Clifford circuits, such codes can be thought of as arising from random Clifford circuits. Rotor cluster-state code › p. 558 

Rotor analogue of the qubit and analog cluster-state codes. The exact rotor cluster state is non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Defined from a real-valued weighted adjacency matrix of a graph [482]. Rotor stabilizer code 

> › p. 558

Rotor code whose codespace is defined as the common +1 eigenspace of a group of mutually commuting rotor generalized Pauli operators. The stabilizer group can be either discrete or continuous, corresponding to modular or linear constraints on angular positions and momenta. Both cases can yield finite or infinite logical dimension. Exact codewords are non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Stabilizer code › p. 559 A code whose logical subspace is the joint eigenspace (usually with eigenvalue +1) of a set of commuting unitary Pauli-type operators forming the code’s stabilizer group. They can be block codes defined on tensor-product spaces of qubits or qudits, or non-block codes defined on single sufficiently large Hilbert spaces such as bosonic modes or other Abelian group spaces. True Galois-qudit stabilizer code › p. 504 

A ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧𝑞 stabilizer code whose stabilizer’s Galois symplectic representation › p. 497 forms a linear subspace. In other words, the set of 𝑞 -ary vectors representing the stabilizer group is closed under both addition and multiplication by elements of F𝑞 . In contrast, Galois-qudit stabilizer codes admit sets of vectors that are closed under addition only.

A non-CSS multimode GKP code defined on a 2D mode lattice that encodes a qudit logical space and whose excitations are characterized by the 𝑈 (1)2𝑛 × 𝑈 (1)−2𝑚 Chern-Simons theory. The code can be obtained from the analog surface code by condensing › p. 559 certain anyons [392].

> › p. 475

Modular-qudit subsystem stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 that is characterized by the chiral semion topological phase. The code admits a set of geometrically local stabilizer generators on a torus. Lattice subsystem code › p. 552 

A geometrically local qubit, modular-qudit, or Galois-qudit subsystem stabilizer code with qudits organized on a lattice modeled by the additive group Z𝐷 for spatial dimension 𝐷 , using either the ordinary block notion of locality or the fermionic/Majorana notion of locality. On an infinite lattice, its gauge group is generated by few-site Pauli operators and their translations, in which case the code is called translationally invariant subsystem code . The stabilizer group may contain generators of unbounded weight, distinguishing these codes from stabilizer codes with bounded-weight generators for which some logical qubits were re-assigned to be gauge qubits. Modular-qudit subsystem color code › p. 482 

An extension of subsystem color codes to modular qudits. Codes are defined analogously to qubit subsystem color codes, but a directionality is required in order to make the modular-qudit stabilizers commute [642, Sec. VII]. QLDPC subsystem code › p. 555 

Member of a family of subsystem stabilizer codes for which the number of sites participating in each gauge generator and the number of gauge generators that each site participates in are both bounded by a constant as 𝑛 → ∞ . The stabilizer group may contain generators of unbounded weight, distinguishing these codes from stabilizer codes with bounded-weight generators for which some logical qubits were re-assigned to be gauge qubits. 𝑞 subsystem code 

› p. 474 

Modular-qudit subsystem code, based on the Kitaev honeycomb model [ 510 ] and its generalization [ 610 ], that is characterized by the Z(1)

𝑞 anyon theory [ 611 ], which is modular for odd prime 𝑞 and non-modular otherwise. Encodes a single 𝑞 -dimensional qudit when put on a torus for odd 𝑞 , and a 𝑞 /2-dimensional qudit for even 𝑞 . 3D fermionic surface code › p. 365 

A non-CSS variant of the 3D Kitaev surface code that realizes Z2 gauge theory with an emergent fermion, i.e., the fermionic-charge bosonic-loop (FcBl) phase [ 435 ]. The model can be defined on a cubic lattice in several ways [ 436 , Eq. (D45-46)]. Realizations on other lattices also exist [437], and the phase of this code also exists in the 3D Kitaev honeycomb model [438]. 3D surface code 

> › p. 366

A generalization of the Kitaev surface code defined on a 3D cubic lattice. Qubits are placed on edges, 𝑍 -type stabilizer generators are placed on square plaquettes oriented in all three directions, and 𝑋 -type stabilizers are placed on the six edges neighboring every vertex [439]. Abelian TQD code 

> › p. 544

TQD code whose codewords realize a 2D Abelian twisted-quantum-double topological order. For Abelian TQDs, the corresponding anyon theory is defined by an Abelian group and a group cocycle built from Type-I, Type-II, or Type-III 3-cocycles [ 388 , 544 , 545 ]. Abelian TQDs with Type-I and -II cocycles account for all 2D Abelian topological orders that admit gapped boundaries [ 546 ]. Abelian TQDs with Type-III cocycles may admit non-Abelian topological orders. Abelian TQD stabilizer code › p. 475 

Modular-qudit stabilizer code whose codewords realize a 2D Abelian twisted-quantum-double topological order on composite-dimensional qudits. For every finite Abelian group 𝐺 = Î𝑖 Z𝑁 𝑖 and every product of Type-I and Type-II cocycles, there is a Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonian realizing the corresponding Abelian TQD [ 388 ]. Equivalently, these codes exhaust the 2D Abelian topological orders that admit gapped boundaries [388, 389]. Abelian quantum-double stabilizer code › p. 474 

Modular-qudit stabilizer code whose codewords realize 2D modular gapped Abelian topological order with trivial cocycle. The corresponding anyon theory is defined by an Abelian group. The 𝐺 = Z2 instance on a torus is the toric code, and cyclic-group instances reduce to modular-qudit surface codes. All such codes can be realized by a stack of modular-qudit surface codes because all finite Abelian groups are direct products of cyclic groups. Abelian topological code › p. 292 

Code whose codewords realize topological order associated with an Abelian anyon theory. In 2D, this is equivalent to a unitary braided fusion category which is also an Abelian group under fusion [ 547 ]. Unless otherwise noted, the phases discussed are bosonic. Brickwork 𝑋𝑆 

stabilizer code › p. 372 

An 𝑋𝑆 stabilizer code that realizes the topological order of the Type-III 𝐺 = Z32 TQD model [ 548 , 549 ], which is the same topological order as the 𝐺 = 𝐷 4 quantum double [ 550 ]. Its qubits are placed on a 2D square lattice, and the stabilizers are defined using two overlapping rectangular tilings. Chen-Hsin invertible-order code › p. 374 

A geometrically local commuting-projector code that realizes beyond-group-cohomology invertible topological phases in arbitrary dimensions. Its code Hamiltonian terms include Pauli-𝑍 operators and products of Pauli-𝑋 operators and 𝐶 𝑍 gates [ 551 , Eq. (3.25)]. Instances of the code in 4D realize the 3D Z2 gauge theory with fermionic charge and either bosonic (FcBl) or fermionic (FcFl) loop excitations at their boundaries [435, 552]; see Ref. [553] for a different lattice-model formulation of the FcBl boundary code. Chiral semion Walker-Wang model code › p. 475 

A 3D lattice modular-qudit stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 whose low-energy excitations on boundaries realize the chiral semion topological order. The model admits 2D chiral semion topological order at one of its surfaces [ 451 , 452 ]. The corresponding phase can also be realized via a non-stabilizer Hamiltonian [453]. Chiral semion subsystem code 

> › p. 475

Modular-qudit subsystem stabilizer code with qudit dimension 𝑞 = 4 that is characterized by the chiral semion topological phase. The code admits a set of geometrically local stabilizer generators on a torus. Clifford-deformed surface code (CDSC) 

> › p. 375

A generally non-CSS derivative of the surface code defined by applying a translationally invariant constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 

to the original (CSS) surface code. Unlike the surface code, CDSCs include codes whose thresholds and subthreshold performance are enhanced under noise biased towards dephasing. Examples of CDSCs include the XY code, XZZX code, and random CDSCs. Compactified R

gauge theory code 

> › p. 518

An integer-homology bosonic CSS code realizing 2D 𝑈 (1) gauge theory on bosonic modes. The code can be obtained from the analog surface code by condensing › p. 559 certain anyons [ 392 ]. This results in a pinning of each mode to the space of periodic functions, which is the Hilbert space of a physical rotor, and can be thought of as compactification of the 2D R gauge theory phase realized by the analog surface code. Cubic honeycomb color code › p. 383 

3D color code defined on a four-colorable bitruncated cubic honeycomb uniform tiling. Cubic theory code 

> › p. 383

A geometrically local commuting-projector code family defined on triangulations in arbitrary spatial dimensions. Its Hamiltonian contains Pauli-𝑍 flux terms and non-Pauli Gauss-law terms built from products of Pauli-𝑋 operators and 𝐶 𝑍 gates. These commuting non-Pauli stabilizers realize higher-form Z32 gauge theories with Abelian electric excitations and non-Abelian magnetic excitations. Dihedral 𝐺 = 𝐷 𝑚 

quantum-double code › p. 545 

Quantum-double code whose codewords realize topological order associated with the dihedral group 𝐷 𝑚 of order 2𝑚 . For 𝑚 ≥ 3,these codes are non-Abelian, with the simplest case given by 𝐷 3 = 𝑆 3, the permutation group on three objects. On an oriented lattice, each edge hosts a 2𝑚 -dimensional group qudit, and the codespace is the ground-state subspace of the corresponding quantum double Hamiltonian [404]. Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theory code 

> › p. 545

A code whose codewords realize 𝐷 -dimensional lattice Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theory [ 557 , 558 ] for a finite group 𝐺 and a 𝐷 + 1-cocycle 𝜔 in the cohomology class 𝐻 𝐷 +1 (𝐺, 𝑈 (1) ) . When the cocycle is non-trivial, the gauge theory is called a twisted gauge theory . There exist lattice-model formulations in arbitrary spatial dimension [ 559 ]. Boundaries and excitations have been studied for arbitrary dimension [560]. Double-semion stabilizer code › p. 476

Its ground-state subspace can be mapped to that of the double-semion string-net model by a finite-depth quantum circuit with ancillas [388]. Double-semion string-net code › p. 384

Under parity-preserving noise, it behaves as the Majorana analogue of the repetition code [532]. Kitaev honeycomb code › p. 409

Its stabilizer group is generated by loop operators, and syndrome extraction can be reduced to ordered measurements of the two-qubit link operators [ 567 , Sec. 3.2]. This is the 𝑞 = 2 instance of the Z(1)

subsystem code and does not encode any logical qubits [567][395, Sec. 7.3]. Kitaev surface code

Variant of the surface code obtained by taking the medial graph of the surface code lattice (treated as a graph) and applying a procedure to construct the check operators [ 406 , 407 ][ 408 , Fig. 8]. On a square lattice, this amounts to a rotation by 45 degrees such that qubits are on vertices, and both 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type check operators occupy plaquettes in an alternating checkerboard pattern. Square-octagon (4.8.8) color code 

> › p. 452

2D color code defined on a patch of the 4.8.8 (square-octagon) tiling, which itself is obtained by applying a fattening procedure to the square lattice [ 411 ]. An equivalent description uses the Tetrakis square tiling (a.k.a. the Union Jack lattice), which is dual to the 4.8.8 lattice [ 412 ]. Among the three semiregular triangular 2D color-code families, the 4.8.8 family uses the fewest physical qubits for a given distance and is the only one of the three with transversal implementations of the full Clifford group [413]. String-net code 

> › p. 566

A non-stabilizer commuting-projector code whose codewords realize a 2D topological order rendered by a Turaev-Viro topological field theory. The corresponding anyon theory is defined by a (multiplicity-free) unitary fusion category C. The code is defined on a cell decomposition dual to a triangulation of a two-dimensional surface, with a qudit of dimension | C | located at each edge of the decomposition. For modular input categories, the emergent anyon theory is the doubled category C ⊗ C ∗ [572 ]. These models realize local topological order (LTO) [573]. Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) code › p. 323 

A code whose codewords form the ground-state or low-energy subspace of a code Hamiltonian realizing symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order. Tetrahedral color code › p. 460 

A 3D color code defined on a colored tetrahedron cut from a suitably colored BCC lattice [ 455 ]. Qubits are placed on tetrahedra, on the triangles covering the tetrahedron faces, on the edges along the tetrahedron edges, and on the tetrahedron vertices. The code has both string-like and sheet-like logical operators [456]. Tetron code › p. 460 A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Three-fermion (3F) Walker-Wang model code › p. 461 

A 3D lattice stabilizer code whose bulk realizes a 3D time-reversal SPT order [ 457 ] and whose gapped boundary supports the 2D three-fermion (3F) topological order. The code can be used as a resource state for fault-tolerant MBQC [458]. Three-fermion (3F) subsystem code 

> › p. 460

2D subsystem stabilizer code whose low-energy excitations realize the three-fermion anyon theory [ 574 –576 ]. One version uses two qubits at each site [ 395 ], while other manifestations utilize a single qubit per site and only weight-two (two-body) interactions [575, 577]. All are expected to be equivalent to each other via a local constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 .Topological code 

> › p. 325

A code whose codewords form the ground-state or low-energy subspace of a (typically geometrically local) code Hamiltonian realizing a topological phase. A topological phase may be bosonic or fermionic , i.e., constructed out of underlying subsystems whose operators commute or anti-commute with each other, respectively. Unless otherwise noted, the phases discussed are bosonic. Toric code › p. 461 Version of the Kitaev surface code on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions, encoding two logical qubits. Being the first manifestation of the surface code, "toric code" is often an alternative name for the general construction. Twisted toric code [ 415 , Fig. 8] refers to the construction on a torus with twisted (a.k.a. shifted) boundary conditions. In the original Hamiltonian construction, open Pauli-𝑍 and Pauli-𝑋 strings create pairs of electric charges and magnetic vortices, and braiding one type around the other yields the nontrivial Abelian anyonic phase [404]. Truncated trihexagonal (4.6.12) color code › p. 465 

2D color code defined on a (typically triangular) patch of the 4.6.12 (truncated trihexagonal or square-hexagon-dodecagon) tiling. Twisted quantum double (TQD) code 

> › p. 560

Code whose codewords realize a 2D topological order rendered by a Chern-Simons topological field theory. The corresponding anyon theory is defined by a finite group 𝐺 and a 3-cocycle 𝜔 ∈ 𝐻 3 (𝐺, 𝑈 (1) ) [ 388 , 544 , 578 ]. Canonical TQD models [ 544 ] are defined on group-valued qudits. Twisted quantum triple (TQT) code 

> › p. 560

Group-based code realizing a 3D topological order rendered by a Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theory. The corresponding anyon theory is defined by a finite group 𝐺 and a Type-IV four-cocycle 𝜔 . Canonical TQT models [ 559 , 579 ] and other formulations whose ground states are in the same phase are all defined on group-valued qudits. Two-gauge theory code › p. 566 

A code whose codewords realize lattice two-gauge theory [ 580 – 588 ] for a finite two-group (a.k.a. a crossed module ) in arbitrary spatial dimension. There exist several lattice-model formulations in arbitrary spatial dimension [ 589 , 590 ] as well as explicitly in 3D [591–594] and 4D [594], with the 3D case realizing the Yetter model [595–598]. Walker-Wang model code › p. 567 

A non-stabilizer commuting-projector 3D topological code defined by a unitary braided fusion category C (also known as a unitary premodular category). The code is defined on a cubic lattice that is resolved to be trivalent, with a qudit of dimension | C | located at each edge. The codespace is the ground-state subspace of the Walker-Wang model Hamiltonian [ 601 ] and realizes the Crane-Yetter model [602–604]. A single-state version of the code provides a resource state for MBQC [458]. 158

> › p. 469

A variant of the surface code whose generators are 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋 and 𝑌𝑌𝑌𝑌 , obtained by mapping 𝑍 → 𝑌 in the surface code. (1, 3) 4D toric code 

> › p. 330

A generalization of the Kitaev surface code defined on a 4D lattice. The code is called a (1, 3) toric code because it admits 1D 𝑍 -type and 3D 𝑋 -type logical operators. In the hypercubic lattice version, qubits are placed on edges, each 𝑍 -type stabilizer generator is supported on cubes on the boundary of a hypercube, and 𝑋 -type stabilizers are placed on the edges neighboring every vertex [ 459 ]. 

(2, 2) Loop toric code › p. 330 

A generalization of the Kitaev surface code defined on a 4D lattice. The code is called a (2, 2) toric code because it admits 2D membrane 𝑍 -type and 𝑋 -type logical operators. Both types of operators create 1D (i.e., loop) excitations at their edges. The code serves as a self-correcting quantum memory [460, 461]. 

𝐺 -enriched Walker-Wang model code › p. 564 

A 3D topological code defined by a unitary 𝐺 -crossed braided fusion category C [ 605 , 606 ], where 𝐺 is a finite group. The model realizes TQFTs that include two-gauge theories, those behind Walker-Wang models, as well as the Kashaev TQFT [ 607 , 608 ]. It has been generalized to include domain walls [609]. 

⟦15 , 1, 3⟧ quantum RM code › p. 335 

A ⟦15 , 1, 3⟧ quantum Reed-Muller code that is most easily thought of as a tetrahedral 3D color code. It can be constructed as a CSS code from the [15 , 5, 8] punctured Reed-Muller code and its even subcode, which explains its transversal 𝑇 † gate [381]. 

⟦17 , 1, 5⟧ 4.8.8 color code › p. 337 

Seventeen-qubit doubly even 2D color code that admits a transversal implementation of the logical Clifford group. The smallest distance-five CSS code has 𝑛 = 17 [ 424 ]. It is also a normal self-dual CSS code whose transversal Hadamard acts logically, making it suitable as an inner code for fifth-order magic-state distillation [89]. 

⟦4, 1, 2⟧

Leung-Nielsen-Chuang-Yamamoto (LNCY) code › p. 343 

A four-qubit CSS stabilizer code that is the only qubit CSS code with such parameters. 

⟦4, 2, 2⟧ Four-qubit code › p. 345 

A four-qubit hyperbolic self-dual CSS stabilizer code that is the smallest two-logical-qubit stabilizer code to detect a single-qubit error. It is unique for its parameters [426, Thm. 8]. 

⟦4, 2, 2⟧𝐺 four group-qudit code 

> › p. 542

⟦4, 2, 2⟧𝐺 group quantum code that is an extension of the four-qubit code to group-valued qudits. 

⟦5, 1, 2⟧ rotated surface code › p. 347 

A rotated surface code on one rung of a ladder, with one qubit on the rung, and four qubits surrounding it. This is the smallest code that implements a fault-tolerant logical 𝑆 gate using a diagonal depth-one Clifford circuit [427]. 

⟦6, 2, 2⟧ 𝐶 6 code 

> › p. 350

Error-detecting normal self-dual CSS code on three qubit pairs that encodes a logical qubit pair and detects any error acting on one pair [428]. In Knill’s 𝐶 4/𝐶 6 architecture, this code is used at the second and higher concatenation levels. 

⟦6, 4, 2⟧

error-detecting code 

> › p. 352

Self-complementary six-qubit code with rate 2/3 that is unique for its parameters, up to equivalence [ 429 , Tab. III]. Concatenations of this code with itself yield the ⟦6𝑟 , 4𝑟 , 2𝑟 ⟧ level-𝑟 many-hypercube code [430]. 

⟦7, 1, 3⟧ Steane code › p. 353 

A ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ self-dual CSS code that is the smallest qubit CSS code to correct a single-qubit error [ 431 ]. The code is constructed using the classical binary [7, 4, 3] Hamming code for protecting against both 𝑋 and 𝑍 errors. 

⟦8, 3, 2⟧ Smallest interesting color code › p. 357 

Smallest 3D color code whose physical qubits lie on vertices of a cube and which admits a (weakly) transversal 𝐶𝐶 𝑍 gate. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Shor code 

> › p. 358

Nine-qubit CSS code › p. 544 that is the first quantum error-correcting code [ 433 , ID 8802]. Among indecomposable ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ CSS codes, the Shor code has the largest automorphism group [434]. 

⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Surface-17 code › p. 359 

A ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ rotated surface code named for the sum of its 9 data qubits and 8 syndrome qubits. It is one of the four inequivalent CSS gauge fixings of the nine-qubit Bacon-Shor code [ 434 ]. It uses the smallest number of qubits to perform fault-tolerant error correction on a surface code with parallel syndrome extraction. 

Z3 × Z9-fusion subsystem code 

> › p. 474

Modular-qudit 2D subsystem stabilizer code whose low-energy excitations realize a non-modular anyon theory with Z3 × Z9 fusion rules. Encodes two qutrits when put on a torus. 

Z(1) 

> 𝑞

subsystem code 

> › p. 474

Modular-qudit subsystem code, based on the Kitaev honeycomb model [ 510 ] and its generalization [ 610 ], that is characterized by the Z(1) 

> 𝑞

anyon theory [ 611 ], which is modular for odd prime 𝑞 and non-modular otherwise. Encodes a single 𝑞 -dimensional qudit when put on a torus for odd 𝑞 , and a 𝑞 /2-dimensional qudit for even 𝑞 . This code can be constructed using geometrically local gauge generators, but does not admit geometrically local stabilizer generators. For 𝑞 = 2, the code reduces to the subsystem code underlying the Kitaev honeycomb model code as well as the honeycomb Floquet code. 159

|0⟩ | 0⟩ | 𝛼 ⟩ for some complex 𝛼 . The dual of a PPM code is obtained by the exchange 0 ↔ 𝛼 .160 

# 4. CODES IN THE CLASSICAL DOMAIN 

It has been only in the past two or three years that the theory of error-correcting codes has advanced sufficiently to provide the basis for practical systems. Computer technology also has continued to advance, decreasing the cost and increasing the speed of equipment used to implement error correction. At the same time, there is a growing need for communication channels of extreme reliability for computers and automatic control systems. As the need grows and as coding theory and computer technology continue to develop, error detection and error correction will play an essential role in the success of complex systems. — W. Wesley Peterson, 1962 

## I. PROPERTY CODES 

𝑡 -DESIGN t-designs  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Quadrature ⊲ Cubature ⊲ Averaging set  

> DESCRIPTION

A code whose codewords are uniformly distributed in a way that is useful for determining averages of polynomials over the code’s underlying space 𝑋 . In that way, the codewords form an approximation of the space. A code is a design on 𝑋 of strength 𝑡 ,i.e., a 𝑡 -design on 𝑋 , if the average of any polynomial of degree up to 𝑡 over its codewords is equal to the uniform average over all of 𝑋 .As such, a design can be used to determine the average of degree-

≤ 𝑡 polynomials 𝑝 over 𝑋 ,

A weighted design is a design for which each term 𝑝 (𝑥 ) in the above sum must be multiplied by a weight 𝑤 (𝑥 ) in order to be equal to the left-hand side. The most well-known examples of weighted designs are exact Gaussian quadrature 

or cubature formulas for integration over the reals [ 362 , 835 – 838 ], 

𝑋 = R𝑛 (with appropriate measure); these tend to be weighted designs. Fixed-weight codewords of a binary code can form a design on 

𝑋 being a Johnson space 𝐽 (𝑛, 𝑤 ), i.e., the space of length-𝑛 binary strings of weight 𝑤 . Such a design is called a combinatorial design  

> › p. 181

(a.k.a. block design or covering design) [ 839 ], which includes Steiner systems as a special case. Other designs exist when 𝑋 is 

𝑞 -ary Hamming space (where they are called orthogonal arrays 

> › p. 231

), ordered Hamming space [ 198 , 199 ], 𝑞 -Johnson space [ 840 , 841 ](where they are called subspace designs › p. 250 ), or a sphere [ 368 ](where they are called spherical designs › p. 278 ). Complex projective designs are designs on complex projective space, i.e., the space of all pure quantum states [ 842 – 844 ]. General-izations to infinite-dimensional spaces yield rigged designs, or more colloquially, continuous-variable (CV) designs [ 845 ], which can be used as operator-valued measures for the space of bosonic quantum states (i.e., Schwartz space over the reals). Designs also exist on groups. Designs on the unitary (projec-tive unitary) group are called strong unitary (unitary) designs › p. 251 

[846 –849 ], while 𝑡 -designs on the permutation group are called per-mutation 𝑡 -designs [850] (a.k.a. 𝑡 -wise independent permutations). Other notable designs not included below include torus designs [851 , 852 ], simplex designs [ 853 – 856 ], quantum-channel designs [857 ], designs on vertex operator algebras (a.k.a. conformal de-signs) [ 858 ], and fractional designs [ 859 ]. Existence has been proven for combinatorial designs [ 860 – 864 ], subspace designs [ 865 , 866 ], as well as designs on continuous topological spaces [867–870].

BATCH CODE [903] batch  

> DESCRIPTION

Binary code designed for minimizing the total amount of storage and the worst-case maximal load on any device in a dis-tributed system. An (𝑛, 𝑁, 𝑘, 𝑚, 𝑡 ) batch code encodes a length-𝑛 string 𝑥 1, · · · , 𝑥 𝑛 

into an 𝑚 -tuple of strings of total length 𝑁 (also called buckets), such that for each 𝑘 -tuple of distinct indices 𝑖 1, 𝑖 2, ..., 𝑖 𝑘 , the entries 

𝑥 𝑖 1 , ..., 𝑥 𝑖 𝑘 can be decoded by reading at most 𝑡 symbols from each bucket. If each bucket of a batch code contains a single symbol, then the (𝑛, 𝑁, 𝑘, 𝑚 ) batch code is primitive .If, for any multiset 𝑖 1, 𝑖 2, ..., 𝑖 𝑘 ∈ [ 𝑛 ], there is a partition of buckets into subsets 𝑆 1, ..., 𝑆 𝑘 ⊂ [ 𝑚 ] such that each 𝑥 𝑖 𝑗 can be recovered by reading at most one symbol from each bucket in 𝑆 𝑗 , then the 

(𝑛, 𝑁, 𝑘, 𝑚 ) code is a multiset batch code . 

> PROTECTION

The Gadget Lemma states that any (𝑛, 𝑁, 𝑘, 𝑚 ) batch code at 𝑡 = 1 can be transformed into a multiset (𝑟𝑛, 𝑟 𝑁, 𝑘, 𝑚 ) batch code for any positive integer 𝑟 [904]. Combining two batch codes 𝐶 1 and 𝐶 2, which are (𝑛 1, 𝑁 1, 𝑘 1, 𝑚 1)

and (𝑛 2, 𝑁 2, 𝑘 2, 𝑚 2) batch codes respectively, yields a composite batch code 𝐶 1 ⊗ 𝐶 2, which is an (𝑛 1, 𝑚 1 𝑁 2, 𝑘 1 𝑘 2, 𝑚 1𝑚 2) batch code.

BLOCK CODE block  

> DESCRIPTION

A code intended to encode a piece, or block, of a data stream on a block of 𝑛 symbols, with each symbol taking values from a fixed alphabet Σ.The overall alphabet of the code is Σ𝑛 , and 𝑛 is called the length of the code [ 912 , Ch. 3]. In some cases, only a subset of Σ𝑛 is available to use for constructing the code. For example, in the case of spherical codes, one is constrained to 𝑛 -dimensional real vectors on the unit sphere. An alternative more stringent definition of the code (not used here) is in terms of a map encoding logical information from Σ𝑘 into 

Σ𝑛 , yielding an (𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 )Σ block code, where 𝑑 is the code distance.  

> PROTECTION

Block codes protect from errors acting on a few of the 𝑛 

symbols. A block code with distance 𝑑 detects errors acting on up to 

𝑑 − 1 symbols, and corrects erasure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 symbols.  

> RATE

Ideal decoding error is suppressed exponentially with the num-ber of subsystems 𝑛 , and the exponent has been studied in Ref. [913–915].  

> DECODING

⊲ Decoding an error-correcting code is equivalent to find-ing the ground state of a statistical mechanical model [916].

CHECKSUM CODE checksum  

> DESCRIPTION

An error-detecting block code that appends to a mes-sage a shorter string, called a checksum, that is computed from the message.  

> PROTECTION

The checksum can be recalculated from the received message and compared with the appended checksum in order to detect certain transmission or storage errors.

⊲ International Standard Book Number (ISBN) code › p. 227 —The last digit of an ISBN-10 string is a check digit computed modulo 11 [ 918 ]. ⊲ [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 𝑞 -ary parity-check code › p. 208 — The 𝑞 -ary parity check code is a simple example of a checksum code, with the parity of the message being the checksum. ⊲ Universal Product Code (UPC) › p. 285 — The last digit of a UPC barcode is a base-10 check digit computed modulo 10 from an alternating weighted sum of the preceding digits [919].

CODE WITH LOCALITY code_with_locality  

> DESCRIPTION

A code has (𝑟, 𝛿 ) locality if each codeword coordinate belongs to a repair group of size at most 𝑟 +𝛿 −1 whose restricted code has minimum distance at least 𝛿 [168 , Sec. 31.3.4.5]. Equivalently, given a codeword 𝑐 and coordinate 𝑐 𝑖 , there exists a coordinate set 

𝑆 𝑖 of size ≤ 𝑟 + 𝛿 − 1 containing 𝑖 such that the restriction 𝐶 |𝑆 𝑖 has minimum distance at least 𝛿 . 

> PROTECTION

There is a generalized Singleton minimum distance bound [922],

CONCATENATED CODE [923] concatenated  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Serially concatenated code  

> DESCRIPTION

A code whose encoding mapping is a composition of two mappings: first the message set is mapped onto the code space of the outer code, then each coordinate of the outer code is mapped onto the code space of the inner code. In the basic construction, the outer code’s alphabet is the finite field F𝑝 𝑚 and the 𝑚 -dimensional inner code is over the field F𝑝 . The construction is not limited to linear codes.  

> RATE

There exist bounds on distance and rate of concatenated codes with a fixed outer and random inner code [924, 925].  

> DECODING

⊲ Generalized minimum-distance decoder [926].  

> PARENT

⊲ Generalized concatenated code (GCC) › p. 166  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Irregular repeat-accumulate (IRA) code › p. 190 — IRA codes can be interpreted as serial concatenated codes [ 927 ]. 

⊲ Binary balanced spherical code › p. 268 — A binary balanced spheri-cal code can be thought of as a concatenation of a constant-weight binary outer code with a shifted and scaled BPSK-like inner code. 

⊲ Polyphase code › p. 274 — A polyphase code can be thought of as a concatenation of a 𝑞 -ary outer code with a PSK inner code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Concatenated quantum code › p. 299 — Quantum codes can be concatenated with classical codes to yield good quantum codes [928 ]. ⊲ Hsu-Anastasopoulos LDPC (HA-LDPC) code › p. 189 — HA-LDPC codes are a concatenation of an LDPC and an LDGM code. 

⊲ Tensor-product code › p. 251 — Tensor-product codes can be viewed both as serial or parallel concatenated codes [ 929 ]. ⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — Concatenations of GRS codes with random linear codes almost surely attain the GV bound › p. 209 [ 930 ]. ⊲ Long-range enhanced surface code (LRESC) › p. 415 — LRESCs are con-structed using a hypergraph product of two copies of a concatenated LDPC-repetition seed code.

DISTRIBUTED-STORAGE CODE distributed_storage  

> DESCRIPTION

Block code designed to encode information into spatial nodes such that it is possible to recover said information after failure of some nodes by accessing the remaining helper nodes with minimal bandwidth.  

> PROTECTION

Typically designed to protect a distributed storage sys-tem against the failure of a single node or multiple nodes.

EDITING CODE [965] insertion_deletion  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Insertion and deletion code  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code designed to protect against insertions, where a new symbol is added somewhere within the string, and deletions, where a symbol at an unknown location is erased.  

> PROTECTION

The metric measuring distance of a received word to the nearest codeword is the Levenshtein deletion distance : given vectors 

𝑢, 𝑣 , this distance is one-half the smallest number of deletions and insertions needed to change 𝑢 to 𝑣 . A code 𝐶 corrects 𝑒 deletions if all codewords are separated by at least 𝑒 + 1 in the deletion distance [966 ]. Similar distances, collectively called editing distances , can be defined for insertions and related operations [967, Sec. 22.7].  

> RATE

An asymptotically good linear code against bit-flip errors can be converted into an asymptotically good code against insertion-deletion errors [968].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Refs. [969, 970][967, Sec. 22.7] for more details.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Block code › p. 161 ⊲ Finite-dimensional error-correcting code (ECC) › p. 165  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Varshamov-Tenengolts (VT) code › p. 204 ⊲ DNA storage code › p. 163 — DNA codes can typically handle base-pair insertions and deletions.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Permutation-invariant (PI) code › p. 313 — PI codes of distance 𝑑 can protect against 𝑑 − 1 (quantum) deletion errors. 

⊲ Combinatorial design › p. 181 — Perfect deletion correcting codes can be constructed using combinatorial design theory [ 124 , 125 ]. 

⊲ Perfect code › p. 232 — Perfect deletion correcting codes can be con-structed using combinatorial design theory [124, 125].

> Finite-field alphabet
> Finite fields:

The most common and useful [ 971 ] alphabets used in block codes are Galois or finite fields F𝑞 , which are sets of 𝑞 ele-ments closed under addition and multiplication. They are finite analogues of the real or complex numbers, and a unique field exists for every power 𝑞 = 𝑝 𝑚 of a prime 𝑝 . The prime-field case reduces to Z𝑝 , a group under addition that is promoted to a field by defining multiplication modulo 𝑝 ; the case 𝑝 = 2 yields the binary field Z2.Every finite field comes with a 0 element (additive identity), a 1 ele-ment (multiplicative identity), and additive (multiplicative) inverses for all (nonzero) elements. An element whose powers exhaust all nonzero field elements is called primitive . Fields come with a trace operation, the field trace , which maps elements 𝛾 ∈ F𝑞 to elements of F𝑝 as tr (𝛾 ) =

under addition. One can check that the trace operation, tr (𝛾 ) =

𝛾 + 𝛾 2, outputs either 0 or 1 for any element 𝛾 ∈ F4. 

> RATE

The Shannon channel capacity (the maximum of the mutual information over input distributions) is the highest rate of informa-tion transmission through a classical (i.e., non-quantum) channel with arbitrarily small error rate [ 1]. The fault-tolerant capacity is the capacity for the more general case where the encoding and decoding 165 maps are also assumed to undergo noise [972]. Corrections to the capacity and tradeoff between decoding error, code rate and code length are determined using small [ 973 – 975 ], moderate [ 976 – 978 ] and large [ 979 – 982 ] deviation analysis. Some-times the difference from the asymptotic rate at finite block length can be characterized by the channel dispersion [975 , 983 ]. Doeblin coefficients [984] for classical channels have been studied [985].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 986 ] for a list of open problems in coding theory. 

⊲ See Refs. [ 987 , 988 ] for reviews of coding theory. ⊲ Classical systems such as RAM [ 989 ], HPC systems [ 990 –992 ], and data centers [993] suffer from noise.  

> PARENT

⊲ Classical-quantum (c-q) code › p. 568 — Any ECC can be em-bedded into a quantum Hilbert space, and thus passed through a quantum channel, by associating elements of the alphabet with ba-sis vectors in a Hilbert space over the complex numbers. In other words, classical codewords are elements of an alphabet, while quan-tum codewords are functions on the alphabet. Classical codes can be unified with quantum codes using various algebraic frameworks [994, 995].

satisfying 𝑑 (𝐸 (𝑒 (𝑥 ))) = 𝑥 for all 𝐸 ∈ E and messages 𝑥 ∈ [ 1 · · · 𝐾 ]

[381]. Finite ECCs can also be defined by axiomatically defining their encoding functions [38].

FRAMEPROOF (FP) CODE [1002, 1003] frameproof  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code designed to prevent a group of users from framing another user outside of the group for creating an unautho-rized copy of data. FP codes help to provide software protection from the illegal distribution and copying of computer software and copyrighted materials. These codes help protect products of dis-tributors as well as other naive users from being framed for illegal activity [1004]. A 𝑐 -separating code has the property that, for any two disjoint sets that each contain at most 𝑐 codewords, there is at least one position where the set of symbols of each set are disjoint [ 1005 ]. Separating codes are, equivalently, codes with the secure FP (SFP) 

property [1003]. Let us define Γ = {𝑤 (1) , . . . , 𝑤 (𝑛 ) } ⊆ F𝑙  

> 2

as an ( 𝑙, 𝑛 )-code. Each codeword 𝑤 (𝑖 ) corresponds to a user 𝑢 𝑖 . Let 𝐶 be a group of users. A bit in position 𝑖 is undetectable for the group 𝐶 when the words assigned to the users in the group match at the same position 𝑖 . The feasible set of the group 𝐶 , denoted 𝐹 (𝐶 ; Γ) or 𝐹 (𝐶 ), for some user 

𝑢 ∈ 𝐶 contains all of the codewords that match the group’s set of undetectable bits. Finally, if every subset 𝑆 ⊂ Γ of size at most 𝑐 

satisfies 𝐹 (𝑆 ) ∩ Γ = 𝑆 , then Γ is a 𝑐 -FP code [1004]. Any 𝑐 -FP code must be of length at least 𝑐 [ 1004 ]. A length-𝑙 𝑞 -ary 

𝑐 -FP code has at most 𝑡𝑞 ⌈𝑙 /𝑐 ⌉ + 𝑂 (𝑞 ⌈𝑙 /𝑐 ⌉− 1) codewords, where 𝑡 is an integer between 1 and 𝑐 , and 𝑡 ≡ 𝑙 modulo 𝑐 [243].  

> RATE

FP codes tend to have large minimum distance and low rate [ 1004 ]. Specifically, for any positive integers 𝑛 and 𝑐 , if 𝑙 = 16 𝑐 2 log 𝑛 ,then there exists a 𝑐 -FP (𝑙, 𝑛 )-code which has rate (log 𝑛 )/ 𝑙 [1004 ]. See Ref. [1006] for other bounds on FP codes.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ FP codes are utilized in digital fingerprinting and watermarking [243].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Block code › p. 161 ⊲ Finite-dimensional error-correcting code (ECC) › p. 165  

> CHILD

⊲ Identifiable parent property (IPP) code › p. 166 — A 𝑡 -IPP code is a 𝑡 -SFP code, which further implies it is a 𝑡 -FP code; see [ 1007 ][ 332 ,Sec. I.C].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Evaluation AG code › p. 219 — Asymptotic bounds on FP codes can be formulated using evaluation AG codes [ 1008 , 1009 ]. A sufficient condition for an evaluation AG code to be FP can be recast as an instance of the Riemann-Roch equation [ 21 , Sec. 15.8.2]. AG-based constructions of binary (2, 1)-separating systems can beat a random-coding lower bound [21, Thm. 15.8.13]. 

⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 — Kerdock codes of sufficient order are separating [1010, 1011]. 166
