GROUP-ORBIT CODE group_orbit  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose set of codewords forms an orbit of some reference codeword under a subgroup of the automorphism group ,i.e., the group of distance-preserving transformations on the metric space defined with the code’s alphabet.  

> PARENT

⊲ Error-correcting code (ECC) › p. 164 — Not all codes are group-orbit codes, and more generally one can classify codewords into orbits of the automorphism group [996].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Binary group-orbit code › p. 180 — Binary group-orbit codes are group-orbit codes in Hamming space. ⊲ Linear code over 𝐺 › p. 286 — The set of codewords of a linear code over 𝐺 can be thought of as an orbit of a particular codeword under the group formed by the code. However, group orbit codes do not have to be linear [ 101 , Remark 8.4.3]. ⊲ Multi-channel group-orbit code › p. 248 

⊲ Slepian group-orbit code › p. 276 — Slepian group-orbit codes are group-orbit codes on spheres.  

> COUSIN

⊲ Group-algebra code › p. 224 — A group-algebra code admits a regular, i.e., free and transitive, action on coordinates by a subgroup of its permutation automorphism group [ 181 , Thm. 16.4.7]. This differs from a group-orbit code, whose defining group action is transitive on codewords. 

IDENTIFIABLE PARENT PROPERTY (IPP) CODE [1016] ipp  

> DESCRIPTION

A code that is embedded in copyrighted content in order to detect unauthorized redistribution of said content by pirates. IPP codes are designed to detect pirates even when segments of content are mixed together so as to conceal the pirates’ identities. A unique codeword of an IPP code is hidden into each copy of the content (say, a movie or videogame) such that reselling a copy would expose the seller as a pirate. To overcome this, a coalition of 𝑡 pirates can mix their copies together so as to obfuscate their identities. The descendant bit-string corresponding to the new mixed copy therefore contains subsets of codeword coordinates of the copies that were used in the mixing. More technically, let 𝐵 = {𝑐 (1) , · · · , 𝑐 (𝑡 ) } be a subset of 𝑡 IPP codewords, corresponding to the copies of the pirate coalition. Then, 

𝑎 is called a descendant of 𝐵 if every coordinate of 𝑎 also exists as a coordinate (in the same position) of at least one of the codewords in 𝐵 . In other words, for all coordinates 𝑖 , there exists some 𝑐 ∈ 𝐵 

such that 𝑎 𝑖 = 𝑐 𝑖 .A 𝑡 -IPP code has the property that, given any descendant, a par-ent codeword can always be identified by examining all possible 

𝑡 -subsets of the code [1007].  

> RATE

A hypergraph approach can be used to show that, for any 𝑡 ≤

𝑞 , there exists a sequence of IPP codes with asymptotically non-vanishing rate [1017].  

> PARENT

⊲ Frameproof (FP) code › p. 165 — A 𝑡 -IPP code is a 𝑡 -SFP code, which further implies it is a 𝑡 -FP code; see [1007][332, Sec. I.C].  

> CHILD

⊲ Traceability code › p. 170 — Traceability codes allow for detec-tion of parents of pirated descendant copies by only determining the closest codeword to the descendant; see [332, Lemma 1.3]. 

LOCALLY CORRECTABLE CODE (LCC) lcc  

> DESCRIPTION

Recall that a block code encodes a length-𝑘 message into a length-𝑛 codeword, which is then sent through a noise channel to yield a received word. Informally, an LCC is a block code for which one can recover any coordinate of a codeword from at most 

𝑟 coordinates of the received word (assuming the received word is within some tolerated corruption rate 𝛿 ). Modified versions of local correctability include relaxed local cor-rectability [1018].  

> PROTECTION

Three-query LCCs have to have length that is superpoly-nomial in the message length [1019].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [ 1020 ] and Ref. [ 1021 ] for an introduction to LDCs and LCCs. ⊲ See a popular summary of the result about three-query LCCs in Quanta Magazine 9. 

> PARENT

⊲ Locally recoverable code (LRC) › p. 167 — LRCs recover a coordinate from a small number of other coordinates of an un-corrupted codeword, while LCCs allow recovery from a corrupted received word within the decoding radius. Since an uncorrupted codeword is a special case of a received word, any LCC is also an LRC.  

> CHILD

⊲ 𝑞 -ary linear LCC › p. 211  

> COUSINS

⊲ Locally decodable code (LDC) › p. 166 — Any family of LCCs can be converted to a family of LDCs whose rate differs by a constant [ 1022 ]; see [ 1021 , Sec. 2.4.1]. ⊲ Locally testable code (LTC) › p. 167 —There are relations between LDCs and LTCs [ 1023 ]. ⊲ Quantum locally recoverable code (QLRC) › p. 316 — A quantum code cannot admit two disjoint local recovery sets for the same qudit unless that qudit is fixed, ruling out a natural quantum analogue of LCCs [ 775 ,Thm. 74]. ⊲ Analog code › p. 256 — LCCs can also be defined over the real or complex numbers, and there are no complex 2-query LCCs [1024].

LOCALLY TESTABLE CODE (LTC) [1043–1046] ltc  

> DESCRIPTION

Code for which one can efficiently check whether a given string is a codeword or is far from a codeword. Efficiency of the verification is quantified by the code’s query complexity 𝑢 , while effectiveness is quantified by the code’s soundness 𝑅 .Typically, one looks at how 𝑅 scales with increasing code size for infinite families of codes, defining LTC families as those for which the soundness is asymptotically constant. Such LTC families with asymptotically constant distance, rate, and query complexity are called 𝑐 3-LTCs . The first two such families are classical codes arising from the expander lifted-product › p. 491 quantum code construction and left-right Cayley complex › p. 192 codes. A technical definition for codes over binary alphabets is provided as follows; for general alphabets, see Ref. [ 1047 ]. The idea behind LTCs is to be able to reliably test whether a given bit-string 𝑥 is in the code by only sampling subsets of 𝑢 bits. To have something to check against, we first have to define a collection of length-𝑢 subsets 

𝑆 of bit locations that are called allowed local views . A code is an LTC if the following two conditions are satisfied [76, Thm. 1.1]. 168 First, if 𝑥 is a codeword, then all of its restrictions 𝑥 |𝑆 to the subsets 𝑆 are allowed local views, 

𝑥 ∈ 𝐶 ⇒ 𝑥 |𝑆 ∈ { allowed local views } . (11) This guarantees that codewords can indeed be determined from this limited sampling procedure. Second, the probability that a given restriction is not an allowed local view is lower-bounded by the relative distance to the code, Pr 𝑆 (𝑥 |𝑆 not allowed local view ) ≥ 𝑅 𝑛 𝐷 (𝑥, 𝐶 ) , (12) where 𝐷 (𝑥, 𝐶 ) is the Hamming distance between 𝑥 and the closest codeword to 𝑥 . This condition ensures that strings 𝑥 can be deemed to be not in the codespace with high probability, i.e., with probability increasing as 𝑥 gets farther from the code.

> CHILD

> COUSINS

— There are relations between LDCs and LTCs [ 1023 ]. ⊲ Locally correctable code (LCC) › p. 166 — There are relations between LDCs and LTCs [ 1023 ]. ⊲ Multiplicity code › p. 230 — Some multiplicity codes are locally testable by an appropriate test [ 1053 , 1054 ]. ⊲ Tanner code › p. 241 — Tanner codes can be generalized to sheaf codes , whose local codes satisfy a certain hierarchy. QUASI-CYCLIC CODE [1066] quasi_cyclic  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code of length 𝑛 is quasi-cyclic if, for each codeword 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 ℓ 𝑐 ℓ+1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the cyclic shift by ℓ positions, 

𝑐 𝑛 −ℓ+1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 −ℓ , is also a codeword. Codes for which ℓ = 1

are cyclic, while codes for which ℓ = 2 are called double circulant .The generator of an [𝑚𝑛 0, 𝑚𝑘 0] quasi-cyclic linear code is repre-sentable as a block matrix of 𝑚 × 𝑚 circulant matrices [34, 1067]. Quasi-cyclic codes can also be understood in terms of cyclic-shift automorphisms. Cyclic codes are invariant under a shift by one 169 position, while quasi-cyclic codes are invariant under a shift by ℓ

positions.

RANDOM CODE [1] random  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose construction is non-deterministic in some way, i.e., codes that utilize an element of randomness somewhere in their construction. Members of this class range from fully non-deterministic codes to codes whose multi-step construction is deter-ministic except for a single step. Typically, random codes are selected with a uniform distribution from some ensemble of codes. For example, a random binary code  

> 10 http://www.tec.hkr.se/~chen/research/codes/qc.htm

is a set of 𝐾 codewords of length 𝑛 chosen uniformly from the en-semble of all 2𝑛 bit-strings. Each bit in each codeword is chosen independently and uniformly. For another example, a random bi-nary linear code is generated from 𝑘 randomly chosen generators of length 𝑛 . Equivalently, it is defined by a random 𝑘 × 𝑛 binary gener-ator matrix whose entries are chosen independently and uniformly. In both of the above random code constructions, the ensemble size scales exponentially with 𝑛 . A common convention is to think of the resulting code constructions as effectively explicit (as opposed to random) in cases where the ensemble size is independent of 𝑛 or even when the size scales polynomially with 𝑛 . 

> RATE

Typical random codes (TRC) or typical random linear codes (TLC) refer to codes in the respective ensemble that satisfy a certain minimum-distance property. The relative fraction of typical codes in the ensemble approaches one as 𝑛 goes to infinity [ 1] (see also Ref. [ 1080 ]). Asymptotically, given relative distance 𝛿 = 𝑑 /𝑛 , the maximum rate for a TRC is 𝑅 = 12 𝑅 𝐺𝑉 (𝛿 ), where 𝑅 𝐺𝑉 (𝛿 ) = 1− ℎ(𝛿 )

is the Gilbert-Varshamov (GV) bound and ℎ(𝛿 ) is the binary entropy function. The maximum rate for a TLC is 𝑅 = 𝑅 𝐺𝑉 (𝛿 ), meaning that TLCs achieve the asymptotic GV bound › p. 209 . 

> DECODING

⊲ Ball-collision decoding [ 1081 ]. ⊲ Information set decoding (ISD) [ 1082 ] and Finiasz and Sendrier (FS-ISD) decoding [1083].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Distributed storage systems [ 302 ]. ⊲ Classical and quantum cryptography based on the learning-with-errors prob-lem, which is related to decoding a random linear code [ 303 ]. 

⊲ Random codes can be used to realize secure computation [304].  

> NOTES

⊲ Shannon’s pioneering work [ 1] analyzes the distance distri-bution of the code given a rate. Given 𝑛 and rate 𝑅 , the minimum distance of a TRC is governed asymptotically by the GV bound › p. 209 

𝑑 = 𝑛𝛿 𝐺𝑉 (2𝑅 ), where 𝛿 𝐺𝑉 (𝑥 ) = ℎ−1 (1 − 𝑥 ) for 0 ≤ 𝑥 ≤ 1. For a TLC, the minimum distance is similarly governed by 𝑑 = 𝑛𝛿 𝐺𝑉 (𝑅 ).

⊲ Fountain code › p. 187 — Fountain codes are typically gen-erated from random sparse encoding ensembles. ⊲ Goldreich-Sudan code › p. 188 — Randomness enters the probabilistic construc-tions associated with Goldreich-Sudan LTCs. ⊲ Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 — LDPC codes are often constructed nonde-terministically. ⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — Concatena-tions of GRS codes with random linear codes almost surely attain the GV bound › p. 209 [930 ]. ⊲ Random quantum code › p. 318 — Ran-dom quantum codes are quantum analogues of random classical codes. ⊲ Expander LP code › p. 491 — Expander lifted-product codes are quantum CSS codes that utilize short classical codes in their construction which need to satisfy some properties [ 169 , Lemma 10]. It is shown that such codes exist, but they are not explicitly con-structed. Such codes can be obtained by repeated random sampling or by performing a search of all codes of desired length. Neverthe-less, since the length of the desired short codes does not scale with 

𝑛 , this construction is effectively explicit. 170 

REVERSIBLE CODE reversible  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code of length 𝑛 over an alphabet is reversible if, for each codeword 𝑐 1𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the reversed string 𝑐 𝑛 · · · 𝑐 2𝑐 1 is also a codeword.  

> NOTES

⊲ Reversible cyclic codes are studied in [58, Sec. 2.10].  

> PARENT

⊲ Block code › p. 161  

> CHILD

⊲ [2𝑚 − 1, 2𝑚 − 1 − 2𝑚, 5] Melas code › p. 172  

> COUSINS

⊲ Cyclic linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 216 — A reversible cyclic code is a cyclic code with self-reciprocal generator polynomial and is an LCD code [ 58 , Thm. 2.10.3]. ⊲ Linear code with complementary dual (LCD) › p. 228 — A reversible cyclic code is a cyclic code with self-reciprocal generator polynomial and is an LCD code [ 58 , Thm. 2.10.3]. 

⊲ Quantum tensor-product code › p. 432 — Reversible cyclic codes can be used to construct quantum tensor-product codes [1084]. 

SKEW-CYCLIC CODE [1085] skew_cyclic  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code 𝐶 of length 𝑛 over an alphabet 𝑅 is skew-cyclic if there exists an automorphism, 𝜃 , of 𝑅 , such that for each string 𝑐 1𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 ∈ 𝐶 , the skew-cyclically shifted string 

𝜃 (𝑐 𝑛 )𝜃 (𝑐 1) · · · 𝜃 (𝑐 𝑛 −1) ∈ 𝐶 . We say that 𝐶 is a 𝜃 -cyclic code over 𝑅 . 

> NOTES

⊲ Computer algebra software is used to find most codes of this type. Ref. [ 1085 ] gives several examples of codes, which have slightly improved minimum distance for some (𝑛, 𝑘 ) codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Block code › p. 161  

> CHILD

⊲ Cyclic code › p. 163 — Skew-cyclic codes with 𝜃 trivial are cyclic.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Quasi-cyclic code › p. 168 — Under certain conditions, there is an equivalent quasi-cyclic or cyclic code for every skew-cyclic code [ 1078 ]. ⊲ Bose–Chaudhuri–Hocquenghem (BCH) code › p. 214 

— There exist skew-BCH codes, which are skew-cyclic versions of BCH codes [ 1085 ]. ⊲ Skew-cyclic CSS code › p. 503 — Skew-cyclic CSS codes are constructed from classical skew-cyclic codes over rings.

TRACEABILITY CODE [1087] traceability  

> DESCRIPTION

An IPP code with which it is possible to detect a parent of a given pirated descendant by finding the closest codeword to that descendant. Codes with strong traceability trace at least one member of a group that has constructed a pirate decoder (i.e., a generic pirate decryption process [ 1087 ]). A code with weak traceability has the ability to ensure that no group is able to frame another user [332].  

> RATE

Suppose 𝑛 is the number of users, 𝑘 is the number of users known by the pirates, and 𝑝 is the probability that the pirates cannot be traced. An open (public) resilient scheme using a hash function has users’ personal keys consisting of 𝑂 (𝑘 2 log 𝑛 ) decryption keys, which is the number of decryptions needed to reveal the informa-tion. The amount of data redundancy overhead is about 𝑂 (𝑘 4 log 𝑛 )

[1087]. A secret resilient scheme using a hash function has users’ per-sonal keys consisting of 𝑂 (𝑘 log (𝑛 /𝑝 )) decryption keys, which is the number of decryptions needed to reveal the information. The amount of data redundancy overhead is about 𝑂 (𝑘 2 log (𝑛 /𝑝 )) 

[1087]. A threshold (secret) scheme using a hash function that is success-ful against pirates which decrypt with probability > 𝑞 has users’ personal keys consisting of (4𝑘 /3𝑞 ) log (𝑛 /𝑝 ) decryption keys (note that this is the same as in the secret resilient scheme above). These types of schemes only need order › p. 161 𝑂 (1) decryption operations performed by users to decrypt the information successfully. Finally, the amount of data redundancy overhead is 4k encrypted keys, a large improvement compared to the above [1087].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Broadcast messages, pay-per-view movies, and pro-tecting copyrighted online material [332].  

> NOTES

⊲ Note that in the feature section above, the hash function maps the users into a set of 2𝑘 2 decryption keys [ 1087 ]. ⊲ For code tables, see Refs. [332, 1087].  

> PARENT

⊲ Identifiable parent property (IPP) code › p. 166 — Traceabil-ity codes allow for detection of parents of pirated descendant copies by only determining the closest codeword to the descendant; see [332, Lemma 1.3].  

> COUSIN

⊲ 𝑞 -ary code › p. 208 — A 𝑞 -ary code with distance 𝑑 ≥ 𝑛 (1 −

1/𝑡 2) has the 𝑡 -traceability property [332, Thm. 4.3]. 171

> DESCRIPTION

(12 , 32 , 5) NADLER CODE [1090] nadler  

> DESCRIPTION

A nonlinear (12 , 32 , 5) binary code that is the largest double-error-correcting code. An inequivalent code with the same parameters was constructed by Van Lint [ 1091 ] and presented in [ 34 , Ch. 2, Sec. 8]. Its automor-phism group is a subgroup of 𝑆 3 × 𝑆 4 [1091]. While the two codes are inequivalent, the (13 , 64 , 5) extension of both codes is unique and is a shortened NR code [1092].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Binary code › p. 179 ⊲ Small-distance block code › p. 170  

> COUSIN

⊲ (16 , 256 , 6) Nordstrom-Robinson (NR) code › p. 171 — The NR code is an extension of the Nadler code [1091, 1092]. 

(16 , 256 , 6) NORDSTROM-ROBINSON (NR) CODE [1093, 1094]  

> nordstrom_robinson
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Semakov-Zinoviev code  

> DESCRIPTION

A nonlinear (16 , 256 , 6) binary code that is the smallest Kerdock code and the smallest Preparata code. The size of this code is larger than the largest possible linear code with the same length and distance. The code can be shortened to produce optimal (15 , 128 , 6),

(14 , 64 , 6) and (13 , 32 , 6) codes, as well as unique (15 , 256 , 5),

(15 , 128 , 6), (14 , 128 , 5), (14 , 64 , 6), (13 , 64 , 5) and (13 , 32 , 6) codes [34 , pg. 74]. Further shortening yields the (12 , 32 , 5) Nadler code [1091]. The automorphism group of the code is Z42 × 𝐴 7 [1095 – 1097 ][ 34 ,pg. 478].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 — The NR code is the smallest Ker-dock code. ⊲ Preparata code › p. 198 — The NR code is the smallest Preparata code. ⊲ Orthogonal array (OA) › p. 231 — The NR code is an orthogonal array of strength 5 [34, pg. 141].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Octacode › p. 284 — The NR code is the image of the octa-code under the Gray map › p. 188 [109 , 1098 ][ 1099 , Sec. 6.3][ 143 , Thm. 12]. — The NR code can be constructed using the extended Golay code by first selecting a set of codewords satisfying certain conditions and then deleting specific coordinates [ 34 , pg. 73]. ⊲ Self-dual linear code › p. 239 — The NR code is self-dual in that its distance distribution is invariant under the MacWilliams transform › p. 209 [ 1101 ]. It maps to the octacode, a self-dual code over Z4 under the Gray map › p. 188 

[109, 1098, 1102][1099, Sec. 6.3].

[2𝑚 − 1, 𝑚, 2𝑚 −1] SIMPLEX CODE [1, 1111] simplex  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Shortened Hadamard code ⊲ RM ∗ (1, 𝑚 ) code 

⊲ Maximum-length feedback-shift-register code  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of the equidistant code family dual to the 

[2𝑚 − 1, 2𝑚 − 𝑚 − 1, 3] Hamming family. The columns of its generator matrix are in one-to-one correspon-dence with the elements of the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (𝑚 − 1, 2), with each column being a chosen representative of the corresponding element. Simplex codes saturate the Plotkin bound and hence have nonzero codewords all of the same weight, 2𝑚 −1 [34 , Th. 11(a)][ 1112 ,Thm. 1.10.5]. The codewords form a (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 + 1) simplex spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 .A punctured simplex code is known as a MacDonald code [1113 ], with parameters [2𝑚 − 2𝑢 , 𝑚, 2𝑚 −1 − 2𝑢 −1] for 𝑢 ≤ 𝑚 − 1 [1114]. The automorphism group of the code is 𝐺 𝐿 (𝑚, F2) [34].  

> PROTECTION

Simplex codes saturate the Plotkin bound [34, pg. 43].  

> DECODING

⊲ Serial orthogonal decoder [ 1115 , 1116 ] ⊲ Quantum decoder [1117].  

> NOTES

⊲ Simplex codes are equivalent to irreducible cyclic codes 

𝐶 (𝑞, 𝑛, 1) when gcd (𝑞 − 1, 𝑚 ) = 1 [58, Exam. 2.5.1].

𝑞 -ary simplex codes reduce to simplex codes for 𝑞 = 2.

[2𝑚 , 𝑚 + 1, 2𝑚 −1] FIRST-ORDER RM CODE biorthogonal   

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Biorthogonal code ⊲ RM (1, 𝑚 ) code 

⊲ Augmented Hadamard code  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of the family of first-order RM codes. Its codewords are the rows of the 2𝑚 -dimensional Hadamard matrix 

𝐻 and its negation −𝐻 with the mapping +1 → 0 and −1 → 1. The family is self-orthogonal for 𝑚 ≥ 3 [31 ]. They form a (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 +1)

biorthogonal spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 .The automorphism group of the code is 𝐺 𝐴 (𝑚, F2) [34].  

> DECODING

⊲ First-order RM codes admit specialized decoders, such as the Fast Hadamard Transform decoder [ 310 ]. ⊲ Maximum-likelihood decoding is practical via the Green Machine decoder [ 34 ,Ch. 14].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ The [32 , 6, 16 ] RM (1, 5) code was used for the 1971 Mariner 9 spacecraft [348].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 1133 ] for the weight distribution of the 226 cosets of the [32 , 6] first-order RM code.  

> PARENT

[2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 ] GOLD CODE [94] gold  

> DESCRIPTION

A cyclic binary linear code characterized by the gen-erator polynomial of degree 𝑟 of two maximum-period sequences of period 2𝑟 − 1 with absolute cross-correlation ≤ 2(𝑟 +2)/ 2. Gold codewords are generated using 𝑚 -sequences 𝑥 and 𝑦 , which are codewords of simplex codes with check polynomials of degree 𝑟 

[94].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Information bits are initialized in the shift registers of the two 𝑚 -sequences 𝑥 and 𝑦 . 

> DECODING

⊲ General decoding is done by building a sparse parity check matrix, followed by applying an iterative message passing algorithm. [1136].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Used for synchronization purposes in telecommuni-cation [349] ⊲ GPS C/A for satellite navigation [350].  

> PARENT

⊲ Cyclic linear binary code › p. 184  

> COUSINS

⊲ [2𝑚 − 1, 𝑚, 2𝑚 −1] simplex code › p. 172 — Simplex codes are used to make gold codes. The dual of a Gold code is the inter-section of the duals of the simplex codes used to construct it [ 1119 ]. 

⊲ [22𝑟 − 1, 3𝑟, 22𝑟 −1 − 2𝑟 −1] Kasami code › p. 172 — Gold and Kasami codes are both constructed by picking a set of cyclically unrelated sequences of binary linear codes with low cross-correlation [ 95 , 96 ]. 

[2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3] HAMMING CODE [1120, 1121] hamming  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ RM ∗ (𝑟 − 2, 𝑟 ) code  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of an infinite family of perfect linear codes with parameters [2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3] for 𝑟 ≥ 2. Their 𝑟 × ( 2𝑟 − 1)

parity-check matrix 𝐻 has all possible nonzero 𝑟 -bit strings as its columns. Adding a parity check yields the [2𝑟 , 2𝑟 −𝑟 − 1, 4] extended Hamming code.  

> PROTECTION

Can detect 1-bit and 2-bit errors, and can correct 1-bit errors.  

> RATE

Asymptotic rate 𝑘 /𝑛 = 1 − log 𝑛 𝑛 → 1 and normalized distance 

𝑑 /𝑛 → 0. 

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Commonly used when error rates are very low, for example, computer RAM or integrated circuits [ 351 ]. ⊲ Hamming-code based matrix embedding used in steganography [352, 353].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Kaiserslautern database [ 1137 ] for explicit codes. 

⊲ See Ref. [ 1112 , Sec. 1.10] for an introduction to Hamming codes, in-cluding their perfectness (Thm. 1.10.4). ⊲ Binary Hamming codes are duals of irreducible cyclic codes 𝐶 (2, 𝑛, 1) [58, Exam. 2.5.1].

[23 , 12 , 7] GOLAY CODE [1121] golay  

> DESCRIPTION

A [23 , 12 , 7] perfect binary linear code with connections to various areas of mathematics, e.g., lattices [ 32 ] and sporadic sim-ple groups [ 34 ]. Up to equivalence, it is unique for its parameters [90 ]. The dual of the Golay code is its [23 , 11 , 8] even-weight subcode [91, 92]. Shortening the Golay code yields shortened Golay codes [996 ] like the [22 , 10 , 8], [22 , 11 , 7], and [22 , 12 , 6] codes. The quadruply short-ened Golay code is optimal [1141]. To construct the Golay code, one can use the great dodecahedron to generate codewords by placing message bits on the faces and calculating the parity bits that live on the 12 vertices of the inner icosahedron. Its generator matrix is [987, Table II]

[24 , 12 , 8] EXTENDED GOLAY CODE [1121] extended_golay  

> DESCRIPTION

A self-dual [24 , 12 , 8] code that is obtained from the Golay code by adding a parity check. Equivalently, puncturing any coordinate yields the [23 , 12 , 7] Golay code. Up to equivalence, it is unique for its parameters [ 90 ], and it is the unique [24 , 12 , 8]

extremal Type II code [33, Rems. 4.3.10 and 4.3.11]. The automorphism group of the extended Golay code is the Math-ieu group M24 , a sporadic simple group [33, Rem. 4.3.11].  

> DECODING

⊲ Majority decoding [ 1096 ]. ⊲ Decoder using the hexa-code [ 1145 ]. ⊲ The extended Golay code has a trellis representa-tion and can thus be decoded using trellis decoding [1142, 1143].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft, transmitting hundreds of color pictures of Jupiter and Saturn in their 1979, 1980, and 1981 fly-bys [ 346 ]. ⊲ American military standards for automatic link establishment in high frequency radio systems [347].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 1112 , Sec. 1.13][ 58 , Sec. 2.5] for an introduction to Golay codes.  

> PARENTS

2, 𝑚 + 1] Karlin code › p. 176 — The extended Golay code is equivalent to the Karlin double circulant code for 𝑚 = 11 [ 34 , Ch. 16]. ⊲ Quasi group-algebra code › p. 235 — The extended Golay code is a quasi group-algebra code for various groups [ 1068 , 1146 , 1147 ]. ⊲ Lexicographic code › p. 227 — The extended Golay code is a lexicode [ 132 , 1148 ][ 34 , pg. 327].

[2𝑚 + 2, 𝑚 + 1] KARLIN CODE [1153] karlin  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of the family of [2𝑚 +2, 𝑚 +1] double circulant codes such that 𝑚 is prime of the form 8𝑘 +3 for some 𝑘 , and 2𝑚 +2 is a multiple of eight. See [ 34 , Ch. 16] for their generator matrix. Karlin codes can be mapped to extended cyclic and extended quadratic-residue codes over F4 [ 97 , 98 ][ 34 , Ch. 16][ 35 , Sec. 2.4.2] by identifying 

(0, 𝜔, ¯𝜔, 1) with (00 ), (10 ), (01 ), (11 ) [97].  

> PARENTS

[𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] SINGLE PARITY-CHECK (SPC) CODE parity_check  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Sum-zero code ⊲ Zero-sum code ⊲ Even-weight code  

> DESCRIPTION

An [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] linear binary code whose codewords consist of the message string appended with a parity-check bit or 

parity bit such that the parity (i.e., sum over all coordinates of each codeword) is zero. If the Hamming weight of a message is odd (even), then the parity bit is one (zero). This code requires only one extra bit of overhead and is therefore inexpensive. Its codewords are all even-weight binary strings, and its parity-check matrix is a row vector of all ones. Its automorphism group is 𝑆 𝑛 . 

> PROTECTION

This code cannot correct errors; it can only detect a single-bit error.  

> RATE

The code rate is 𝑛 −1 

> 𝑛

→ 1 as 𝑛 → ∞ . 

> DECODING

⊲ If the receiver finds that the parity information of a codeword disagrees with the parity bit, then the receiver will discard the information and request a resend. ⊲ Wagner’s rule yields a procedure that is linear in 𝑛 [1160 ] (see [ 179 , Sec. 29.7.2] for a description).  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Can be realized on almost every communication device. SPCs are some of the earliest error-correcting codes [ 280 ,Ch. 27].  

> NOTES

⊲ A parity-check code is the mod-two version of the casting out nines procedure [1161, 1162].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Cyclic redundancy check (CRC) code › p. 185 — A CRC us-ing the divisor 11 is a single parity-check code [ 233 , Sec. 2.3.3].

⊲ Lexicographic code › p. 227 — SPCs are lexicodes [ 132 ]. ⊲ 𝑞 -ary sharp configuration › p. 212 — The SPC code is a binary sharp configu-ration [184, Table 12.1].  

> COUSINS

BINARY BCH CODE [1181–1183] bch  

> DESCRIPTION

Cyclic binary code of odd length 𝑛 whose zeroes are consecutive powers of a primitive 𝑛 th root of unity 𝛼 (see Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ). More precisely, the generator polynomial of a BCH code of designed distance 𝛿 ≥ 1 is the lowest-degree monic polynomial with zeroes {𝛼 𝑏 , 𝛼 𝑏 +1, · · · , 𝛼 𝑏 + 𝛿 −2 } for some 𝑏 ≥ 0. BCH codes are called narrow-sense when 𝑏 = 1, and are called primitive when 𝑛 = 2𝑟 − 1 for some 𝑟 ≥ 2.The code dimension is related to the multiplicative order of 2 mod-ulo 𝑛 , i.e., the smallest integer 𝑚 such that 𝑛 divides 2𝑚 − 1. The dimension of a BCH code with 𝛿 = 2𝑡 + 1 is at least 𝑛 − 𝑚𝑡 . The field 

F2𝑚 is the smallest field containing the above root of unity 𝛼 , and is the splitting field of the polynomial 𝑥 𝑛 − 1 (see Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ).  

> PROTECTION

By the BCH bound, a BCH code with designed distance 

𝛿 has true distance 𝑑 ≥ 𝛿 . BCH codes with different designed dis-tances may coincide, and the largest possible designed distance for a given code is the Bose distance ; the true distance may still be larger than that.  

> RATE

Primitive BCH codes are asymptotically bad [58, Thm. 2.6.3].  

> DECODING

⊲ Peterson decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 3)

[1184 , 1185 ] (see exposition in Ref. [ 1186 ]). ⊲ Berlekamp-Massey decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2) [1187 , 1188 ] and mod-ification by Burton [ 1189 ]; see also [ 950 , 979 ]. ⊲ Sugiyama et al. modification of the extended Euclidean algorithm [ 1190 , 1191 ]. 

⊲ Guruswami-Sudan list decoder [1192, 1193].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Satellite communication [219]  

> NOTES

⊲ See books [ 34 , 112 , 1194 ][ 1112 , Sec. 1.14][ 58 , Secs. 2.6-2.6.3] for expositions on BCH codes and code tables. ⊲ See Kaiser-slautern database [ 1137 ] for explicit codes. ⊲ See corresponding MinT database entry [1195].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Cyclic linear binary code › p. 184 

⊲ Bose–Chaudhuri–Hocquenghem (BCH) code › p. 214  

> CHILDREN

⊲ [23 , 12 , 7] Golay code › p. 175 — The Golay code is equiv-alent to a BCH code with Bose distance 5 [ 34 , Ch. 20]. ⊲ [2𝑟 −

1, 2𝑟 − 𝑟 − 1, 3] Hamming code › p. 174 — Binary Hamming codes are binary primitive narrow-sense BCH codes [ 112 , Corr. 5.1.5]. Binary Hamming codes can be written in cyclic form [918, Thm. 12.22].  

> COUSINS

BINARY CODE bits_into_bits  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Binary Kingdom › p. 11 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) in 𝑛 binary coordinates and has distance 𝑑 . Usually denoted as (𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 ). The distance is the minimum Hamming distance between a pair of distinct codewords. The coordinate permutation group 𝑆 𝑛 of order 𝑛 ! is formed by 

𝑛 -dimensional matrices with a 1 in each row and column [ 34 , Ch. 8][ 32 , Ch. 3]. The group of isometries of Hamming space is the hyperoctahedral group Z2 ≀ 𝑆 𝑛 = Z𝑛  

> 2

⋊ 𝑆 𝑛 , i.e., the permutation group together with the group formed by the action of binary space on itself (under addition). Two binary codes are equivalent if the codewords of one code can be mapped into those of the other under a hyperoctahedral group element [ 1112 , Def. 1.8.8][ 60 , Sec. 3.2]. Determining equivalence of two codes can be done by putting each in a canonical form and mapping to a graph isomorphism problem [1201][60, Def. 3.2.18 and Sec. 3.2.2].  

> PROTECTION

A binary code 𝐶 corrects 𝑡 errors in the Hamming dis-tance if 

∀𝑥 ∈ 𝐶 , 𝐷 (𝑥, 𝑥 + 𝑦 ) < 𝐷 (𝑥 ′, 𝑥 + 𝑦 ) (17) for all codewords 𝑥 ′ ≠ 𝑥 and all 𝑦 such that |𝑦 | = 𝑡 , where 𝐷 is the 

Hamming distance and |𝑦 | = 𝐷 (𝑦, 0). A code corrects 𝑡 errors if and only if 𝑑 ≥ 2𝑡 + 1, i.e., a code corrects errors on 𝑡 ≤ ⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋

coordinates. The number of correctable errors is called the decoding radius , and it is upper bounded by half of the distance. In addition, a code detects errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 coordinates, and corrects erasure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 coordinates. A binary code 𝐶 is distance invariant if it has the same Hamming weight distribution as that of its translates 𝑐 + 𝐶 for all codewords 𝑐 . 

> RATE

The rate of a binary code is usually defined as 𝑅 = 1 

> 𝑛

log 2 𝐾 

bits per symbol. The maximum rate of a binary code with linear distance is upper bounded by the McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch (MRRW) bound [ 1202 ] (see Refs. [ 1203 – 1208 ] for other proofs).  

> GATES

⊲ The group of reversible binary operations is the permuta-tion group 𝑆 2𝑛 of all possible 𝑛 -bit strings. Reversible gate sets have been classified [1209].  

> DECODING

⊲ For few-bit codes ( 𝑛 is small), decoding can be based on a lookup table. For infinite code families, the size of such a table scales exponentially with 𝑛 , so approximate decoding algorithms scaling polynomially with 𝑛 have to be used. The decoder deter-mining the most likely error given a noise channel is called the 

maximum-likelihood decoder . ⊲ Given a received string 𝑥 and an error bound 𝑒 , a list decoder returns a list of all codewords that are at most 𝑒 from 𝑥 in Hamming distance. The number of codewords in a neighborhood of 𝑥 has to be polynomial in 𝑛 in order for this decoder to run in time polynomial in 𝑛 .

𝑞 = 2. Ternary computing may be more applicable than binary computing to cryptographic schemes [1210, 1211].

BINARY DUADIC CODE [1217] binary_duadic  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a pair of cyclic linear binary codes that satisfy certain relations, depending on whether the pair is even-like 

or odd-like duadic. Binary duadic codes generalize binary quadratic-residue codes [ 58 , Sec. 2.7]. Duadic codes exist for lengths 𝑛 that are products of powers of primes, with each prime being ±1 modulo 8

[59]. Duadic codes come in two pairs, an even-like duadic pair and an odd-like duadic pair. All codewords in an even-like pair are even-like ,i.e., Í𝑖 𝑐 𝑖 = 0. By contrast, an odd-like pair is not even-like, i.e., it contains at least one codeword with Í𝑖 𝑐 𝑖 = 1.Duadic code pairs can be defined in terms of their idempotent generators (see Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ). A pair of even-like codes 𝐶 1 and 𝐶 2 with respective idempotents 𝑒 1 and 𝑒 2 is an even-like duadic pair if (1) 𝑒 1 (𝑥 )+ 𝑒 2 (𝑥 ) = 1− 1 

> 𝑛

(1+𝑥 +𝑥 2 +· · ·+ 𝑥 𝑛 −1)

and (2) there exists a multiplier 𝜇 such that 𝐶 1 𝜇 = 𝐶 2 and 𝐶 2 𝜇 = 𝐶 1.There is an odd-like duadic pair {𝐷 1, 𝐷 2 } associated with the even-like pair {𝐶 1, 𝐶 2 }, where 1 − 𝑒 2 (𝑥 ) generates 𝐷 1 and 1 − 𝑒 1 (𝑥 )

generates 𝐷 2. The even-pair codes are [𝑛, 𝑛 −12 ] codes while the odd-pair codes are [𝑛, 𝑛 +12 ] codes. Families of binary duadic codes were constructed in Ref. [1218].  

> PROTECTION

For odd-like duadic codes, the common minimum odd-like weight 𝑑 𝑜 satisfies 𝑑 2 

> 𝑜

≥ 𝑛 ; if the splitting is given by 𝜇 = −1,then 𝑑 2 

> 𝑜

− 𝑑 𝑜 + 1 ≥ 𝑛 [58, Thm. 2.7.1].

BINARY QUADRATIC-RESIDUE (QR) CODE binary_quad_residue  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a quadruple of cyclic binary codes of prime length 𝑛 = 8𝑚 ± 1 for 𝑚 ≥ 1 constructed using quadratic residues and nonresidues of 𝑛 [60, Def. 3.2.8]. The roots of the generator polynomial 𝑟 (𝑥 ) of the first code (see Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ) are all of the inequiva-lent quadratic residues of 𝑛 , and the second code’s generator poly-nomial is (𝑥 − 1)𝑟 (𝑥 ). The roots of the generator polynomial 𝑎 (𝑥 ) of the third code are all inequivalent nonresidues of 𝑛 , and the fourth code’s generator polynomial is (𝑥 − 1)𝑎 (𝑥 ). The codes correspond-ing to polynomials 𝑟, 𝑎 are often called augmented quadratic-residue codes, while the remaining codes are called expurgated .The extended versions of odd-like binary quadratic-residue codes have automorphism groups containing 𝑃𝑆𝐿 (2, 𝑝 ) by the Gleason-Prange theorem [ 60 , Thm. 3.2.11]; the extensions of the [7, 4, 3]

Hamming and [23 , 12 , 7] Golay codes are exceptional examples with larger automorphism groups [60, Rem. 3.2.12].  

> PROTECTION

For odd-like quadratic-residue codes of prime length, the common minimum distance 𝑑 satisfies 𝑑 2 ≥ 𝑛 ; if −1 is a quadratic non-residue, then 𝑑 2 − 𝑑 + 1 ≥ 𝑛 [58, Thm. 2.7.4].

COMBINATORIAL DESIGN combinatorial_design  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Block design ⊲ Covering design ⊲ Support design  

> DESCRIPTION

A constant-weight binary code that is mapped into a combinatorial 𝑡 -design. The mapping proceeds as follows for a length-𝑛 code with code-words of constant weight 𝑤 . A codeword 𝑐 corresponds to a block of the design, with the codeword’s 𝑗 th coordinate labeling whether or not element 𝑗 is contained in the block. There are a total of 𝑛 elements ,and the constant weight of the code implies that each block con-tains a fixed number 𝑤 of elements. The code supports an 𝑆 (𝑡, 𝑤, 𝑛 )

Steiner system if each subset of 𝑡 ≤ 𝑤 elements is contained in ex-actly one block. More generally, the code supports a combinatorial 

𝑡 -design , or, more precisely, a 𝑡 -(𝑛, 𝑤, 𝜆 )-design, if each such 𝑡 -subset is contained in exactly 𝜆 ≥ 1 blocks. A combinatorial 2-design with two block intersection sizes is called a quasi-symmetric design . A 

3-(𝑞 𝑑 + 1, 𝑞 + 1, 1) combinatorial design is sometimes called a Witt design (a.k.a. a spherical geometry design ) [ 1237 , 1238 ][ 1239 , Remark 6.10]. For example, the seven codewords of weight 𝑤 = 3 of the [7, 4, 3]

Hamming code support a 2-(7, 3, 1)-design a.k.a. an 𝑆 (2, 3, 7) Steiner system. The codeword 1000110 corresponds to a block containing elements 1, 5, and 6. Similarly, the other six codewords correspond to blocks 257, 367, 147, 246, 345, and 123. Each pair of elements is contained in exactly one block. Combinatorial 𝑡 -designs exist for all 𝑡 [860 – 864 ]. Existence of certain quasi-symmetric designs has also been established [1240].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [ 120 , 139 , 1241 ] for reviews on combinatorial designs. 

⊲ See [148, 208, 1239, 1242] for books on combinatorial designs.

CONSTANT-WEIGHT CODE constant_weight  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ One-weight code  

> DESCRIPTION

A binary code whose codewords are all constrained to have the same Hamming weight 𝑤 . In the linear setting, this usually refers to all nonzero codewords having the same weight, since every linear code contains the zero codeword. The complement of a constant-weight code is a constant-weight code obtained by interchanging zeroes and ones in the codewords. Constant-weight codes that contain all strings of some fixed Ham-ming weight are known as 𝑚 -in-𝑛 or ␀ 𝑛 𝑚 

 codes. The set of all weight-𝑤 binary strings of length 𝑛 forms the Johnson space 𝐽 (𝑛, 𝑤 ), a finite two-point homogeneous space 𝐺 /𝐻 with 𝐺 =

𝑆 𝑛 and 𝐻 = 𝑆 𝑤 × 𝑆 𝑛 −𝑤 [ 156 , 839 , 871 , 943 ][ 944 , Sec. 4.2.1][ 942 , Table 2]. In these coordinates, the Johnson metric is half the Hamming distance between characteristic vectors [ 156 ]. The number of such binary strings is the binomial coefficient ␀ 𝑛 𝑤 

.Nontrivial linear binary codes cannot have all codewords of the same weight, but they can have all nonzero codewords of the same weight. All such codes are equidistant, and Bonisoli”s theorem states that any equidistant linear binary code is a direct sum of simplex codes [945] (see also Refs. [38, 39]).  

> PROTECTION

See Ref. [ 1244 ] for upper bounds on dimension. See book [34] for (Johnson) bounds on size.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Radio-network frequency hopping [223].  

> NOTES

𝑛 > 28 [223].

CONSTANTIN-RAO (CR) CODE [1246] constantin_rao  

> DESCRIPTION

A nonlinear single-asymmetric-error code that general-ize VT codes and that is constructed from an Abelian group. A CR code for an Abelian group 𝐺 of order 𝑛 + 1 and fixed group element 𝑔 consists of all binary strings 𝑐 = 𝑐 1𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 that satisfy 

Í𝑛 𝑖 =1 𝑐 𝑖 𝑔 𝑖 = 𝑔 [1139 , Def. 1.3]. Here, addition is the group operation, the multiplication 1𝑔 𝑖 = 𝑔 𝑖 , and 0𝑔 𝑖 = 𝑔 0 is the identity element. CR codes can be generalized to the 𝑞 -ary case and also to codes correcting more than one asymmetric error [1138].  

> PROTECTION

Protect against single errors induced by the asymmetric noise channel. Codes for some groups, and in particular, the VT codes, also protect against single deletions and insertions [1247].  

> RATE

CR codes for particular groups have higher rates than distance-one codes under the binary asymmetric channel for all lengths except 𝑛 = 2𝑟 − 1, in which case CR codes reduce to Hamming codes [ 1138 ]; see Ref. [ 1139 ]. Size analysis is presented in Refs. [ 1248 , 1249 ].

CYCLE CODE [61, 1105, 1252–1256] homological_classical  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Graph theoretic code ⊲ Graph homology code ⊲ Graph code  

> DESCRIPTION

A code whose parity-check matrix is obtained from the incidence matrix of a graph over F2. This code’s properties are derived from the size two chain complex associated with the graph. Not every binary linear code is homological, but there exist homological families that asymptotically saturate the Hamming bound [61]. Let 𝐺 be a finite, undirected, connected graph without loops and multiple edges. Let |𝑉 | be its number of vertices and |𝐸 | be its num-ber of edges. Its incidence matrix is a |𝑉 | × | 𝐸 | matrix whose rows are indexed by the vertices of 𝐺 , and whose columns are indexed by the edges of 𝐺 . The matrix element 𝐻 𝑖 𝑗 = 1 if vertex 𝑖 belongs to the edge 𝑗 and 𝐻 𝑖 𝑗 = 0 otherwise. Over F2, one row is redundant for a connected graph, so a parity-check matrix of the cycle code can be taken to be any full-rank set of |𝑉 | − 1 rows.  

> PROTECTION

More generally, an [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] cycle code constructed out of a connected graph has 𝑛 = |𝐸 | and 𝑘 = 1 − 𝜒 (𝐺 ) = 1 − | 𝑉 | + | 𝐸 |,where 𝜒 (𝐺 ) is the Euler characteristic of the graph [ 1257 ]. The code distance is equal to the shortest size of a cycle, guaranteed to exist since 𝐺 is not a tree.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 ⊲ Projective geometry code  

> › p. 233

— Incidence matrices of graphs have no repeated columns since that would correspond to multi-edges. Therefore, cycle codes can be interpreted as projective codes.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Hoffman-Singleton cycle code › p. 189 ⊲ [15 , 6, 5] Pe-tersen cycle code › p. 171 ⊲ Cycle LDPC code › p. 184  

> COUSINS

⊲ Graph-adjacency code › p. 188 — Graph-adjacency (cycle) codes’ generator (parity-check) matrices are defined using adjacency (incidence) matrices of graphs. ⊲ Quantum-inspired classical block code › p. 235 — Cycle codes have been known in classical coding theory, and have been rediscovered in the quantum context; see Ref. [1257 ] for a brief exposition. ⊲ Generalized homological-product code › p. 546 — Cycle codes have been known in classical coding theory, and have been rediscovered in the quantum context; see Ref. [ 1257 ]for a brief exposition. ⊲ Homological code › p. 400 — Cycle codes fea-ture in generalizations of the surface code [ 1257 ]. ⊲ Perfect binary code › p. 197 — A family of cycle codes saturate the asymptotic Ham-ming bound [ 61 ]. ⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 — Cycle codes, including the Petersen cycle and Hoffman-Singleton cycle codes, feature in magic-state distillation protocols [89, Appx. CYCLE LDPC CODE [1105] cycle_ldpc  

> DESCRIPTION

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix forms the incidence matrix of a graph, i.e., has weight-two columns.  

> PROTECTION

The minimum distance of a cycle LDPC code is 𝑑 ≥ 𝑔 /2,where 𝑔 is the girth of the code’s Tanner graph [ 85 , Remark 21.2.13].  

> RATE

Cycle codes are not asymptotically good [1258].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Linear-time encoder [1259].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Cycle LDPC codes have been proposed to be used for MIMO channels [231].

CYCLIC LINEAR BINARY CODE binary_cyclic  

> DESCRIPTION

A binary code of length 𝑛 is cyclic if, for each codeword 

𝑐 1𝑐 2 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 , the cyclically shifted string 𝑐 𝑛 𝑐 1 · · · 𝑐 𝑛 −1 is also a code-word. A cyclic code is called primitive when 𝑛 = 2𝑟 − 1 for some 

𝑟 ≥ 2.A shortened cyclic code is obtained from a cyclic code by taking only codewords with the first 𝑗 zero entries, and deleting those zeroes. For odd 𝑛 , cyclic binary codes can also be described by defining sets of roots of generator polynomials, and by equivalent generating-idempotent and trace constructions [58, Secs. 2.3 and 2.4].  

> PROTECTION

The BCH and Hartmann-Tzeng bounds give lower bounds on the distance of cyclic binary codes [ 58 , Sec. 2.4]; the shift bound [1261] gives another lower bound.  

> DECODING

⊲ Meggitt decoder [ 340 ]. ⊲ Information set decoding (ISD) [ 1262 ], a probabilistic decoding strategy that essentially tries to guess an information set of 𝑘 correct positions in the received word, where 𝑘 is the code dimension. Then, an error vector is constructed to map the received word onto the nearest codeword, assuming those 𝑘 positions are error-free. When the Hamming weight of the error vector is low enough, that codeword is assumed to be the intended transmission. ⊲ Permutation decoding [1263].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [ 34 , Ch. 7][ 58 , Secs. 2.1-2.4] for expositions on cyclic codes. ⊲ See Ref. [1264] for tables of the best binary cyclic codes of odd lengths 101 to 127.

CYCLIC REDUNDANCY CHECK (CRC) CODE [950, 1194, 1270] crc  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Frame check sequence (FCS)  

> DESCRIPTION

A generalization of the single parity-check code in which the generalization of the parity bit is the remainder of the data string (mapped into a polynomial via the Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ) divided by some generator polynomial. A no-table family of codes is referred to as CRC-(𝑚 − 1), where 𝑚 is the length of the generator polynomial.  

> PROTECTION

Detects any burst error up to the length of the generator polynomial.  

> DECODING

⊲ GRAND [1271].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ CRC-16 and CRC-32 are used in data transmission, e.g., IEEE 802.16e, IEEE 802.3 [ 232 ] and TCP/IP communication [ 233 ,Sec. 2.3.3].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 1272 ] and book [ 1273 ] for introductions to CRC codes. ⊲ See Refs. [ 1274 , 1275 ] for exhaustive lists of CRC poly-nomials, as well as the CRC Polynomial Zoo website 11 by Philip Koopman.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Cyclic linear binary code › p. 184 ⊲ Checksum code › p. 162  

> CHILD

⊲ [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2] Single parity-check (SPC) code › p. 177 — A CRC using the divisor 11 is a single parity-check code [233, Sec. 2.3.3].

DELSARTE-GOETHALS (DG) CODE [1279] delsarte_goethals  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of (22𝑡 +2, 2(2𝑡 +1) ( 𝑡 −𝑟 +2)+ 2𝑡 +3, 22𝑡 +1 −

22𝑡 +1−𝑟 ) binary nonlinear codes for parameters 𝑟 ≥ 1 and 𝑚 =

2𝑡 + 2 ≥ 4, denoted by DG (𝑚, 𝑟 ), that generalizes the Kerdock code. The code DG (𝑚, 𝑟 ) is a nonlinear subcode of the second-order Reed-Muller code RM (2, 𝑚 ), and equals RM (2, 𝑚 ) at 𝑟 = 1 [34 , pg. 461]. The code is the union of certain cosets of RM (1, 𝑚 ) in RM (2, 𝑚 )

that are specified by bilinear forms [ 1279 ]. The code DG (𝑚, 𝑟 + 1) is a union of disjoint translates of DG (𝑚, 𝑟 ). 

> 11 https://users.ece.cmu.edu/~koopman/crc/crc32.html

While DG (𝑚, 𝑟 ) is not generally linear, it is the Gray map image of a certain extended cyclic linear code over Z⋭ [ 143 ]. These codes are distance invariant [ 143 ], so the distance and weight distributions are the same. Their automorphism groups are determined in Ref. [1280].  

> DECODING

⊲ Since the equivalent Z⋭ codes are extended cyclic codes, efficient encoding and decoding is possible [143].

DIFFERENCE-SET CYCLIC (DSC) CODE [1282] difference_set  

> DESCRIPTION

Cyclic LDPC code constructed deterministically from a difference set. Certain DSC codes satisfy more redundant con-straints than Gallager codes and thus can outperform them [62].  

> NOTES

EXPANDER CODE [1285] expander  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Sipser-Spielman code  

> DESCRIPTION

LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is derived from the adjacency matrix of a bipartite expander graph [ 64 ] such as a Ramanujan graph or a Cayley graph of a projective special linear group over a finite field [ 65 , 66 ]. Expander codes admit efficient encoding and decoding algorithms and yield an explicit (i.e., non-random) asymptotically good LDPC code family. The rate and distance of the expander code depend on specific parameters of the corresponding graph. A ( 𝑛, 𝑚, 𝐷, 𝛾, 𝛼 ) bipartite expander graph is defined as a 𝐷 -left-regular graph with 𝑛 left nodes and 𝑚 right nodes such that for any subset of left nodes 𝑆 of size at most 𝛾𝑛 , the neighborhood 𝑁 (𝑆 ) has size at least 𝛼 |𝑆 |. Given a (𝑛, 𝑚, 𝐷, 𝛾, (1 − 𝜖 )𝐷 ) expander graph, the corresponding expander code has rate at least 1 − 𝑚 /𝑛 and distance at least 2(1 − 𝜖 )𝛾𝑛 for any 𝜖 < 1/2. Explicit constructions for expander graphs [ 64 ] with any ratio 𝑛 /𝑚 are known where 𝐷 = polylog (𝑛 /𝑚 ), 𝛾 = Ω (1/𝐷 )

and arbitrary 𝜖 [170].  

> PROTECTION

There exist minimum distance bounds [ 1285 , 1286 ] as well as bounds on decoding performance [ 1287 – 1289 ] in terms of features of the expander graph.  

> RATE

The rate is at least 1 − 𝑚 /𝑛 , where 𝑛 is the number of left nodes and 𝑚 is the number of right nodes in the bipartite expander graph. Expander codes yield an explicit (i.e., non-random) asymptotically good LDPC code family [1285].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Multiplication by generator matrix with runtime 𝑂 (𝑛 2) 

> DECODING

⊲ Decoding can be done in 𝑂 (𝑛 ) runtime using a greedy 

flip decoder [ 1285 ] (see also [ 1290 ]). The algorithm consists of flipping a bit of the received word if it will result in a greater number of satisfied parity checks. This is repeated until a codeword is reached. 

⊲ ’Find erasures and Decode’ a.k.a. Viderman’s algorithm correcting order › p. 161 Ω(𝑛 ) errors in order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 ) time [1291].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ The flip decoding algorithm is fault tolerant against parity-check errors [1292]; see also [1293].  

> PARENT

⊲ Regular LDPC code › p. 201 — Expander codes yield an ex-plicit (i.e., non-random) asymptotically good LDPC code family [1285].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Locally decodable code (LDC) › p. 166 — Expander codes are locally decodable provided that the inner code satisfies cer-tain properties; there exist code families with rate approaching one [ 1034 ]. ⊲ Left-right Cayley complex code › p. 192 — Left-right Cayley complex codes can be viewed as Tanner-like codes on ex-pander graphs [ 64 ], but with bits defined on squares and con-straints on edges (as opposed to edges and vertices, respectively, for expander codes). Expander codes are also typically not lo-cally testable [ 1294 ]. ⊲ 𝑞 -ary LDPC code › p. 210 — Asymptotically good non-binary expander codes can be constructed [ 1295 ][ 1296 ,Thm. 7.16] by generalizing the originally binary expander con-structions [ 1285 , 1297 ]. ⊲ Self-correcting quantum code › p. 319 —Constant-rate random (quantum) expander codes are self-correcting (quantum) memories, but have no thermodynamic phase transi-tions [ 811 ]. ⊲ Quantum expander code › p. 426 — Quantum expander codes are quantum analogues of expander codes. ⊲ Galois-qudit expander code › p. 494 — The explicit expander-code construction of [ 657 ] yields ⟦𝑁, 𝐾 ≥ 𝑁 1− 𝜖 , 𝐷 ≥ 𝑁 1/𝑟 /poly (log 𝑁 )⟧ 𝑞 QLDPC Galois-qudit quantum expander codes with transversal 𝐶 𝑟 −1 𝑍 gates. Bal-anced products of the same expander-code complexes also yield 

[𝑛, 𝑘 ≥ 𝑛 1− 𝜖 , 𝑑 ≥ 𝑛 /poly (log 𝑛 )] 𝑞 LTCs exhibiting the multiplica-tion property. ⊲ Expander LP code › p. 491 — Expander LP codes are lifted products of expander codes with different local codes [169].

FIBONACCI CODE [1301] fibonacci_model  

> DESCRIPTION

Quantum-inspired binary linear code defined on an 

𝐿 × 𝐿 /2 lattice with one bit on each site, where 𝐿 = 2𝑁 for an integer 

𝑁 ≥ 2. The codewords are defined to satisfy the condition that, for each lattice site (𝑥, 𝑦 ), the bits on (𝑥, 𝑦 ), (𝑥 + 1, 𝑦 ), (𝑥 − 1, 𝑦 ) and 

(𝑥, 𝑦 + 1) (where the lattice is taken to be periodic in both directions) contain an even number of 1’s.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against small weight errors and string-like er-rors. The code distance is more than 𝐿 , but the exact value is un-known.  

> ENCODING

⊲ The codewords can be generated using a cellular au-tomaton of length 𝐿 (periodic). The 2𝐿 possible initial states corre-spond to the 2𝐿 codewords. For each generation, the state of each cell is the XOR sum of that cell and its two neighbors in the previous generation. After 𝐿 /2 − 1 generations, the entire history generated by the automaton corresponds to a codeword, where the initial state is the first row of the lattice, the first generation is the second row, etc. In polynomial language, the update rule is 𝑓 (𝑥 ) = 1 + 𝑥 + 𝑥 2

over F2, so the resulting fractal has dimension log 2 (1 + √5) [1301].  

> DECODING

⊲ An efficient algorithm based on minimum-weight per-fect matching [ 1302 ], which can correct high-weight errors that span rows and columns of the 2D lattice, with failure rate decaying super-exponentially with 𝐿 . 

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 ⊲ Quantum-inspired classical block code › p. 235  

> COUSINS

⊲ Haah cubic code (CC) › p. 395 — The Fibonacci code is de-signed to mimic the fractal properties of (quantum) Haah cubic code so that studying the former can help us toward the development of an efficient algorithm for the latter [1302]. ⊲ Fibonacci fractal spin-liquid code › p. 390 — The Fibonacci fractal spin-liquid code is a hypergraph product of the repetition code and the Fibonacci code [1301], and can be formulated directly as a BP code [1303].

FOUNTAIN CODE [86] fountain  

> DESCRIPTION

Code based on the idea of generating an endless stream of custom encoded packets for the receiver. The code is designed so that the receiver can recover the original transmission of size 𝐾𝑙 

bits after receiving at least 𝐾 packets each of 𝑙 bits. The simplest example of a fountain code is the random linear fountain code. Take some message of size 𝐾𝑙 and split into 𝐾 packets, 

𝑝 0, 𝑝 1, ..., 𝑝 𝐾 . For each packet ˆ𝑝 𝑛 to be transmitted do the following: Generate 𝐾 random bits 𝐺 𝑛𝑘 and let ˆ𝑝 𝑛 be the bitwise sum of the source packets when 𝐺 𝑛𝑘 is 1,

> PROTECTION

Designed to protect against erasures during broadcast-ing of information by a sender to multiple receivers.  

> RATE

Random linear fountain codes approach the Shannon limit as the file size 𝐾 increases. However, they do not have a fixed encoding rate.  

> DECODING

⊲ Invert the fragment generator matrix resulting from the continuous encoding process. If exactly 𝐾 packets are received, then the probability of decoding correctly is 0.289 . Extra packets increase this probability exponentially. The decoding runtime is dominated by the matrix inversion step, which takes order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 3) time.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Designed for servers sending data to many recip-ients, such as during broadcasting or file distribution [ 240 , 241 ].

GALLAGER (GL) CODE [1313, 1314] gallager  

> DESCRIPTION

The first LDPC code. The rows of the parity-check ma-trix of this regular code are divided into equal subsets, and columns in the first subset are randomly permuted to yield the corresponding rows in subsequent subsets. For example, the parity-check matrix 

©«

1 1 0 00 0 1 11 0 1 00 1 0 1

ª®®®¬

(20) contains two subsets, each consisting of two rows, and the last two rows are obtained from the first two by exchanging the second and third columns.  

> PROTECTION

With high probability, random GL codes have minimum distance that grows linearly with block length [ 1314 ]. There exist GL codes that are able to correct errors of weight less than 𝑐𝑛 for some constant 𝑐 in order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 log 𝑛 ) decoding operations [1315].  

> RATE

GL codes nearly achieve Shannon capacity against binary-input additive Gaussian white noise using iterative decoding [ 1316 , 1317 ]. GL codes can outperform RS codes at short block length [62].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Regular LDPC code › p. 201 — GL codes are the first LDPC codes. ⊲ Generalized Gallager code › p. 187  

> COUSIN

⊲ Combinatorial design › p. 181 — Some Steiner systems can be used to construct Gallager codes [62]. 

GAUSS’ LAW CODE [68, 69] gauss_law  

> DESCRIPTION

An [𝑚 + 𝐷𝑚, 𝐷𝑚, 3] linear binary code for 𝑚 ≥ 3𝐷 , de-fined by the Gauss’ law constraint of a 𝐷 -dimensional fermionic Z2

gauge theory [ 68 , Thm. 1]. The code can be rephrased as a distance-one stabilizer code whose stabilizers consist of gauge-group ele-ments. It can be concatenated to form a stabilizer code for fault-tolerant quantum simulation of the underlying gauge theory [ 68 , 69 ].  

> PARENTS

> COUSINS

⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 — Gauge-group elements of a 𝐷 -dimensional fermionic Z2 gauge theory can arise from a single-error-correcting linear binary code [ 68 , Thm. 1]. There is a general correspondence between stabilizer codes and gauge theory, with the stabilizer group playing the role of the gauge group [ 1318 ], and with the Gauss’ law code being a specific example. ⊲ Fermion-into-qubit code › p. 389 — Gauge-group elements of a 𝐷 -dimensional fermionic Z2 gauge theory can arise from a single-error-correcting linear binary code [68, Thm. 1]. ⊲ Concatenated qubit code › p. 380

GRAY CODE [70, 1327, 1328] gray  

> DESCRIPTION

The first Gray code [70], now called the binary reflected Gray code , is a trivial code that orders length-𝑛 binary strings such that nearest-neighbor strings differ by only one digit via what is known as the Gray map › p. 188 .

Gray map: The Gray map converts a quaternary string over Z4 into a binary string such that the Hamming distance of the binary repre-sentation is one between any two consecutive quaternary digits. For a single digit, the mapping is 0 → 00 , 1 → 01 , 2 → 11 , and 3 → 10 .This differs from the usual binary expansion of the natural numbers, which maps 0 → 00 , 1 → 01 , 2 → 10 , and 3 → 11 . A linear code 𝐶 

over Z4 can be mapped, via the Gray map, to a distance invariant binary code [ 143 , Thm. 2]. The binary code is linear if and only if doubling the component-wise product of any two codewords in 

𝐶 yields another codeword in 𝐶 [1099 , Sec. 6.3][ 112 , Thm. 12.2.3]. The map converts Lee to Hamming weight, and Lee distance to Hamming distance [1099, Sec. 6.3][109, Thm. 3.1 and Prop. 3.3]. Gray codes have been generalized such that nearest-neighbor strings differ by only one digit when the strings are arranged in higher-dimensional hypercubes [ 1327 ]. Further generalizations called combinatorial Gray codes [ 1328 ] refer to methods to organize combinatorial objects such that successive objects differ in some particular way. Particular 𝑞 -ary extensions [ 1329 ] of Gray codes may be useful in digital imaging and signal processing.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Efficient encoder for binary reflected Gray code [ 1330 ].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Three-dimensional imaging [ 257 ]. ⊲ Broadcasting and communication [258].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Refs. [1331–1333] reviews of various Gray codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — A linear code 𝐶 over Z4 can be mapped, via the Gray map › p. 188 , to a binary code. The binary code is linear if and only if doubling the component-wise product of any two codewords in 𝐶 yields another codeword in 𝐶 [ 112 , Thm. 12.2.3].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 — Gray codes are useful for optimizing qubit unitary circuits [ 1334 ] and for encoding qudits in multiple qubits [ 481 ]. ⊲ Linear code over Z4 › p. 283 — A linear code 𝐶 over 

Z4 can be mapped, via the Gray map › p. 188 , to a binary code. The binary code is linear if and only if doubling the component-wise product of any two codewords in 𝐶 yields another codeword in 𝐶 

[112 , Thm. 12.2.3]. More specifically, a linear quaternary code over 

Z4 of length 𝑛 , type 4𝑘 1 2𝑘 2 , and minimum Lee weight 𝑑 maps under the Gray map › p. 188 to a binary code of length 2𝑛 , cardinality 22𝑘 1 +𝑘 2 ,and minimum Hamming weight 𝑑 [1099 , Sec. 6.3]. ⊲ Quadrature-amplitude modulation (QAM) format › p. 261 — 2D Gray codes are often concatenated with 𝑛 = 1 lattice-based QAM codes so that the Ham-ming distance between the bitstrings encoded into the points is a discretized version of the Euclidean distance between the points. 

⊲ Hergert code › p. 189 — Hergert codes can be seen, via the Gray map

, as linear codes over Z4 [109 , 143 ]. ⊲ Preparata code › p. 198 —The binary Preparata code is the Gray-map image of the quaternary code QRM (𝑚 − 2, 𝑚 ) [143 , Thm. 19]. ⊲ Delsarte-Goethals (DG) code › p. 185 — DG codes can be seen, via the Gray map › p. 188 , as ex-tended linear cyclic codes over Z4 [ 143 ]. ⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 —The binary Kerdock code is the Gray-map image of the quaternary code QRM (1, 𝑚 ), an extended cyclic code over Z4 [ 143 , Thm. 19] (see also Ref. HERGERT CODE [1279] hergert  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Goethals-Delsarte (GD) code  

> DESCRIPTION

A nonlinear subcode of an RM code that is a formal dual of a nonlinear DG code in the sense that its distance distribution is equal to the MacWilliams transform › p. 209 of the distance distribution of the corresponding DG code. The Hergert code for 𝑚 /2 ≥ 𝑟 ≥ 2 is a nonlinear subcode of RM (𝑚 − 2, 𝑚 ), and equals RM (𝑚 − 2, 𝑚 ) at 𝑟 = 1 [1279 , Thm. 2]. For each DG (𝑚, 𝑟 ) code, the Hergert code is defined as the union of cosets of RM (𝑚 − 3, 𝑚 ) in RM (𝑚 − 2, 𝑚 ), with coset representa-tives obtained by applying a particular linear bijection to the coset representatives of the DG code [1279].  

> DECODING

⊲ Since the equivalent Z4 codes are extended cyclic codes, efficient encoding and decoding is possible [143, 1336].

⊲ Binary code › p. 179

HOFFMAN-SINGLETON CYCLE CODE [71, 1326] hoffman-singleton  

> DESCRIPTION

HOFFMAN-SINGLETON GRAPH-ADJACENCY CODE [71, 1326]  

> hoffman-singleton_graph
> DESCRIPTION

A graph-based code whose generator matrix is the row space of the adjacency matrix of the Hoffman-Singleton graph [ 72 ]. This [50 , 22 , 7] code is dual to a [50 , 28 , 8] code [71, Table III].  

> DECODING

⊲ The rows of the adjacency matrix serve as orthogonal parity checks enabling majority decoding of the [50 , 28 , 8] dual code up to three errors (its full error-correcting capacity) [71].

HSU-ANASTASOPOULOS LDPC (HA-LDPC) CODE [1339] ha_ldpc  

> DESCRIPTION

A regular LDPC code obtained from a concatenation of a certain random regular LDPC code and a certain random 190 LDGM code. An (𝑙, 𝑟, 𝑔 )-HA-LDPC code can be written using punc-tured LDPC and LDGM parts, and it is dual to the corresponding 

(𝑟, 𝑙, 𝑔 )-MN-LDPC code [ 73 ]. Using rate-one LDGM codes eliminates high-weight codewords while admitting an amount of low-weight codewords that asymptotically vanishes, allowing code families to achieve the GV bound › p. 209 with high probability. An (𝑙, 𝑟, 𝑔 )-HA-LDPC code can be written using punctured LDPC and LDGM parts, and it is dual to the corresponding (𝑟, 𝑙, 𝑔 )-MN-LDPC code [73].  

> RATE

HA-LDPC codes achieve capacity on the BEC channel under BP decoding [ 1339 ] and the memoryless binary-input output-symmetric (MBIOS) channels under ML decoding [ 1339 ] and under MAP decod-ing [ 73 ]. Bounded-density spatially coupled HA-LDPC codes have BEC BP thresholds close to the Shannon limit [ 73 ]. They also achieve the GV bound › p. 209 with asymptotically high probability when the concatenation is with a rate-one LDGM code [1339].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Regular LDPC code › p. 201 ⊲ Multi-edge LDPC code › p. 196 

— HA-LDPC codes can be formulated as multi-edge LDPC codes [ 73 ].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Low-density generator-matrix (LDGM) code › p. 194 — HA-LDPC codes are a concatenation of an LDPC and an LDGM code. 

⊲ Concatenated code › p. 162 — HA-LDPC codes are a concatenation of an LDPC and an LDGM code. ⊲ MacKay-Neal LDPC (MN-LDPC) code › p. 195 — HA-LDPC and MN-LDPC codes are dual to each other [73 ]. ⊲ Dual linear code › p. 218 — HA-LDPC and MN-LDPC codes are dual to each other [ 73 ]. ⊲ Spatially coupled LDPC (SC-LDPC) code  

> › p. 203

— Spatial coupling of HA-LDPC protographs yields bounded-density SC-HA codes with BEC BP thresholds close to the Shannon limit [73]. 

IRREGULAR LDPC CODE [1340, 1341] irregular_ldpc  

> DESCRIPTION

An LDPC code whose parity-check matrix has a variable number of entries in each row or column.  

> RATE

Nearly achieve capacity against binary-input additive Gaussian white noise using iterative decoding [ 1342 , 1343 ]. Such sequences have sublinearly growing distance per block length [1344].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Satellite communication after concatenating with a modulation scheme [260].  

> NOTES

⊲ Regular LDPC code › p. 201 — Irregular LDPC codes have vari-able node and check node degrees, while regular LDPC codes have fixed node degrees. Irregular LDPC codes with optimized degree distributions can outperform regular ones under iterative decoding [1317, 1348]. 

IRREGULAR REPEAT-ACCUMULATE (IRA) CODE [263, 1349, 1350]  

> ira
> DESCRIPTION

A generalization of the RA code in which the outer 1-in-3 repetition encoding step is replaced by an LDGM code. A simple version is when different bits in the RA block are repeated a different number of times. IRA codes can be optimized against various noise channels [ 1351 ].  

> RATE

IRA codes nearly achieve the Shannon capacity of the binary erasure channel using iterative decoding [ 1349 ]. Puncturing lessens the decoding complexity while still allowing sequences of codes to achieve capacity [1352].  

> ENCODING

⊲ One linear-time encoder for a systematic IRA code con-sists of first encoding into an [𝑛, 𝑘 ] LDGM binary linear code, ap-plying a random permutation, and then applying an accumulator to obtain 

(𝑢 1, 𝑢 1 + 𝑢 2, · · · , 𝑢 1 + · · · + 𝑢 𝑁 ) , (21) where 𝑁 is the length of the permuted LDGM output.  

> DECODING

⊲ Linear-time decoder [1349].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ LDPC codes used for digital satellite video broadcast-ing per the DVB-S2 standard [ 261 , 262 ] utilize IRA code features and were subject to litigation; see Ref. [ 263 ]. ⊲ Apple and Broadcom Wi-Fi devices utilize IRA encoding and decoding features and are subject to ongoing litigation; see Ref. [263].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Irregular LDPC code › p. 190 ⊲ Protograph LDPC code  

> › p. 198

— IRA codes can be formulated as protograph LDPC codes [ 1165 ]. 

⊲ Concatenated code › p. 162 — IRA codes can be interpreted as serial concatenated codes [927].  

> CHILD

⊲ Repeat-accumulate (RA) code › p. 201 — IRA codes for which the outer code is a 1-in-3 repetition code reduce to RA codes.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Low-density generator-matrix (LDGM) code › p. 194 — IRA codes replace the outer 1-in-3 repetition encoding step in RA codes with an LDGM code. ⊲ MacKay-Neal LDPC (MN-LDPC) code › p. 195

JUSTESEN CODE [1356] justesen  

> DESCRIPTION

Binary linear code resulting from generalized concate-nation of an outer RS code with multiple inner codes sampled from the Wozencraft ensemble, i.e., 𝑁 distinct binary inner codes of di-mension 𝑚 and length 2𝑚 . Justesen codes were among the first explicit asymptotically good codes [60, Sec. 3.3.3]. Justesen codes are parameterized by 𝑚 , with length 𝑛 = 2𝑚𝑁 

and dimension 𝑘 = 𝑚𝐾 , where (𝑁 = 2𝑚 − 1, 𝐾 ) is the RS outer code over F2𝑚 . Further modifications have improved code parameters [1357–1359].  

> RATE

The first asymptotically good codes. Rate is 𝑅 𝑚 = 𝑘 /𝑛 =

𝐾 /2𝑁 ≥ 𝑅 and the relative minimum distance satisfies 𝛿 𝑚 =

𝑑 𝑚 /𝑛 ≥ 0.11 (1 − 2𝑅 ), where 𝐾 = ⌈2𝑁 𝑅 ⌉ for asymptotic rate 

0 < 𝑅 < 1/2; see [34, pg. 311]. The code can be improved and the range of 𝑅 extended from 0 to 1 by puncturing , i.e., by erasing 𝑠 digits from each inner codeword. This yields a code of length 𝑛 = (2𝑚 − 𝑠 )𝑁 and rate 𝑅 = 𝑚𝑘 /( 2𝑚 −

𝑠 )𝑁 . The lower bound on the relative distance of the punctured code approaches 𝑑 𝑚 /𝑛 = (1 − 𝑅 /𝑟 )𝐻 −1 (1 − 𝑟 ) as 𝑚 goes to infinity, where 

𝑟 is the maximum of 1/2 and the solution to 𝑅 = 𝑟 2/( 1 + log (1 −

ℎ−1 (1 − 𝑟 ))) , and ℎ is the binary entropy function.  

> DECODING

⊲ Generalized minimum distance decoding [1356].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Generating small-bias sample spaces, i.e., probabil-ity distributions that parity functions cannot typically distinguish from the uniform distribution [264].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 ⊲ Generalized concatenated code (GCC) › p. 166 — Justesen codes can be considered as a generalized concatenation of an outer RS code with 𝑁 distinct binary inner codes.

LAPLACIAN CODE [1303] laplacian  

> DESCRIPTION

A binary linear code whose parity-check matrix is the graph Laplacian reduced mod 2. For an undirected graph Γ with degree matrix 𝐷 and adjacency matrix 𝐴 , the parity-check matrix is the symmetric matrix 𝐻 = (𝐷 − 𝐴 ) mod 2 . 

> PROTECTION

A connected graph always contributes at least one logi-cal bit. For generic sparse bounded-degree graph ensembles, the logical dimension stays 𝑂 (1), while highly symmetric graphs such as square lattices or complete graphs can have much larger rank deficiency [1303].  

> RATE

Generic sparse-graph Laplacian-code families have vanishing rate with only 𝑂 (1) logical bits, whereas more symmetric families can exhibit enhanced rank deficiency [1303].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 ⊲ Projective geometry code  

> › p. 233

— Incidence matrices of graphs have no repeated columns since that would correspond to multi-edges. Therefore, Laplacian codes can be interpreted as projective codes. ⊲ Quantum-inspired classical block code › p. 235  

> COUSINS

⊲ Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 — Laplacian codes on bounded-degree graph families are classical LDPC codes. 

⊲ Pinwheel code › p. 232 — The pinwheel code is derived from the graph Laplacian of the pinwheel tiling, with a fraction of boundary checks removed. ⊲ Anisotropic Z2 Laplacian model code › p. 368 —The anisotropic Z2 Laplacian model is the hypergraph product of a cyclic repetition code and a Laplacian code [1303].

LEFT-RIGHT CAYLEY COMPLEX CODE [76] lr-cayley-complex  

> DESCRIPTION

Binary code constructed on a left-right Cayley complex using a pair of base codes 𝐶 𝐴 , 𝐶 𝐵 and an expander graph [ 64 ]. Bits live on the squares of the complex, while local constraints are im-posed on edges; for a fixed graph vertex, the incident symbols form a codeword of the tensor code 𝐶 𝐴 ⊗ 𝐶 𝐵 . A family of such codes is one of the first 𝑐 3-LTCs [76].  

> PARENT

⊲ Binary linear LTC › p. 180 — Left-right Cayley complex codes yield one of the first two families of 𝑐 3-LTCs.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Tensor-product code › p. 251 — Left-right Cayley complex codewords for a fixed graph vertex are codewords of a tensor code. 

⊲ Expander code › p. 186 — Left-right Cayley complex codes can be viewed as Tanner-like codes on expander graphs [ 64 ], but with bits defined on squares and constraints on edges (as opposed to edges and vertices, respectively, for expander codes). Expander codes are also typically not locally testable [ 1294 ]. ⊲ Balanced product (BP) code › p. 489 — Left-right Cayley complexes can be obtained via a balanced product of 𝐺 -graphs [ 76 ]. ⊲ Quantum Tanner code › p. 431 

— Applying the CSS construction to two left-right Cayley complex codes yields quantum Tanner codes, and one can simultaneously prove a linear distance for the quantum code and local testability for one of its constituent classical codes [1367].

LINEAR BINARY CODE binary_linear  

> DESCRIPTION

An (𝑛, 2𝑘 , 𝑑 ) linear code is denoted as [𝑛, 𝑘 ] or [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ],where 𝑘 is the code’s dimension, and where 𝑑 is the code’s distance. Its codewords form a linear subspace, i.e., for any codewords 𝑥, 𝑦 ,

𝑥 + 𝑦 is also a codeword. A code that is not linear is called nonlinear .Linear codes can be defined in terms of a generator matrix 𝐺 ,whose rows form a basis for the 𝑘 -dimensional codespace. Given a message 𝑥 , the corresponding encoded codeword is 𝐺 𝑇 𝑥 . The generator matrix can be reduced via coordinate permutations to its standard form or systematic form 𝐺 = [𝐼 𝑘 𝐴 ], where 𝐼 𝑘 is a 𝑘 × 𝑘 

identity matrix and 𝐴 is a 𝑘 × ( 𝑛 − 𝑘 ) binary matrix. The automorphism group of a linear binary code is the largest subgroup of coordinate permutations that maps the code onto itself. Two linear binary codes are equivalent if the codewords of one code can be mapped into those of the other under a permutation [ 60 ,Remark 3.2.1][34, Ch. 8][32, Ch. 3].  

> PROTECTION

Distance 𝑑 of a linear code is the number of nonzero entries in the (nonzero) codeword with the smallest such number. Corrects any error set for which no two elements of the set add up to a codeword. Linear codes admit a parity check matrix 𝐻 , whose columns make up a set of parity checks , i.e., a maximal linearly independent set of vectors that are in the kernel of 𝐺 . It follows that 

𝐺𝐻 T = 0 mod 2 . (22) The decision problem corresponding to finding the minimum distance is also 𝑁 𝑃 -complete [ 1369 ], and approximating the weight enumerator is #𝑃 -complete [1370]. There are several standard procedures for increasing or decreas-ing the length of an [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code [34, Ch. 1]: (1) Puncturing : removing a coordinate to yield a code whose length is shorter by one and whose distance is ≥ 𝑑 − 1.(2) Expurgating : removing odd-weight codewords of a non-even-weight code to yield a code whose dimension is 𝑘 − 1.(3) Augmenting : adding the all-ones codeword to a code without it to yield a code whose dimension is 𝑘 + 1.(4) Lengthening : adding the all-ones codeword and then adding a parity check to yield a code whose size and dimension in-crease by one. (5) Shortening : keeping only codewords which have a zero in a fixed coordinate and removing that coordinate to yield a code whose length is shorter by one.  

> RATE

A family of linear codes 𝐶 𝑖 = [𝑛 𝑖 , 𝑘 𝑖 , 𝑑 𝑖 ] is asymptotically good if the asymptotic rate lim 𝑖 →∞ 𝑘 𝑖 /𝑛 𝑖 and asymptotic distance 

lim 𝑖 →∞ 𝑑 𝑖 /𝑛 𝑖 are both positive. Nearly all good linear binary codes for the asymmetric channel are also good for the symmetric channel [1371]; this is not the case for non-binary codes [1139]. Binary linear codes on 𝐷 -dimensional Euclidean lattices are lim-ited by the classical Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal (BPT) bound [ 1372 , 1373 ], which states that 𝑑 = 𝑂 (𝑛 1−1/𝐷 ) and that 𝑘 𝑑 1/𝐷 = 𝑂 (𝑛 ) (using asymptotic notation › p. 161 ). This bound is the classical analogue of the BPT bound › p. 551 for qubit stabilizer codes and the subsystem BT bound › p. 553 for subsystem qubit stabilizer codes.  

> DECODING

⊲ Decoding an arbitrary linear binary code is 𝑁 𝑃 -complete [ 1374 , 1375 ]. ⊲ Slepian’s standard-array decoding [ 1221 ]. 

⊲ Recursive maximum likelihood decoding [ 1376 ]. ⊲ Deep learn-ing [ 1377 ] and a transformer graph neural net (GNN) for soft decod-ing [ 1378 ]. ⊲ Chase decoding, which uses channel measurement information [1379].

LOW-DENSITY GENERATOR-MATRIX (LDGM) CODE ldgm  

> DESCRIPTION

Binary linear code with a sparse generator matrix. Al-ternatively, a member of an infinite family of [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] codes for which the number of nonzero entries in each row and column of the generator matrix are both bounded by a constant as 𝑛 → ∞ . The dual of an LDGM code has a sparse parity-check matrix and is called an LDPC code.  

> RATE

Certain LDGM codes come close to achieving Shannon capacity [1394].

LOW-DENSITY PARITY-CHECK (LDPC) CODE [1313, 1314, 1402]  

> ldpc
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Sparse graph code  

> DESCRIPTION

A binary linear code with a sparse parity-check matrix. Often a member of an infinite family of [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] codes for which the numbers of nonzero entries in each row and in each column of the parity-check matrix are both bounded above by a constant as 

𝑛 → ∞ .An LDPC code is ( 𝑗, 𝑘 )-regular if the parity-check matrix has a fixed number of 𝑗 nonzero entries in each column and 𝑘 entries 195 in each row; otherwise, the LDPC code is irregular . Irregular LDPC codes are characterized by the fractions 𝑣 𝑗 of columns of weight 𝑗 

as well as the fractions ℎ 𝑗 of rows of weight 𝑗 ; these are collectively called the degree distribution .A parity check is performed by taking the inner product of a row of the parity-check matrix with a codeword that has been affected by a noise channel. A parity check yields either zero (the parity constraint is satisfied) or one (the parity constraint is violated). In alternative conventions (not used here), LDPC codes are re-ferred to as simple LDPC codes, as opposed to generalized LDPC codes, also called Tanner codes.  

> RATE

Some LDPC codes achieve the Shannon capacity of the binary symmetric channel under maximum-likelihood decoding [ 1313 , 1317 ,1403 ]. Other LDPC codes achieve capacity for smaller block lengths under belief-propagation decoding [ 1404 ]. Random LDPC codes achieve list-decoding capacity [1405].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Almost linear-time encoder based on transforming the parity-check matrix into upper triangular form [1406].  

> DECODING

⊲ Gallager introduced a hard-decision iterative decoder that flips any digit contained in more than a fixed number of unsat-isfied parity checks [ 1314 , Ch. 4]. ⊲ Gallager also introduced an iterative probabilistic decoding procedure on the computation tree; this is a precursor to modern message-passing, belief-propagation (BP), and sum-product decoding [ 1348 , 1407 – 1409 ][ 1314 , Ch. 4] (see also [ 1194 , 1410 ]). ⊲ Soft-decision Sum-Product Algorithm (SPA) [ 1348 , 1409 ] and its simplification the Min-Sum Algorithm (MSA) [ 1411 ]. ⊲ Linear programming [ 1412 – 1414 ]. ⊲ Iterative decoder using stochastic computation [ 1415 ]. ⊲ Iterative LDPC decoders can get stuck at stopping sets of their Tanner graphs [ 1416 ], with decoder performance improving with the size of the small-est stopping set; see [ 85 , Sec. 21.3.1] for more details. The small-est stopping set size can reach the minimum distance of the code [1417 ]. ⊲ Ensembles of random LDPC codes under iterative de-coders are subject to the concentration theorem [1342 , 1348 ]; see [ 85 ,Thm. 21.7.1] for the case of the BEC. ⊲ Reinforcement learning [1418]. ⊲ Quantum-enhanced BP decoding [1419].  

> NOTES

⊲ The potential of LDPC codes was noted by Margulis [ 41 ], but realized by the broader community [ 1316 , 1317 ] much later after their discovery by Gallager [ 1313 , 1314 ]. ⊲ See books [ 905 , 1420 , 1421 ]and reviews [ 1422 –1425 ] for introductions to LDPC codes, belief-propagation decoding, and connections to statistical mechanics. Other introductory references include Refs. [ 82 , 1426 –1428 ] as well as a review of LDPC codes circa 2005 [ 1429 ]. ⊲ See Kaiserslautern database [ 1137 ] for explicit representatives of several classes of LDPC codes, including 𝑞 -ary, WiMAX, multi-edge, and spatially-coupled. 

⊲ See pretty-good-codes database [ 1430 ] for explicit representatives and benchmarking. ⊲ See the Encyclopedia of sparse graph codes for explicit representatives [ 1431 ] ⊲ LDPC codes have been con-sidered for quantum key distribution [ 1432 ]. ⊲ Codes have been benchmarked using AFF3CT toolbox [1433]. ⊲ LDPC Python soft-ware library for decoding LDPC and QLDPC codes [1434, 1435].

LUBY TRANSFORM (LT) CODE [1442] luby_transform  

> DESCRIPTION

Erasure codes based on fountain codes. They improve on random linear fountain codes by having a much more efficient encoding and decoding algorithm. LT codes can be constructed as follows. First, randomly choose a degree 𝑑 𝑛 from a degree distribution depending on total size 𝐾 .Then, randomly choose 𝑑 𝑛 distinct source packets and let the packet to be transmitted ˆ𝑝 𝑛 be the bitwise sum of the chosen input packets. This forms a graph connecting encoded packets to source packets.  

> DECODING

⊲ Sum-Product Algorithm (SPA), often called a peeling decoder [1443, 1444], similar to belief propagation [1445].  

> PARENT

⊲ Raptor (RAPid TORnado) code › p. 199 — Raptor codes using a trivial pre-code are LT codes. Typically, Raptor codes have constant-sized overhead but are faster to decode. 

MACKAY-NEAL LDPC (MN-LDPC) CODE [1317, 1446] mn_ldpc  

> DESCRIPTION

A code whose parity-check matrix is constructed non-deterministically via the MacKay-Neal prescription. An (𝑙, 𝑟, 𝑔 )-MN-LDPC code is a non-systematic two-edge-type LDPC code whose parity-check matrix is of the form (𝐻 1 𝐻 2), where 

𝐻 1 is a random binary matrix of column weight 𝑙 and row weight 𝑟 ,and 𝐻 2 is a random binary matrix of column and row weight 𝑔 ; the bits corresponding to 𝐻 1 are punctured [73].  

> RATE

Certain sequences of optimally decoded codes can nearly achieve the Shannon capacity [ 1317 , 1446 ]. A sequence of codes achieves the capacity of memoryless binary-input symmetric-output channels under MAP decoding [ 73 ]. Standard MN-LDPC codes have no BP threshold, while bounded-density spatially coupled MN-LDPC codes have BEC BP thresholds close to the Shannon limit [73].  

> DECODING

⊲ Free-energy minimization and a BP decoder [1446]. 196  

> PARENTS
