HANSEN TORIC CODE [1814, 1815] toric_classical  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation code of a linear space of polynomials eval-uated on points lying on an affine or projective toric variety. If the space is taken to be all polynomials up to some degree, the code is called a toric RM-type code of that degree.  

> PROTECTION

Parameters of toric RM-type codes and various general-izations have been determined in Refs. [1816–1821].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 1821 ] for various examples and implementations in Magma.  

> PARENT

⊲ Polynomial evaluation code › p. 232 — Hansen toric codes are polynomial evaluation codes with X being a toric variety.  

> COUSIN

⊲ Toric code › p. 461 — The toric code is not to be confused with the CSS code constructed from a polynomial evaluation code on a toric variety [1822]. 

HERMITIAN CODE [1753, 1823][1265, Sec. 4.4.3] hermitian  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Hermitian AG code  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation AG code of rational functions on a Hermitian curve over F𝑞 2 .A standard affine model of the curve is 

𝑦 𝑞 + 𝑦 = 𝑥 𝑞 +1 , (61) and this curve has 𝑞 3 + 1 rational points and genus 𝑔 = 𝑞 (𝑞 − 1)/ 2.Hermitian codes are usually defined as one-point AG codes 

𝐶 𝐿 (𝐷, 𝑚𝑃 ∞), where 𝐷 is the sum of the 𝑞 3 affine rational points and 

𝑃 ∞ is the unique point at infinity. They provide much longer code lengths than Reed-Solomon codes over the same alphabet, since the standard one-point construction has length 𝑞 3 over F𝑞 2 .There exists a family of Hermitian codes with automorphism group 𝑃𝐺 𝐿 (2, F𝑞 ) [1824].  

> PROTECTION

Distance is determined by the divisor and the geometry of the Hermitian curve [ 1825 ]; see [ 27 , Sec. 5.3] for the general result. For the standard one-point code 𝐶 𝐿 (𝐷, 𝑚𝑃 ∞) of length 𝑛 = 𝑞 3, the designed distance satisfies 𝑑 ≥ 𝑛 − 𝑚 . 

> RATE

For the standard one-point code 𝐶 𝐿 (𝐷, 𝑚𝑃 ∞) with genus 𝑔 =

𝑞 (𝑞 − 1)/ 2, Riemann-Roch gives 

𝑘 = 𝑚 − 𝑔 + 1 (62) whenever 2𝑔 − 2 < 𝑚 < 𝑛 = 𝑞 3. 

> DECODING

⊲ Unique decoding using syndromes and error locator ideals for polynomial evaluations. Note that Hermitian codes are linear codes so we can compute the syndrome of a received vector. Moreover, akin to the error-locator ideals found in decoding RS codes, for the multivariate case we must define an error locator ideal Λ such that the variety of this ideal over F2 

> 𝑞

is exactly the set of errors. The Sakata algorithm uses these two ingredients to get a unique decoding procedure [1746].  

> NOTES

⊲ Certain structured classical optimization problems can be mapped into decoding and list decoding Hermitian codes via the Decoded Quantum Interferomentry (DQI) algorithm [1826].  

> PARENT

⊲ Norm-trace code › p. 231 — Hermitian codes are evaluation AG codes with X being a Hermitian curve [ 1753 ][ 27 , Exam. 2.74]. This curve is maximal, meaning that Hermitian codes are evaluation AG codes with maximum possible length given a fixed genus. They are a special case of norm-trace codes [1754].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — Hermitian codes are concatenated GRS codes [ 1786 ]. ⊲ Group-algebra code › p. 224 

— Some Hermitian codes are group-algebra codes [ 1813 ][ 181 , Re-mark 16.4.14]. ⊲ Hermitian-hypersurface code › p. 226 — Hermitian-hypersurface codes reduce to Hermitian codes of polynomials when the hypersurface is a curve. ⊲ Barg-Tamo-Vladut code › p. 214 —226 Hermitian-curve examples of these codes are given in [ 21 , Rem. 15.9.16]. ⊲ Quantum Hermitian AG code › p. 502 — Quantum Hermi-tian AG codes are quantum analogues of Hermitian codes.

KLEIN-QUARTIC CODE [1838] klein_quartic  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation AG code over F8 of rational functions eval-uated on points lying on the Klein quartic, which is defined by the equation 𝑥 3 𝑦 + 𝑦 3 𝑧 + 𝑧 3𝑥 = 0 [27, Ex. 2.75].  

> PROTECTION

Dimension 𝑘 = 8 and distance 𝑑 ≥ 13 . Concatenation with the [4, 3, 2] single parity check code, conversion to a binary code by expressing F8 elements as vectors over F2, and puncturing yields a [91 , 24 , 25 ] binary code that set the world record for codes of length 91 [1839].  

> PARENT

LINEAR 𝑞 -ARY CODE q-ary_linear  

> DESCRIPTION

An (𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 )𝑞 linear code is denoted as [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 , where 

𝑘 = log 𝑞 𝐾 is an integer. Its codewords form a linear subspace, i.e., for any codewords 𝑥, 𝑦 , 𝛼𝑥 + 𝛽𝑦 is also a codeword for any field elements 𝛼, 𝛽 ∈ F𝑞 . This extra structure yields much information about their properties, making them a large and well-studied subset of codes. Linear codes can be defined in terms of a generator matrix 𝐺 ,whose rows form a basis for the 𝑘 -dimensional codespace. Given a message 𝑥 , the corresponding encoded codeword is 𝐺 𝑇 𝑥 . The 228 generator matrix can be reduced via coordinate permutations to its 

standard form or systematic form 𝐺 = [𝐼 𝑘 𝐴 ], where 𝐼 𝑘 is a 𝑘 × 𝑘 

identity matrix and 𝐴 is a 𝑘 × ( 𝑛 − 𝑘 ) 𝑞 -ary matrix. The code also comes with a parity check matrix 𝐻 , whose columns make up a maximal linearly independent set of vectors that are in the kernel of 𝐺 . For an error vector 𝑒 , the associated error syndrome is 𝐻𝑒 .The monomial group of order (𝑞 −1)𝑛 𝑛 ! is formed by 𝑛 -dimensional matrices with one nonzero field element in each row and column. Two linear 𝑞 -ary codes are (monomial) equivalent if the codewords of one code can be mapped into those of the other under a monomial group element [ 34 , Ch. 8][ 32 , Ch. 3]. The automorphism group of a linear 𝑞 -ary code is the largest subgroup of the monomial group that maps the code onto itself.  

> PROTECTION

Distance 𝑑 of a linear code is the number of nonzero entries in the (nonzero) codeword with the smallest such number. A linear code corrects an error set precisely when the difference of any pair of distinct errors is not a codeword, equivalently when distinct errors have distinct syndromes under the parity check matrix.  

> RATE

Any code admitting a two-transitive automorphism group achieves capacity under the binary erasure channel [ 1519 , 1520 ,1614].  

> DECODING

⊲ Maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. This algorithm decodes a received word to the most likely sent codeword based on the received word. ML decoding of reduced complexity is possible for virtually all 𝑞 -ary linear codes [ 1841 ]. ⊲ Optimal symbol-by-symbol decoding rule [ 1842 ]. ⊲ Information set decoding (ISD) [1843 ], a probabilistic decoding strategy that essentially tries to guess 

𝑘 correct positions in the received word, where 𝑘 is the size of the code. Then, an error vector is constructed to map the received word onto the nearest codeword, assuming the 𝑘 positions are er-ror free. When the Hamming weight of the error vector is low enough, that codeword is assumed to be the intended transmission. 

⊲ Generalized minimum-distance decoder [ 926 ]. ⊲ Soft-decision maximum-likelihood trellis-based decoder [ 1844 ]. ⊲ Random lin-ear codes over large fields are list-recoverable and list-decodable up to near-optimal rates [ 1845 ]. ⊲ Extensions of algebraic-geometry decoders to linear codes [1846, 1847].  

> NOTES

⊲ The two extreme examples of codes are the [𝑛, 0, 𝑛 ]𝑞 

zero code and its dual the [𝑛, 𝑛 ]𝑞 universe code . ⊲ University of Salzburg’s MinT application 20 generates an optimal parameter table for a linear code [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 , contingent on an optional fluctuation of maximal Hamming code distance, rank, and length, along with other specifications. ⊲ CodingTheory Julia software library [ 1848 ].

MAXIMUM DISTANCE SEPARABLE (MDS) CODE [1857] mds  

> DESCRIPTION

A 𝑞 -ary linear code whose parameters satisfy the Sin-gleton bound with equality. An [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 code is MDS if parameters 𝑛 , 𝑘 , 𝑑 , and 𝑞 are such that the Singleton bound 

𝑑 ≤ 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1 (64) becomes an equality. Equivalently, a code with minimum distance 

𝑑 and dual distance 𝑑 ′ is MDS precisely when 𝑑 + 𝑑 ′ = 𝑛 + 2 and all distances occur [ 184 , Thm. 12.3.1]. A code is called almost MDS 

(AMDS) when 𝑑 = 𝑛 − 𝑘 . A bound for general (i.e., nonlinear or unrestricted) 𝑞 -ary codes can also be formulated; see [ 1112 , Thm. 1.9.10]. A code is near MDS (NMDS) if both the code and its dual are AMDS. The codes [𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ]𝑞 , [𝑛, 𝑛 −1, 2]𝑞 , [𝑛, 𝑛 ]𝑞 for any 𝑞 are MDS codes. These are called the trivial MDS codes [ 60 , Sec. 3.3.2]. The only binary MDS codes are the trivial ones. Many, but not all, 𝑞 -ary MDS codes are related to RS codes and their extensions; see, e.g., [ 180 ,Prob. 11.11].  

> PROTECTION

Given 𝑛 and 𝑘 , MDS codes have the highest distance possible of all codes and so have the best possible error-correction properties.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Automatic repeat request (ARQ) data transmission protocols [230, Ch. 7].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Refs. [ 1858 ][ 180 , Sec. 11.4 notes][ 34 , Ch. 11 notes] for more on MDS codes and the MDS conjecture. ⊲ An MDS code with 𝑘 = 2 is equivalent to a set of 𝑛 − 𝑘 mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order 𝑞 [34, Ch. 11 notes].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 227 ⊲ Optimal LRC › p. 168 — The gen-eralized Singleton bound becomes the Singleton bound for 𝑘 = 𝑟 ,so optimal LRCs with that constraint are MDS. ⊲ Universally opti-mal 𝑞 -ary code › p. 242 — MDS codes are LP universally optimal codes [158 , 1859 ]. ⊲ Orthogonal array (OA) › p. 231 — An MDS code is an OA 1 (𝑘, 𝑛, 𝑞 ) [60, Thm. 3.3.19].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — GRS codes have dis-tance 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1, saturating the Singleton bound. ⊲ Roth-Lempel code › p. 238 — Roth-Lempel codes are examples of MDS codes that are not GRS codes. ⊲ [10 , 5, 6]9 Glynn code › p. 205 — The Glynn code is a rare example of an MDS code that is not related to an RS code. 

⊲ Hirschfeld code › p. 226 — The Hirschfeld code is a rare example of an MDS code that is not related to an RS code. ⊲ [4, 2, 3]4 RS 4

code › p. 207 ⊲ Griesmer code › p. 224 — Singleton bound implies the Griesmer bound.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Dual linear code › p. 218 — A linear binary or 𝑞 -ary [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑛 −

𝑘 + 1] code is MDS if and only if its dual [𝑛, 𝑛 − 𝑘, 𝑘 + 1] is MDS [ 1112 ,Thm. 1.9.13]. ⊲ Projective geometry code › p. 233 — A linear code is MDS (almost MDS) if and only if columns of its parity-check matrix form an 𝑛 -arc ( 𝑛 -track) in projective space [ 1807 , 1831 , 1860 , 1861 ]. The dual of a MDS code is an MDS code, so MDS codes are pro-jective. All [9, 3] MDS codes have been tabulated [ 1862 ] in terms of 9-arcs in the projective plane. ⊲ Repetition code › p. 202 — Bi-nary repetition codes are trivial MDS codes [ 184 , Thm. 12.3.1][ 60 ,Sec. 3.3.2]. ⊲ MDS array code › p. 248 — MDS array codes are MDS codes when each matrix codeword is treated as a vector by con-verting each column into a single coordinate via subpacketization. 

⊲ Distributed computation code › p. 246 — The first matrix multipli-cation code encoded each entry of the matrices to be multiplied into an MDS code [ 1863 ]. ⊲ Maximum-sum-rank distance (MSRD) code › p. 248 — MSRD codes generalize MDS codes from the Hamming metric to the sum-rank metric. ⊲ Maximum-rank distance (MRD) code › p. 247 — MRD codes are matrix-code analogues of MDS codes. 

⊲ Algebraic-geometry (AG) code › p. 213 — Near MDS [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] 𝑝 𝑚 AG codes exist when 𝑛, 𝑝, 𝑚 satisfy certain relations according to the Tsfasman-Vladut bound [ 55 , 1265 – 1267 ]. ⊲ Elliptic code › p. 219 —Elliptic codes can be MDS [ 21 , Exam. 15.5.3][ 1267 , pg. 310][ 1265 ,Sec. 4.4.2]. ⊲ Extended GRS code › p. 221 — A GRS code can be extended to an MDS code [ 112 , Thm. 5.3.4]. Extended and dou-bly extended narrow-sense RS codes are MDS [ 112 , Thms. 5.3.2 and 5.3.4], and there is an equivalence between the two for odd prime 𝑞 [1762 ]. ⊲ Narrow-sense RS code › p. 230 — Extended and doubly extended narrow-sense RS codes are MDS [ 112 , Thms. 5.3.2 and 5.3.4][ 180 , Ch. 11], and there is an equivalence between the two for odd prime 𝑞 [1762 ]. ⊲ Reed-Solomon (RS) code › p. 236 —Reed-Solomon codes are important examples of MDS codes, and for prime 𝑞 , every [𝑞 + 1, 𝑘, 𝑞 − 𝑘 + 2]𝑞 MDS code is Reed-Solomon; for non-prime 𝑞 , non-equivalent maximal-length MDS codes also exist [1762 ][ 60 , Sec. 3.3.2][ 180 , Ch. 11]. ⊲ Generalized Srivastava code  

> › p. 223

— Generalized Srivastava codes for 𝑚 = 1 are MDS codes [ 34 ,pg. 359]. ⊲ [6, 3, 4]4 Hexacode › p. 207 — The hexacode is an MDS code [ 112 , Exer. 578]. ⊲ [𝑛, 𝑛 − 1, 2]𝑞 𝑞 -ary parity-check code › p. 208 

⊲ [4, 2, 3]3 Tetracode › p. 206 — The tetracode is a unique MDS code [ 1616 , 1617 ]. ⊲ EA mixed-alphabet Reed-Solomon c-q code › p. 568 —EA mixed-alphabet RS c-q codes can saturate a block-erasure bound and, in some parameter ranges, exceed the classical Singleton bound 230 for ordinary 𝑞 -ary codes [ 1864 ]. ⊲ Quantum maximum-distance-separable (MDS) code › p. 317 — Quantum MDS codes are quantum ana-logues of MDS codes. ⊲ Perfect-tensor code › p. 312 — MDS codes can be used to obtain cluster states that are AME with minimal support [ 136 , 1865 –1869 ]. ⊲ Quantum tensor-product code › p. 432 —MDS codes can be used to construct quantum tensor-product codes [1084 ]. ⊲ EA MDS code › p. 491 — MDS codes give rise to families of EA Galois-qudit codes that saturate the original (erroneous) EAQECC Singleton bound [1870]. 

MEIR CODE [1871] meir  

> DESCRIPTION

Locally testable [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 code with query complex-ity poly (log 𝑘 ) and rejection ratio 𝑅 /𝑛 = 1/poly (log 𝑘 ). The code construction is probabilistic and combinatorial.  

> PARENTS

⊲ 𝑞 -ary linear LTC › p. 211 — Meir codes stand out in that they are based on a combinatorial construction, while other LTCs often use algebraic tools. ⊲ Random code › p. 169 — Meir codes are defined using a probabilistic combinatorial construction. 

MULTIPLICITY CODE [164–166] multiplicity  

> DESCRIPTION

A generalization of an 𝑚 -variate polynomial evaluation code based on evaluating polynomials together with their Hasse derivatives up to order 𝑠 − 1 at all points in F𝑚 𝑞 . Originally proposed for coding using the Rosenbloom-Tsfasman metric [ 164 ]. Univariate (𝑚 = 1) [ 164 , 165 ] and multivariate ( 𝑚 > 1) [ 166 ] codes have been proposed.  

> PROTECTION

The multiplicity Schwartz-Zippel Lemma provides a lower bound on code distance [1872].  

> RATE

Multiplicity codes achieve relaxed generalized Singleton bounds [1765].  

> DECODING

⊲ Multivariate multiplicity codes can be decoded up to half of the minimum distance in polynomial time [ 1873 , 1874 ]. 

⊲ Univariate [ 165 ] and multivariate [ 1873 ] multiplicity codes can be list-decoded up to the Johnson bound. Certain univariate code fam-ilies achieve the list-decoding capacity for sufficiently large field characteristic [1873, 1875].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [1876] for a review of multiplicity codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Group-algebra code › p. 224 — Multiplicity codes of order 𝑠 

are Abelian group-algebra codes whose corresponding polynomial that is modded out is (𝑥 − 𝛼 𝑗 )𝑠 for each evaluation point 𝛼 𝑗 [1770].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Reed-Solomon (RS) code › p. 236 — Univariate multiplicity codes of degree 𝑠 = 1 reduce to RS codes. ⊲ Generalized RM (GRM) code › p. 222 — Multivariate multiplicity codes of degree 𝑠 = 1

reduce to GRM codes.  

> COUSINS

⊲ 𝑞 -ary linear LCC › p. 211 — There exist multiplicity codes with rate arbitrarily close to one that are locally decodable and lo-cally correctable from a constant error fraction [ 166 ]. ⊲ Locally testable code (LTC) › p. 167 — Some multiplicity codes are locally testable by an appropriate test [ 1053 , 1054 ]. ⊲ Polynomial eval-uation code › p. 232 — A multiplicity code is a generalization of an 

𝑚 -variate polynomial evaluation code based on evaluating polyno-mials together with their Hasse derivatives up to order 𝑠 − 1 at all points in F𝑚 𝑞 . ⊲ Batch code › p. 161 — Multiplicity codes can be used to construct batch codes [ 910 ]. ⊲ Private information retrieval (PIR) code › p. 168 — Multiplicity codes can be used to construct PIR codes [910].

NORM-TRACE CODE [1754] norm_trace  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation AG code of rational functions evaluated on points lying on a Miura-Kamiya curve in either affine or projective space. The family is named as such because the equations defining the curves can be expressed in terms of the field norm and field trace › p. 164 . 

> PROTECTION

Minimum distance is determined by an order bound [1754].  

> PARENT

⊲ Evaluation AG code › p. 219 — Norm-trace codes are evalua-tion AG codes with X being a Miura-Kamiya curve [1754].  

> CHILD

⊲ Hermitian code › p. 225 — Hermitian codes are evaluation AG codes with X being a Hermitian curve [ 1753 ][ 27 , Exam. 2.74]. This curve is maximal, meaning that Hermitian codes are evaluation AG codes with maximum possible length given a fixed genus. They are a special case of norm-trace codes [1754].

PERFECT CODE perfect  

> DESCRIPTION

A type of 𝑞 -ary code whose parameters satisfy the Ham-ming bound with equality. An (𝑛, 𝐾, 2𝑡 + 1)𝑞 code is perfect if parameters 𝑛 , 𝐾 , 𝑡 , and 𝑞 are such that the Hamming (a.k.a. sphere-packing) bound

> 𝑗 =0

𝑛 𝑗

≤ 𝑞 𝑛 /𝐾 (68) becomes an equality. In other words, the code’s packing radius matches its covering radius. For example, for a binary 𝑞 = 2 code with one logical bit ( 𝐾 = 2)and 𝑡 = 1, the bound becomes 𝑛 + 1 ≤ 2𝑛 −1. Perfect codes are those for which balls of Hamming radius 𝑡 exactly fill the space of all 𝑛 𝑞 -ary strings. Any perfect linear code over F𝑞 is either a repetition code, a Hamming code, or a binary or ternary Golay code [ 1452 ][ 60 , Thm. 3.3.1]. If 𝑞 is a prime power, any nontrivial perfect unrestricted code that is not equivalent to a linear code has the same length, size, and minimum distance as a Hamming code [ 60 , Thm. 3.3.1]; see [ 120 ,pg. 100] for more details. There are many nonlinear perfect codes [201, 1103, 1456–1459, 1897–1903].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 1112 , Def. 1.9.8] for an introduction to perfect codes. ⊲ See book [1904] on perfect codes for more details.

⊲ Perfect binary code › p. 197 ⊲ 𝑞 -ary Hamming code › p. 210 

⊲ [5, 3, 3]4 Shortened hexacode › p. 207 — The shortened hexacode is perfect [ 112 , Exer. 578]. ⊲ [11 , 6, 5]3 Ternary Golay code › p. 205 —The ternary Golay code is perfect [184, Thm. 12.3.3 and Def. 12.3.4].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Combinatorial design › p. 181 — Perfect codes and combina-torial designs are related [ 134 , 135 ]. ⊲ Mixed code › p. 287 — Perfect mixed codes with minimum distance 3 can be constructed from partitions of vector spaces [ 60 , Thm. 3.3.13]. ⊲ Editing code › p. 164 

— Perfect deletion correcting codes can be constructed using combi-natorial design theory [ 124 , 125 ]. ⊲ Perfect quantum code › p. 312 —A classical (quantum) perfect code saturates the classical (quantum) Hamming bound. 

PINWHEEL CODE [1303] pinwheel  

> DESCRIPTION

A geometrically local binary LDPC code defined on pla-nar graphs obtained from the pinwheel tiling [ 81 ]. Both bits and checks live on vertices of the graph. If 𝐿 𝑁 is the graph Laplacian at generation 𝑁 , the undepleted check matrix is ˜𝐻 𝑁 = (𝐿 𝑁 −I) mod 2,and the actual parity-check matrix 𝐻 𝑁 is obtained by removing an evenly spaced fraction of boundary checks. The construction was introduced as a concrete aperiodic seed code whose hypergraph products realize local Type-I and Type-II fracton models.  

> PROTECTION

For boundary-depletion period 𝑝 , the family has 𝑘 ≈√𝑛 /𝑝 and distance 𝑑 ∼ 𝑛 [ 1303 ], saturating the classical BPT bound  

> › p. 551

𝑘 √𝑑 = 𝑂 (𝑛 ). The same work gives numerical evidence for confinement.  

> RATE

The encoding rate vanishes asymptotically because 𝑘 ∼ √𝑛 

while the block length grows with the substitution generation [ 1303 ].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Quantum-inspired classical block code › p. 235 ⊲ Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194  

> COUSINS

⊲ Laplacian code › p. 192 — The pinwheel code is derived from the graph Laplacian of the pinwheel tiling, with a fraction of bound-ary checks removed. ⊲ Hypergraph product (HGP) code › p. 406 —The hypergraph product of a pinwheel code with a cyclic repetition code yields a local Type-I fracton model in three dimensions, while the hypergraph product of two pinwheel codes yields a local Type-II fracton model in four dimensions [ 1303 ]. ⊲ Repetition code › p. 202

POSET CODE [1908] poset  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Galois-field Kingdom › p. 11 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) in 𝑛 𝑞 -ary coordinates over the field F𝑞 , with its distance evaluated in the poset metric.  

> PROTECTION

Poset codes are quantified with respect to the poset metric [ 967 ]. This metric is based on a partial ordering ≤ on [𝑛 ] =

{1, 2, · · · , 𝑛 } and the notion of ideals generated by the support of a 𝑞 -ary string. An ideal ⟨supp (𝑥 )⟩ generated by 𝑥 ∈ F𝑛 𝑞 contains all elements of [𝑛 ] that are less than or equal to some element in the support of 𝑥 in the partial ordering. The poset metric between two strings 𝑥, 𝑦 is then the cardinality of the ideal generated by the support of 𝑥 − 𝑦 , 𝑑 𝑃 (𝑥, 𝑦 ) = |⟨ supp (𝑥 − 𝑦 )⟩| .Generalizations of various bounds for ordinary 𝑞 -ary codes have been developed for poset codes, including generalizations of MacWilliams identities › p. 209 [199, 1909]; see [967].

PROJECTIVE GEOMETRY CODE projective  

> DESCRIPTION

Linear 𝑞 -ary [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code whose generator matrix 𝐺 

does not contain any repeated columns or the zero column. That way, each column corresponds to a distinct point in the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (𝑘 − 1, 𝑞 ) arising from a 𝑘 -dimensional vector space over 

F𝑞 . A choice of 𝑘 linearly independent columns determines an 

information set . Columns of a code’s parity-check matrix can sim-ilarly correspond to points in projective space. This formulation yields connections to projective geometry, which can be applied to determine code properties. Recall that a linear code encodes a message ℎ into a codeword 

𝑐 = ℎ𝐺 . The 𝑖 th coordinate of a codeword is given by the dot product 

ℎ · 𝐺 𝑖 , with 𝐺 𝑖 being the 𝑖 th column of the generator matrix. The zero-coordinate condition ℎ · 𝑥 = 0 defines a hyperplane of points 

𝑥 with normal vector ℎ. Therefore, the Hamming weight of the corresponding codeword is the number of points 𝐺 𝑖 not contained in that hyperplane. In general, linear codes can admit repeated columns or columns proportional to each other. In that case, the columns correspond to a multiset of not-necessarily-distinct nonzero points of projective space [ 55 , 1804 ]. Multisets can also be used to construct parity-check matrices of linear codes.  

> PROTECTION

Distance 𝑑 is 𝑛 minus the maximum number of points that are contained in a hyperplane. For 𝑛 ≥ 3, a code is projective if and only if the distance of its dual code is at least three. The weight enumerator of the code comes from the Tutte polyno-mial associated with the projective code [1913].  

> NOTES

⊲ See corresponding definition in MinT 21 . 

> 21 https://web.archive.org/web/20240228180821/http://mint.sbg.ac.at/glossary.php\#GProjectiveCode

234  

> PARENT

⊲ Linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 227 — Columns of the generator matrix of a projective linear [𝑛, 𝑘 ]𝑞 code correspond to distinct nonzero points in projective space. In general, linear codes admit repeating columns or columns proportional to each other. In that case, the columns correspond to a multiset of non-distinct nonzero points, and multisets are in one-to-one correspondence to arcs in projective space [1804, Thm. 1.1].

PROJECTIVE TWO-WEIGHT CODE projective_two_weight  

> DESCRIPTION

A projective code whose codewords all have one of two possible nonzero Hamming weights. There is a correspondence between projective two-weight codes, projective two-character sets, and certain strongly regular graphs [1925 ][ 157 , Sec. 19.3.3]. As such, projective two-weight codes have been classified and can be constructed out of quadrics [1859, 1926], maximal arcs and hyperovals, Baer spaces, or Hermitian quadrics [157 , Secs. 19.7.1-19.7.5]. There are also several sporadic examples [157, Table 19.1]. 235  

> PROTECTION

In a projective two-weight code, the difference between the two nonzero weights is a power of the characteristic [ 157 , Sec. 19.3.6].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Projective geometry code › p. 233 — Projective two-weight codes are projective codes by definition [ 157 , Sec. 19.2] (see also [188 , 1914 , 1915 ]). ⊲ Two-weight code › p. 242 — Projective two-weight codes are two-weight codes by definition [ 157 , Def. 19.1] (see also [188, 1914, 1915]).  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Ovoid code › p. 231 — The ovoid code is a two-weight pro-jective code [ 1609 , 1610 ][ 190 , Table 7.1]. ⊲ Denniston code › p. 217 

— Denniston codes are projective two-weight codes on maximal arcs [ 1720 ][ 157 , Sec. 19.7.3]. ⊲ Hill projective-cap code › p. 226 — Hill projective-cap codes are projective two-weight codes on projective caps [157, Table 19.1].  

> COUSINS

⊲ [11 , 6, 5]3 Ternary Golay code › p. 205 — The dual of the ternary Golay code is a projective two-weight subcode [ 1609 ,1610 ][ 157 , Exam. 19.3.2][ 190 , Table 7.1]. ⊲ Hyperoval code › p. 226

QUADRATIC-RESIDUE (QR) CODE q-ary_quad_residue  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a quadruple of cyclic 𝑞 -ary codes of prime length 𝑛 where 𝑞 is prime and a quadratic-residue modulo 𝑛 [ 60 , Def. 3.2.8]. The codes are constructed using quadratic residues and non-residues of 𝑛 . The definition extends to prime-power alphabet sizes and to prime-power lengths [ 159 , 160 ][ 60 , Rem. 3.2.9]. A quadratic-residue code of prime length 𝑝 has dimension ( 𝑝 + 1)/ 2 [60 , Sec. 3.2.1]. The roots of the generator polynomial 𝑟 (𝑥 ) of the first code (see Cyclic-to-polynomial correspondence › p. 216 ) are all of the inequiva-lent quadratic residues of 𝑛 , and the second code’s generator poly-nomial is (𝑥 − 1)𝑟 (𝑥 ). The roots of the generator polynomial 𝑎 (𝑥 ) of the third code are all inequivalent nonresidues of 𝑛 , and the fourth code’s generator polynomial is (𝑥 − 1)𝑎 (𝑥 ). The codes correspond-ing to polynomials 𝑟, 𝑎 are often called augmented quadratic-residue codes, while the remaining codes are called expurgated .The extended versions of odd-like quadratic-residue codes have automorphism groups containing 𝑃𝑆𝐿 (2, 𝑝 ) [ 60 , Thm. 3.2.11]; such codes are the only codes with these symmetries [1928].  

> PROTECTION

For odd-like quadratic-residue codes of prime length, the common minimum distance 𝑑 satisfies 𝑑 2 ≥ 𝑛 ; if −1 is a quadratic non-residue, then 𝑑 2 − 𝑑 + 1 ≥ 𝑛 [58, Thm. 2.7.4].  

> RATE

Achieve capacity of the binary erasure channel; see Ref. [ 1614 ].  

> NOTES

⊲ Introduction of quadratic-residue codes in Refs. [ 34 ,112][58, Sec. 2.7].  

> PARENT

⊲ 𝑞 -ary duadic code › p. 210 — QR codes are duadic codes of prime length satisfying certain relations [59].

QUASI-PERFECT CODE quasi_perfect  

> DESCRIPTION

Perfect codes (𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 )𝑞 are those for which balls of Hamming radius 𝑡 = ⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋ exactly fill the space of all 𝑛 𝑞 -ary strings. Quasi-perfect codes are those for which balls of Hamming radius 𝑡 are disjoint, while balls of radius 𝑡 + 1 cover the space with possible overlaps. In other words, any 𝑞 -ary string is at most 𝑡 + 1

bit flips away from a codeword of a quasi-perfect code.  

> PROTECTION

Correct errors of weight 𝑡 as well as some errors of weight 𝑡 + 1. 

> PARENTS

⊲ Uniformly packed code › p. 242 — Quasi-perfect codes are uniformly packed [ 1697 , Def. 2.5]. ⊲ Weighted-covering code › p. 242 

— A quasi-perfect code is a special case of an 𝑚 -weighted covering code with 𝑚 -covering radius 𝑟 = 𝑡 + 1 [227, Ch. 13].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Nearly perfect code › p. 196 — Nearly perfect codes are quasi-perfect [ 34 , pg. 533]. ⊲ Zetterberg code › p. 204 — Zetterberg codes are quasi-perfect, with each 𝑛 -bit string at most three bit-flips away from a codeword [1596].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Binary BCH code › p. 179 — Only double error-correcting BCH codes [2𝑚 − 1, 𝑛 − 2𝑚, 5] are quasi-perfect [ 1196 , 1197 ] (see also [34 , Ch. 9]). ⊲ Preparata code › p. 198 — Shortened Preparata codes are quasi-perfect [34, pg. 475]. 

REED-SOLOMON (RS) CODE [1618, 1877, 1878] reed_solomon  

> DESCRIPTION

An [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1]𝑞 linear code based on polynomials over F𝑞 .Let {𝛼 1, · · · , 𝛼 𝑛 } be 𝑛 distinct points in F𝑞 . An RS code encodes a message 𝜇 = {𝜇 0, · · · , 𝜇 𝑘 −1 } into { 𝑓 𝜇 (𝛼 1), · · · , 𝑓 𝜇 (𝛼 𝑛 )} using a message-dependent polynomial 

𝑓 𝜇 (𝑥 ) = 𝜇 0 + 𝜇 1𝑥 + · · · + 𝜇 𝑘 −1𝑥 𝑘 −1 . (71) In other words, each message 𝜇 is encoded into a string of values of the corresponding polynomial 𝑓 𝜇 at the points 𝛼 𝑖 ,

𝜇 → ␀ 𝑓 𝜇 (𝛼 1) , 𝑓 𝜇 (𝛼 2) , · · · , 𝑓 𝜇 (𝛼 𝑛 ) . (72) The dual of an RS code is an RS code [34, pg. 296].  

> PROTECTION

Since each polynomial 𝑓 𝜇 is of degree less than 𝑘 , it has less than 𝑘 roots; this is called the degree mantra . Therefore, the polynomial can be determined from its values at 𝑘 points. This means that RS codes can correct erasures on up to 𝑛 − 𝑘 registers. The resulting distance, 𝑑 = 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1, saturates the Singleton bound.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Bit-serial encoder [ 1934 ]. ⊲ [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑛 − 𝑘 + 1] RS code requires an order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2) operations while encoding if a straight-forward matrix multiplication is employed and 𝑘 = 𝑂 (𝑛 ). Using the FFT algorithm, complexity of evaluating a polynomial at 𝑛 roots of unity becomes 𝑂 (𝑛 log 𝑛 ). The FFT can be generalized to finite fields and rings, which is referred as Number-theoretic Transform (NTT). However, for some values of 𝑛 , which can not be factorized into small primes or do not have 𝑛 roots of unity, the FFT algorithm fails. Independently developed by [ 1935 , 1936 ] and generalized in Ref. [ 1937 ], the additive FFT solves this problem by evaluating the polynomial at 𝑛 − 1 roots of unity when 𝑛 is power of 2.  

> DECODING

⊲ Decoding general RS codes is 𝑁 𝑃 -hard [1938 ]. 

⊲ Although using iFFT has its counterpart iNNT for finite fields, the decoding is usually standard polynomial interpolation in 𝑘 =

𝑂 (𝑛 log 2 𝑛 ). However, in erasure decoding, encoded values are only erased in 𝑟 points, which is a specific case of polynomial inter-polation and can be done in 𝑂 (𝑛 log 𝑛 ) by computing product of the received polynomial and an erasure locator polynomial and using long division to find an original polynomial. The long divi-sion step can be omitted to increase speed further by only dividing the derivative of the product polynomial, and derivative of erasure locator polynomial evaluated at erasure locations. ⊲ Berlekamp-Massey decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2) [ 1187 , 1188 ]. 

⊲ Gorenstein-Peterson-Zierler decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 

𝑂 (𝑛 3) [1184 , 1687 ] (see exposition in Ref. [ 1186 ]). ⊲ Berlekamp-Welch decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 3) [ 1939 ] (see exposi-tion in Ref. [ 1940 ]), assuming that 𝑡 ≥ ( 𝑛 + 𝑘 )/ 2. ⊲ Sugiyama et al. modification of the extended Euclidean algorithm [ 1190 , 1191 , 1941 ]. 

⊲ Gao decoder using extended Euclidean algorithm [ 1942 ]. ⊲ Fast-Fourier-transform decoder with runtime of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 polylog 𝑛 )

[1943 ]. ⊲ List decoders try to find a low-degree bivariate polyno-mial 𝑄 (𝑥, 𝑦 ) such that evaluation of 𝑄 at (𝛼 𝑖 , 𝑦 𝑖 ) is zero. By choosing proper degrees, it can be shown such polynomial exists by drawing an analogy between evaluation of 𝑄 (𝛼 𝑖 , 𝑦 𝑖 ) and solving a homoge-neous linear equation (interpolation). Once this is done, one lists roots of 𝑦 that agree at ≥ 𝑡 points. The breakthrough Sudan list-decoding algorithm corrects up to 1 − √2𝑅 fraction of errors asymp-totically in 𝑛 [1944 ]. Roth and Ruckenstein proposed a modified key equation that allows for correction of more than ⌊( 𝑛 − 𝑘 )/ 2⌋ errors [1945 ]. The Guruswami-Sudan algorithm improved the Sudan algo-rithm to 1 − √𝑅 [ 1193 ], meaning that RS codes achieve list-decoding capacity; see Ref. [ 1946 ] for bounds. It was later shown that generic RS codes achieve list-decoding capacity [ 1947 ]. A modification of the Guruswami-Sudan algorithm by Koetter and Vardy is used for soft-decision decoding [ 1784 ] (see also Ref. [ 1690 ]). Subcodes of RS codes whose evaluation points lie in a subfield › p. 164 can be decoded up to the 1−𝑅 [ 841 ]. List decoding of RS codes is known as noisy poly-nomial interpolation in cryptography [ 1948 ]. ⊲ The ubiquity of RS codes has yielded off-the-shelf VLSI integrated-circuit decoding hardware [1949] (see also [230, Chs. 5 and 10]).  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ RS Product Code (RSPC) was used in DVDs [ 230 , Ch. 4]. ⊲ DSL technologies and their variants against impluse noise [ 311 ]. ⊲ Cryptographic primitives based on the hardness of decod-ing RS codes for more than 1 −√︁ 𝑘 /𝑛 + 𝜖 errors. This is equivalent to the polynomial reconstruction problem [ 312 ]. ⊲ RS codes as outer codes concatenated with convolutional codes are used indi-rectly in space exploration programs such as Voyager and Galileo. RS codes were part of a telemetry channel coding standard issued by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems [ 230 , Ch. 3]. 

⊲ Automatic repeat request (ARQ) data transmission protocols [ 230 ,Ch. 7]. ⊲ Slow-frequency-hop spread-spectrum transmission [ 230 ,Chs. 8-9]. ⊲ RS codes over 𝑞 = 2𝑚 are used in RAID 6 [ 313 , 314 ]; 237 see [ 174 ]. ⊲ Coded sharding designs in blockchains to increase ef-ficiency [ 315 ]. ⊲ Used in QR-Codes to retrieve damaged barcodes [316 ]. ⊲ Wireless communication systems such as 3G, DVB, and WiMAX [ 317 ]. ⊲ Correcting pooled testing results for SARS-CoV-2 [318]. ⊲ DNA storage [319].

RESIDUE AG CODE residue  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Differential code  

> DESCRIPTION

Linear 𝑞 -ary code defined using a set of F𝑞 -rational points P = (𝑃 1, 𝑃 2, · · · , 𝑃 𝑛 ) on an algebraic curve X and a linear space Ω of certain rational differential forms 𝜔 [21, Def. 15.3.2]. Codewords are evaluations of residues of the differential forms at the specified points, 

␀Res 𝑃 1 (𝜔 ), Res 𝑃 2 (𝜔 ), · · · , Res 𝑃 𝑛 (𝜔 ) ∀𝜔 ∈ Ω . (73) The code is denoted as 𝐶 Ω (X , P, 𝐷 ), where the divisor 𝐷 determines which rational differential forms to use.  

> PROTECTION

Riemann-Roch theorem yields code length 𝑛 , dimension 

𝑘 , and a lower bound on distance in terms of the divisor 𝐷 and the genus of the curve X [ 21 , Cor. 15.3.13]. Distance bounds can also be derived from how an algebraic curve X is embedded in the ambient projective space [1905]. 238  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Improvements over the McEliece public-key cryp-tosystem to linear AG codes on curves of arbitrary genus [ 323 ]. Only the subfield › p. 164 subcode proposal remains resilient to attacks [21 , Sec. 15.7.5.3]. ⊲ Algebraic-geometric secret-sharing schemes [324].  

> PARENT

⊲ Evaluation AG code › p. 219 — Any residue AG code of dif-ferential forms can be restated, up to diagonal equivalence, as an evaluation AG code of functions [ 1265 – 1267 ][ 21 , Lemma 15.3.10][ 27 ,Thm. 2.72]. Evaluation and residue AG codes are dual to each other [27][21, Thm. 15.3.3].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — GRS (RS) codes are in one-to-one correspondence with both evaluation AG codes of univariate polynomials 𝑓 [ 21 , Thm. 15.3.24] and residue AG codes of univariate differential forms [ 21 , Prop. 15.3.26], with X being the projective (affine) line [ 27 , 1265 , 1266 ][ 1267 , Ch. 3.2]. The 𝐶 𝐿 and 

𝐶 Ω constructions yield the same family of codes on the projective line (up to diagonal equivalence). ⊲ Tsfasman-Vladut-Zink (TVZ) code › p. 241 — TVZ codes can be formulated as residue AG codes on algebraic curves.  

> COUSIN

⊲ Cartier code › p. 215 — Every Cartier code is contained in a subfield › p. 164 subcode of a residue AG code. Cartier codes share similar asymptotic properties to subfield › p. 164 subcodes of residue AG codes, with both families admitting sequences of codes that achieve the GV bound › p. 209 .

RULED-SURFACE CODE [28, 29] ruled_surface  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation code obtained by evaluating global sections of a line bundle, or equivalently suitable polynomial functions, on rational points of a ruled surface over a finite field. Such codes extend algebraic-geometry constructions from curves to certain projective surfaces [28, 29].  

> PARENT

> PROTECTION

Minimum distance bounds computed in Refs. [ 1960 –1962].  

> PARENT

SEGRE-VARIETY RM-TYPE CODE [30] serge  

> DESCRIPTION

Evaluation code of multihomogeneous polynomials evaluated on points of a Segre variety, i.e., on the Segre embedding of a product of projective spaces. These codes are Reed-Muller-type analogues adapted to product projective geometries [30].  

> PARENT

⊲ Polynomial evaluation code › p. 232 — Segre-variety RM-type codes are polynomial evaluation codes with X being a Segre variety. 

SELF-DUAL ADDITIVE CODE self_dual_additive  

> DESCRIPTION

An additive 𝑞 -ary code 𝐶 ⊆ F𝑛 𝑞 that is equal to its dual,

Self-dual additive codes that contain at least one codeword of odd weight are called Type I additive . Even self-dual additive codes are called Type II additive , existing only for even 𝑛 [ 112 , Sec. 9.10]. Type I (type II) additive codes with length up to seven (eight) have been classified [36]. Much is known about codes up to length 16 [1963]. Two self-dual additive codes are equivalent if they can be mapped into each other by a map that preserves self-duality [1598].

SELF-DUAL LINEAR CODE self_dual  

> DESCRIPTION

An [𝑛, 𝑛 /2]𝑞 code that is equal to its dual, 𝐶 ⊥ = 𝐶 ,where the dual is defined with respect to an inner product, most commonly either Euclidean or Hermitian. Self-dual codes exist only for even lengths and have dimension 𝑘 = 𝑛 /2. A code that is equivalent to its dual is called isodual . Any self-dual code is isodual, and hence formally self-dual [33, Rem. 4.2.2]. A binary singly even (doubly even) self-dual code is called Type I (Type II), a ternary self-dual code is called Type III, and a Hermitian self-dual code over F4 is called Type IV [ 33 , Rems. 4.1.10 and 4.3.2]. Type III codes are 3-divisible, while Type IV codes are 2-divisible [33 , Thm. 4.1.9]. Self-dual doubly even binary codes exist iff 8|𝑛 ,self-dual ternary codes exist iff 4|𝑛 , and Hermitian self-dual codes over F4 exist iff 𝑛 is even [33, Thm. 4.1.13].  

> PROTECTION

The generator matrix of the Hermitian dual of a code with generator matrix 𝐺 = [𝐼 𝑘 𝐴 ] is [− ¯𝐴 𝑇 𝐼 𝑛 −𝑘 ], where ¯𝐴 contains matrix elements of 𝐴 raised to the 𝑝 th power. A code is Hermitian self-dual if and only if 𝐴 ¯𝐴 𝑇 = −𝐼 𝑛 /2.The minimum distance of a formally self-dual even binary code, a Type II binary self-dual code, a Type III ternary self-dual code, and a Type IV Hermitian self-dual code over F4 satisfies

24 , in which case 𝑑 ≤ 4⌊𝑛 /24 ⌋ + 6 [ 33 , Thm. 4.3.6]. A self-dual code meeting the relevant upper bound is called extremal [33 , Def. 4.3.7]. Fixed-weight codewords of extremal Type II codes of length di-visible by 24 form combinatorial 5-designs [ 33 , Thm. 4.3.16(a)]. The extended Golay code and the [48 , 24 , 12 ] self-dual code are two such codes. It is not yet known whether a [72 , 36 , 16 ] self-dual code exists [33, Rem. 4.3.11]; see also [986, 1964, 1967]. > COUSINS

⊲ Divisible code › p. 217 — Binary self-orthogonal codes are even, doubly even binary codes are self-orthogonal, and binary self-dual codes split into singly-even Type I and doubly-even Type II families [ 33 , Def. 4.1.6][ 33 , Rems. 4.1.7 and 4.1.10]. ⊲ Conformal-field theory (CFT) code › p. 382 — Even self-dual binary codes and even unimodular lattices define CFTs [ 1975 – 1977 ]. Self-dual ternary codes define superconformal field theories (SCFTs) [1978 ]. ⊲ Niemeier lattice › p. 260 — The nine inequivalent [24 , 12 ]

doubly even self-dual codes [ 1968 ] yield certain Niemeier lattices via Construction A › p. 258 [ 1979 ]. Niemeier lattices can be constructed from ternary self-dual codes of length 24 [ 1980 ]. ⊲ Unimodular lattice › p. 262 — Unimodular lattices are lattice analogues of self-dual codes. There are several parallels between (doubly even) self-dual binary codes and (even) unimodular lattices [ 32 , 35 , 1981 ]. TANNER CODE [1535] tanner  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Generalized LDPC (GLDPC) code  

> DESCRIPTION

A linear 𝑞 -ary code defined on a bipartite graph similar to a Tanner graph. This generalized Tanner graph consists of variable nodes and constraint nodes, with the generalization being that the constraint nodes of degree 𝑟 now represent a linear code of length 

𝑟 .A string is in the Tanner code if all substrings satisfy their corre-sponding constraints, i.e., all substrings are members of the linear codes represented on the constraint nodes. A code is called regular if the corresponding bipartite graph is regular. Expansion properties of the underlying graph can yield efficient decoding algorithms.  

> DECODING

⊲ Min-sum and sum-product iterative decoders for binary Tanner codes [ 1989 , 1990 ]; see also [ 1191 , 1991 ]. These decoders can be improved using a probabilistic message-passing schedule [ 1992 ]. 

⊲ Any code can be put into normal form without significantly alter-ing the underlying graph or the decoding complexity [ 1993 ]. For an algebraic viewpoint on decoding, see [ 1994 ]. ⊲ Iterative decoding is optimal for Tanner graphs that are free of cycles [ 1990 ]. However, codes that admit cycle-free representations have bounds on their distances [1535, 1995]; see [85, 1996].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Linear 𝑞 -ary code › p. 227 ⊲ Parallel concatenated code  

> › p. 168

— Tanner codes are examples of parallel concatenation [929].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Regular binary Tanner code › p. 201 — Regular binary Tan-ner codes are binary Tanner codes defined on regular sparse bi-partite graphs, with the inner code being the same for all vertices. 

⊲ 𝑞 -ary LDPC code › p. 210 — 𝑞 -ary LDPC codes are 𝑞 -ary Tanner codes on sparse bipartite graphs whose constraint nodes represent 𝑞 -ary parity-check codes.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Generalized homological-product CSS code › p. 546 — Tan-ner codes can be generalized to sheaf codes , whose local codes satisfy a certain hierarchy. This allows for a way to formulate and under-stand many generalized homological-product CSS codes [ 1055 ] and LTCs [ 1056 ]. ⊲ Locally testable code (LTC) › p. 167 — Tanner codes can be generalized to sheaf codes , whose local codes satisfy a certain hierarchy. This allows for a way to formulate and understand many generalized homological-product CSS codes [1055] and LTCs [1056]. 

TSFASMAN-VLADUT-ZINK (TVZ) CODE [1668] shimura  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of AG codes obtained from algebraic curves via the residue or evaluation construction. Sequences of curves with many rational points, such as Drinfeld modular curves, classical modular curves, or Garcia-Stichtenoth curves, yield the asymptotic parameters of the TVZ bound [21, Sec. 15.4.2].  

> RATE

TVZ codes, either in the residue AG or evaluation AG construc-tions, exceed the asymptotic GV bound › p. 209 [1668 ] (see also Ref. [1997 ]). For square 𝑞 ≥ 49 , these codes improve on the GV bound; for smaller 𝑞 , they do not [ 21 , Sec. 15.4.2]. Roughly speaking, this result implies that AG codes can outperform random codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Residue AG code › p. 237 — TVZ codes can be formulated as residue AG codes on algebraic curves.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Evaluation AG code › p. 219 — TVZ codes can also be formu-lated as evaluation AG codes on algebraic curves; these are dual to the corresponding residue AG codes. ⊲ Quantum AG code › p. 501 —The AG codes used in an asymptotically good construction of quan-tum AG codes with non-Clifford transversal gates [ 665 ] are those of the TVZ codes. 

TURBO CODE [1998, 1999] turbo  

> DESCRIPTION

Code obtained from a parallel concatenation of two or more convolutional codes with permutations interleaving the indi-vidual encodings. The choice of interleaver is important to the code design [ 2000 ,2001].  

> PROTECTION

Parallel concatenated turbo codes have typical min-imum distance with upper bound 𝑂 (log (𝑛 )) . Truhachev, Lent-macher, and Zignagirov produced a sequence of turbo codes with minimum distance of order › p. 161 Θ(log (𝑛 )) . [ 2002 ]. Various bounds on code parameters exist [2003, 2004].  

> RATE

Turbo codes nearly achieve the Shannon capacity [1999].  

> DECODING

⊲ Turbo decoder [ 1999 ], an instance of BP decoding [ 2005 ]. 

⊲ Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) decoder [ 2006 ] and a soft output derivative [ 2007 ]. The use of soft outputs can improve code perfor-mance [ 2008 ]. ⊲ List decoding [ 2009 ]. ⊲ VLSI integrated-circuit decoding hardware [2010]. ⊲ Autoencoder [2011].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Several standards related to wireless communication, including W-CDMA, DVB-RCS, TD-SCDMA, 802.16, and CDMA2000 [335].

UNIVERSALLY OPTIMAL 𝑞 -ARY CODE [156, 158, 873, 2030–2033]  

> univ_opt_q-ary
> DESCRIPTION

A 𝑞 -ary code that (weakly) minimizes all completely monotonic potentials on Hamming space [ 158 ]. Equivalently, its binomial moments are minimal among all codes with the same size and block length [158, Lemma 4]. All codes that attain the linear programming (LP) bound by Del-sarte [ 193 ] are universally optimal [ 158 ]. Such codes are called LP universally optimal or extremal . If universal optimality is proved by these LP bounds, then deleting any one codeword yields another universally optimal code [ 158 , Thm. 2]. However, not all univer-sally optimal codes attain the Delsarte LP bound (for example, the 

[23 , 12 , 7] Golay code [ 158 ][ 184 , Table 12.1]). See [ 184 , Table 12.1][ 158 ,Table 1] for a list of (LP) universally optimal codes. See [ 184 , Sec. 12.3] for further discussion. All codes that attain the Levenshtein bound [ 156 , 873 , 2030 , 2031 ], which estimates the solution to Delsarte’s linear program, are uni-versally optimal [ 2032 ]; see [ 184 , Thm. 12.3.23]. However, not all universally optimal codes attain the Levenshtein bound.  

> PARENTS

⊲ 𝑞 -ary code › p. 208 ⊲ Universally optimal code › p. 291  

> CHILDREN

⊲ [23 , 12 , 7] Golay code › p. 175 — The Golay code and several of its extended, shortened, and punctured versions are LP univer-sally optimal codes [ 158 ]. ⊲ Conference code › p. 182 — Conference codes are LP universally optimal codes [ 158 ]. ⊲ Maximum dis-tance separable (MDS) code › p. 229 — MDS codes are LP universally optimal codes [ 158 , 1859 ]. ⊲ 𝑞 -ary Hamming code › p. 210 — Ham-ming codes and their once-punctured and once-shortened versions are LP universally optimal codes [ 158 ]. ⊲ [11 , 6, 5]3 Ternary Golay code › p. 205 — The ternary Golay code and several of its extended, shortened, and punctured versions are LP universally optimal codes [ 158 ]. The [11 , 6, 5]3 code is universally optimal but not sharp. ⊲ 𝑞 -ary sharp configuration › p. 212 — All 𝑞 -ary sharp configurations are universally optimal 𝑞 -ary codes [158], but the converse is not true.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Constant-weight code › p. 183 — Some constant-weight codes, such as simplex codes, are also universally optimal bi-nary codes. ⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 — Kerdock codes are asymp-totically close to the LP and universal-energy bounds [ 184 , Exam. 12.3.25]. ⊲ [2𝑚 , 𝑚, 2𝑚 −1] Hadamard code › p. 173 — Several punc-tured Hadamard codes are LP universally optimal codes [ 158 ].

ARRAY CODE array  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ RAID code ⊲ Disk array code  

> DESCRIPTION

Matrix code over F𝑞 designed for use in distributed storage, with the first such application being a RAID-type array of hard drives such that information is protected against erasure of one or more hard drives. Each column of a matrix codeword is typically treated as a single codeword coordinate via subpacketiza-tion (defined below) and represents a large data block. Array codes are denoted by (𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑚 ), where 𝑛 is the number of nodes, 𝑘 is the number of nodes needed to recover the data, and 𝑚 is the column dimension of each codeword a.k.a. the subpacketization level. Classical array codes also include block and convolutional fami-lies whose parity checks run along rows, columns, or diagonals, with applications to burst correction, multitrack magnetic recording, and disk arrays [174].  

> PROTECTION

Since they are designed to protect against corruption of nodes in a distributed storage network, many array codes are analyzed in terms of their erasure capabilities. An analogue of the Hamming metric for array codes comes from counting the number of column positions in which two codewords differ. Equivalently, one may treat each length-𝑚 column as a single symbol from an alphabet of size 𝑞 𝑚 ; this interpretation underlies the subpacketization viewpoint. Array codes are typically F𝑞 -linear as matrix codes. In some constructions, after choosing an identifi-cation of columns with symbols from an extension field F𝑞 𝑚 , one also obtains an F𝑞 𝑚 -linear code. There are other notions of distance for array codes, including the rank metric and its generalization the sum-rank metric.

CLIFFORD GROUP [429, 2041–2046] clifford_group  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Clifford-Weil group ⊲ Normalizer of a group of symplectic type  

> DESCRIPTION

The Clifford group on 𝑛 qubits is a subgroup of the uni-tary group 𝑈 (2𝑛 ) that is the normalizer of the Pauli group › p. 433 , that forms a unitary 3-design, and that is closely related to the auto-morphism group of BW lattices. The group features prominently in quantum information, with the rest of the entry given in that context.  

> Clifford group:

The 𝑛 -qubit Clifford group consists of the Pauli group as well as elements that permute Pauli operators amongst them-selves. Up to any phases and Pauli strings, the group is equivalent to the symplectic group 𝑆 𝑝 (2𝑛, Z2). A Clifford circuit is a quantum circuit, defined on some qubit geometry and consisting of only Clif-ford gates. See Refs. [ 381 , 2046 – 2049 ] for generators, relations, and normal form. The Clifford group cannot be expressed as a semidirect product of the Pauli and symplectic groups [ 416 ]. Restricting the group to real-valued elements yields the real Clifford group [ 2050 , 2051 ], and including complex conjugation yields the extended Clifford group 

[2052]. Single-qubit Clifford gates, together with Paulis, realize a group with 192 elements. Modding out phases yields the 48 -element 2𝑂 245 binary octahedral subgroup of 𝑆𝑈 (2). Further modding out the Pauli group, which corresponds to the quaternion group 𝑄 , yields the permutation group 𝑆 3, which consists of permutations of the three non-identity single-qubit Pauli matrices. The two-qubit Clifford group, modded out by the Pauli group and phases, is isomorphic to 𝑆 6, and its subgroups have been classified [2053]. The commutant of four-fold [ 765 , 2054 ] and higher transversal representations of the Clifford group consists of qubit permutations and projections onto the ⟦2𝑚, 2𝑚 − 2, 2⟧ error-detecting code [ 766 ]. In particular, the fourth tensor-power commutant is generated by tensor-factor permutations and the projector onto this special sta-bilizer code [ 765 , Thm. 1]. Although generic Clifford orbits are not projective 4-designs, exact projective 4-designs can be constructed from Clifford orbits, and random Clifford orbits are typically close to 4-designs [765]. Clifford-group elements can be sampled efficiently [2055].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [35, preface] for a history of the Clifford group.  

> PARENT

⊲ Unitary 𝑡 -design › p. 251 — Stabilizer states on 𝑛 qubits form 3-designs on complex projective spaces C𝑃 2𝑛 

[896 ]. The Clifford group › p. 244 is a unitary 2-design [ 897 ] and a 3-design [ 898 , 899 ][ 900 ,Thm. 1.6(B)][ 35 , pg. 191] on 𝑈 (2𝑛 ). The ⟦2𝑚, 2𝑚 − 2, 2⟧ code when 

2𝑚 is a multiple of four obstructs the Clifford group from being a 4-design [765].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — Computing with Clifford gates › p. 244 , Pauli measurements, and classical feedforward acting on stabilizer states only can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer by tracking stabilizer and logical generators, according to the Gottesman-Knill theorem [2056 , 2057 ]. Stabilizer states can be mapped into the first lattice shell of a BW lattice over a cyclo-tomic field, while the Clifford group › p. 244 is related to the symmetry group of the lattice [ 2058 ]. ⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 — Kerdock codes correspond to cluster states, and the corresponding Clifford-group automorphisms of this set form a particular group [ 893 ] that is a unitary 2-design on 𝑈 (2𝑛 ) [894 ]. ⊲ Barnes-Wall (BW) lattice › p. 257 — Stabilizer states can be mapped into the first lattice shell of a BW lattice over a cyclotomic field, while the Clifford group › p. 244 is related to the symmetry group of the lattice [ 2058 ]. ⊲ Real-Clifford subgroup-orbit code › p. 275 — The automorphism group of BW lattices is a subgroup of index 2 of a real Clifford group › p. 244 [ 2050 , 2051 ] (see [ 2045 , 2058 ] for an explana-tion). ⊲ Haar-random qubit code › p. 395 — Approximating the ran-dom projections through 𝑡 -designs is necessary in order to make the Haar-random qubit protocol practical. There is a canonical form for Clifford circuits › p. 244 [ 2059 , 2060 ] and many algorithms for simulating them [ 2061 – 2063 ]. Universal quantum computing can be achieved using Clifford gates › p. 244 and a single type of non-Clifford › p. 244 gate, such as the 𝑇 gate [ 2064 ]. More gen-erally, the Solovay-Kitaev theorem [ 1587 , 2065 ] states that any subset of gates that generates a dense subgroup of the full 𝑛 -qubit gate group can be used to construct any gate to arbitrary accuracy (see [ 2066 ][ 2067 , Appx. 3]). The task of approximating a desired gate by Clifford gates › p. 244 and a fixed set of non-Clifford › p. 244 gates is called 

gate compilation or circuit synthesis .

CONSTANT-DIMENSION CODE [275] finite_grassmann  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

> DESCRIPTION

A subspace code whose codewords are 𝑘 -dimensional subspaces of F𝑛 𝑞 for fixed 𝑘 . Constant-dimension codes are equiva-lent to linear authentication codes [152, Thm. 4.1]. Each 𝑘 -dimensional subspace of F𝑛 𝑞 is a point on the finite-field Grassmannian (a.k.a. Grassmannian variety or 𝑞 -Johnson space). The number of such subspaces is a 𝑞 -binomial coefficient [ 2068 ][ 872 ,Sec. 8.6].  

> PROTECTION

Johnson-type bounds have been developed [2069].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Linear authentication [152].

DISTRIBUTED COMPUTATION CODE matrix_computation  

> DESCRIPTION

Encoding that provides extra redundancy for dis-tributed matrix computation algorithms such as matrix multipli-cation. Parallelized algorithms distribute a desired computation over many nodes, and a key performance bottleneck is due to some nodes completing their individual tasks much later than other nodes. Matrix computation codes provide a layer of redundancy such that the computation can be performed without having all nodes finish their piece of the computation.  

> PROTECTION

Allows computation to complete without waiting for 

stragglers , or nodes that either do not finish or finish their portion of the computation much later than all other nodes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Matrix-based code › p. 247  

> COUSIN

⊲ Maximum distance separable (MDS) code › p. 229 — The first matrix multiplication code encoded each entry of the matrices to be multiplied into an MDS code [1863]. 

EVENODD CODE [2072] evenodd  

> DESCRIPTION

Binary array code EO 2 (𝑚 ) with independent horizontal and diagonal parity columns, designed to retain optimal double-erasure protection while simplifying small updates [174].  

> PROTECTION

Corrects any two erased columns whenever 𝑚 is prime, and has minimum column distance three in that case [174].  

> DECODING

⊲ Efficient decoding algorithm against two erasures [2072].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Can be implemented on standard RAID-5 controllers without extra finite-field hardware [174].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Generalized EVENODD code › p. 247 — Generalized EVEN-ODD codes reduce to EVENODD codes for 𝑟 = 2 [ 174 ]. ⊲ MDS array code › p. 248 — EVENODD codes are examples of MDS array codes [ 177 ].  

> COUSIN

⊲ B-code › p. 244 — EVENODD avoids the recursive parity up-dates of B2 (𝑚 ) while retaining optimal two-erasure correction [ 174 ].

LINEARIZED RS CODE [1212, 2083, 2084] linearized_reed_solomon  

> DESCRIPTION

A code obtained by linearizing a skew RS code, i.e., by translating evaluations of skew polynomials into operator evalua-tions over blocks. The general definition over arbitrary division rings was in-troduced in [ 1212 ]. Earlier finite-field subfamilies include skew-polynomial constructions and the pasting MDS construction [2083, 2084].  

> PROTECTION

RANK-METRIC CODE [2074] rank_metric  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Delsarte rank-metric code  

> DESCRIPTION

Each codeword is a matrix over F𝑞 , with codewords forming a F𝑞 -linear subspace, and with the metric being the rank of the difference of matrices. The distance 𝑑 is the minimum rank of all nonzero matrices in the code. Rank-metric codes on 𝑛 × 𝑚 

matrices are denoted as [𝑛 × 𝑚, 𝑘, 𝑑 ]𝑞 .The number of codewords satisfies 𝑘 ≤ max (𝑛, 𝑚 )𝑀 , where 𝑀 

is the maximum rank of all matrices in the code. Codes that achieve this bound with equality are called Delsarte optimal anticodes . 

> PROTECTION

Protects against errors with rank ≤ ⌊ 𝑑 −12 ⌋.In particular, this includes criss-cross errors confined to a small number of rows and/or columns whenever the corresponding error matrix has sufficiently small rank [174, Sec. 5]. The complexity of decoding rank-metric codes is unknown but expected to be harder than that of binary linear codes [2091]. Linear programming bounds have been derived [ 2074 , 2092 , 2093 ]. See Ref. [2077] for a discussion of MacWilliams identities › p. 209 . 

> DECODING

⊲ Polynomial-reconstruction Berlekamp-Welch based de-coder [2094]. ⊲ Berlekamp-Massey based decoder [2095].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Identity-Based Encryption [ 305 ]. ⊲ Digital water-marking [ 306 ]. ⊲ Network coding and streaming media broadcast-ing [307].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [905, 2096, 2097][174, Sec. 5] for more details.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Two-point homogeneous-space code › p. 291 — Matrices of dimen-sion 𝑚 × 𝑛 over F𝑞 under the rank metric form a finite two-point homogeneous space [2074, 2092, 2093][942, Table 2].  

> CHILDREN

REGENERATING CODE (RGC) [2090] regenerating  

> DESCRIPTION

An [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑, 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝑀 ]𝑞 Regenerating Code C is an erasure-correcting code that encodes 𝑀 symbols from F𝑞 into an 

𝛼 × 𝑛 matrix over F𝑞 , with each column of the matrix treated as a coordinate of a codeword. The code has the following properties. Any 𝑘 coordinates of the codeword can be used to recover the original 𝑀 symbols. Any erased coordinate, i.e., the 𝛼 symbols of that coordinate, can be recovered by contacting any 𝑑 other coordinates and collecting 𝛽 symbols from each one of them, where 𝑘 ≤ 𝑑 ≤ 𝑛 − 1 and 𝛽 ≤ 𝛼 .The connection of such codes to distributed storage is as follows. A file of size 𝑀 symbols is encoded using the code, and the 𝛼 symbols of each coordinate are stored in geographically separated storage nodes. Accessing any 𝑘 such nodes gives back the original file. Node failures are considered erasures in the codeword, and any such failed node can be regenerated by contacting 𝑑 surviving nodes and downloading 𝛽 symbols from each of them.  

> PROTECTION

Corrects up to 𝑛 − 𝑘 erasures on coordinates. For stan-dard erasure codes, like RS codes, total download bandwidth for recovery of a single node is 𝑘𝛼 due to the MDS property. For regen-erating codes, it is 𝑑𝛽 which can be significantly less. It was shown by network coding arguments that 𝑀 ≤ Í𝑘 −1 

> 𝑖 =0

min {𝛼, (𝑑 − 𝑖 ) 𝛽 }. De-pending on the relative values of 𝛼 and 𝛽 , a trade-off between storage per node and download bandwidth arises. Two extreme points of this trade-off curve are the MBR ( 𝛼 = 𝑑𝛽 ) and MSR ( 𝛼 = (𝑑 − 𝑘 +1) 𝛽 )codes.  

> DECODING

⊲ If the recovered symbols are exactly equal to the erased symbols, the repair is called an exact repair . ⊲ If the recovered symbols are not exactly equal to the erased symbols but still preserve the code properties, the repair is called a functional repair . 

> PARENT

⊲ Array code › p. 244  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Determinant code › p. 246 ⊲ Minimum-bandwidth re-generating (MBR) code › p. 248 — MBR codes are minimum-bandwidth extreme points in the storage-bandwidth trade-off curve and are characterized by 𝛼 = 𝑑𝛽 . ⊲ Minimum-storage regenerating (MSR) code › p. 248 — MSR codes are extreme points in the storage-bandwidth trade-off curve and are characterised by 𝛼 = (𝑑 − 𝑘 + 1) 𝛽 .

SPACETIME BLOCK CODE (STBC) [2086, 2099–2101] spacetime_block  

> DESCRIPTION

In a space-time block code, 𝑛 transmitting antennas send symbols to 𝑚 receiving antennas over 𝑇 time slots. These symbols can be arranged in a 𝑛 ×𝑇 matrix where the rows correspond to the transmitting antennas, and the columns correspond to the time slots. The codewords {𝑋 } making up the code are thus 𝑛 × 𝑇 

matrices. 250  

> PROTECTION

Provides protection against errors due to thermal noise and destructive interference arising from traversing an environment with scattering, reflection, and/or refraction. Transmission occurs from 𝑛 transmitting antennas to 𝑚 receiv-ing antennas over 𝑇 time slots. The typical noise model, a fading channel [ 2102 ], multiplies an incoming codeword by an 𝑚 × 𝑛 fading matrix or damping matrix 𝐻 and adds random (typically Gaussian) noise using an 𝑚 × 𝑇 matrix 𝑍 ,

𝑋 → 𝐻 𝑋 + 𝑍 = 𝑌 . (87) If 𝐻 is known (unknown) to the receiver, then the receiver is called coherent (incoherent). Decoding corresponds to choosing the codeword 𝑋 that, when transformed under the channel, is closest to the corrupted output 𝑌 

in the Frobenius norm, 

min  

> 𝑋 ∈𝐶

∥𝑌 − 𝐻 𝑋 ∥2 . (88)  

> RATE

If a codeword encodes 𝑘 information symbols over 𝑇 channel uses, then its rate is 𝑘 /𝑇 symbols per channel use. A spacetime block code is said to be full rate when this equals the number 𝑛 of transmit antennas, i.e., when 𝑘 = 𝑛𝑇 . 

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ High data-rate wireless communication, e.g., WiMAX (IEEE 802.16m) [325–327].

SPACETIME CODE (STC) [2103] spacetime  

> DESCRIPTION

Code designed for wireless transmission over multiple antennas and multiple time slots. A spacetime code uses a modula-tion scheme to encode a message into signals that are transmitted at different times from different antennas, thereby utilizing both spatial and temporal (i.e., spacetime ) degrees of freedom.  

> RATE

Shannon capacity of various multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels has been determined [ 2104 – 2107 ]. MIMO channel capacity when the channel is unknown to the sender and receiver [2099 , 2108 ] can be interpreted as a problem of placing points on the Grassmannian [2109].

SUBSPACE CODE [275, 2114, 2115] subspace  

> DESCRIPTION

A code that is a set of subspaces of F𝑛 𝑞 . Codewords are the subspaces themselves, often represented by generator matrices in reduced-row echelon form, and distance is governed by various notions of subspace overlap.  

> PROTECTION

Subspace codes are quantified with respect to the sub-space distance [275] or injection distance [2114]. Generalizations of various bounds for ordinary 𝑞 -ary codes have been developed for subspace codes; see [330].  

> DECODING

⊲ List decoding up to the Singleton bound [841].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Packet-based transmission over linear networks [ 275 ,276, 330].  

> NOTES

> DESCRIPTION

Bounds on design size have been computed [2132].

## V. ANALOG KINGDOM 

So one of the fundamental problems in communication theory is determining the densest packing of balls in high-dimensional spaces. This geometrical way of representing signals, at the heart of Shannon’s mathematical theory of communication, underlies the high-speed modems that we now take for granted. One of the most common coding schemes in use today works so well because the signals are represented as points in eight-dimensional space. — Neil J. A. Sloane, 1998

Z𝑛 HYPERCUBIC LATTICE hypercubic  

> DESCRIPTION

Lattice-based code consisting of all integer vectors in 

𝑛 dimensions. Its generator matrix is the 𝑛 -dimensional identity matrix. Its automorphism group consists of all coordinate permuta-tions and sign changes.  

> PROTECTION

The Z integer lattice solves the lattice quantization prob-lem in one dimension with a second moment of 𝐺 1 = 1/12 . The lattice has determinant 1, kissing number 2𝑛 , packing radius 1/2,covering radius √𝑛 /2, and density 𝑉 𝑛 /2𝑛 (with 𝑉 𝑛 the volume of the unit 𝑛 -sphere). See Ref. [2150] for further characterization.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Unimodular lattice › p. 262 — The hypercubic lattice is odd and unimodular. ⊲ Root lattice › p. 261  

> COUSINS

0 BW lattice. ⊲ Hypercube code › p. 271 — Hypercube codewords form the minimal lattice shell code of the Z𝑛 hypercubic lattice when the lattice is shifted such that the center of a hypercube is at the origin. ⊲ Square-lattice GKP code › p. 530 — GKP codewords, when written in terms of coherent states, form a square lattice in phase space. ⊲ Square-octagon (4.8.8) color code › p. 452 — The 4.8.8 (square-octagon) tiling is obtained by applying a fattening procedure to the square lattice [ 411 ]. ⊲ 3D Bacon-Shor code › p. 364 — 3D Bacon-Shor codes are defined on a hypercubic lattice. ⊲ CSS-Plaquette code › p. 382 — CSS-Plaquette codes are defined on a hypercubic lattice.

𝐷 3 FACE-CENTERED CUBIC (FCC) LATTICE dthree  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Cannonball lattice  

> DESCRIPTION

Laminated three-dimensional lattice consisting of lay-ers of triangular lattices.  

> PROTECTION

The 𝐷 3 fcc lattice exhibits the densest packing and high-est kissing number of 12 in three dimensions. The Kepler conjecture 

[2164] states that the 𝐷 3 fcc lattice has the densest packing in 3D. It was first proven that this lattice was the densest 3D lattice pack-ing [ 2165 ]. Determining the maximum density of any sphere pack-ing in 3D was then reduced to a computationally tractable problem [2155 ], which was solved [ 2166 ] and formalized in automated proof checking software [2167].  

> PARENTS

⊲ 𝐷 𝑛 checkerboard lattice › p. 255 — The 𝐷 3 root lattice is equivalent to the 𝐴 3 root lattice [ 101 , Ch. 10]. ⊲ 𝐴 𝑛 lattice › p. 254 —The 𝐷 3 fcc lattice is equivalent to the 𝐴 3 root lattice [ 32 , Ch. 1, pg. 13].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Rhombic dodecahedron code › p. 275 — The Voronoi cell of the 𝐷 3 fcc lattice is a rhombic dodecahedron [ 32 , Ch. 21, pg. 464].

DUAL LATTICE dual_lattice  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Reciprocal lattice ⊲ Polar lattice  

> DESCRIPTION

For any dimensional lattice 𝐿 , the dual lattice is the set of vectors whose inner products with the elements of 𝐿 are integers. More technically, the dual lattice is 

𝐿 ⊥ = {𝑦 ∈ R𝑛 | 𝑥 · 𝑦 ∈ Z ∀ 𝑥 ∈ 𝐿 }, (101) where the Euclidean inner product is used. A lattice that is contained in its dual, 𝐿 ⊆ 𝐿 ⊥, is called integral .The Gram matrix of such a lattice has integer entries, and its dual is contained in a suitably scaled version of itself, 𝐿 ⊥ ⊆ 𝐿 /det 𝐿 .Integral lattices are classified into even or odd : an even lattice has every squared norm even, while an odd lattice has at least one vector of odd squared norm. A lattice that is equal to its dual, 𝐿 ⊥ = 𝐿 , is called unimodular or 

self-dual . 

> PROTECTION

The Gram matrix of 𝐿 ⊥ is the inverse of that of 𝐿 . The generator matrix of 𝐿 ⊥ is the transposed inverse of that of 𝐿 . 

> PARENT

⊲ Lattice › p. 259  

> CHILD

⊲ Unimodular lattice › p. 262  

> COUSINS

⊲ Dual linear code › p. 218 — Dual lattices are lattice analogues of dual codes. ⊲ Body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice › p. 257 — The bcc and fcc lattices are dual to each other.

HONEYCOMB TILING honeycomb  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Hexagonal tiling  

> DESCRIPTION

A two-dimensional point set whose points are vertices of hexagons. It is not a lattice since its points do not form a group under addition. As a tiling, its dual (whose points lie at the centers of each triangle) is the triangular tiling. The ruby tiling is a fattened honeycomb tiling interpolating between the honeycomb tiling and triangular lattice.  

> PARENT

⊲ Analog code › p. 256  

> COUSINS

⊲ 𝐴 2 triangular lattice › p. 254 — The Voronoi cell of the trian-gular lattice (honeycomb tiling) is a hexagon (triangle). Triangular and hexagonal tilings are dual to each other as tilings, i.e., the ver-tices of one tiling lie at the centers of faces of the other. Points of the honeycomb tiling form two triangular lattices. The ruby tiling is a fattened honeycomb tiling interpolating between the honeycomb tiling and triangular lattice. ⊲ Polygon code › p. 273 — The faces of the honeycomb tiling are hexagons, while the faces of its dual triangular tiling are triangles. ⊲ Ruby Floquet code › p. 449 — The ruby Floquet code is defined on the ruby tiling. ⊲ Honeycomb Floquet code › p. 403 — The honeycomb Floquet code is defined on the honeycomb tiling. ⊲ Non-Abelian Kitaev honeycomb code › p. 419 —The Kitaev honeycomb model is defined on the honeycomb tiling. 

⊲ Truncated trihexagonal (4.6.12) color code › p. 465 — The 4.6.12 (trun-cated trihexagonal or square-hexagon-dodecagon) tiling is obtained by applying a fattening procedure to the honeycomb tiling [ 411 ]. 

⊲ Honeycomb (6.6.6) color code › p. 402 — The 6.6.6 color code is de-fined on the honeycomb tiling. ⊲ Kitaev honeycomb code › p. 409 —The Kitaev honeycomb code is defined on the honeycomb tiling.

LATTICE points_into_lattices  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes states (codewords) in coordinates of an 𝑛 -dimensional lattice, i.e., a discrete set of points in Euclidean space 

R𝑛 that forms a group under vector addition when translated so that one point is at the origin. The number of codewords may be infinite because the ambient Euclidean space is unbounded, so various re-stricted versions have to be constructed in practice. Since lattices are closed under addition, lattice-based codes can be thought of as linear codes over the reals. An 𝑛 -dimensional lattice-based code can be defined using a gen-erator matrix 𝐺 of rank 𝑛 , where the rows of 𝐺 are the lattice transla-tion vectors 𝑔 𝑖 . Any lattice point 𝑥 is a linear combination of transla-tion vectors with integer coefficients 𝑐 𝑖 , 𝑥 = 𝑐 1𝑔 1 +𝑐 2𝑔 2 +· · ·+ 𝑐 𝑛 𝑔 𝑛 . A lattice-based code can also be defined using the Gram matrix 𝐺𝐺 𝑇 .The automorphism group of a lattice is the group of all isometries that preserve the origin and map the lattice into itself. This group is a subgroup of the orthogonal group 𝑂 (𝑛 ), which is the group of isometries in Euclidean space. An orthogonal matrix 𝑈 leaves the lattice invariant if there exists an integer matrix 𝐴 of determinant 

±1 such that 

𝐴𝐺 = 𝐺𝑈 . (102) The affine automorphism group is the group obtained from adding lattice translations to the automorphism group. Two lattices with generator matrices 𝐺, 𝐺 ′ are equivalent if one is obtained from the other by the following combination of an or-thogonal matrix 𝑈 and a change of scale 𝑐 ≠ 0,

𝐺 ′ = 𝑐 𝐴𝐺𝑈 , (103) where 𝐴 is an integer matrix of determinant ±1. 

> PROTECTION

Lattices are characterized by the minimum (Euclidean) distance 𝑑 min between two lattice points, the kissing number 𝐾 min of nearest neighbors at each lattice point, and the volume 𝑉 = | det 𝐺 |,which is the volume of the lattice’s fundamental region that can be used to tile all of R𝑛 .The minimum Euclidean distance is an analogue of the minimum distance of binary codes. Half of this distance is called the packing radius .The nominal coding gain 𝛾 𝑐 (a.k.a. Hermite parameter ) of an 𝑛 -dimensional lattice is

The shortest vector problem (SVP) asks for the shortest nonzero vector in a given lattice and is related to cryptographic protocols. MODULATION SCHEME modulation  

> DESCRIPTION

A sphere packing mapped into a time-dependent elec-tromagnetic signal [ 178 , 179 ]. There is a close relation between ab-stract real-space encodings and modulation schemes, and certain simple sphere packings are often synonymous with their correspond-ing modulation schemes. Linear modulation schemes encode points into amplitudes of basis waveforms. Pulse-amplitude modulation (PAM) associates each point with a real-valued amplitude of one quadrature of an electro-magnetic waveform [ 179 , Sec. 10.5]. Quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) associates each point in a two-dimensional constellation with a complex-valued two-quadrature amplitude of a band-limited signal [179, Ch. 16].  

> NOTES

⊲ See books [ 2218 , 2219 ] for an introduction to modulation schemes.

SPHERE PACKING sphere_packing  

> DESCRIPTION

An analog code whose points can be thought of as form-ing centers of spheres that pack Euclidean space R𝑛 . Such packings can also be interpreted as complex sphere packings by mapping pairs of real coordinates to the complex plane. Sphere packings provide ways of encoding digital or analog information into the fre-quency, amplitude, and phase of one or more analog waveforms for transmission through, e.g., an optical fiber or free space. This is due to Kotelnikov’s [ 2233 ] and Shannon’s [ 2234 ] fundamental observation that a discretized electromagnetic signal of finite bandwidth and average power 𝑃 can be represented as a vector in R𝑛 with squared norm 𝑛𝑃 . Questions of capacity of electromagnetic communication channels then translate to packing problems in R𝑛 [32]. In the electromagnetic context, the information stored in the code is called the bitstream , coordinates used for encoding are often called signal points and form a constellation , and R𝑛 is called the 

signal space . 

> PROTECTION

Sphere packings can be used to transmit information using electromagnetic signals. The primary noise channel for such signals is the additive white Gaussian channel (AWGN) , which adds a random Gaussian-distributed displacement with variance 𝜎 2 to each signal point. Protection of a constellation thus depends on how far apart its points are in terms of the Euclidean distance. As usual, there is a tradeoff between packing of space and level of protection. For a given 𝑛, 𝑀, 𝑃 , the Gaussian channel coding problem 

asks to find a set of 𝑀 codewords of norm ≤ 𝑛𝑃 that minimizes the error probability during transmission; see [32, Ch. 3]. The minimum distance 𝑑 of a constellation is the infimum over distances between any two of its points. The corresponding packing radius is 𝑑 /2. The density Δ is the fraction of the total volume of space that is occupied by spheres of packing radius centered at each point in the sphere packing. Defining a density for infinite constellations can be done using a limit [101, pg. 349]. The Kabatiansky-Levenshtein bound [ 2235 ][ 32 , Ch. 9] says that any sphere packing must satisfy 1 

> 𝑛

log 2 Δ ≲ −0.5990 asymptotically with dimension 𝑛 . This bound improved over the Rogers bound [2236 ] and the Sidelnikov bound [ 2237 ]. Afterwards came the Lev-enshtein bound [ 156 , 873 , 2030 , 2214 , 2215 ], Cohn-Elkies LP bounds [2216 ], and, most recently, an improvement of the Rogers bound [2238 ]. For more details, see [ 101 , Ch. 10.4][ 32 , Ch. 1]. There exists an 𝑛 -dimensional sphere packing whose density is at least 𝑐𝑛 2/2𝑛 

for 𝑐 being a universal constant [2239]. The covering problem asks how one can cover all of space by over-lapping spheres in the most efficient way. The thickness Θ (a.k.a. covering density or sparsity) of a covering is defined in the same way as the (packing) density, but with the spheres’ covering radius 

now being the smallest one such that the spheres cover all space. There is an upper bound on the thickness of a covering in dimen-sions 𝑛 > 3 [2240] as well as an asymptotic lower bound [2241], 

𝑛 𝑒 √𝑒 ≲ Θ ≤ 𝑛 ln 𝑛 + 𝑛 ln ln 𝑛 + 5𝑛 . (109) Sphere packings can be used as quantizers or analog-to-digital con-verters , which perform data compression by rounding a vector of real numbers to the point in the packing that is closest to the vector. The set of all points closest to a point 𝑥 is called the Voronoi cell of 

𝑥 . The quantizer problem asks for a sphere packing that minimizes a dimensionless quantity proportional to the average mean-squared error per dimension; see [ 32 , Sec. 3.2]. For dimension 𝑛 , this mini-mum is known as 𝐺 𝑛 . It is known only for 𝑛 = 1, 2 and is attained by the integer and triangular lattices, respectively.  

> RATE

The rate of a code consisting of 𝑀 codewords that represent a signal of bandwidth 𝑊 and duration 𝑇 is defined as 

𝑅 = 1

𝑇 log 2 𝑀 bits/s . (110) The Shannon capacity of the AWGN channel for a signal whose power is 𝑃 is 

𝐶 = 𝑊 log 2

> DESCRIPTION

ANTIPRISM CODE antiprism  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical (3, 2𝑞 ) code for 𝑞 ≥ 2 whose codewords are the vertices of a 𝑞 -antiprism.  

> PROTECTION

The antiprism vertices consists of two 𝑞 -gon vertices with the 𝑞 -gons rotated by 2𝜋 /𝑞 degrees. The relative height and radii of the 𝑞 -gons can be modulated while still staying on the sphere. For the case when the two 𝑞 -gons are such that the 𝑞 = 2, 3 cases re-duce to the tetrahedron and octahedron, respectively, the antiprism is a spherical 3-design for 𝑞 ≥ 3, and a 2-design for 𝑞 = 2 [2272 ]. This can be seen as a consequence of [215, Lemma 6.11].  

> NOTES

𝑞 ≥ 3, and a 2-design for 𝑞 = 2 [ 2272 ]. This can be seen as a conse-quence of [ 215 , Lemma 6.11]. ⊲ Biorthogonal spherical code › p. 268
