BINARY ANTIPODAL CODE binary_antipodal  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Binary signal constellation  

> DESCRIPTION

An (𝑛, 𝐾, 4𝑑 /𝑛 ) spherical code obtained from a binary 

(𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 ) code via the antipodal mapping › p. 267 .

Antipodal mapping: The antipodal mapping, also known as a 

Euclidean-space image or 𝑌 2 construction), is a component-wise map-ping from binary space into Euclidean space. Each coordinate of a binary string is mapped into a sign, 0 → + 1 and 1 → − 1 [101 ,Example 1.2.1].  

> PARENT

⊲ Polyphase code › p. 274 — The polyphase mapping for 𝑞 = 2

reduces to the antipodal mapping › p. 267 . 

> CHILDREN

⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) modulation format › p. 268 — A binary antipodal code can be thought of as a concatenation of a binary outer code with a BPSK inner code. A single-bit binary code yields a spherical (𝑛, 2, 4) spherical code under the antipodal mapping 

> › p. 267

, which is equivalent to the BPSK code for dimension 𝑛 = 2.

⊲ Kerdock spherical code › p. 272  

> COUSINS

⊲ Binary code › p. 179 — Binary antipodal codes are spheri-cal codes obtained from binary codes via the antipodal mapping 

> › p. 267

. ⊲ Slepian group-orbit code › p. 276 — Any length-𝑛 binary lin-ear code can be used to define a diagonal subgroup of 𝑛 -dimensional rotation matrices with ±1 on the diagonals via the antipodal map-ping › p. 267 0 → + 1 and 1 → − 1. The orbit of this subgroup yields the corresponding Slepian group-orbit code; see [ 101 , Thm. 8.5.2]. 

⊲ Biorthogonal spherical code › p. 268 — Each first-order RM (1, 𝑚 )

code maps to a (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 +1) biorthogonal spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 [ 1134 ][ 1118 , Sec. 6.4][ 101 , pg. 19]. In other words, first-order RM (biorthogonal spherical) codes form ortho-plexes in Hamming (Euclidean) space. ⊲ Hypercube code › p. 271 

— Binary antipodal codes are subcodes of a hypercube code since the hypercube code corresponds to the Hamming 𝑛 -cube (a.k.a. Boolean hypercube) embedded into the unit 𝑛 -sphere. ⊲ Simplex 268 spherical code › p. 276 — Binary simplex codes map to (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 + 1)

simplex spherical codes under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 [1118 ,Sec. 6.5.2][ 101 , pg. 18]. In other words, simplex (simplex spherical) codes form simplices in Hamming (Euclidean) space. 

BINARY BALANCED SPHERICAL CODE binary_balanced  

> DESCRIPTION

An (𝑛 − 1, 𝐾, 𝑛𝑑 𝑛𝑤 −𝑤 2 ) spherical code obtained from a constant-weight-𝑤 binary (𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 ) code via the component-wise binary balanced mapping. The binary balanced mapping (also known as the CW 2 construction )is defined as 

0 →√︂ 𝑤 𝑛 (𝑛 − 𝑤 )

1 → − √︂ 𝑛 − 𝑤 𝑛𝑤 .

(113) This construction can be extended to the general balanced binary construction CW 𝑞 for spherical code alphabets of size 𝑞 [ 101 , Sec. 6.6].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [101, Sec. 6.2] for more details.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Spherical code › p. 277 ⊲ Concatenated code › p. 162 — A bi-nary balanced spherical code can be thought of as a concatenation of a constant-weight binary outer code with a shifted and scaled BPSK-like inner code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Constant-weight code › p. 183 — Binary balanced spherical codes are obtained from constant-weight binary codes. ⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) modulation format › p. 268 — A binary balanced spherical code can be thought of as a concatenation of a constant-weight binary outer code with a shifted and scaled BPSK-like inner code. 

BINARY PSK (BPSK) MODULATION FORMAT [2274] bpsk  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) modulation code ⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) modulation scheme ⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) signaling format ⊲ Binary antipodal modulation ⊲ Phase-reversal keying (PRK) ⊲ Antipodal signaling  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes one bit of information into a constellation of antipodal points ±𝛼 for complex 𝛼 . These points are typically associated with two phases of an electromagnetic signal.  

> RATE

Achieves capacity of AWGN in the low signal-to-noise regime [2220 ] (see also [ 2274 ]). BPSK concatenated with classical-quantum polar codes approaches the Holevo capacity of the pure-loss › p. 508 

optical channel in the low-photon-number regime [2275].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Telephone-line modems throughout 1950s and 1960s: Bell 103 and 202, as well as international standards V.21 [ 220 ] and V.23 [221].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Phase-shift keying (PSK) modulation format › p. 273 — BPSK is also known as 2-PSK. ⊲ Binary antipodal code › p. 267 — A binary antipodal code can be thought of as a concatenation of a binary outer code with a BPSK inner code. A single-bit binary code yields a spherical (𝑛, 2, 4) spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 ,which is equivalent to the BPSK code for dimension 𝑛 = 2. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Pulse-amplitude modulation (PAM) format › p. 260 — BPSK for real 𝛼 is the simplest non-trivial PAM encoding. ⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — Concatenating binary linear codes with BPSK yields a standard way of digitizing the analog AWGN channel [ 179 , Ch. 29]. ⊲ Two-component cat code › p. 534 — BPSK (two-component cat) codes are used to transmit classical (quantum) information using (superpositions of) antipodal coherent states over classical (quan-tum) channels. ⊲ Polar c-q code › p. 570 — BPSK concatenated with classical-quantum polar codes approaches the Holevo capacity of the pure-loss › p. 508 optical channel in the low-photon-number regime [2275 ]. ⊲ Turbo code › p. 241 — Turbo codes can be concatenated with BPSK codes [ 2018 ]. ⊲ Binary balanced spherical code › p. 268 

— A binary balanced spherical code can be thought of as a concate-nation of a constant-weight binary outer code with a shifted and scaled BPSK-like inner code. ⊲ BPSK c-q modulation format › p. 571 

— BPSK (BPSK c-q) codes are used to transmit classical information using antipodal coherent states over classical (quantum) channels. 

⊲ Hadamard BPSK c-q modulation format › p. 572 — The Hadamard BPSK c-q code can be thought of as a concatenation of the Hadamard binary linear code with BPSK for the purposes of transmission of classical information over quantum channels. 

BIORTHOGONAL SPHERICAL CODE biorthogonal_spherical  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Cross polytope code ⊲ Hyperoctahedron code ⊲ Orthoplex code ⊲ Co-cube code  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical (𝑛, 2𝑛, 2) code whose codewords are all per-mutations of the 𝑛 -dimensional vectors (0, 0, · · · , 0, ±1), up to nor-malization. The code makes up the vertices of an 𝑛 -orthoplex (a.k.a. hyperoctahedron or cross polytope). For 𝑛 = 3, biorthogonal spherical codewords make up the vertices of an octahedron. For 𝑛 = 4, codewords make up the vertices of a 16-cell, or, equivalently, the Möbius-Kantor complex polygon. A quaternion realization of the vertices yields the quaternion group 

𝑄 .The set of permutations of (0, 0, · · · , 0, 1) forms an orthogonal set and yields the biorthogonal code when combined with the set of permutations of (0, 0, · · · , 0, −1). 

> PROTECTION

Biorthogonal spherical codes saturate the absolute bound for antipodal codes and the third Rankin bound [ 101 ]. Biorthogonal codes are unique up to equivalence [ 101 , pg. 19], which follows from saturating the Boroczky bound [ 2267 ]. The octahedron is the optimal antipodal configuration of 6 points in 3D space [ 2276 ].  

> NOTES

⊲ See the corresponding Bendwavy database entry [2277].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Polytope code › p. 274 — Biorthogonal spherical codewords in 2 (3, 4, 𝑛 ) dimensions form the vertices of a square (octahe-dron, 16-cell, 𝑛 -orthoplex). ⊲ Spherical sharp configuration › p. 279 

⊲ Lattice-shell code › p. 272 — Biorthogonal codewords form the mini-mal shell of the Z𝑛 hypercubic lattice. ⊲ Permutation spherical code › p. 273  

> CHILD

⊲ Quadrature PSK (QPSK) modulation format › p. 275 — The QPSK is equivalent to the biorthogonal spherical code for 𝑛 = 2. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Spherical design › p. 278 — Biorthogonal spherical codes are the only tight spherical 3-designs [ 101 , Tab. 9.3]. A suitable weighted union of the vertices of a hypercube and an orthoplex forms a weighted spherical 5-design in dimensions ≥ 3 [362 , Sec. 8.6, Ex. 5-2][ 363 , Exam. 2.6]. ⊲ 24-cell code › p. 266 — Vertices of a 24-cell can be split up into vertices of three 16-cells, which are biorthogonal spherical codes for 𝑛 = 4 [163 ]. The vertices of a 24-cell are a union of the vertices of a tesseract and a 16-cell [ 363 ,Exam. 2.6]. ⊲ Dual polytope code › p. 270 — Orthoplexes and hyper-cubes are dual to each other. ⊲ Hypercube code › p. 271 — Ortho-plexes and hypercubes are dual to each other. A suitable weighted union of the vertices of a hypercube and an orthoplex forms a 269 weighted spherical 5-design in dimensions ≥ 3 [362 , Sec. 8.6, Ex. 5-2][ 363 , Exam. 2.6]. ⊲ Binary antipodal code › p. 267 — Each first-order RM (1, 𝑚 ) code maps to a (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 +1) biorthogonal spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 [ 1134 ][ 1118 , Sec. 6.4][ 101 , pg. 19]. In other words, first-order RM (biorthogonal spherical) codes form orthoplexes in Hamming (Euclidean) space. ⊲ Antiprism code › p. 267 — The antiprism reduces to the octahedron for 𝑞 = 3.

⊲ [2𝑚 , 𝑚 + 1, 2𝑚 −1] First-order RM code › p. 173 — Each first-order RM code maps to a (2𝑚 , 2𝑚 +1) biorthogonal spherical code under the antipodal mapping › p. 267 [1134 ][ 1118 , Sec. 6.4][ 101 , pg. 19]. In other words, first-order RM (biorthogonal spherical) codes form ortho-plexes in Hamming (Euclidean) space. ⊲ Pulse-position modu-lation (PPM) format › p. 274 — PPM codewords form a spherical code whose constellation consists of the standard basis vectors. Adjoin-ing negatives yields the corresponding biorthogonal spherical code. 

⊲ Rhombic dodecahedron code › p. 275 — The vertices of a rhombic dodecahedron are a union of the vertices of a cube and an octahe-dron. ⊲ Kerdock spherical code › p. 272 — Kerdock spherical codes form spherical 3-designs because their codewords are unions of 

22𝑟 −1 + 1 orthoplexes [ 369 ]. ⊲ Polyphase code › p. 274 — Biorthog-onal spherical codes for dimension 𝑛 = 𝑝 with 𝑝 an odd prime admit a polyphase realization [ 101 , Sec. 7.7]. ⊲ Pulse-position (PPM) c-q modulation format › p. 574 — PPM c-q codewords are c-q spherical codes whose constellation consists of the standard basis vectors. Adjoining negatives yields the corresponding biorthogonal c-q spherical code. 

CAMERON-GOETHALS-SEIDEL (CGS) ISOTROPIC SUBSPACE CODE [2278] cgs_spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a (𝑞 (𝑞 2 − 𝑞 + 1), (𝑞 + 1)( 𝑞 3 + 1), 2 − 2/𝑞 2)

family of spherical codes for any prime-power 𝑞 . Constructed from generalized quadrangles, which in this case correspond to sets of totally isotropic points and lines in the projective space 𝑃𝐺 (5, 𝑞 )

[101 , Exam. 9.4.5]. There exist multiple distinct spherical codes using this construction for 𝑞 > 3 [105, 369].

CONSTANT-ENERGY SPHERICAL CODE points_into_spheres  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Spherical Kingdom › p. 12 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords are points on a real or complex sphere whose radius squared is called the energy . Typically, only angular distances between points are relevant for code performance, so one can normalize codewords of a constant-energy code to obtain up a spherical code, i.e., a constant energy code with energy one.  

> PROTECTION

Constant-energy codes are sphere packings constrained to lie on a sphere, meaning that they can be used to transmit in-formation through the AWGN channel. For a given dimension 𝑛 ,number of codewords 𝑀 , and average energy 𝑃 , the constant-energy Gaussian channel coding problem asks to find a set of 𝑀 codewords of energy 𝑛𝑃 that minimizes the error probability during transmission; see [32, Ch. 3].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [101, Ch. 7] for more details.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bounded-energy code › p. 257 — Constant-energy codes are bounded-energy codes constrained to lie on a sphere. ⊲ Two-point homogeneous-space code › p. 291 — Real spheres are compact connected two-point homogeneous spaces with quotient 𝑆𝑂 (𝐷 +

1)/ 𝑆𝑂 (𝐷 ) [942 , Table 1]. Complex spheres can be treated as real spheres of twice the dimension over R, with quotient 𝑆𝑈 (𝐷 +

1)/ 𝑆𝑈 (𝐷 ). In fact, spheres are compact three-point homogeneous spaces [2180, Sec. 6.6.1.1].  

> CHILD

⊲ Spherical code › p. 277  

> COUSINS

⊲ Real projective space code › p. 289 — Real projective space can be obtained from the sphere by identifying antipodal points, i.e., R𝑃 𝑁 = 𝑆 𝑁 /Z2. As such, real projective space codes are in one-to-one correspondence with antipodal spherical codes, with each antipodal pair of spherical codewords corresponding to one line in projective space. ⊲ Quantum spherical code (QSC) › p. 529 —QSCs are quantum counterparts of spherical and constant-energy codes because they store information in quantum superpositions of points on a sphere in quantum phase space.

DISPHENOIDAL 288-CELL CODE disphenoidal288cell  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical (4, 48 , 2 − √2) code [101, Exam. 1.2.6] whose codewords are the vertices of the disphenoidal 288-cell. Codewords are the union of two 24-point lattice shells of the 𝐷 4 lattice. DUAL POLYTOPE CODE dual_polytope  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Reciprocal polytope code  

> DESCRIPTION

For a spherical code whose codewords are vertices of a convex polytope, the dual code consists of codewords corresponding to the facets of the original polytope, i.e., to the vertices of the polar dual polytope. For regular polytopes, these dual codewords can be represented by the normalized centers of the facets of the original polytope. The dual codewords make up the vertices of the polytope dual to the original polytope. If the dual polytope is the same as the original polytope, the original polytope is said to be self-dual . Self-dual polytopes have the same number of facets as vertices.  

> PARENT

⊲ Polytope code › p. 274

Optimal configuration of 12 points in 3D space [101, pg. 76]. Saturates the absolute bound for antipodal codes [101, pg. 314].  

> NOTES

KERDOCK SPHERICAL CODE [1364, 2295, 2296] kerdock_spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

[ 101 , pg. 157]. These codes are optimal for their parameters for

LATTICE-SHELL CODE [2299, 2300] lattice_shell  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical code whose codewords are scaled versions of points on a lattice. A 𝑚 -shell code consists of normalized lattice vectors 𝑥 with squared norm ∥𝑥 ∥2 = 𝑚 . Each code is constructed by normalizing a set of lattice vectors in one or more shells , i.e., sets of lattice points lying on a hypersphere.

PERMUTATION SPHERICAL CODE [2306, 2307] permutation_spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

Slepian group-orbit code whose codewords are con-structed from an arbitrary unit vector in two possible variants. Vari-ant 1 consists of codewords that are permutations of the vector’s coordinates, while Variant 2 consists of such permutations and all possible sign changes of the vector’s components.  

> RATE

Number of codewords cannot increase exponentially with di-mension 𝑛 [2308]  

> DECODING

⊲ Efficient maximum-likelihood decoder determining the Voronoi region of an error word.  

> NOTES

⊲ See [ 101 , Ch. 4] for more details and tables of optimal codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Slepian group-orbit code › p. 276 — Permutations and sign changes can be implemented on vectors by orthogonal matrices, so permutation spherical codes are Slepian group-orbit codes.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Biorthogonal spherical code › p. 268 ⊲ Simplex spherical code › p. 276 

PETERSEN SPHERICAL CODE [373] petersen_spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

A (4, 10 , 1/6) spherical code whose codewords corre-spond to vertices of the Petersen graph. Its Gram matrix is con-structed by putting −2/3 whenever two vertices are adjacent in the graph, and 1/6 otherwise. The code is optimal for its parameters [373].  

> PARENT

⊲ Spherical design › p. 278 — The Petersen spherical code forms a spherical 2-design [373].  

> COUSINS

⊲ [15 , 6, 5] Petersen cycle code › p. 171 — The Petersen spheri-cal code is a spherical realization associated with the Petersen cycle code. ⊲ Simplex spherical code › p. 276 — Codewords of the Petersen spherical code correspond to midpoints of the 5-cell [373]. 

PHASE-SHIFT KEYING (PSK) MODULATION FORMAT psk  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Phase-shift keying (PSK) modulation code 

⊲ Phase-shift keying (PSK) modulation scheme ⊲ Phase-shift key-ing (PSK) signaling format  

> DESCRIPTION

A 𝑞 -ary phase-shift keying ( 𝑞 -PSK) encodes one 𝑞 -ary digit of information into a constellation of 𝑞 points distributed equidistantly on a circle in C or, equivalently, R2.For example, such a constellation could be 

{1, 𝑒 𝑖 2 𝜋 𝑞 , · · · , 𝑒 𝑖 2 𝜋 𝑞 (𝑞 −1) } . (114) Each point is typically associated with a complex amplitude of an electromagnetic signal, and information is encoded into the phase of that signal. Concatenating PSK with 𝑞 -ary codes yields a natural non-binary way of digitizing the analog AWGN channel [2309, 2310].  

> RATE

As the constellation size 𝑞 grows, 𝑞 -PSK approaches the Shan-non AWGN capacity of the corresponding two-dimensional signal set [2224, Fig. 11.7].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Telephone-line modems: 1967 Milgo 4400/48 and international standard V.27 used 8-PSK [287].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Polygon code › p. 273 — The PSK constellation forms a 𝑞 -gon. ⊲ Polyphase code › p. 274 — A polyphase code can be thought of as a concatenation of a 𝑞 -ary outer code with a PSK inner code. When the outer code is trivial, the construction reduces to a PSK code. ⊲ Modulation scheme › p. 260 — PSK is a modulation whose constellation consists of points arranged equidistantly on a circle.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Binary PSK (BPSK) modulation format › p. 268 — BPSK is also known as 2-PSK. ⊲ Quadrature PSK (QPSK) modulation format › p. 275 — The QPSK is also known as 4-PSK.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Gray code › p. 188 — 1D Gray codes are often concatenated with PSKs so that the Hamming distance between the bitstrings encoded into the points is a discretized version of the Euclidean distance between the points. ⊲ Cat code › p. 515 — PSK (cat) codes are used to transmit classical (quantum) information using (super-positions of) single-mode coherent states distributed on a circle over classical (quantum) channels. ⊲ Hyperbolic sphere packing › p. 289 

— Hyperbolic PSK constellations may yield improved performance over Euclidean ones [ 2311 ]. ⊲ PSK c-q modulation format › p. 573 —PSK (PSK c-q) codes are used to transmit classical information using single-mode coherent states distributed on a circle over classical (quantum) channels.

POLYPHASE CODE [2313–2323] polyphase  

> DESCRIPTION

A spherical code obtained from a binary code, 𝑞 -ary code, or 𝑞 -ary code over Z𝑞 via a component-wise mapping of each 

𝑞 -ary digit to a 𝑞 th root of unity in a generalization of the antipodal mapping › p. 267 .For example, for the case 𝑞 = 4, one can map either the ring-based alphabet Z4 = {0, 1, 2, 3} or the field-based alphabet F22 =

{00 , 01 , 10 , 11 } to the set {1, 𝜃, 𝜃 2, 𝜃 3 } for some fourth root of unity 𝜃 .

POLYTOPE CODE polytope  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical code whose codewords are the vertices of a polytope, i.e., a geometrical figure bounded by lines, planes, and hyperplanes in either real [ 163 ] or complex [ 214 ] space. A polytope in two (three, four) dimensions is called a polygon (polyhedron, polychoron).

REAL-CLIFFORD SUBGROUP-ORBIT CODE [2050, 2051] sidelnikov  

> DESCRIPTION

Slepian group-orbit code of dimension 2𝑟 , approximate asymptotic size 2.38 · 2𝑟 (𝑟 +1)/ 2+1, and distance 1. Code is constructed by applying elements of an index-two subgroup of the real Clif-ford group › p. 244 , when taken as a subgroup of the orthogonal group [2045 ], onto the vector (1, 0, 0, · · · , 0). This group is the automor-phism group of the BW lattice, and the resulting codes coincide with the optimal spherical codes for dimensions {4, 8, 16 }.Taking the orbit under the entire real Clifford group › p. 244 yields spherical codes with twice the points and distance 2 − √2. 

> PARENTS

⊲ Slepian group-orbit code › p. 276 ⊲ Spherical design › p. 278 

— The orbit of any point under the real Clifford subgroup is a spheri-cal 7-design [374], and some are 11-designs [375].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ 𝐵𝑊 32 lattice-shell code › p. 265 — The minimal 𝐵𝑊 32 

lattice-shell code is equivalent to the real Clifford subgroup-orbit code for 𝑛 = 32 . ⊲ Λ16 lattice-shell code › p. 264 — The minimal Λ16 

lattice-shell code is equivalent to the real Clifford subgroup-orbit code for 𝑛 = 16 . ⊲ 24-cell code › p. 266 — The 24-cell code is equiva-lent to the real Clifford subgroup-orbit code for 𝑛 = 4. ⊲ Witting polytope code › p. 279 — The Witting polytope code is equivalent to the real Clifford subgroup-orbit code for 𝑛 = 8. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Barnes-Wall (BW) lattice › p. 257 — The automorphism group of BW lattices is a subgroup of index 2 of a real Clifford group  

> › p. 244

[ 2050 , 2051 ] (see [ 2045 , 2058 ] for an explanation). ⊲ Clifford group › p. 244 — The automorphism group of BW lattices is a subgroup of index 2 of a real Clifford group › p. 244 [ 2050 , 2051 ] (see [ 2045 , 2058 ]for an explanation). ⊲ Disphenoidal 288-cell code › p. 270 — The disphenoidal 288-cell code is a group-orbit code with the group being the real Clifford group › p. 244 in 4 dimensions. ⊲ Clifford subgroup-orbit QSC › p. 517 — Clifford group-orbit QSCs are quantum counterparts of real Clifford subgroup-orbit codes.

SIMPLEX SPHERICAL CODE simplex_spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical (𝑛, 𝑛 +1, 2+2/𝑛 ) code whose codewords are all permutations of the 𝑛 + 1-dimensional vector (1, 1, · · · , 1, −𝑛 ), up to normalization, forming an 𝑛 -simplex. Codewords are all equidistant and their components add up to zero. Simplex spherical codewords in 2 (3, 4) dimensions form the vertices of a triangle (tetrahedron, 5-cell). In general, the code makes up the vertices of an 𝑛 -simplex. The union of a simplex and its antipodal simplex forms the vertices of a bi-simplex, which has 2(𝑛 + 1) vertices. See [101, Sec. 7.7] for a parameterization.  

> PROTECTION

Simplex spherical codes saturate the absolute bound, the Levenshtein bound and, for 2 < 𝜌 ≤ 4, the first two Rankin bounds [ 101 ]. All simplex codes are unique up to equivalence [ 101 ,pg. 18], which follows from saturating the Boroczky bound [2267].  

> NOTES

⊲ See the corresponding Bendwavy database entry for the 5-cell [2329].

⊲ Self-dual polytope code › p. 276 — The simplex is self-dual.

SLEPIAN GROUP-ORBIT CODE [2330–2332] slepian_group  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical code in 𝑛 dimensions whose codewords cor-respond to points in an orbit of some initial vector under a generating group 𝐺 , which is a subgroup of the orthogonal group 𝑂 (𝑛 ) acting by Euclidean isometries. Neither the vector nor the group are unique for a given code.  

> PROTECTION

Code properties depend on the relationship between the group and the initial vector, and the number of codewords is the number of cosets of an initial vector’s symmetry subgroup in 𝐺 per the orbit-stabilizer theorem. See Refs. [ 2333 – 2336 ] for allowed code parameters.  

> NOTES

⊲ See [2337][101, Ch. 8] for more details and code tables.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Spherical code › p. 277 ⊲ Group-orbit code › p. 166 — Slepian group-orbit codes are group-orbit codes on spheres.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Permutation spherical code › p. 273 — Permutations and sign changes can be implemented on vectors by orthogonal matri-ces, so permutation spherical codes are Slepian group-orbit codes. 

⊲ Real-Clifford subgroup-orbit code › p. 275 ⊲ Torus-layer spherical 277 code (TLSC) › p. 279 — Polyphase codewords can be implemented by acting on the all-ones initial vector by block-diagonal orthogonal matrices whose 2 × 2 rotation blocks encode the codeword com-ponents [ 101 , Ch. 8]. TLSC codes are generalizations of polyphase codes to other initial vectors and are examples of Abelian Slepian-group codes. ⊲ Polytope code › p. 274 — Vertices of polytope codes typically form an orbit of the polytope’s symmetry group.

SPHERICAL CODE spherical  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords are points on an 𝑛 -dimensional sphere 𝑆 𝑛 −1 with radius one. A spherical code is typically denoted by parameters (𝑛, 𝑀, 𝜌 ),where 𝑛 is the ambient dimension, 𝑀 is the size or number of code-words, and 𝜌 is the squared minimum distance , i.e., the smallest squared Euclidean distance between pairs of distinct codewords, 

𝜌 = min ∥𝑥 − 𝑦 ∥2 s.t. 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐶, 𝑥 ≠ 𝑦 . (115) A spherical code can be defined using the Gram matrix 𝐺 = 𝑋 𝑋 𝑇 ,where the rows of 𝑋 are the codeword vectors. The Gram matrix is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and has all diagonal elements equal to one. The code dimension is equal to the rank of 𝐺 , which can be less than the dimension of the codeword vectors. Spherical codeword components are often taken from a discrete set of real values called an alphabet . For example, codewords of any length-𝑛 binary code can be mapped into spherical codewords with alphabet {± 1/√𝑛 } via the antipodal mapping › p. 267 0 → + 1 and 

1 → − 1 [101, Example 1.2.1].  

> PROTECTION

The Euclidean distance between two points is related to the dot product as 

∥𝑥 − 𝑦 ∥2 = 2 − 2𝑥 · 𝑦 , (116) where 𝑥 · 𝑦 is the Euclidean inner product. As a result, the angular distance ,

𝜃 = arccos (𝑥 · 𝑦 ) ∈ [ 0, 𝜋 ] , (117) can be equivalently used to quantify code performance. The size of an (𝑛, 𝑀, 𝜌 ) spherical code with 𝑑 distances between distinct points satisfies the absolute bound , [368]

SPHERICAL DESIGN [368] spherical_design  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical code whose codewords are uniformly dis-tributed in a way that is useful for determining averages of polyno-mials over the real sphere. A spherical code is a spherical design of 

strength 𝑡 , i.e., a 𝑡 -design, if the average of any polynomial of degree up to 𝑡 over its codewords is equal to the average over the entire sphere. A weighed spherical design is a generalization in which the average over codewords is non-uniform. Spherical designs can also be defined for complex spheres, and there are ways to convert between the two [366, Lemma 3.6].  

> PROTECTION

The number of points |𝑋 | of an 𝑛 -dimensional spherical design 𝑋 is bounded by [368] 

|𝑋 | ≥ 

(␀𝑛 +𝑠 −1

> 𝑛 −1

 + ␀𝑛 +𝑠 −2

> 𝑛 −1

 𝑡 = 2𝑠 

2␀𝑛 +𝑠 −1

> 𝑛 −1

 𝑡 = 2𝑠 + 1 , (121) and designs saturating the above inequality are called tight .Spherical designs with asymptotically optimal cardinality exist for all 𝑛 [2350], proving the Korevaar-Meyers conjecture [2351].

TORUS-LAYER SPHERICAL CODE (TLSC) [2355] tlsc  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords are elements of a foliation of the 

2𝑛 −1-dimensional hypersphere 𝑆 2𝑛 −1 using flat tori 𝑆 1 × 𝑆 1 ×· · ·× 𝑆 1.Related constructions include the spherical codes by Hopf foliations (SCHF) [2356].  

> DECODING

> NOTES

⊲ See [2357, Sec. 5.2] for an exposition.

WITTING POLYTOPE CODE witting_polytope  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ 421 polytope code ⊲ Gosset polytope code  

> DESCRIPTION

Spherical (8, 240 , 1) code whose codewords are the ver-tices of the Witting complex polytope, the 421 polytope, and the minimal lattice-shell code of the 𝐸 8 lattice. The code is optimal and unique up to equivalence [ 32 , 110 , 111 ]. Antipodal pairs of points of the 421 polytope code correspond to the 120 tritangent planes of a canonical sextic curve in C𝑃 3 [103–106]. A representation of the codewords consists of the 112 vectors obtained from permutations of (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, ±2, ±2) together with the 128 vectors (± 1)×8 for which the number of minus signs is even. After normalization, these are precisely the 240 minimal vectors of the 𝐸 8 lattice. See [214, pg. 132] for a complex representation. Recursively taking its kissing configurations yields the (7, 56 , 1/3),

(6, 27 , 1/4), (5, 16 , 1/5), (4, 10 , 1/6), and (3, 6, 1/7) spherical codes [110].  

> PROTECTION

Code yields an optimal solution to the kissing problem in 8D [ 2264 , 2265 ], saturates the Levenshtein bound [ 2251 ], and is unique up to equivalence [ 110 ]. It carries a 4-class association 280  

> FIG. 57: Projection of the coordinates of the Witting polytope.

scheme, and the inner products with respect to any codeword are 

±1, ±1/2, and 0 with multiplicities 1, 56 , and 126 , respectively [110].

𝑅 -LINEAR CODE rings_linear  

> DESCRIPTION

A code of length 𝑛 over a ring 𝑅 is 𝑅 -linear if it is a submodule of 𝑅 𝑛 . Axiomatically, one can define such a code by assuming that the message set is a module over the alphabet and that encoding functions are module homomorphisms [38]. For finite commutative Frobenius rings, the standard inner prod-uct, duality, and MacWilliams identities extend from the field case [1099 , Secs. 6.4 and 6.5]. There is a standard form for codes over finite chain rings with maximal ideals [2370, Thm. 2.12].

LINEAR CODE OVER Z4 quaternary_over_z4  

> DESCRIPTION

A code that forms a subgroup of Z𝑛  

> 4

under addition. More technically, linear codes over Z4 are submodules of Z𝑛  

> 4

.Linear codes over Z4 can be defined in terms of a generator matrix 

𝐺 , whose rows generate the 𝑘 -dimensional codespace. Given a message (i.e., logical string) 𝑥 , the corresponding encoded codeword is 𝐺 𝑇 𝑥 .A code’s generator matrix can be reduced via coordinate permu-tations to its standard form 

 𝐼 𝑘 1 𝐴 𝐵 

0 2𝐼 𝑘 2 2𝐶 



, (125) where 𝐴, 𝐶 are binary matrices, and where 𝐵 is a quaternary matrix. Such a code encodes 4𝑘 1 2𝑘 2 codewords, consisting of 𝑘 1 logical qua-ternary digits and 𝑘 2 logical bits. It is called an (𝑛, 4𝑘 1 2𝑘 2 )Z4 linear code over Z4 of type 4𝑘 1 2𝑘 2 . The generator matrix forms a basis when there are no logical bits, i.e., the submodule is free if and only if 

𝑘 2 = 0 [109]. Two linear codes over Z4 are monomially equivalent if the code-words of one code can be mapped into those of the other under a permutation and coordinate sign flips. The monomial automorphism group of a linear code over Z4 is the largest subgroup of coordinate permutations and sign flips that maps the code onto itself.  

> PROTECTION

Quaternary codes over Z4 come with a Hamming dis-tance, which is the minimum number of nonzero coordinates of a nonzero codeword. They also protect from cyclic shifts in each quaternary digit, which are quantified by the Lee metric. The Lee weight of a digit is given by 𝑤 𝐿 (0) = 0, 𝑤 𝐿 (1) = 1, 𝑤 𝐿 (2) = 2, and 

𝑤 𝐿 (3) = 1, and the Lee weight of a string is the sum of the Lee weights of its digits. The Lee distance of a code is the minimum Lee weight of a nonzero codeword [1099, Secs. 6.2 and 6.3]. The Lee distance 𝑑 𝐿 between two digits 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ Z4 governs how many cyclic shifts it takes to connect them, and is thus related to the Euclidean distance between the vectors 𝑖 𝑎 and 𝑖 𝑏 as 2𝑑 𝐿 (𝑎, 𝑏 ) =

∥𝑖 𝑎 − 𝑖 𝑏 ∥2. Quaternary codes over the Lee metric are thus naturally mapped to QPSK codes. Weight enumerators › p. 209 have also been extended to the Lee metric [2373].

> DESCRIPTION

A code encoding 𝐾 states (codewords) in 𝑛 coordinates over the ring Z𝑞 of integers modulo 𝑞 that forms an Abelian sub-group of Z𝑛 𝑞 under addition. Since addition of 𝑚 identical elements is equivalent to multiplying by 𝑚 , linear codes over Z𝑞 are automat-ically closed under scalar multiplication. More technically, linear codes over Z𝑞 are submodules of Z𝑛 𝑞 .Linear codes can be defined using generator matrices [ 154 , 2375 ,2376 ]. There is a standard form of the generator matrix for even 

𝑞 and an upper-triangular permutation-equivalent standard form when 𝑞 is a prime power [1152, 2248].

QUATERNARY RM (QRM) CODE [143] quaternary_reed_muller  

> DESCRIPTION

A quaternary linear code over Z4 whose binary mod-two reduction is an RM code. This code family includes the quaternary codes whose Gray images are the binary Kerdock and Preparata codes. The code is usually noted as QRM (𝑟, 𝑚 ), with its mod-two reduction yielding the RM code RM (𝑟, 𝑚 ) [143, Thm. 19].  

> DECODING

⊲ QRM codes whose Gray images are Preparata codes can be decoded using a syndrome-calculation-based algorithm to correct all error patterns of Lee weight at most 2 and detect all (or, for some constructions, a subset of) error patterns of Lee weight 3 or 4 [143].  

> PARENT

⊲ Linear code over Z4 › p. 283  

> COUSINS

⊲ Reed-Muller (RM) code › p. 199 — The mod-two reduc-tion of the QRM (𝑟, 𝑚 ) code is the RM (𝑟, 𝑚 ) code [ 143 , Thm. 19]. 

⊲ Dual code over Z4 › p. 282 — The dual of a QRM (𝑟, 𝑚 ) code is the QRM (𝑚 − 𝑟 − 1, 𝑚 ) code [ 143 , Thm. 19]. ⊲ Preparata code › p. 198 —The binary Preparata code is the Gray-map image of the quaternary code QRM (𝑚 − 2, 𝑚 ) [ 143 , Thm. 19]. ⊲ Kerdock code › p. 191 — The binary Kerdock code is the Gray-map image of the quaternary code QRM (1, 𝑚 ), an extended cyclic code over Z4 [ 143 , Thm. 19] (see also Ref. CODE IN PERMUTATIONS [2306, 2385–2388] binary_permutation  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Permutation-based code  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes codewords into permutations of 𝑛 objects. Per-mutations can be mapped to inversion vectors [ 2389 ] over a mixed alphabet.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against errors in the Kendall tau distance on the space of permutations. The Kendall distance between permu-tations 𝜎 and 𝜋 is defined as the minimum number of adjacent transpositions required to change 𝜎 into 𝜋 . Various bounds have been developed [ 2389 , 2390 ], including LP bounds [ 2391 , 2392 ]. The mapping to inversion vectors is not distance preserving, but the ℓ1

distance between inversion vectors is a lower bound on the Kendall tau distance [2389]. Other distances include the Ulam distance [2393].  

> RATE

Asymptotically good codes in the Ulam metric exist [2394].  

> NOTES

⊲ Review of parallels between linear binary codes and per-mutation groups [2395].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Group-alphabet code › p. 286 — Codes in permutations are group-alphabet codes for the symmetric group 𝐺 = 𝑆 𝑛 .

⊲ Symmetric-space code › p. 290 — The permutation group can be viewed as a finite symmetric space 𝐺 /𝐻 with 𝐺 = 𝑆 𝑛 × 𝑆 𝑛 and 

𝐻 = 𝑆 𝑛 [2391, 2392][942, Table 3].  

> CHILD

⊲ Rank-modulation code › p. 287  

> COUSINS

⊲ Convolutional code › p. 215 — Convolutional codes in per-mutations have been constructed [ 1707 ]. ⊲ Mixed code › p. 287 —Permutation group elements can be mapped to inversion vectors [2389 ] over a mixed alphabet. ⊲ 𝑡 -design › p. 160 — The 𝐺 𝐴 (𝑛, F𝑞 )

group is a permutation 2-design for general 𝑞 , and a 3-design for 

𝑞 = 2. This follows from the fact that the group acts transitively on ordered pairs of distinct points, and on ordered triples of distinct points for 𝑞 = 2 [878].

LINEAR CODE OVER 𝐺 [2331, 2402, 2403] group_linear  

> DESCRIPTION

Block code that encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) in 𝑛 coor-dinates over a group 𝐺 such that the codewords form a subgroup of 287 

𝐺 𝑛 . In other words, the set of codewords is closed under the compo-nentwise group operation. This notion generalizes linear codes over finite fields, but it does not require 𝐺 to be a field or even Abelian. For codes endowed with the Hamming metric on 𝐺 𝑛 , the ambi-ent isometry group contains coordinate permutations together with coordinatewise left translations › p. 549 by elements of 𝐺 . The auto-morphism group of a particular group code is the subgroup of those isometries that preserves the code, rather than the entire ambient group.  

> RATE

Linear codes over non-Abelian 𝐺 cannot have better parame-ters than those for Abelian groups [ 2404 ] and are asymptotically bad [2405, 2406].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Canonical encoder [2407].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Group-alphabet code › p. 286 ⊲ Group-orbit code › p. 166 —The set of codewords of a linear code over 𝐺 can be thought of as an orbit of a particular codeword under the group formed by the code. However, group orbit codes do not have to be linear [ 101 , Remark 8.4.3]. ⊲ Block code › p. 161 — Linear codes over 𝐺 are linear block codes with Σ = 𝐺 . 

> CHILDREN

⊲ Lattice › p. 259 — Lattice-based codes are linear codes over 

𝐺 = R. Because any orthogonal matrix leaving the lattice invariant has a corresponding integer matrix (see lattice description), integer representations of groups can be used to obtain lattices [ 32 , Ch. 3, Sec. 4.2]. ⊲ Additive 𝑞 -ary code › p. 213 — Additive 𝑞 -ary codes are linear over the additive group 𝐺 = F𝑞 . If 𝑞 = 𝑝 𝑚 , they are always 

F𝑝 -linear, but for 𝑚 > 1 they need not be F𝑞 -linear. ⊲ 𝑅 -linear code › p. 281 — 𝑅 -linear codes are linear over 𝐺 = 𝑅 since rings and submodules are Abelian groups under addition.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Group GKP code › p. 548 — Group GKP codes are quantum analogues of linear codes over groups. ⊲ Slepian group-orbit code  

> › p. 276

— Any finite-group code can be mapped to a Slepian group-orbit code by representing the group using orthogonal matrices [2331].

RANK-MODULATION CODE [1849, 2389, 2409] rank_modulation  

> DESCRIPTION

A permutation code designed for storing information in the relative rank order of a collection of cell levels rather than in their absolute values. Many rank-modulation codes are obtained from 𝑞 -ary linear codes, such as Lee-metric codes, RS codes [ 1849 ], quadratic-residue codes, and most binary codes.  

> RATE

Rank modulation codes with code distance of order › p. 161 𝑑 =Θ(𝑛 1+𝜖 ) for 𝜖 ∈ [ 0, 1] achieve a rate of 1 − 𝜖 [2410].  

> REALIZATIONS

HOMOGENEOUS-SPACE CODE homogeneous_space_classical  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Coset-space code ⊲ 𝐺 /𝐻 code  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Homogeneous-space Kingdom › p. 12 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) into a homogeneous (a.k.a. coset) space 𝐺 /𝐻 , where 𝐺 is a group and 𝐻 is a subgroup of 

𝐺 . The space is labeled by cosets of 𝐻 in 𝐺 . Notable groups include compact groups, locally compact Abelian groups, and finite groups. 289 The two-sphere is a simple example of a homogeneous space with 

𝐺 /𝐻 = 𝑆𝑂 (3)/ 𝑆𝑂 (2). Any point on the sphere can be obtained from any other point by a proper (i.e., 𝑆𝑂 (3)) rotation, which is equivalent to saying that 𝑆𝑂 (3) acts transitively . One can then show that any point is invariant under the subgroup of rotations around the axis parallel to the point. This means that one can associate each point with a coset of 𝑆𝑂 (2) in 𝑆𝑂 (3). 

> PROTECTION

The space of normalizable functions on a homogeneous space, 𝐿 2 (𝐺 /𝐻 ), carries a representation of 𝐺 , which can further be decomposed into irreducible representations (irreps) and their multiplicities. Functions on 𝐺 /𝐻 that transform as an irrep of 𝐺 

are called 𝐺 -harmonics .If the decomposition of a homogeneous space into 𝐺 -irreps is 

multiplicity free , there are no multiplicities, and the irreps and their internal indices are sufficient to completely label a basis for the space. In this case, the pair (𝐺, 𝐻 ) is called a Gelfand pair. For example, the integer angular momentum 𝐽 and its 𝑧 -axis projec-tion 𝑚 are sufficient to completely label the spherical harmonics (i.e., form a good set of quantum numbers), which in turn can be used to expand any function on the two-sphere 𝑆 2 = 𝑆𝑂 (3)/ 𝑆𝑂 (2).Therefore, (𝑆𝑂 (3), 𝑆𝑂 (2)) is a Gelfand pair. Functions that correspond to projections onto irreps are called 

zonal spherical functions [ 2423 ]; these correspond to functions on the double coset space 𝐻 \𝐺 /𝐻 [2424 , Eq. (2.9)] and can be obtained by averaging harmonics over 𝐻 .The matrix algebra of zonal spherical functions is non-Abelian when there are multiplicities in the irrep decomposition since irrep projections can be tensored with arbitrary matrices on the irreps’ multiplicity space and still commute with the group action, but not with each other. For multiplicity-free spaces such as symmetric spaces, the zonal spherical functions form an Abelian algebra, and the behavior of such functions can be used to obtain bounds on code parameters such as the Levenshtein bound [156, 873, 2030, 2214, 2215].

⊲ See Refs. [942, 944][32, Ch. 9] for reviews.

[2401 , pg. 60]. ⊲ Stiefel code › p. 290 — Homogeneous spaces 𝐺 /𝐻

HYPERBOLIC SPHERE PACKING [2223, 2425, 2426] hyperbolic  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes states (codewords) as points in hyperbolic space (in particular, the hyperbolic plane for dimension 𝐷 = 2). Distances are measured using the hyperbolic geodesic metric, and finite codebooks correspond to hyperbolic constellations/sphere packings.  

> PROTECTION

Designed to communicate information over channels for which a Lorentzian metric is appropriate [ 2427 ]. Linear pro-gramming (LP) bounds exist for hyperbolic spaces and for closed hyperbolic surfaces [2428–2432].  

> PARENT

the proper Lorentz group and 𝐻 = 𝑂 (𝐷 ). The hyperbolic plane is the case 𝐷 = 2. In fact, hyperbolic spaces are noncompact three-point homogeneous spaces [2180, Sec. 6.6.1.1].

REAL PROJECTIVE SPACE CODE real_projective  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ R𝑃 𝑁 code ⊲ Packing in R𝑃 𝑁  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) into a real projective space R𝑃 𝑁 , the space of lines in real space. The space for 𝑁 = 2 is called the projective plane.  

> PROTECTION

A common distance-related quantity on real projective space is the absolute inner product (a.k.a. coherence). Equiangular lines are sets of lines which have the same inner product between each other; these lines are points in real projective space. Sets of lines minimizing coherence are called Grassmannian frames [255 ], and equiangular tight frames are important examples of optimal line packings [ 2433 ]. The Welch bound is a lower bound on the worst-case coherence of a code [2434].

⊲ Two-point homogeneous-space code › p. 291 — Compact two-point homogeneous spaces 𝐺 /𝐻 reduce to real projective spaces for 𝐺 = 𝑆𝑂 (𝐷 + 1) and 𝐻 = 𝑂 (𝐷 ) [32 , Ch. 9][ 942 , Table 1]. 

⊲ Grassmannian code › p. 288 — Real projective spaces R𝑃 𝑁 are real Grassmannians 𝐺 /𝐻 for 𝐺 = 𝑂 (𝑁 + 1) and 𝐻 = 𝑂 (𝑁 ) × 𝑂 (1).

SYMMETRIC-SPACE CODE symmetric_space  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) into a symmetric space, which is a homogeneous space 𝐺 /𝐻 with an additional symmetry property whose definition depends on whether the space is continu-ous or finite. Continuous symmetric spaces are homogeneous spaces for which every point admits an involutive isometry fixing that point and re-versing geodesics through it. The sphere is a basic example, giv-ing the 𝐷 -dimensional spherical symmetric space family 𝑆𝑂 (𝐷 +

1)/ 𝑆𝑂 (𝐷 ). Cartan classified the compact symmetric spaces whose 

𝐺 are simple real Lie groups [ 2180 , 2436 ]. These spaces include spheres, projective spaces, and Grassmannians. Noncompact sym-metric spaces include Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. Finite symmetric spaces are defined in coding theory as spaces admitting a generously transitive group action, i.e., for all pairs of points 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝐺 /𝐻 , there exists a 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 such that 𝑔.𝑥 = 𝑦 and 

𝑔.𝑦 = 𝑥 [944, Def. 4.5][942, Sec. 3.4].  

> PROTECTION

The decomposition of a symmetric space into 𝐺 -irreps is multiplicity free. Optimal codes have been formulated for quater-nionic and octonionic projective spaces [876, 2437].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [942, 944] for reviews.

For multiplicity-free spaces such as symmetric spaces, the zonal spherical functions form an Abelian algebra, and the behavior of such functions can be used to ob-tain bounds on code parameters such as the Levenshtein bound [156, 873, 2030, 2214, 2215].

TWO-POINT HOMOGENEOUS-SPACE CODE [2235] 2pt_homogeneous  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Rank-one symmetric space code  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 states (codewords) into a two-point homo-geneous space 𝐺 /𝐻 , i.e., a homogeneous space with a 𝐺 -invariant metric whose symmetry group acts transitively on pairs of points at any fixed distance. In the compact connected case, these are pre-cisely the rank-one symmetric spaces. Finite examples tag along as the corresponding combinatorial analogues, where pairs of points are indistinguishable up to the symmetry group once their mutual distance is fixed. More technically, a two-point homogeneous space 𝐺 /𝐻 is a homogeneous space with a 𝐺 -invariant metric such that for any 

𝑥, 𝑥 ′, 𝑦, 𝑦 ′ ∈ 𝐺 /𝐻 , there exists 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 with 𝑔𝑥 = 𝑥 ′ and 𝑔𝑦 = 𝑦 ′

whenever 𝑑 (𝑥, 𝑦 ) = 𝑑 (𝑥 ′, 𝑦 ′) [944 , Def. 4.7]. For finite spaces, this is the metric-space analogue of distance transitivity on pairs, not ordinary two-transitivity on all ordered pairs [942, Table 2]. Two-point homogeneous spaces for compact connected 𝐺 have been classified and include spheres, the real, complex, and quater-nionic projective spaces, and the octonionic projective (a.k.a. Cay-ley) plane [ 2438 ][ 32 , Ch. 9]. These compact examples have positive sectional curvature [2439][2440, Fig. 1]. Examples of two-point homogeneous spaces for finite 𝐺 include Hamming space, Johnson space, and distance-transitive graphs [1338 ]. Finite spaces have yet to be classified [ 944 ][ 32 , Ch. 9][ 942 ,Table 2]. Infinite two-point homogeneous spaces with constant curvature include spheres, Euclidean spaces, and hyperbolic spaces. These spaces are three-point homogeneous (a.k.a. satisfy the mobility axiom), meaning that the 𝐺 action maps any triangle to any other triangle with the same parameters [2180, Sec. 6.6.1.1].  

> PROTECTION

The zonal spherical functions of two-point homoge-neous spaces depend only on the distance between points due to the pairwise distance-homogeneity of the 𝐺 action. For the compact connected families, these spherical functions are Jacobi polynomi-als; in the spherical case, they reduce to Gegenbauer polynomials [942 , Table 1]. This yields a general series of bounds on packings in 

𝐺 /𝐻 originating with the Kabatiansky-Levenshtein bound [ 2235 ][ 32 ,Ch. 9]; see Ref. [873] for a review.

# 5. CODES IN THE QUANTUM DOMAIN 

Many of us are hopeful that quantum computers will become practical and useful computing devices some time during the 21st century. It is probably fair to say, though, that none of us can now envision exactly what the hardware of that machine of the future will be like; surely, it will be much different than the sort of hardware that experimental physicists are investigating these days. But of one thing we can be quite confident—that a practical quantum computer will incorporate some type of error correction into its operation. Quantum computers are far more susceptible to making errors than conventional digital computers, and some method of controlling and correcting those errors will be needed to prevent a quantum computer from crashing. — John Preskill, 1997

ABELIAN TOPOLOGICAL CODE topological_abelian  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords realize topological order asso-ciated with an Abelian anyon theory. In 2D, this is equivalent to a unitary braided fusion category which is also an Abelian group under fusion [ 547 ]. Unless otherwise noted, the phases discussed are bosonic. 

> 2D Abelian topological codes

A theory is defined by an Abelian group 𝐴 of anyon types whose multiplication relations define the fusion rules, and a set of exchange statistics 𝜃 (𝑎 ) ∈ 𝑈 (1) obtained by exchanging two anyons of type 

𝑎 ∈ 𝐴 . The exchange statistics in turn define braiding relations, 

𝐵 (𝑎, 𝑏 ) = 𝜃 (𝑎𝑏 )

𝜃 (𝑎 )𝜃 (𝑏 ) , (129) between all anyon pairs 𝑎, 𝑏 .All 2D Abelian bosonic topological orders can be understood within the subsystem stabilizer formalism [ 395 ]. As such, many of the operations one can perform on such codes have both a stabilizer and a topological-phase interpretation. Stabilizer generators of 2D topological codes acting on 1D loops of qubits can be interpreted as one-form symmetries of the underlying phase realized by the code. Identification of an anyon 𝑎 with the vacuum is equivalent to adding string excitation operators corresponding to 𝑎 to the stabilizer group and taking the center to get another stabilizer group. Code states of this new stabilizer code correspond to a condensed phase › p. 559 of the parent topological phase. A related subsystem-code operation is to gauge out › p. 485 anyon types by adjoining their short string operators to the gauge group; unlike condensation, the gauged-out anyons need not be bosons and are not identified with the vacuum [ 395 ]. The remaining unidentified parent-phase anyons behave differently with respect to the new condensed-phase state. Some become confined 

while the remaining ones pick up new braiding relations. A 2D Abelian anyon theory admits a gapped boundary iff it has a Lagrangian subgroup, i.e., a maximal subgroup of bosons with trivial mutual statistics whose order squares to that of the anyon group [ 388 , 389 , 546 ]. It is conjectured that the logical dimension of an Abelian topological code on a torus is always a square [546]. 

> 3D Abelian topological codes

While excitations are point-like in 2D topological codes, they can have higher dimension in 3D topological codes. For example, there are three types of Z2 Abelian topological orders in 3D: one with bosonic charge and loop excitations (BcBl) and two with fermionic charge excitations and bosonic (FcBl) or fermionic (FcFl) loop exci-tations, respectively [ 435 , 552 ]. The first two correspond to the 3D surface code and 3D fermionic surface code, while the FcFl case 293 is purported not to have a commuting projector Hamiltonian re-alization [ 435 ]. There exists an invariant that distinguishes these [435].  

> RATE

Z𝑞 topological order cannot exist on any fractal geometry that is embeddable in two Euclidean dimensions [2444].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Any local quantum circuit connecting ground states of topological orders with non-isomorphic Abelian groups must have depth that is at least linear in the diameter of the system [2445].  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford gates can be implemented by braiding defects; for qubit-based stabilizer codes realizing Abelian topological phases, see Refs. [ 2446 , 2447 ]. Most of such designs focus on the surface code [422, 2448–2452].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant logical operations can be inter-preted as anyon condensation › p. 559 events [ 2453 ]. ⊲ Modular de-coding, designed to overcome the backlog problem, is applicable to fault-tolerant protocols based on topological qubit stabilizer codes [2454].

APPROXIMATE QUANTUM ERROR-CORRECTING CODE (AQECC) [820, 2065, 2464, 2465, 2473–2475] approximate_qecc  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes quantum information so that it is possible to approximately recover that information from noise up to an error bound in recovery. Many families of approximate block quantum codes become ex-act in the 𝑛 → ∞ limit (see children). More generally, codes that become exact for some parameter values are called quasi-exact [ 754 ].  

> PROTECTION

Many of the state fidelity conditions that hold exactly for (exact) QECCs › p. 304 can be shown to hold up to some error 𝜖 for approximate QECCs. Approximate correction has been formulated for certain types of correlated noise [2476]. 

> Input-output fidelity

This is the primary notion of closeness between states before and after error correction. It is defined as 

⟨𝜓 |N (| 𝜓 ⟩⟨ 𝜓 |)| 𝜓 ⟩ , (135) where N is the combination of encoding, noise, and recovery chan-nels. This quantity is difficult to compute, and there exist other quantities that are easier to work with and that also become 1 in the limit of perfect error correction. 

> Entanglement fidelity

> Other metrics of approximate error correction

(1) Code space complexity: One can relate robustness of an ap-proximate quantum code to the quantum circuit complexity 

[2484 – 2487 ] of creating states in the codespace. For a family of block codes, scaling as order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑘 /𝑛 ) of a code param-eter called the subsystem variance characterizes the transition between code subspaces with low and high circuit complexity [ 2488 ]. The Lovasz local lemma yields a trade-off between circuit complexity and local indistinguishability [2489]. (2) Integrity measures how well a code state 𝜓 and an orthogonal state can be distinguished in trace distance after noise and recovery are applied [2490].

The infidelity of a modified Petz recovery map under erasure can be bounded using the conditional mutual information via the approximate Petz theorem [2491 , 2514 , 2515 ]. In the case of topological codes, the Petz infidelity is related to the topological entanglement entropy [ 2516 ]. Modifications include the Petz-like decoder [ 2517 ], the temporal Petz recovery map for dynamical codes [ 2518 ], and a syndrome-based Petz recovery [ 2519 ]. The Petz map is related to quantum Bayes’ rule [2520 ]. ⊲ The Yoshida-Kitaev decoder for the Hayden-Preskill pro-tocol [ 2521 ] can be extended to general QECCs [ 2517 ]. ⊲ If parts of the Knill-Laflamme conditions › p. 304 are violated, a deterministic recovery operation is not possible. However, a probabilistic recov-ery and a modified version of the conditions can still be constructed [2522].

ASYMMETRIC QUANTUM CODE (AQC) [822, 2534] asymmetric_qecc  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Noise-biased quantum code  

> DESCRIPTION

Quantum systems can be roughly characterized by two types of noise, a bit-flip noise that maps canonical basis states into each other, and a phase-flip noise that induces relative phases be-tween superpositions of such basis states. A code cannot protect against both types of noise arbitrarily well, and there is a tradeoff between the two types of protection. An AQC is one that performs much better against one type of noise than the other type. Such codes typically have tunable distances against each noise type and include CSS codes, GKP codes, and QSCs.  

> PROTECTION

Noise channels for which one type of noise is more prominent than the other are called asymmetric-noise channels or 

biased-noise channels . An example of a noise-biased channel is a Pauli channel of independent 𝑋 and 𝑍 -type noise with 𝑝 𝑋 ≫ 𝑝 𝑍 or vice versa. In the context of comparing weight as well as of determining distances for noise models biased toward 𝑋 - or 𝑍 -type errors, an extended notation for asymmetric CSS block quantum codes is 297 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, (𝑑 𝑋 , 𝑑 𝑍 )⟧ or ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 𝑋 /𝑑 𝑍 ⟧, where 𝑑 𝑋,𝑍 are the 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -distances, respectively [ 424 ]. An asymmetric Singleton bound and linear programming bounds for asymmetric CSS codes have been formulated [ 1308 ], as well as asymmetric quantum GV bounds [ 2535 ]and Hamming and Singleton bounds for general asymmetric subsys-tem codes [ 2536 ]. Asymmetric MDS codes have been characterized [2536, 2537].  

> GATES

⊲ Taking into account noise bias can reduce resource over-head in magic-state distillation schemes [ 2538 ]. ⊲ A CNOT gate continuously connected to the identity cannot be noise-bias-preserving in finite dimensions [ 2539 ][ 2540 , Appx. A]. ⊲ Qubit gates that preserve noise bias (after but not during each gate) cor-respond to permutations in the Pauli-𝑋 basis [ 2541 ]. There is a bias-preserving Hadamard test [2541] (see also Ref. [2542]).  

> DECODING

⊲ Measurement-free error correction has been optimized for biased noise [2543].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant noise-bias-preserving computa-tion scheme [ 2539 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant circuits converting between asymmetric and symmetric subsystem codes [2544, 2545].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ A lower bound on concatenated thresholds › p. 435 with CSS codes under biased noise [2546].

BLOCK QUANTUM CODE block_quantum  

> DESCRIPTION

An encoding of quantum information into a subspace of a multi-partite (a.k.a. many-body ) quantum system, a physical space consisting of a tensor product of 𝑛 > 1 identical factors. Each factor is referred to as a subsystem , register , site , party , or body , depending on context. The subsystems include qubits, modular qudits, Galois qudits, oscillators, groups, or categories. For finite dimensional codes, the dimension of the underlying subsystem is denoted by 𝑞 

and is sometimes called the local dimension .298 While codewords 𝑐 of block codes are elements of Σ𝑛 for some alphabet Σ, quantum states of block quantum codes are 𝐿 2-normalizable functions on Σ𝑛 . Put differently, the configuration space of the canonical (a.k.a. computational) basis states |𝑐 ⟩ of an 𝑛 -body quantum system is the classical 𝑛 -coordinate alphabet 

Σ𝑛 ∋ 𝑐 . 

> PROTECTION

A block quantum code over a finite alphabet Σ with dis-tance 𝑑 detects errors acting on up to 𝑑 − 1 subsystems, corrects erasure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 subsystems, or corrects errors acting on up to ⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋ subsystems. The subsystems that are erased are known to the receiver, and erasures of subsystems at unknown locations are called deletion errors [2579 – 2582 ]. More general forms of noise are caused by insertion errors [2579 – 2582 ], where subsys-tems are inserted into the block, and synchronization errors (a.k.a. misalignment) [ 1199 ], where the code block is misplaced in a larger block by one or more locations. There are relations between deletion and insertion errors [2583, 2584]. The weight of an operator on a tensor-product Hilbert space is the number of subsystems on which the operator acts non-trivially. For example, an operator acting on two subsystems is called a weight-two operator or a two-body operator. General noise models for block codes include stochastic noise , in which every possible error is assigned a probability. In the case of local stochastic noise , the probability decreases rapidly (typically, exponentially) with the number of subsystems that an error acts on. On the other hand, the adversarial noise model consists of errors act-ing on at most a fixed number of subsystems. Independent channels that are close to the identity can be approximated by adversarial 

𝑡 -subsystem error maps with an error that is exponentially small in 

𝑡 + 1, motivating the study of 𝑡 -subsystem errors even when the phys-ical noise is memoryless [ 381 , Ch. 1]. Errors acting on subsystems in a geometrically local region are called burst errors [2585, 2586]. 

> Bounds on code parameters

Bounds on finite dimensional block code performance include the quantum Singleton bound, quantum Hamming bound, quantum GV bound › p. 298 , various quantum linear programming (LP) bounds [2587 , 2588 ] (see the book [ 381 ]), and other bounds [ 2589 , 2590 ]. A code whose parameters attain the quantum Hamming bound (quan-tum Singleton bound) is called a perfect quantum code (a quantum MDS code). We are often interested in how parameters of particular infinite block quantum code families scale with increasing block length 𝑛 , necessitating the use of asymptotic notation › p. 161 . A code family is called good when its rate 𝑘 /𝑛 and relative error-correction capability 𝑡 /𝑛 , equivalently relative distance up to constant factors, remain bounded away from zero as 𝑛 → ∞ [381, Ch. 2].

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ 

> Eastin-Knill theorem:

Transversal gates are logical gates on block codes that can be realized as tensor products of unitary operations acting on subsets of subsystems whose size is independent of 𝑛 . For sub-sets of size one, gates are sometimes called strongly transversal if the single-subsystem unitaries are identical, and weakly transversal oth-erwise. A universal gate set for a finite-dimensional block quantum code cannot be transversal for any code that detects single-block errors due to the Eastin-Knill theorem [687]. 

⊲ A qudit code of length 𝑛 with permutation automorphism subgroups 𝑁 ⊳ 𝐺 ≤ PAut (𝑄 ) and simple non-Abelian quotient 𝐺 /𝑁 

must satisfy 𝑛 ≥ 𝜇 (𝐺 /𝑁 ) [688, Thm. S5].

COMMUTING-PROJECTOR HAMILTONIAN CODE  

> commuting_projector
> DESCRIPTION

Hamiltonian-based code whose Hamiltonian terms can be expressed as orthogonal projectors (i.e., Hermitian operators with eigenvalues 0 or 1) that commute with each other.  

> PROTECTION

Geometrically local commuting-projector code Hamil-tonians on Euclidean manifolds are stable with respect to small perturbations when they satisfy the TQO conditions › p. 326 , mean-ing that a notion of a phase can be defined [ 2598 – 2601 ]. This no-tion can be extended to semi-hyperbolic manifolds [ 2602 ] and non-geometrically local QLDPC codes exhibiting check soundness [ 2603 ](see also [ 2604 ]). Hamiltonians satisfying a Peierls condition are stable to off-diagonal perturbations [2605]. 2D topological order on qubit manifolds requires weight-four (four-body) commuting-projector Hamiltonian terms, i.e., it cannot be stabilized via weight-two (two-body) or weight-three (three-body)   

> 37 https://www.codetables.de/
> 38 https://magma.maths.usyd.edu.au/magma/handbook/text/1976

299 terms on nearly Euclidean geometries of qubits or qutrits [ 2606 –2608]. Ground-state spaces of commuting-projector Hamiltonians with weight-two (two-body) terms cannot be used to suppress errors in adiabatic quantum computation [ 2609 ], but this can be circum-vented with excited-state subspaces [ 2610 ] or ground-state subspaces of subsystem code Hamiltonians, e.g., using BBS codes [ 640 , 2611 ]. No eigenspace of a weight-two commuting-projector Hamiltonian can simultaneously have 𝑑 > 2 and dimension greater than 1 [ 2610 ].  

> PARENT

⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 — Geometrically local commuting-projector code Hamiltonians on Euclidean manifolds are stable with respect to small perturbations when they satisfy the TQO conditions › p. 326 , meaning that a notion of a phase can be de-fined [ 2598 – 2601 ]. This notion can be extended to semi-hyperbolic manifolds [ 2602 ] and non-geometrically local QLDPC codes exhibit-ing check soundness [ 2603 ] (see also [ 2604 ]). Hamiltonians admit-ting a Peierls condition are stable to off-diagonal perturbations [2605].

CONCATENATED QUANTUM CODE [2617] quantum_concatenated  

> DESCRIPTION

A combination of two quantum codes, an inner code 

𝐶 in and an outer code 𝐶 out , where the physical subspace used for the inner code consists of the logical subspace of the outer code. In other words, one first encodes in the inner code, and then encodes each of its physical registers in the outer code. An inner 𝐶 in =

(( 𝑛 1, 𝐾, 𝑑 1)) 𝑞 1 and outer 𝐶 out = (( 𝑛 2, 𝑞 1, 𝑑 2)) 𝑞 2 block quantum code yield an (( 𝑛 1𝑛 2, 𝐾, 𝑑 ≥ 𝑑 1 𝑑 2)) 𝑞 2 concatenated block quantum code [381]. More generally, one can concatenate in blocks: several physical registers of the inner code can be grouped together so that each such block carries one logical register of the outer code. Encoding then proceeds by first applying the inner encoding to each block and then applying the outer encoding across the resulting blocks. Concatenating an (( 𝑛, 𝑞, 𝑑 )) 𝑞 block quantum code can be done re-cursively, with the 𝑟 th level of concatenation yielding an (( 𝑛 𝑟 , 𝑞, 𝑑 𝑟 )) 𝑞 

code. Other ways to combine quantum codes include pasting [ 1645 ], and generalizations of concatenation exist [2618, 2619].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Standard encoding proceeds by first encoding into the inner code and then encoding each physical register of the inner code into the outer code.  

> DECODING

⊲ Standard decoding proceeds in the reverse order: first decode the outer code blocks and then use the resulting data to decode the inner code. ⊲ Maximum-likelihood decoding can be formulated as contraction of a tree tensor network, yielding exact de-coders that improve on minimum-distance decoding for recursively concatenated block codes [383, 2620].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Recursive concatenation is the standard route to threshold-theorem constructions: if one level of a fault-tolerant simulation suppresses logical error below the physical error rate, then further concatenation suppresses it rapidly, yielding the family of protocols used in polylogarithmic-overhead threshold theorems [381, Chs. 10 and 14]. 300  

> NOTES

⊲ See the book [381] for an introduction.

CONSTANT-EXCITATION (CE) CODE [2628–2630] constant_excitation  

> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords lie in an eigenspace of fixed total energy or fixed total excitation number for the underlying quantum system. For qubit codes, such a Hamiltonian is often the 

total spin Hamiltonian , 𝐻 = Í𝑖 𝑍 𝑖 . For spin-𝑆 codes, this general-izes to 𝐻 = Í𝑖 𝐽 (𝑖 ) 

> 𝑧

, where 𝐽 𝑧 is the spin-𝑆 𝑍 -operator. For bosonic (and, similarly, for fermion) codes, such as Fock-state codes, code-words are often in an eigenspace with eigenvalue 𝑁 > 0 of the total excitation or energy Hamiltonian , 𝐻 = Í𝑖 ˆ𝑛 𝑖 . 

> PROTECTION

CE codewords have to lie in the same excitation subspace in order to protect against changes in the total excitation number. Fock-state CE codes lie in the constant-excitation Fock space and are in one-to-one correspondence with points on the discrete simplex › p. 261 . They are protected from identical AD › p. 508 acting on all modes because the damping acts on all codewords identically [820 , 2524 ]. The all-zero AD › p. 508 Kraus operator acts identically on every state and so can be exactly correctable in the case of Fock-state CE codes. For example, this operator’s acting on a Fock state |𝒎 ⟩

depends only on the total occupation number |𝒎 | = Í 𝑗 𝑚 𝑗 and not on the individual occupation numbers 𝑚 𝑗 ,

𝐸 ⊗𝑛  

> 0

|𝒎 ⟩ = (1 − 𝛾 )|𝒎 |/ 2 |𝒎 ⟩ . (148) This effect extends to the damping portion, (1 − 𝛾 ) ˆ𝑛 /2, of any ℓ ≠ 0

AD › p. 508 Kraus operators. In similar fashion, qubit CE codes are protected from coherent noise in the form of transversal 𝑍 -rotations because such rotations act identically on all codewords [ 772 , 2631 ]. In the case of CSS codes, all codes oblivious to such rotations are CE codes [772, 2631]. Stabi-lizer codes can be extended to codes that are protected against such coherent noise via an enlargement procedure [772].  

> RATE

Fock-state CE codes can be used in a protocol that achieves the two-way quantum capacity of the AD › p. 508 Gaussian channel [ 2632 ]. For every 𝐾, 𝑡 ≥ 2, there are explicitly constructible 𝐾 -dimensional Fock-state CE codes with 𝑞 = 𝑁 = (𝐾 − 1)𝑡 (𝑡 + 1) modes, total excitation 𝑁 , and distance 𝑡 + 1; there also exist families with logical dimension 𝐾 = 𝑜 (2𝑁 ) and distance of order › p. 161 𝑜 (𝑁 /log 𝑁 ) [ 475 ].

COVARIANT BLOCK QUANTUM CODE [2441] covariant  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Equivariant block quantum code  

> DESCRIPTION

A block code on 𝑛 subsystems that admits a group 𝐺 of transversal gates. The group has to be finite for finite-dimensional codes due to the Eastin-Knill theorem › p. 298 . Continuous-𝐺 covari-ant codes, necessarily infinite-dimensional, are relevant to error correction of quantum reference frames [ 2441 ] and error-corrected parameter estimation. Denoting the code’s encoding map as 𝑈 , covariance is equivalent to 

> 𝑛

Ì

> 𝑗 =1

𝑉 𝑗 (𝑔 )

!

𝑈 = 𝑈𝑉 𝐿 (𝑔 ) ∀𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 , (149) where 𝑉 𝑗 (𝑔 ) is a unitary representation of 𝑔 acting on the 𝑗 subsys-tem, and 𝑉 𝐿 is a unitary representation acting on the unencoded logical information. In this way, covariant encoding maps are equiv-ariant (i.e., commute) with group actions on the logical and physical spaces. Almost always, the physical representation is defined to be the transversal one (with respect to some tensor-product decomposi-tion), but can reduce to any representation when the code is a sub-space of a larger space that is not expressed as a tensor product (𝑛 = 1). More generally, a code is sometimes said to be time-covariant 

if it admits a continuous-parameter 𝑈 (1) family of gates, not neces-sarily transversal [2639].  

> PROTECTION

Finite-dimensional codes correcting a single-subsystem erasure and admitting a continuous-parameter family of transversal gates (assuming 𝑛 > 1) cannot exist in finite dimensions due to the Eastin-Knill theorem › p. 298 . As a result, there is generally a tradeoff between covariance and error correction. Exact error-correcting 𝐺 -covariant codes can exist in infinite di-mensions, but their codewords are non-normalizable, meaning that approximate constructions have to be considered that are only ap-proximately error correcting. On the other hand, there exist exact error-correcting codes in finite dimensions that are approximately covariant [ 2640 , 2641 ]. Various bounds quantify the covariance-performance tradeoff [ 2489 , 2640 – 2646 ]. In particular, an approxi-mate Eastin-Knill theorem implies that an 𝑆𝑈 (𝑑 𝐿 )-covariant code satisfies 𝜖 worst ≳ [2𝑛 max 𝑖 ln 𝑑 𝑖 ]−1, so for fixed 𝑛 the local subsys-tem dimensions must grow exponentially in 1/𝜖 worst to support a universal transversal gate set [2642, Thm. 4].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ 𝐺 -covariant codes de-fined on a tensor product space consisting of 𝑛 subsystems are equiv-alent to codes with a transversal gate set realizing 𝐺 . 

> PARENT

⊲ Block quantum code › p. 297 — Covariant codes for 𝑛 > 1 are block quantum codes.

VIII.B]. ⊲ 𝐺 -covariant era-sure code › p. 292 — In a proof of principle demonstration, error-correcting codes that are finite-𝐺 covariant can be constructed from a base encoding 𝑈 0. ⊲ 𝑈 (𝑑 )-covariant approximate era-sure code › p. 292 ⊲ W-state code › p. 327 — The W-state code approxi-mately protects against a single erasure while allowing for a uni-versal transversal set of gates. ⊲ Group-representation code › p. 306 

— Group-representation code projections are onto a single irrep of a subgroup of canonical or distinguished unitary operations on a Hilbert space. This makes them covariant w.r.t. that subgroup. More general covariant codes need not be projections onto a single irrep. Removing the restriction to distinguished operations and allowing all operations, every code projection on an 𝑁 -dim Hilbert space can be expressed as a projection onto the irrep formed by the code-preserving subgroup of 𝑈 (𝑁 ). The same idea holds when 𝑁 is taken to infinity. In other words, while all codes are covariant w.r.t. some group, group-representation codes are covariant w.r.t. a canonical or distinguished subgroup.

CYCLIC QUANTUM CODE [2652] quantum_cyclic  

> DESCRIPTION

DYNAMICALLY GENERATED QECC [2654] dynamic_gen  

> DESCRIPTION

Block quantum code whose natural definition is in terms of a many-body scaling limit of a local dynamical process. Such processes, which are often non-deterministic, update the code structure and can include random unitary evolution or non-commuting projective measurements.  

> NOTES

ENTANGLEMENT-ASSISTED (EA) HYBRID QECC [641, 2657, 2658]  

> eacq
> DESCRIPTION

Code that encodes quantum and classical information and requires pre-shared entanglement for transmission. EA hybrid block quantum codes on 𝑛 Galois qudits of dimension 

𝑞 are denoted by (( 𝑛, 𝑘 : 𝑐, 𝑑 ; 𝑒 )) 𝑞 , where 𝑘 (𝑐 ) is the number of encoded logical qudits (classical symbols), where 𝑑 is the distance, and where 𝑒 is the required number of pre-shared ebits. Similarly, block codes on 𝑛 modular qudits are denoted by (( 𝑛, 𝑘 : 𝑐, 𝑑 ; 𝑒 )) Z𝑞 .In alternative conventions (not used here), EA hybrid codes are called entanglement-assisted classical-quantum (EACQ) codes. Here, we use the term classical-quantum for codes for transmitting classi-cal information over quantum channels.  

> PROTECTION

If an EA hybrid code is viewed as transmitting 𝐶 cbits, 𝑄 

qubits, and consuming 𝐸 ebits, then the EA hybrid Singleton bound is the set of triples (𝐶, 𝑄, 𝐸 ) for which there exists a parameter 

𝑡 ∈ [ 0, log 𝑞 ] such that 

𝐶 + 2𝑄 ≤ ( 𝑛 − 𝑑 + 1)( log 𝑞 + 𝑡 ) , (150) 

𝑄 − 𝐸 ≤ ( 𝑛 − 2𝑑 + 2)𝑡 , (151) 

𝐶 + 𝑄 − 𝐸 ≤ ( 𝑛 − 𝑑 + 1) log 𝑞 − ( 𝑑 − 1)𝑡 , (152) for 𝑞 -ary physical systems [2659, Thm. 8].  

> RATE

Trade-off between classical communication, quantum commu-nication, and entanglement distribution has been examined [ 2660 –2662]; see also Ref. [2663].

The EA quantum capacity is the highest rate of quantum infor-mation transmission through a quantum channel with arbitrarily small error rate and access to arbitrary amounts of entanglement [2668 ]. ENTANGLEMENT-ASSISTED OPERATOR-ALGEBRA QECC (EAOA QECC) [818] eaoaecc  

> DESCRIPTION

A code family that encompasses ordinary (i.e., sub-space) codes, subsystem codes, classical-quantum codes, hybrid codes, and their entanglement-assisted counterparts using an operator-algebraic framework. In the EAOAQEC framework, the original EAQEC, EAOQEC, and EACQ formalisms appear as special cases, and the operator-algebra perspective also yields EA hybrid subspace and EA subsystem codes beyond those earlier settings [818].  

> PROTECTION

For Pauli noise with noiseless receiver ebits, the EAOAQEC framework gives a unified error-correction criterion and an associated distance notion that specialize to the corresponding conditions for EAQEC, EAOQEC, and EACQ codes [818].

ERROR-CORRECTED SENSING CODE [2672, 2673] metopt  

> DESCRIPTION

Code that can be obtained via an optimization proce-dure that ensures correction against a set E of errors as well as guaranteeing optimal precision in locally estimating a parameter using a noiseless ancilla. For tensor-product spaces consisting of 

𝑛 subsystems (e.g., qubits, modular qudits, or Galois qudits), the procedure can yield a code whose parameter estimation precision satisfies Heisenberg scaling , i.e., scales quadratically with the number 

𝑛 of subsystems. The conditions required for a code are that it corrects errors in the set E and admits a continuous-parameter 𝑈 (1) group of logical gates generated by some signal Hamiltonian 𝐻 (with the time of evo-lution by 𝐻 the parameter that is to be estimated). This means that 𝐻 cannot itself be a detectable error, i.e., 𝐻 cannot be ex-pressed as a linear combination of the errors, a condition known as the Hamiltonian-not-in-Kraus-span (HNKS) condition [ 2674 ] (alterna-tively, Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span, or HNLS, for Markovian noise [ 2673 ]; see also [ 2675 ]). If these conditions are satisfied, a semidefinite-program based optimization procedure yields a metro-logically optimal code. The procedure has been generalized to more general groups, corresponding to multiparameter estimation [ 2676 ]. If these conditions are not satisfied, Heisenberg scaling is not achievable, but metrologically optimal codes can still be obtained via another semidefinite-program based optimization procedure [2674, 2677]. Metrologically optimal QECCs require error-free ancillas for op-timal local parameter estimation using an entangling gate. In this sense, such codes can be thought of as being entanglement-assisted. 

Ancilla-free versions exist in the case when the noise commutes with the signal Hamiltonian [2678, 2679].  

> DECODING

⊲ There is a condition under which autonomous QEC gives rise to metrology with optimal Heisenberg scaling [2680].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ A single physical qubit entangled with an NV spin was used to measure an incoming signal in a way that bit-flip errors on the qubit were correctable [2681].  

> PARENT

⊲ Finite-dimensional quantum error-correcting code › p. 304 304 — Semidefinite-program optimization procedure for finding a metro-logically optimal code holds for finite-dimensional spaces.  

> CHILD

⊲ Chebyshev code › p. 517  

> COUSINS

⊲ Entanglement-assisted (EA) QECC › p. 303 — Metrologically optimal codes can be thought of as being entanglement-assisted because they require error-free ancillas for optimal local parame-ter estimation, and the estimation procedure uses an entangling gate. ⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 — Metrologically optimal codes admit a 𝑈 (1) set of gates generated by a signal Hamiltonian 

𝐻 , meaning that there exists a basis of codewords that are eigen-states of the 𝐻 . ⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 — Qubit CSS codes can be used for sensing whenever the HNLS condition is satisfied, with the quantum Fisher information related to the number of weight-two codewords of the dual code [ 2682 ]. ⊲ Metrological code › p. 310 

— Error-corrected sensing codes are required to satisfy the Knill-Laflamme conditions › p. 304 , while metrological codes need only sat-isfy the conditions partially. ⊲ GNU PI code › p. 394 — GNU codes can be used to sense signals within the PI subspace [2683].

Encodes quantum information in a 𝐾 -dimensional ( log-ical ) subspace of an 𝑁 -dimensional ( physical ) Hilbert space such that it is possible to recover said information from errors. The logi-cal subspace is spanned by a basis comprised of code basis states or

> Knill-Laflamme error-correction conditions

Equivalently, correction capability is determined by the quantum error-correction conditions. A code that satisfies these conditions approximately, i.e., up to some small quantifiable error, is called an approximate code › p. 294 . 

> Knill-Laflamme conditions:

The Knill-Laflamme error-correction con-ditions [ 2684 – 2686 ][ 2503 , Thm. 10.1] are necessary and sufficient conditions for a code to successfully correct a set of errors in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A code (defined by a partial isometry 𝑈 )with code space projector Π = 𝑈𝑈 † can correct a set of errors {𝐸 𝑗 }

if and only if

By linearity of quantum error correction, if a code corrects a set of errors E, then it also corrects span E.For codewords whose basis states are chosen far enough apart (in some notion of distance) so that the off-diagonal conditions are automatically zero, the remaining diagonal conditions correspond to a system of non-linear constraints on the basis-expansion coef-ficients of the codewords. basis elements [ 621 , Thm. 4], a consequence of the Tverberg theo-rem [570 , 2687 , 2688 ]. For 𝐾 = 2 this theorem reduces to Radon’s theorem [569, 570]. The Knill-Laflamme conditions can alternatively be expressed in terms of the complementary channel › p. 304 , in an entropic information-theoretic way via a data processing inequality [ 2689 –2693 ], or can be interpreted thermodynamically [ 2694 ]. They mo-tivate higher-rank numerical ranges, which are generalizations of the numerical range of an operator [ 2695 – 2697 ]. They have been extended to sequences of multiple errors and rounds of correction [2698].  

> Degeneracy:

A code is degenerate with respect to a noise model if different errors map code states to the same error subspace. For a linearly independent error set E, degeneracy is equivalent to rank (𝑐 𝑖 𝑗 ) < |E| [381].

> Coherent information:

Given a bipartite state 𝜌 𝑅𝑄 , the coherent infor-mation › p. 305 in subsystem 𝑄 is 

𝐼 𝑐 (𝜌 𝑅𝑄 ) = 𝑆 (𝜌 𝑄 ) − 𝑆 (𝜌 𝑅𝑄 ) . (158) For a channel E : 𝐿 → 𝑄 and a pure input state 𝜌 on 𝑅 ⊗ 𝐿 , the coherent information › p. 305 of the channel is 

𝐼 𝑐 (E , 𝜌 ) = 𝑆 (E ( 𝜌 𝐿 )) − 𝑆 (( id ⊗ E)( 𝜌 )) . (159) Coherent information › p. 305 cannot increase under further process-ing of the output, a statement known as the quantum data processing inequality [381, 2689–2693]. Exact correctability is equivalent to preservation of coherent in-formation › p. 305 : a channel E is exactly correctable on a code iff the coherent information › p. 305 after encoding and noise is the same as that of the logical input for every pure input state, and it is enough to check this on a maximally entangled state between the logical system and a reference [381, 2689, 2691].  

> RATE

The quantum channel capacity, i.e., the regularized coherent information › p. 305 , is the highest rate of quantum information trans-mission through a quantum channel with arbitrarily small error rate [2701 – 2703 ]. In other words, the capacity formula implies that one can achieve a transmission rate 𝑟 over a quantum channel E iff, for sufficiently large 𝑛 , 𝑚 = ⌊𝑟𝑛 ⌋, and for all 𝜖 > 0,

∥DEU − 𝐼 ⊗𝑚 ∥1 ≤ 𝜖 (160) for some encoding channel U and some recovery channel D. The quantum capacity 𝑄 of E is defined as the supremum over 𝑛 of achievable transmission rates [ 2704 ]. See [ 508 , Ch. 24] for definitions and a history. The fault-tolerant capacity is the capacity for the more general case where the encoding and decoding maps are also assumed to undergo noise [972]. Doeblin coefficients [ 984 ] for quantum channels have been stud-ied [985].

⊲ The operation D in the definition of this code is called the decoder.
