CAMPBELL DOUBLE HOMOLOGICAL PRODUCT CODE [644]  

> double_homological_product
> DESCRIPTION

A multi-dimensional HGP code derived from two appli-cations of the hypergraph product to a classical code, resulting in a length-4 chain complex. The construction method allows for the use of two different classical codes as inputs, with Ref. [ 644 ] assuming identical input codes for simplicity. Explicitly, the resulting chain complex is 

𝐴 −2

> 𝜕 −2

−−→ 𝐴 −1

> 𝜕 −1

−−→ 𝐴 0

> 𝜕 0

−→ 𝐴 1

> 𝜕 1

−→ 𝐴 2 . (263) The boundary maps 𝜕 𝑗 are constructed using tensor products of the original boundary maps, ensuring the chain condition 𝜕 𝑗 +1 𝜕 𝑗 = 0.The additional parts of the chain complex yield metachecks to detect measurement errors, enabling single-shot error correction.  

> PROTECTION

For the minimal length-one chain complex associated with a classical [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code, the double homological product yields a quantum code with parameters ⟦𝑛 4 +4𝑛 2 (𝑛 −𝑘 )2 +( 𝑛 −𝑘 )4, 𝑘 4, ≥ 𝑑 ⟧

and single-shot distance 𝑑 ss = ∞ [644]. In this minimal-input setting, the Campbell double homological product code is (𝑑, 𝑓 )-sound with 𝑓 (𝑥 ) = 𝑥 3/4, meaning that small syndromes can be explained by errors whose weight grows at most cubically in the syndrome weight [ 644 ]. Its check redundancy is bounded by < 2, and the construction preserves LDPC properties if the original classical-code family is LDPC.  

> RATE

If the input classical-code family has asymptotically constant rate, then the resulting Campbell double homological product family also has asymptotically constant rate because both 𝑘 𝑄 and 𝑛 𝑄 scale as 𝑛 4 [644].  

> DECODING

⊲ The minimum-weight decoder optimizes the recovery operation 𝐸 rec to minimize the residual error 𝐸 rec · 𝐸 given a noisy syndrome 𝑠 = 𝜎 (𝐸 ) + 𝑢 . The decoder’s performance is intrinsi-cally tied to the code’s soundness: when the code is (𝑡, 𝑓 )-sound, the minimum-weight decoder guarantees that the residual error’s min-weight scales as 𝑓 (2|𝑢 |) for measurement errors |𝑢 | < 𝑡 /2

[644 ]. This property is particularly robust in double homological product codes, where soundness follows a cubic scaling ( 𝑓 (𝑥 ) ∼ 𝑥 3). 

⊲ A meta-check-based decoder operates through a two-stage pro-cess: first, it identifies a minimal correction 𝑠 rec to the syndrome 

𝑠 such that the repaired syndrome 𝑠 + 𝑠 rec satisfies all metachecks (𝐻 (𝑠 + 𝑠 rec ) = 0). Second, it computes a minimal-weight physical error 𝐸 rec consistent with the repaired syndrome. This approach uniquely tolerates up to ⌊( 𝑑 ss − 1)/ 2⌋ measurement errors in a single round (where 𝑑 ss is the single-shot distance), eliminating the need for repeated syndrome measurements.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Higher-dimensional homological product code › p. 399 

⊲ Single-shot code › p. 320 — For a minimal input chain complex associ-ated with a classical [𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ] code, the Campbell double homological product code is a single-shot code with 𝑑 ss = ∞, (𝑑, 𝑓 )-soundness for 𝑓 (𝑥 ) = 𝑥 3/4, and check redundancy bounded by < 2 [644].  

> COUSIN

⊲ (2, 2) Loop toric code › p. 330 — The 4D loop planar (toric) code on a hypercubic lattice can be obtained from a particular choice of chain complex from a hypergraph product of four repetition codes [ 1565 ]. As such, it is a particular Campbell double homological product code [644, table I]. 

CAPPED COLOR CODE (CCC) [3415] capped_color  

> DESCRIPTION

CHAMON MODEL CODE [3416, 3417] chamon  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Chamon-Bravyi-Leemhuis-Terhal (CBLT) code  

> DESCRIPTION

A foliated type-I fracton non-CSS code defined on a cubic lattice using one weight-eight stabilizer generator acting on the eight vertices of each cube in the lattice [436, Eq. (D38)]. In the realization as an XYZ product of three repetition codes [ 618 ,Sec. 3.4], qubits live on the vertices and faces of a cubic lattice, each stabilizer generator has weight six, and the natural logical operators are membrane-like rather than string-like [618]. Variants include a CSS model that is expected to have the same excitation structure [ 216 ] and a modified Chamon code based on the XYZ product code construction [618]. 374  

> PROTECTION

Flexible string operators confined to planes orthogonal to [1, 1, 1]𝑇 imply 𝑑 = 𝑂 (√𝑁 ) for the stabilizer version [618].  

> RATE

For the stabilizer version on an 𝑛 1 × 𝑛 2 × 𝑛 3 lattice, the number of logical qubits is 𝑘 = 4 gcd (𝑛 1, 𝑛 2, 𝑛 3) [618].  

> DECODING

⊲ Repetition-based decoder, based on the three underly-ing repetition codes and improved by pre-treatment with a proba-bilistic greedy local algorithm [3418].    

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Depolarizing noise: 4.92% with repetition-based decoder [3418].  

> PARENTS

⊲ XYZ product code › p. 469 — The Chamon model code can be obtained from an XYZ product of three repetition codes [ 1564 ], in a construction different from the 3D surface code; see [ 618 , Sec. 3.4]. 

⊲ Fracton stabilizer code › p. 476 — The Chamon model is a 4-foliated type-I fracton code [ 3419 ] and is the first example of a fracton phase [436].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Repetition code › p. 202 — The Chamon model code can be obtained from an XYZ product of three repetition codes [ 1564 ], in a construction different from the 3D surface code; see [ 618 , Sec. 3.4]. ⊲ 3D surface code › p. 366 — The 3D planar and toric code on a cubic lattice can be obtained from a hypergraph product of three repetition codes [ 1565 ][ 1566 , Exam. A.1]. The Chamon code is an XYZ product of three repetition codes [ 618 , Sec. 3.4]. ⊲ XZZX surface code › p. 470 — The Chamon model code can be obtained from an XYZ product of three repetition codes [ 1564 ]; see [ 618 , Sec. 3.4]. Using only two repetition codes in the analogous 2D construction yields the XZZX code, making it a 2D analogue of the Chamon code [618, Sec. 2]. 

CHECKERBOARD MODEL CODE [3420] checkerboard  

> DESCRIPTION

A foliated type-I fracton code defined on a cubic lattice that admits weight-eight 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type stabilizer generators on the eight vertices of each cube in the lattice. A tetrahedral Ising model can be used to obtain the checkerboard model by gauging [ 216 ,442 – 450 ] its subsystem symmetry [ 216 ]. In that construction, the checkerboard model is self-dual under exchange of 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type stabilizers, and its composites include dimension-1 and dimension-2 excitations, i.e., lineons and planons in later terminology, with anyonic mutual and self-statistics [216]. Variants include the twisted checkerboard model [3421].  

> DECODING

⊲ Parallelized matching decoder [3422].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Independent 𝑋, 𝑍 noise: ≈ 7.5% , higher than 3D surface code and color code [3423].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 

⊲ Fracton stabilizer code › p. 476 — The checkerboard model is equivalent to two copies of the X-cube model via a local constant-depth unitary [ 3424 ]. Hence, it is a foliated type-I fracton code. 

⊲ Lifted-product (LP) code › p. 500 — The checkerboard model code can be formulated directly as an LP code [1303].  

> COUSINS

𝐶𝐶𝑍 gate [ 506 ]. ⊲ Fracton Floquet code › p. 391 — The ISG of the Fracton Floquet code can be that of the X-cube model code or the checkerboard model code.

> circuit_to_hamiltonian
> DESCRIPTION

CLIFFORD-DEFORMED SURFACE CODE (CDSC) [2549]  

> clifford-deformed_surface
> DESCRIPTION

A generally non-CSS derivative of the surface code de-fined by applying a translationally invariant constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 to the original (CSS) surface code. Unlike the surface code, CDSCs include codes whose thresholds and subthreshold per-formance are enhanced under noise biased towards dephasing. Ex-amples of CDSCs include the XY code, XZZX code, and random CDSCs.  

> PROTECTION

As a stabilizer code, ⟦𝑛 = 𝑂 (𝑑 2), 𝑘 = 𝑂 (1), 𝑑 ⟧. 

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ In order to leverage the benefits of CDSCs into practical universal computation, we have to implement syndrome measurement circuits and fault-tolerant logical gates in a bias-preserving way.  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Depolarizing noise: the threshold un-der ML decoding corresponds to the value of a critical point of the weight-two (two-body) two-dimensional random-bond Ising model (RBIM) on the Nishimori line [ 460 , 2549 , 3426 ]. Utilizing this statistical mechanical mapping yields a phase diagram for a CDSC. ⊲ A class of random CDSCs, parametrized by the probabili-ties Π𝑋𝑍 , Π𝑌 𝑍 of 𝑋 ↔ 𝑍 and 𝑌 ↔ 𝑍 Pauli permutations, respec-tively, has 50% code capacity threshold at infinite 𝑍 bias. Certain translation-invariant CDSCs such as the XY code and the XZZX code also have 50% code capacity threshold at infinite 𝑍 bias. ⊲ XZZX code and the (0.5, Π𝑌 𝑍 ) random CDSCs have a 50% code capacity threshold for noise infinitely biased towards either Pauli-𝑋 , 𝑌 , or 𝑍 

errors.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Abelian quantum-double stabilizer code › p. 474 — When treated as ground states of the code Hamiltonian, surface codewords realize Z2 topological order, a topo-logical phase of matter that also exists in Z2 lattice gauge theory [3427]. Local Clifford deformation preserves this topological order.  

> CHILD

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — CDSC codes are deformations of the surface code via constant-depth Clifford circuits › p. 244 that may not be CSS.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Dynamically generated QECC › p. 302 — To create CDSCs, a dynamical process is applied on top of the surface code [ 2549 ]. 

⊲ Random stabilizer code › p. 557 — Many useful CDSCs are con-structed using random Clifford circuits › p. 244 . ⊲ 3D lattice sta-bilizer code › p. 543 — Applying Clifford deformations to various 3D stabilizer codes, including the 3D surface code, 3D color code, X-cube model code, and Sierpinski prism model code, yields a 50% 

code capacity threshold under infinitely biased Pauli noise [ 2550 ]. 

⊲ Asymmetric quantum code (AQC) › p. 296 — Random Clifford defor-mation can improve performance of surface codes against biased noise [ 2549 , 2550 ]. ⊲ Compass code › p. 380 — Clifford deformation can enhance the performance of compass codes against biased noise [2575]. 

CLIFFORD-HIERARCHY STABILIZER CODE [690] clifford_hierarchy  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit code whose codespace is a joint eigenspace of a subset of operators in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 . The stabilizing set, which need not be a group, contains Pauli strings and opera-tors at any level 𝑚 of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 , generalizing qubit stabilizer codes ( 𝑚 = 1) and Clifford stabilizer codes (𝑚 = 2). Clifford-hierarchy codes in 𝐷 spatial dimensions include (𝐷 + 1)-dimensional Dijkgraaf-Witten gauge theories with non-Abelian topo-logical order [ 690 ]. CLUSTER-STATE CODE [3428] cluster_state  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Graph-state code  

> DESCRIPTION

A code based on a cluster state (a.k.a. graph state) and often used in measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) [409 , 410 ] (a.k.a. one-way quantum processing), which substitutes the temporal dimension necessary for decoding a conventional code with a spatial dimension. This is done by encoding the computation into the features of the cluster state’s graph. Cluster states are stabilizer states defined on a graph. There is one stabilizer generator 𝑆 𝑗 per graph vertex 𝑗 of the form 

𝑆 𝑗 = 𝑋 𝑗 

Ö     

> 𝑘 ∈𝑁 (𝑗 )

𝑍 𝑘 , (266) where the neighborhood 𝑁 ( 𝑗 ) is the set of vertices which share an edge with 𝑗 .A type of cluster-state code can be built from a cluster state by applying the CWS construction using a linear binary code, in which codewords are obtained by applying 𝑍 -type operators defined by the code to the cluster state; see, e.g., Ref. [ 3429 ]. Pure › p. 434 CWS codes can be constructed from uniform graphs [2853]. By contrast, MBQC schemes utilize single cluster states. An MBQC scheme can be constructed out of any qubit CSS code (via foliation 

[3430 ]; see also Ref. [ 3431 ]) or qubit stabilizer code [ 3432 ]. In the fault-complex formalism, foliation of a CSS code is expressed as a homological product of the code’s chain complex with a repetition-code complex [ 3084 ]. The original one-way MBQC scheme uses a two-dimensional cluster state [ 409 , 410 ]. Fault-tolerant MBQC based on topological error correction uses the three-dimensional RBH cluster state on the bcc lattice [3433, 3434]. Since they are stabilizer states, two cluster states are considered local-Clifford equivalent if they can be mapped into each other un-der a tensor product of arbitrary single-qubit Clifford › p. 244 opera-tions. For graph states, any such equivalence can be generated by a finite sequence of local complementations (LCs), where local com-plementation about a vertex complements the induced subgraph on its neighborhood [ 3435 , 3436 ]. More generally, any two local-unitary equivalent cluster states can be mapped into each other by operations at some level of the hierarchy [ 3437 ], meaning that general tensor-product unitaries are not needed. Cluster states on 

≤ 19 qubits are LC equivalent if and only if they are local-unitary equivalent [ 3437 ], and there exists a cluster state on 27 qubits that is local-unitary but not LC equivalent [ 3438 – 3440 ]. Local complemen-tation has been generalized to graphically characterize local unitary equivalence under local Clifford operations and, more generally, at other levels of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 [3437].  

> PROTECTION

Protection is related to the stabilizer code underlying the cluster state. There is no physical error correction, and decoding output is simply used to update the Pauli frame. There exist necessary and sufficient conditions for a family of cluster states to exhibit TQO-1 › p. 326 [3064 ]. Quantum weight enu-merators › p. 434 of cluster state codes are known as sector weights [3441–3444]. Potential and limits of MBQC using probabilistic gates has been studied [3445]. Cluster states can be optimized to be robust against qubit erasure [3446].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Initialization of all qubits in the |+⟩ state and action of 

𝐶𝑍 gates along the edges of the graph. ⊲ Optimal-depth prepa-ration based on graph coloring [ 3447 ]. ⊲ A cluster-like state, or a state that is in the same SPT phase as a cluster state, can be prepared in finite time [ 3004 ]. ⊲ ZX calculus based encoder representation [3429].  

> GATES

⊲ In the original one-way MBQC scheme on a square-lattice cluster state, 𝑍 -basis measurements remove qubits from the re-source, 𝑋 -basis measurements teleport quantum information along a wire, adaptive equatorial-basis measurements on a five-qubit chain implement arbitrary single-qubit 𝑆𝑈 (2) rotations, and a four-qubit pattern implements CNOT. Random measurement outcomes gener-ate Pauli byproduct operators that are tracked classically and can modify later measurement bases [ 410 ]. ⊲ The computation is en-coded in pre-determined fashion via topological features of the clus-ter state’s graph, such as boundaries, defects, or twists. Such features can be created using 𝑍 -type measurements, which effectively cut a qubit off from the cluster state. Non-Clifford gates are performed by inserting non-Clifford › p. 244 states into particular singular qubits. More generally, any gate protocol of a qubit stabilizer code yields an MBQC protocol [ 3432 ]. To perform the computation, subsets qubits are measured, e.g., along one two-dimensional slice of a 3D lattice for each time step. This effectively teleports the logical information into the remaining unmeasured portion of the cluster state. The computation terminates after all qubits are measured. The entire cluster state does not need to be created at the start of the computa-tion. Instead, the portion of the cluster state in the extra dimension can be initialized as the computation progresses. ⊲ Single-qubit Clifford operations mapping one cluster state to another can be re-alized as local complementations acting on the underlying graph [ 3436 ]. In one-way computation, Clifford gates can be parallelized [3448].  

> DECODING

⊲ MBQC syndrome extraction is performed by multiply-ing certain single-qubit 𝑋 -type measurements, which yield syn-drome values.  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Photonic architecture [ 3449 ]. ⊲ Generalized foliation procedures exist for noise-bias preserving MBQC [ 2558 ]. 

⊲ Fault complexes provide a representation of foliated cluster-state protocols that makes fault distances, logical correlations, and related fault-tolerance properties computable from the underlying CSS code [3084].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Independent 𝑋, 𝑍 noise: 𝑝 𝑋 = 2.9% un-der MWPM decoding [ 3433 ]. The threshold under ML decoding cor-responds to the value of a critical point of the 3D random-plaquette 

Z2 gauge theory (3D-RPGM) via the statistical mechanical mapping [460], calculated to be 3.3% [3450] (see also [3451]).  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ There is a simple proof of a threshold for MBQC [ 3452 ].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Polarizations of photons: quantum computation [3453, 3454] and single-qubit error correction on an 8-qubit cluster state [3455].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Refs. [ 3456 , 3457 ] for a review of cluster states and their applications. ⊲ Cluster states are useful for entanglement purification [ 3458 ]. ⊲ The original one-way MBQC paper also 377 noted that universal computation remains possible on irregular occupied 2D clusters above the percolation threshold, and that finite clusters can be reused by re-entangling successive computation segments [ 410 ]. ⊲ Graph-State Compass (GSC) Python software library for manipulating local Clifford equivalence classes of cluster states [3440, 3459, 3460].

⊲ Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) code › p. 323 — Cluster states defined on various lattices are representatives of SPT phases, and states realizing these phases can be resources for MBQC. In 1D, cluster states are examples of SPT phases with global symmetries [2982 , 2988 – 2991 ] and enable MBQC on a single qubit [ 409 , 410 ]. The square-lattice cluster state, which is the prototypical resource for universal MBQC [ 409 , 410 ], and other 2D cluster states [ 2992 – 2994 ]have SPT order protected by subsystem symmetries [ 2992 , 2995 ,2996 ]. States like AKLT states and SPT fixed-point states can be efficiently converted into cluster states using local measurements and subsequently used as resources for MBQC [ 2989 , 2997 –3001 ]. In 3D, cluster states belong to SPT phases protected by higher-form symmetries [ 3002 ] and enable universal fault-tolerant MBQC [ 3003 ]. A cluster-like state, or a state that is in the same SPT phase as a cluster state, can be prepared in finite time [ 3004 ]. Cluster states can be created on various lattices [3005].

CODEWORD STABILIZED (CWS) CODE [814, 817] cws  

> DESCRIPTION

A code defined using a cluster state and a set of 𝑍 -type Pauli strings defined by a binary classical code. The CWS construction takes in Q = (G , C) , where G is a graph, and where C is an (𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 ) binary code. From the graph, we form the unique cluster state |G⟩ . From the binary code, we form Pauli 

𝑍 -type operators 𝑊 𝑖 = 𝑍 𝑐 𝑖, 1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑍 𝑐 𝑖,𝑛 , where 𝑐 𝑖, 𝑗 is the 𝑗 -th coordinate of the 𝑖 -th classical codeword. The CWS codewords are then |𝑖 ⟩ = 𝑊 𝑖 |G⟩ .The above definition corresponds to the standard form of CWS codes. Since any stabilizer state is equivalent to a cluster state un-der a single-qubit Clifford circuit › p. 244 [3436 ][ 3462 , Appx. A], any code whose underlying state is a non-cluster stabilizer state can be rewritten in standard CWS form [814]. The term CWS was coined in Ref. [ 814 ], and their approach is equivalent to another approach [ 817 ] based on Boolean functions (see Ref. [ 3481 ]). In an alternative convention (not used here), CWS codes are defined from an underlying stabilizer state that is not necessarily a cluster state.  

> PROTECTION

In standard form, error detection reduces to detecting the induced binary error patterns 𝐶 𝑆 (𝐸 ) with the underlying clas-sical code, together with the requirement that any error satisfying 

𝐶 𝑆 (𝐸 ) = 0 commute with every word operator [ 814 ]. The code distance of Q = (G , C) is upper bounded by the distance of the classical code C. A CWS code is degenerate if and only if it is impure  

> › p. 434

[ 3482 ]. The pure distance › p. 434 is upper bounded by 𝛿 + 1, where 

𝛿 is the minimum degree of G [ 3483 , 3484 ]. For additive CWS codes realizable from a fixed graph G, Ref. [ 418 ] derives upper bounds on the distance and proves a Gilbert-Varshamov existence bound matching the standard pure-stabilizer bound up to the graph-state distance 𝑑 ′ (G) . 

> ENCODING

⊲ If the classical code C has an encoder of complexity 

𝑓 (𝑛 ), then the CWS code Q = (G , C) has an encoder of complexity 

max (𝑛 2, 𝑓 (𝑛 )) , obtained by preparing the graph state and applying the classical encoder [ 814 ]. ⊲ Sequential encoder related to MBQC [2853].  

> DECODING

⊲ There is no known efficient algorithm to decode 

non-additive (non-stabilizer) CWS codes. ⊲ Clustered bounded-distance decoder [ 3485 –3487 ]. ⊲ Structured error recovery [ 3482 ], which reduces to syndrome-based recovery for additive (i.e., stabi-lizer) CWS codes.  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [3075] for an overview of CWS codes.

COHERENT-PARITY-CHECK (CPC) CODE [821, 3187, 3489] cpc  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit stabilizer code for which two binary linear codes are used to directly construct encoding and decoding circuits against 

𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type errors, respectively, via ZX calculus [ 3490 , 3491 ]. CPC codes can be obtained from numerical search [3187].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — CPC codes are a type of stabi-lizer code. A teleported version of the CPC construction, the Clifford noise reduction (CliNR) scheme, can reduce noise in Clifford circuits  

> › p. 244

with Pauli measurements with at most a three-fold overhead 379 in the number of qubits and gates [ 3492 , 3493 ]. There is a simple formula for the probability that a Clifford circuit › p. 244 contains a logical error [3489].

COLOR CODE [411, 677] color  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of qubit CSS codes defined on par-ticular 𝐷 -dimensional graphs. In the colex realization introduced in [ 411 ], qubits are placed on vertices of a 𝐷 -colex, and for any integers 𝑝, 𝑞 ∈ { 1, . . . , 𝐷 − 1} with 

𝑝 + 𝑞 = 𝐷 , 𝑍 -type stabilizers are attached to ( 𝑝 + 1)-cells while 𝑋 -type stabilizers are attached to (𝑞 + 1)-cells. On a closed 𝐷 -manifold, the resulting commuting-projector Hamiltonian encodes 𝑘 = ␀𝐷 𝑝 

 ℎ𝑝 

logical qubits, where ℎ𝑝 is the 𝑝 th Betti number [411]. One family is defined on a 𝐷 -dimensional graph which satis-fies two properties: (1) the graph is a homogeneous simplicial 𝐷 -complex obtained as a triangulation of the interior of a 𝐷 -simplex, and (2) the graph is 𝐷 + 1-colorable. Qubits are placed on the 

𝐷 -simplices and generators are supported on suitable simplices [691 , 3317 , 3494 ]. Admissible graphs can be obtained via a fattening procedure [ 411 ]. See also a construction based on the more general quantum pin codes [669].  

> PROTECTION

As with the surface code, the code distance depends on the specific kind of lattice used to define the code. More precisely, the distance depends on the homology of logical string operators [3494].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Some color codes on 

𝐷 -dimensional lattices can transversally implement a gate at the 

𝐷 th level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 in the form of a 𝑍 -rotation by angle 𝜋 /2𝐷 −1 [691, Fig. 3].  

> DECODING

⊲ In contrast to the surface code, the color code can suf-fer from unremovable hook errors › p. 435 due to the specifics of its syndrome extraction circuits. Fault-tolerant decoders thus have to utilize additional flag qubits.  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

COMBINATORIAL PI CODE [3077] combinatorial_permutation_invariant  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ AAB code  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of a family of PI quantum codes whose cor-rection properties are derived from solving a family of combinatorial identities. The code encodes one logical qubit in superpositions of Dicke states › p. 422 whose coefficients are square roots of ratios of binomial coefficients.  

> PROTECTION

A code 𝑄 𝑔,𝑚, 𝛿, 𝜖 is defined for nonnegative integers 𝑔 ,

𝑚 , and 𝛿 as well as a sign 𝜖 [ 3077 , Construction 5.1]. The number of qubits is 𝑛 = 2𝑔 + 𝑚 + 𝛿 + 1. The code corrects errors on up to 𝑡 qubits for 𝑚 ≥ 𝑡 , 𝛿 ≥ 2𝑡 , and either (𝑔 ≥ 2𝑡, 𝜖 = −) or (𝑔 ≥ 2𝑡 + 1, 𝜖 = +) .Under the same conditions, the code also corrects all patterns of 2𝑡 

deletions [3077].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

COMPASS CODE [2574] compass_model  

> DESCRIPTION

Subspace or subsystem CSS code defined by gauge-fixing the Bacon-Shor code, i.e., the code whose gauge group consists of terms in the compass model Hamiltonian [ 628 –630 ] on a square lattice. Families of random codes perform well against biased noise and spatially dependent (i.e., asymmetric) noise. The gauge fixing proceeds by denoting plaquettes by 𝑋 or 𝑍 type using two colors, and fixing or cutting the corresponding 𝑋 or 𝑍 -type gauge generators at the respective plaquettes. A fully colored lattice yields a subspace code, but allowing for non-colored plaquettes yields a subsystem code. A fully non-colored lattice reduces to the Bacon-Shor code. The surface-density compass code family is obtained by randomly cutting 𝑋 -type stabilizers at only plaquettes of one color in a checker-board coloring; it interpolates between Bacon-Shor codes and ro-tated surface codes. The Shor-density compass code family is ob-tained by randomly cutting 𝑋 -type stabilizers at any plaquette; it interpolates between Bacon-Shor codes and QPCs.  

> PROTECTION

Provides some protection against coherent noise [ 3497 ].  

> DECODING

⊲ Asymmetrically-weighted variant of the union-find de-coder [2574].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ See [ 2574 , Sec. IV] for tables of code-capacity thresholds against spatially dependent and biased noise.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Subsystem qubit CSS code › p. 456 ⊲ Lattice subsystem code › p. 552  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Bacon-Shor code › p. 368 — A compass code on a fully non-colored lattice reduces to the Bacon-Shor code. ⊲ Heavy-hexagon code › p. 396 — The heavy-hex code is a compass code on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, combining weight-two 𝑋 𝑋 and 𝑍 𝑍 gauge operators that are partially gauge-fixed to yield surface-code 𝑍 -type stabilizers and Bacon-Shor 𝑋 -type stabilizers [3498].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Rotated surface code › p. 448 — The surface-density com-pass code family interpolates between Bacon-Shor codes and ro-tated surface codes. ⊲ Quantum parity code (QPC) › p. 427 — The Shor-density compass code family interpolates between Bacon-Shor codes and QPCs. ⊲ Random stabilizer code › p. 557 — Compass code families are constructed by randomly assigning stabilizers to plaque-ttes of a square lattice. ⊲ Clifford-deformed surface code (CDSC)  

> › p. 375

— Clifford deformation can enhance the performance of com-pass codes against biased noise [ 2575 ]. ⊲ Asymmetric quantum code (AQC) › p. 296 — Families of random compass codes perform well against biased noise and spatially dependent (i.e., asymmetric) noise [2574 ]. Clifford deformation can enhance the performance of com-pass codes against biased noise [2575]. 

CONCATENATED QUBIT CODE qubit_concatenated  

> DESCRIPTION

A concatenated code whose outer code is a qubit code. In other words, a qubit code that can be thought of as a concate-nation of an inner qubit code and an outer qubit code. An inner 

𝐶 in = (( 𝑛 1, 𝐾, 𝑑 1)) and outer 𝐶 out = (( 𝑛 2, 2, 𝑑 2)) qubit code yield an 

(( 𝑛 1𝑛 2, 𝐾, 𝑑 ≥ 𝑑 1 𝑑 2)) concatenated qubit code. Concatenating an (( 𝑛, 2, 𝑑 )) qubit code can be done recursively, with the 𝑟 th level of concatenation yielding an (( 𝑛 𝑟 , 2, 𝑑 𝑟 )) code.  

> PROTECTION

Any distance-three recursively concatenated code pro-tects against an open set of errors [ 3499 ]. Concatenating stabilizer codes can help protect against catastrophic errors such as cosmic rays [3500].  

> DECODING

⊲ Adaptive syndrome extraction for a concatenation of a small error-detecting code and a high-rate, high-distance QLDPC code [ 3200 ]. ⊲ The effective channel for a concatenation of codes is the composition of the codes’ effective channels [ 3225 ]. 

⊲ Message passing algorithm for concatenated codes can be equiva-lent to ML decoding [2620].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant message passing between devices [ 3501 ]. ⊲ Blocklet concatenation uses concatenation and transver-sal gates in a way that is tailored to FBQC platforms [3502].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ The first methods to achieve a concatenated threshold  

> › p. 435

against local stochastic noise use concatenated qubit stabilizer codes [490, 493, 494, 788, 3266, 3503–3505]; see the book [381].

CONFORMAL-FIELD THEORY (CFT) CODE [555, 556, 2488] cft  

> DESCRIPTION

Approximate code whose codewords lie in the low-energy subspace of a conformal field theory, e.g., the quantum Ising model at its critical point [ 555 , 556 ]. Its encoding is argued to perform source coding (i.e., compression) as well as channel coding (i.e., error correction) [555].  

> PROTECTION

Code performance is quantified by a lower bound on the entanglement fidelity in terms of the conditional mutual infor-mation [ 555 , Eq. (9)]; see also [ 2532 , Appx. A]. Certain CFT codes have indefinite codespace complexity › p. 295 , and their protection de-pends on the minimum scaling dimension of the underlying CFT [2488 ]. The coherent information of a combined noise and recovery channel can be perturbatively expanded [556].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Threshold under dephasing depends on the structure of the conformal field theory, with the 1D critical Ising model admitting a finite threshold against certain dephasing noise [556].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 —CFT codewords lie in the low-energy subspace of a conformal field theory (CFT), e.g., the quantum Ising model at its critical point. ⊲ Approximate quantum error-correcting code (AQECC)  

> › p. 294

⊲ Holographic code › p. 308 — CFT codewords lie in the low-energy subspace of a conformal field theory (CFT), e.g., the quantum Ising model at its critical point.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Unimodular lattice › p. 262 — Even self-dual binary codes and even unimodular lattices define CFTs [ 1975 –1977 ]. ⊲ Sphere packing › p. 262 — The Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound can be recast as a conformal bootstrap problem, which is a way of utilizing symmetry to constrain correlation functions of conformal field the-ories [ 2244 –2246 ]. ⊲ Self-dual linear code › p. 239 — Even self-dual binary codes and even unimodular lattices define CFTs [ 1975 – 1977 ]. Self-dual ternary codes define superconformal field theories (SCFTs) [1978 ]. ⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 — There is a holographic relation between qubit CSS codes describing CFTs and qubit stabilizer codes describing path integrals over certain topologies [3512]. 

CRYSTALLINE-CIRCUIT QUBIT CODE [3513] crystalline_dynamic_gen  

> DESCRIPTION

Code dynamically generated by constant-depth unitary Clifford circuits › p. 244 defined on a lattice with some crystalline sym-metry. A notable example is the circuit defined on a rotated square lattice with vertices corresponding to iSWAP gates and edges deco-rated by 𝑅 𝑋 [𝜋 /2], a single-qubit rotation by 𝜋 /2 around the 𝑋 -axis. This circuit is invariant under space-time translations by a unit cell 

(𝑇, 𝑎 ) and all transformations of the square lattice point group 𝐷 4.The input state to the circuit is taken to be a product stabilizer state with finite entropy density. If the input is translation-invariant, then this periodicity is preserved by the circuit at all later times, so the code is a quantum quasi-cyclic code with unit cell 𝑎 . The initial product state recurs after a time 𝜏 (𝑛 ) that is linear in 𝑛 for 𝑛 = 𝑎 2𝑘 ,but is thought to be exponential for generic 𝑛 . 

> PROTECTION

The code protects against Pauli errors. The circuit com-posed of iSWAP and 𝑅 𝑋 [𝜋 /2] gates on the square lattice is a "good scrambler" with non-fractal operator spreading and thus behaves like a random circuit in that regard, motivating the use of contiguous code distance as a proxy for code distance. For the 𝐷 4 example above, the unit cell 𝑎 = 2, and the initial product group is chosen to have code rate 1/2. The parameters of the code are ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 /2, 𝑑 (𝑡 )⟧ , and the contiguous code distance [ 2910 ]grows linearly before saturating at 𝑂 (𝑛 ).Selecting the code defined by the stabilizer group at the time when the contiguous distance is maximized and subjecting it to random erasures, an optimal threshold of 1/4 is achieved for a subset of system sizes [ 3366 , 3514 ]. The subthreshold scaling is competitive with random codes, which obey the random matrix theory ansatz [3514].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Clifford quantum cellular automaton (CQCA) that pre-serves crystalline symmetry.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Random stabilizer code › p. 557

CUBIC THEORY CODE [549] cubic_theory  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Magic stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

A geometrically local commuting-projector code fam-ily defined on triangulations in arbitrary spatial dimensions. Its Hamiltonian contains Pauli-𝑍 flux terms and non-Pauli Gauss-law terms built from products of Pauli-𝑋 operators and 𝐶𝑍 gates. These commuting non-Pauli stabilizers realize higher-form Z32 gauge the-ories with Abelian electric excitations and non-Abelian magnetic excitations. For 𝑙 = 𝑚 = 𝑛 = 2 in 𝐷 = 6 spacetime dimensions, the code is a candidate non-Abelian self-correcting quantum memory with Abelian loop excitations and non-Abelian membrane excitations [549]. The construction is based on first constructing a model for an SPT phase [ 3010 , 3519 ], gauging its symmetries [ 216 , 442 –450 ], and making all terms commute outside of the ground-state subspace by projecting them to zero flux.

DYNAMICAL CODE [509, 2459] da   

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Dynamical automorphism (DA) code 

⊲ Floquet code  

> DESCRIPTION

Dynamically generated stabilizer-based code whose (not necessarily periodic) sequence of few-body measurements im-plements state initialization, logical gates and error detection. After each measurement in the sequence, the codespace is a joint 

+1 eigenspace of an instantaneous stabilizer group (ISG) , i.e., a par-ticular stabilizer group corresponding to the measurement. The ISG specifies the state of the system as a Pauli stabilizer state at a particular round of measurement, and it evolves into a (potentially) different ISG via code switching › p. 559 using the group F of check operators measured in the next step in the sequence. As opposed to subsystem codes, only specific measurement se-quences maintain the codespace, and not all sequences implement error detection. Aperiodic measurement sequences provide a way to implement logical gates [2459]. For dynamical codes based on topological phases, the phase as-sociated with each ISG of the code can be obtained from a single 

parent topological phase associated with the dynamical code [ 2453 ] via anyon condensation › p. 559 . In this way, measurements cycle logical quantum information between the various condensed phases. 

> PROTECTION
> Classification of stabilizers by masking

There exists an efficient classical algorithm that tracks informa-tion learned by syndrome extraction at each step [ 3528 ]. The algo-rithm performs the following classification of stabilizers into un-masked, temporarily masked, and permanently masked stabilizers. An unmasked stabilizer is a stabilizer whose outcome can be obtained by measurements. In general, it is not obvious to determine if a stabilizer can be unmasked as its eigenvalue may only be revealed indirectly as a product of several measurements. A temporarily masked stabilizer is a stabilizer whose syndrome cannot be obtained by the given sequence but could possibly be obtained with future measurements. A permanently masked stabilizer is a stabilizer whose outcome is irreversibly lost by the given sequence. For a masked stabilizer code with a set 𝑈 of 𝑙 masked stabilizers, its masked distance is given by: 

𝑑 u = min wt {N(𝑈 )\ G} . (267) Above, G is a gauge group defined from the algorithm that depends partly on the freedom in the choice of destabilizers › p. 443 for the temporarily masked stabilizers, and partly on the measurement sequence which fixes the destabilizers › p. 443 for the permanently masked stabilizers.  

> ENCODING

⊲ A dynamical code with 𝑟 stabilizer generators can be initialized by a measurement sequence in at most 𝑟 cycles [3528].  

> GATES

⊲ Code bounds for gates in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 (sim-ilar to the BK bounds › p. 552 ) can be formulated for QLDPC codes that are embedded in a 𝐷 -dimensional lattice but that admit some long-range connectivity [3528].  

> DECODING

⊲ Temporal Petz recovery map [2518].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Modular-qudit dynamical code › p. 480  

> CHILDREN

⊲ 2D DA color code › p. 363 — The 2D DA color code is a dy-namical code with an aperiodic measurement sequence realizing Clifford logical gates. ⊲ 3D DA color code › p. 365 — The 3D DA color code is a dynamical code with an aperiodic measurement sequence realizing a non-Clifford logical gate. ⊲ Hastings-Haah Floquet code › p. 396 — Periodic Floquet codes are dynamical codes with peri-odic measurement sequences.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 — Useful measurement se-quences of dynamical codes can be extracted from topological quan-tum field theory [ 2459 ]. ⊲ Approximate quantum error-correcting code (AQECC) › p. 294 — Approximate versions of dynamical codes have been formulated [ 2518 ]. ⊲ Subsystem qubit stabilizer code  

> › p. 457

— A dynamical code can be viewed as a subsystem qubit sta-bilizer code, albeit one with fewer logical qubits. ⊲ Monitored random-circuit code › p. 310 — Both dynamical and monitored ran-dom circuit codes can have an instantaneous stabilizer group which evolves through unitary evolution and measurements. However, dynamical codewords are generated via a specific prescribed se-quence of measurements, while random-circuit codes maintain a 386 stabilizer group after any measurement. Dynamical codes have the additional capability of detecting errors induced during the mea-surement process; see Appx. A of Ref. [ 509 ]. ⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 — Dynamical codes are viable candidates for storage in Majorana-qubit devices [ 3529 ]. ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 — Using ZX calculus, an ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code admitting stabilizer generators of weight no more than 𝑚 can be Floquetified into an 

⟦𝑛 + ⌈ 𝑚 /2⌉ + ℓ, 𝑘, 𝑑 ′⟧ dynamical code with single- and two-qubit operations, where ℓ ≤ log 2 𝑚 and 𝑑 ′ ≥ 𝑑 [ 3198 ] (see also Ref. [ 3197 ]). A more general locality-preserving spacetime concatenation proce-dure yields a dynamical code out of any qubit stabilizer code by structuring measurement gadgets using low-weight measurements while ensuring the preservation of logical information [ 3530 ]. In particular, spacetime concatenation reformulates the notion of a dynamical code associated with a stabilizer code in terms of code concatenation for every qubit (spatial concatenation) and measure-ments between these codes (temporal concatenation), leading to a temporal evolution of the stabilizer state [ 3530 ]. A matrix rank condition on the bond operators connecting the gadgets, called the Bond-Kernel-Rank Condition, and a strict locality preservation con-dition (SLPC), along with preservation of the operator algebra of the stabilizer code under the gadget action, preserves fault-tolerance and the spacetime distance of the code [3530].

EA QUBIT STABILIZER CODE [1382, 1383] eastab  

> DESCRIPTION

A code constructed using a variation of the stabilizer formalism designed to utilize pre-shared entanglement between sender and receiver. A code is typically denoted as ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 ; 𝑒 ⟧ or 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ; 𝑒 ⟧, where 𝑑 is the distance of the EA code and 𝑒 is the number of required pre-shared maximally entangled Bell states (ebits). While other entangled states can be used, there is always a choice of generators such that Bell states suffice while still using the fewest ebits. The dual of an EA qubit stabilizer code is also an EA qubit stabi-lizer code whose logical qubits and ebits are interchanged, 𝑘 ↔ 𝑒 

[3536]. An ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 + 𝑒 ; 𝑒 ⟧ EA stabilizer code can be constructed from an or-dinary ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 ⟧ stabilizer code with check matrix 𝐻 = ( 𝐴 |𝐵 ), where the required number of ebits is 𝑒 = rank ( 𝐴𝐵 𝑇 + 𝐵𝐴 𝑇 )/ 2 [3539 ]. Ancillary shared entanglement is assumed to be per-fect, but this assumption can be relaxed [ 3540 ]. There are quantum Griesmer [ 3541 ] and Plotkin [ 3542 ] bounds for EA qubit stabilizer codes.

EAOA QUBIT STABILIZER CODE [818] eaoa_stabilizer  

> DESCRIPTION

Entanglement-assisted qubit stabilizer code in the operator-algebra framework. In the generalized stabilizer formal-ism of [ 818 ], such a code is specified on an extended qubit space by Pauli data consisting of stabilizer, gauge, logical, and sector-labeling operators, and is viewed on the original system as using noiseless ebits shared with a receiver. EAOA qubit stabilize codes are denoted by ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 ; 𝑟, 𝑒, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧ or 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ; 𝑟, 𝑒, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧, where 𝑛 is the number of transmitted physical qubits, 𝑘 is the number of logical qubits, 𝑟 is the number of gauge qubits, 𝑒 is the number of ebits, and 𝑐 𝑏 is the number of classi-cal strings encoded. When the hybrid component encodes 𝑐 clas-sical bits, one has 𝑐 𝑏 = 2𝑐 . This family encompasses ordinary entanglement-assisted qubit stabilizer codes, entanglement-assisted subsystem stabilizer codes, entanglement-assisted hybrid stabilizer codes, and operator-algebra generalizations described within that stabilizer formalism. The framework also exhibits EA hybrid sub-space and EA subsystem stabilizer codes that lie outside the earlier EACQ and EAOQECC formalisms [818]. There exist four constructions of EAOA qubit stabi-lizer codes with distance lower bounds: gauge fixing

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ; 𝑟, 0, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧ → ⟦ 𝑛 − 𝑒, 𝑘, 𝑑 ′; 𝑟, 𝑒, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧, entanglement-assisted gauge fixing ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ; 𝑟, 0, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧ → ⟦ 𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ′; 𝑟 −𝑒, 𝑒, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧, and general gauge fixing ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ; 𝑟, 𝑒, 𝑐 𝑏 ⟧ → ⟦ 𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ′; 𝑟 − 𝑦 𝐼 − 𝑦 𝑆 , 𝑒 + 𝑦 𝑆 , ≤

EIGENSTATE THERMALIZATION HYPOTHESIS (ETH) CODE [ 3550 ] 

> eth
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Thermodynamic code  

> DESCRIPTION

An 𝑛 -qubit approximate code whose codespace is formed by eigenstates of a translationally-invariant quantum many-body system which satisfies the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypoth-esis (ETH). ETH ensures that codewords cannot be locally distin-guished in the thermodynamic limit. Relevant many-body systems include 1D non-interacting spin chains or frustration-free systems such as Motzkin chains and Heisenberg models. ETH requires that for ordered energy eigenstates |𝐸 𝑙 ⟩ and any local observable 𝑂 ,

|⟨ 𝐸 𝑙 |𝑂 |𝐸 𝑙 ⟩ − ⟨ 𝐸 𝑙 +1 |𝑂 |𝐸 𝑙 +1⟩| ≤ exp (− 𝑐𝑛 ) (268) for a constant 𝑐 . This implies that energy eigenstates around some energy ¯𝐸 are approximately locally indistinguishable from one an-other, as their reduced density matrices on any subsystem are both approximately thermal at energy ¯𝐸 . In this way, global informa-tion is protected from local measurements by the environment as 

𝑛 → ∞ . 

> PROTECTION

Approximately protects against erasure errors at known locations. Translation invariance alone is sufficient for good ap-proximate error-correcting properties in a many-body spectrum, including in integrable models [ 3550 ]. The ETH code generated 389 from the spectrum of the translation-invariant 1D Heisenberg spin chain [ 3550 ] has recovery infidelity against the erasure of a constant number of sites scaling as 𝜖 worst = 𝑂 (1/𝑛 ) [2642]. The ETH code defined on a Heisenberg spin chain has unbounded codespace complexity › p. 295 [2488].  

> DECODING

⊲ An explicit universal recovery channel for the ETH code is given in [3551].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 — ETH codewords are eigenstates of a local Hamiltonian whose eigenstates satisfy ETH. ⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 — ETH codewords are eigenstates of a local Hamil-tonian whose eigenstates satisfy ETH, and many example codes are eigenstates of frustration-free Hamiltonians. ⊲ Approximate quantum error-correcting code (AQECC) › p. 294 — ETH codes approxi-mately protect against erasures in the thermodynamic limit. There is a link between ETH and approximate QEC, with fluctuations of the infinite-time average of certain observables expressible in terms of code error [2526].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Topological code › p. 325 — ETH codewords, like topolog-ical codewords, are locally indistinguishable. ⊲ PI qubit code  

> › p. 422

— Several instances of ETH codes contain PI qubit codewords. 

⊲ Spin code › p. 540 — Relevant many-body systems housing ETH codes include 1D non-interacting spin chains or frustration-free systems such as Motzkin chains and Heisenberg models. ⊲ Frustration-free Hamiltonian code › p. 305 — ETH codewords are eigenstates of a local Hamiltonian whose eigenstates satisfy ETH, and many example codes are eigenstates of frustration-free Hamiltonians. 

⊲ Covariant block quantum code › p. 301 — ETH codes consisting of Dicke states › p. 422 are approximately 𝑈 (1)-covariant and nearly satu-rate certain covariance-performance bounds [ 2640 , 2642 ]. ⊲ W-state code › p. 327 — The W-state is not a unique ground state of any local Hamiltonian [ 3073 ]. ⊲ Magnon code › p. 539 — Magnon codes have been shown to protect against non-geometrically local noise, while ETH codes protect only against erasures on geometrically local patches. 

FERMION CODE [530] fermions  

> DESCRIPTION

Finite-dimensional quantum error-correcting code en-coding a logical qudit or fermionic Hilbert space into a physical Fock space of fermionic modes. Codes are typically described using Majorana operators, which are linear combinations of fermionic creation and annihilation operators [ 530 ]. Majorana operators may either be considered individually or paired in various ways into cre-ation and annihilation operators to yield fermionic modes. They form a Clifford algebra and can be interpreted as Ising anyons in certain contexts. Admissible codewords include fermionic states, a subset of which is the Gaussian fermionic states [ 3552 – 3556 ]. Gaussian fermionic states are analogues of (non-displaced) Gaussian bosonic states; they are labeled by points in a Grassmannian and are sometimes called fermionic coherent states [ 3557 ]. Fermionic analogues of ordinary (bosonic) coherent states are the fermionic coherent states labeled by Grassmann numbers [ 3558 , 3559 ]. A Wigner function formalism has been developed for fermionic states [3560].  

> PROTECTION

Majorana analogues of common qubit noise channels have been developed [3561].  

> ENCODING

⊲ A fermionic code using fermion Fock states as code-words cannot protect against occupation-number errors (i.e., de-phasing) and does not admit fermionic logical operators [ 532 , 3562 ].  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford operations on fermionic codes, shown [ 3552 ] to be equivalent to match gates [ 3563 ], can be formulated using Fermionic Linear Optics , a classically simulable model of computation [ 3552 –3556 , 3564 ]. The structure of the Majorana Clifford group has been studied [ 3565 ]. ⊲ Non-Clifford gates can be done using gate tele-portation, in which a gate can be obtained from a particular magic state (a.k.a. resource state) [ 3564 , 3566 –3569 ]. ⊲ General gates in-clude qubit-like 𝑆 , 𝑇 , and 𝐶𝑍 gates acting on either logical qubit or logical fermionic encodings. Fermionic gates include braiding gates which correspond to exchanging Majorana modes. Hybrid gates in-clude 𝐶𝑍 𝑞 𝑓 gates between a logical qubit and a logical fermion. The braiding, 𝐶𝑍 𝑓 , 𝐶𝑍 𝑞 𝑓 , Hadamard, 𝑆 , and 𝑇 gates are universal [ 532 ]. 

⊲ Logical-fermion circuits constructed out of certain transversal gates do not admit a lower 𝑇 gate count than logical-qubit circuits [532 ]. ⊲ Using fermion codes with logical fermion encodings and the fermionic fast Fourier transform [ 3570 ] can yield exponential improvements in circuit depth over fermion-into-qubit encodings [532].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 3571 ] for an introduction to Majorana-based qubits.  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 — The Majorana operator algebra is iso-morphic to the qubit Pauli-operator algebra via various fermion-into-qubit encodings.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ SYK code › p. 459 ⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417  

> COUSINS

⊲ Bosonic code › p. 512 — Bosonic (fermionic) codes are asso-ciated with bosonic (fermionic) degrees of freedom. ⊲ Fermion-into-qubit code › p. 389 — Fermion (fermion-into-qubit) codes encode logical information into a physical space of fermionic modes (qubits). The Majorana operator algebra is isomorphic to the qubit Pauli-operator algebra via various fermion-into-qubit encodings. Using fermion codes with logical fermion encodings and the fermionic fast Fourier transform [ 3570 ] can yield exponential improvements in circuit depth over fermion-into-qubit encodings [532]. 

⊲ Constant-excitation (CE) code › p. 300 — Fermion codewords lying in a fixed fermion-number subspace have to lie in the same subspace in order to protect against changes in fermion number [532]. 

FERMION-INTO-QUBIT CODE fermions_into_qubits  

> DESCRIPTION

Qubit stabilizer code encoding a logical fermionic Hilbert space into a physical space of 𝑛 qubits. Such codes are primarily intended for simulating fermionic systems on quantum computers, and some of them have error-detecting, correcting, and transmuting properties. The first fermion-into-qubit code is the Jordan-Wigner transfor-mation code, a trivial ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 ⟧ stabilizer code encoding Majorana op-erators into Pauli strings of weight 𝑂 (𝑛 ). This is necessary to ensure that Majorana operators satisfy the proper anti-commutation rela-tions. Subsequent encodings consisted of stabilizer codes with 𝑘 < 𝑛 ,ensuring anti-commutation through the long-range entanglement of the codestates. This makes it possible to reduce the Pauli weight of a Majorana operator by multiplying by a stabilizer. For example, for stabilizer constraints associated with loops of a 2D lattice, applying loop constraints to high-weight fermionic string-like operators yields operators of lower weight. See [ 393 , Table I][ 387 , Table I] for comparisons of various fermion-into-qubit codes. On the square lattice, explicit local 2D encodings with qubit-fermion ratios 2, 1.5, and 1.25 are exhibited in Ref. [ 387 ]. 390 In addition to the children of this entry, various custom encodings exist [ 3522 , 3572 –3576 ] that can be tailored to the quantum simula-tion problem of interest.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Any two locality-preserving fermion-into-qubit map-pings in two spatial dimensions can be related by a finite-depth generalized local unitary transformation [387].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — Fermion-into-qubit codes are qubit stabilizer codes that encode a logical fermionic Hilbert space into a physical space of 𝑛 qubits.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Auxiliary qubit mapping (AQM) code › p. 368 ⊲ Bravyi-Kitaev transformation (BKT) code › p. 372 ⊲ Bosonization code  

> › p. 371

⊲ Jordan-Wigner transformation code › p. 408 ⊲ Ternary-tree fermion-into-qubit code › p. 459  

> COUSINS

⊲ Twist-defect surface code › p. 465 — Treating a twist-defect surface codespace as a logical fermion encoding yields a fermion-into-qubit code [ 3577 ]. ⊲ Gauss’ law code › p. 187 — Gauge-group el-ements of a 𝐷 -dimensional fermionic Z2 gauge theory can arise from a single-error-correcting linear binary code [ 68 , Thm. 1]. 

⊲ Fermion code › p. 389 — Fermion (fermion-into-qubit) codes encode logical information into a physical space of fermionic modes (qubits). The Majorana operator algebra is isomorphic to the qubit Pauli-operator algebra via various fermion-into-qubit encodings. Using fermion codes with logical fermion encodings and the fermionic fast Fourier transform [ 3570 ] can yield exponential improvements in circuit depth over fermion-into-qubit encodings [532].

FUSION-BASED QUANTUM COMPUTING (FBQC) CODE [3584]  

> fusion
> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codewords are resource states used in an FBQC scheme. FBQC is a fault-tolerant model of quantum computation built from small constant-sized entangled resource states together with destructive entangling measurements called fusions [ 3584 ]. Resource states are stabilizer states and can be described, up to local Clifford transformations, by graph states [ 3584 ]. Unlike standard MBQC, which first prepares a large cluster state and then computes using single-qubit measurements, FBQC integrates entanglement genera-tion, syndrome extraction, and logical processing into the fusion measurements themselves. This makes FBQC particularly natural for photonic platforms, where Bell-type fusion measurements are native operations.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against erasure, Pauli errors, photon loss › p. 508 ,fusion failure from non-determinism, and faults in resource-state preparation. Redundancy in fusion outcomes is captured by the check-operator group. Fusion measurement outcomes form a syn-drome that can be decoded to infer the logical Pauli frame, rather than by applying physical recovery operations [3584].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Resource-state generators, which produce small constant-sized stabilizer states, together with Bell-fusion measure-ments.  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford gates › p. 244 are performed by introducing and ma-nipulating topological features such as boundaries, defects, or twists through modified fusion bases and, in some constructions, single-qubit measurements. Logical gates can also be performed by code deformation. Non-Clifford gates are performed by magic-state in-jection.  

> DECODING

⊲ Surface-code-based FBQC schemes often admit a syndrome-graph description, allowing the use of decoders such as minimum-weight matching and union-find [3068, 3584].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fusion networks can be constructed so that the surviving stabilizers and check operators realize topological surface-code fault tolerance [ 3584 ]. ⊲ More generally, any three-dimensional cell complex in which each edge has four incident faces defines a surface-code fusion complex, yielding a large family of FBQC fault-tolerant protocols [3069].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Under the hardware-agnostic fusion error model, ped-agogical FBQC schemes have reported thresholds of 11 .98% against erasure in each fusion measurement and 1.07% against Pauli error [3584 ]. ⊲ For a linear-optical ballistic scheme, reported thresh-olds include 43 .2% against fusion failure and 10 .4% photon loss › p. 508 

per fusion [ 3584 ]. ⊲ For surface-code logical blocks compiled to FBQC, the threshold for fault-tolerant logical gates was found to agree, within numerical uncertainty, with the bulk memory thresh-old [3068].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — The resource states in FBQC are small stabilizer states, and the surviving stabilizers after fusion determine the encoded output state (conditioned on measurement outcomes).  

> COUSINS

⊲ Topological code › p. 325 — Surface-code-based topological fault-tolerant protocols can be realized in FBQC, including topo-logical features such as boundaries, defects, and twists, by mod-ifying fusion measurements and, in some constructions, adding single-qubit measurements [ 3068 , 3069 ]. ⊲ Dual-rail quantum code › p. 520 — FBQC resource states are concatenated with dual-rail codes to increase loss detection. ⊲ Dynamically generated QECC  

> › p. 302

— Building a fusion network is done using a measurement-based dynamical process. ⊲ Concatenated cat code › p. 519 — The four-component cat code can be concatenated with the XZZX code to yield a fusion-based computation scheme on a 2D lattice [ 3585 ]. 

⊲ Square-lattice GKP code › p. 530 — GKP states can be used to perform computation in a fusion-based encoding [3586]. ⊲ Concatenated qubit code › p. 380 — Blocklet concatenation uses concatenation and transversal gates in a way that is tailored to FBQC platforms [ 3502 ]. 

⊲ Cluster-state code › p. 376 — FBQC and MBQC are both computational models in which computation is done by measuring resource states (which are qubit stabilizer states). The difference between the two is in how the states are constructed. FBQC is based exclusively on two-qubit measurements tailored to photonic platforms. These mea-surements require a foliation with more qubits but one which can be built by fusing smaller modules. 393 

GENERALIZED FIVE-SQUARES CODE [567, 632, 633] five_squares  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of subsystem codes that are general-izations [ 632 , 633 ] of a code defined on a three-valent hypergraph as-sociated with the five-squares lattice [ 567 ]. The original five-squares code is a 2D topological subsystem code with local two-qubit gauge generators; on a torus, it encodes two logical qubits [567].

⊲ For the original five-squares code, preprocessing maps decoding onto two copies of the toric code, after which one can use minimum-weight matching or renormalization-group decoding [567 ]. ⊲ Generalized five-squares codes can also be decoded via a mapping to two copies of the surface code [633].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ For depolarizing noise, the original five-squares code has a threshold around 1.5% under the simple decoder and around 2% under the improved decoder [567].  

> PARENTS

HAAH CUBIC CODE (CC) [2942] haah_cubic  

> DESCRIPTION

A 3D lattice stabilizer code on a length-𝐿 cubic lattice with one or two qubits per site. Admits two types of stabilizer gen-erators with support on each cube of the lattice. In the non-CSS case, these two are related by spatial inversion. For CSS codes, we require that the product of all corner operators is the identity. We lastly require that there are no non-trivial string operators, meaning that single-site operators are a phase, and any period one logical operator 𝑙 ∈ S⊥ is just a phase. Haah showed in his original construction that there is exactly one non-CSS code of this form, and 17 CSS codes [ 2942 ]. The non-CSS code is labeled code 0, and the rest are numbered from 1 - 17. Codes CC1-CC4, CC7, CC8, and CC10 do not have string logical operators [436 , 2942 ]. The original cubic code in this family can be obtained by gauging [ 216 , 442 –450 ] a fractal-symmetry Ising model [ 444 , Sec. IV.B]; related fracton gauging constructions also appear in [ 216 , 444 ]. Under renormalization group flow [ 3594 ], cubic code 1 fragments into itself and the Haah B-code (a.k.a. CC1B ), which has four qubits per unit cell [ 3595 ][ 436 , Eq. (D2)]. In this context, cubic code 1 is sometimes called the Haah A-code or CC1A . Cubic codes 11-17 frag-ment into combinations of themselves, their corresponding B-codes, and stacks of surface codes [3595, Table 1]. The Haah A-code can be written in a similar form as the Sierpinski prism model code [ 3072 ]. The Haah B-code admits a topological defect network construction out of two copies of the 3D surface code [3071]. Encodings using geometries with boundaries as well as lattice defects have been studied [ 3596 ]. CC1A and CC1B have been gener-alized to manifolds more general than 3D lattices [3597, 3598].  

> PROTECTION

Cubic codes protect against simultaneous independent Pauli errors on different sites (not qubits, since there can be 2 qubits per site). Codes CC0-CC4 are known to have distance 𝑑 ≥ 𝐿 , mean-ing they can achieve macroscopic code distance as 𝐿 → ∞ . 

> DECODING

⊲ Hard-decisions RG decoder [ 2946 ]. ⊲ BP-OSD de-coder [1200].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ The encoding rate depends on the code implemented, but code CC0 has been shown to have 𝑘 ≥ 𝐿 on a periodic finite cubic lattice of side length 𝐿 . In general, we expect the number of logical qubits to scale as 𝑘 = Ω (𝐿 ). 

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Qudit cubic code › p. 484  

> COUSINS

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — Under renormalization group flow [ 3594 ], cubic codes 11-17 fragment into combinations of them-selves, their corresponding B-codes, and stacks of surface codes [3595 , Table 1]. ⊲ 3D surface code › p. 366 — The Haah B-code ad-mits a topological defect network construction out of two copies of the 3D surface code [ 3071 ]. ⊲ 3D color code › p. 364 — The 3D color and cubic code families both include 3D codes that do not admit string-like operators. ⊲ (2, 2) Loop toric code › p. 330 — The energy of any partial implementation of CC1 is proportional to the boundary length, similar to the 4D toric code. This can potentially suppress the effects of thermal errors, but it is currently an open problem.

HAAR-RANDOM QUBIT CODE [ 2498 , 2702 , 2703 , 3599 ] haar_random  

> DESCRIPTION

Haar-random codewords are generated in a process involving averaging over unitary operations distributed according to the Haar measure. Haar-random codes are used to prove statements about the capacity of a quantum channel to transmit quantum in-formation [ 508 ], but encoding and decoding in such 𝑛 -qubit codes quickly becomes impractical as 𝑛 → ∞ .There are different approaches to create Haar-random codewords. In the construction of Ref. [ 2498 ], codewords are produced by per-forming a unitarily covariant projective measurement on a typical 

subspace of a tensor-power state. Reference [ 2498 ] showed that coherent-information rates are achievable by encoding in such Haar-random codes. In particular, Haar-random codes achieve asymptot-ically vanishing decoding error in the 𝑛 → ∞ limit by proving that the encoded information becomes decoupled from the environment. This is a necessary and sufficient condition for successful decoding since measurements of the environment should never reveal the encoded information [2689]. Intuitively, coupling with the environment can be decreased by projecting the system onto a random codespace. The more qubits that are randomly discarded, the more the codespace is decoupled from the environment. One may ask what is the least amount of qubits that can be discarded, i.e. the largest remaining codespace, that still achieves decoupling. It can be shown through the decou-pling inequality [ 3600 ] that the largest possible dimension of the random codespace that achieves arbitrarily large decoupling is expo-nential in the coherent information of the channel. Therefore, there exist codes that can transmit information at rates governed by coher-ent information. Furthermore, these codes can be constructed with high probability by performing a Haar-random isometry embedding 

𝑘 logical qubits into an 𝑛 -qubit physical space. Such an isometry can be produced by QR decomposition of a Gaussian random matrix [3601].  

> RATE

Haar-random qubit codes attain the regularized coherent in-formation of certain noise channels in the limit of large 𝑛 [3602].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Haar-random qubit codes have a measurement thresh-old › p. 435 of one [3118].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Random-circuit code › p. 318 396  

> COUSINS

⊲ Local Haar-random circuit qubit code › p. 415 — Approxi-mating the random projections through 𝑡 -designs is necessary in order to make the Haar-random qubit protocol practical. Replacing with random Clifford gates › p. 244 is especially convenient since the Clifford group › p. 244 forms a unitary 2-design and produces stabi-lizer codes. ⊲ Clifford group › p. 244 — Approximating the random projections through 𝑡 -designs is necessary in order to make the Haar-random qubit protocol practical. Replacing with random Clif-ford gates › p. 244 is especially convenient since the Clifford group › p. 244 

forms a unitary 2-design and produces stabilizer codes. 

HASTINGS-HAAH FLOQUET CODE [509] floquet  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Periodic Floquet code  

> DESCRIPTION

Dynamical code whose sequence of check-operator measurements is periodic. The original Hastings-Haah construc-tion introduced periodic measurement schedules that dynamically generate logical qubits even when the underlying subsystem code has fewer or no logical qubits [ 509 ]. Its basic examples are the 2D honeycomb Floquet code and the 1D ladder Floquet code.  

> PROTECTION

In the original Hastings-Haah examples, periodic mea-surements protect against single-qubit Pauli faults and measure-ment faults: the honeycomb Floquet code on a torus stores two logical qubits with distance proportional to linear size, while the ladder Floquet code is an error-detecting toy model [ 509 ]. Spacetime errors for periodic Floquet codes have been studied in Ref. [3603].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Periodic Floquet codes on tri-colorable lattices can be made fault-tolerant in the presence of dead qubits [ 3604 ,3605].  

> PARENT

⊲ Dynamical code › p. 385 — Periodic Floquet codes are dy-namical codes with periodic measurement sequences.

HEAVY-HEXAGON CODE [3498] heavy_hex  

> DESCRIPTION

Subsystem stabilizer code on the heavy-hexagonal point set that combines Bacon-Shor and surface-code stabilizers. Encodes one logical qubit into 𝑛 = (5𝑑 2 − 2𝑑 − 1)/ 2 physical qubits with distance 𝑑 . The heavy-hexagonal point set allows for low degree (at most 3) connectivity between all the data and ancilla qubits, which is suitable for fixed-frequency transmon qubits subject to frequency collision errors. The code can be split into a surface and a Bacon-Shor code, with the idling qubits of one code serving as the physical qubits of the other [634]. Data qubits and ancillas of the code are placed on a heavy-hexagonal point set, i.e., the vertices and edges of a tiling of hexagons. A subset of the ancilla qubits are flag qubits used for detecting high-weight errors arising from fewer faults. The code stabilizers for detecting 𝑋 -type errors are measured by measur-ing weight-two 𝑍 -type gauge operators whose product produces stabilizers of the surface code. 𝑋 -type stabilizers are column opera-tors corresponding to stabilizers of the Bacon-Shor code, which are measured by taking products of weight-four and weight-two 𝑋 -type gauge operators.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against Pauli noise. The code has no threshold for 𝑍 -type Pauli errors since they are detected by Bacon-Shor-type stabilizers.  

> RATE

1/𝑛 for a distance-𝑑 heavy-hexagon code on 𝑛 = (5𝑑 2 −2𝑑 −1)/ 2

qubits.  

> ENCODING

⊲ For a logical-zero state, prepare all data qubits in the physical-zero state and then measure the 𝑋 -type Bacon-Shor stabilizers. For logical-plus state, prepare all data qubits in the physical-plus state and then measure 𝑍 -type surface code stabilizers. 

⊲ Stabilizer measurement encoding circuits have a constant depth of 10 time steps (excluding ancilla state preparation and measure-ment).  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ CNOT gates are transver-sal for this code. However, for most architectures, all logical gates would be implemented using lattice surgery methods.  

> GATES

⊲ Universal gate set achieved with magic state injection and lattice surgery. ⊲ Magic-state injection with and without flag qubits [3606].  

> DECODING

⊲ Any graph-based decoder can be used, such as MWPM and Union Find. However, edge weights must be dynamically renormalized using flag-qubit measurement outcomes after each syndrome measurement round. ⊲ Machine-learning [ 3607 ] and neural-network [3608] decoders.  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ All logical gates can be fault-tolerantly im-plemented using lattice surgery and magic state injection. 

⊲ Stabilizer measurements are measured fault-tolerantly using one-flag circuits since some single-fault events can result in weight-two data qubit errors which are parallel to the code’s logical operators. Hence, using information from the flag-qubit measurements is cru-cial to fault-tolerantly measure the code stabilizers.  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ 0.45% for 𝑋 errors under a full circuit-level depolariz-ing noise model (obtained from Monte Carlo simulations). ⊲ 𝑍 -errors have no threshold given the 𝑋 -type Bacon-Shor stabilizers.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Superconducting qubits: Logical state preparation and flag-qubit error correction realized in superconducting-circuit devices (specifically, fixed-frequency transmon qubit architectures) by IBM for 𝑑 = 2 [3167 , 3184 ] and 𝑑 = 3 [3609 ]. Simultaneous syndrome extraction and logical Bell-state preparation for both the embedded surface and Bacon-Shor codes of distance ≤ 4 on an IBM 133-qubit device [ 634 ]. Embedded rotated surface code magic-state injection implemented on IBM fez device [3610].  

> PARENT

⊲ Compass code › p. 380 — The heavy-hex code is a compass code on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, combining weight-two 𝑋 𝑋 and 

𝑍 𝑍 gauge operators that are partially gauge-fixed to yield surface-code 𝑍 -type stabilizers and Bacon-Shor 𝑋 -type stabilizers [3498]. 397  

> COUSINS

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — Surface code stabilizers are used to measure the Z-type stabilizers of the code. There are var-ious ways to embed the surface code into the heavy-hex lattice [3611 ]. ⊲ Bacon-Shor code › p. 368 — Bacon-Shor stabilizers are used to measure the X-type stabilizers of the code. ⊲ ⟦4, 1, 2⟧ Leung-Nielsen-Chuang-Yamamoto (LNCY) code › p. 343 — Magic states pre-pared using a ⟦4, 1, 2⟧ subcode can be injected into the heavy-hex code [ 3167 , 3168 ]. The 𝑑 = 2 heavy-hex code is closely related to the 

⟦4, 1, 2⟧ LNCY code. 

⊲ Rotated surface code › p. 448 — A rotated surface code can be mapped onto a heavy square lattice, resulting in a code similar to the heavy-hexagon code [ 3498 ]. ⊲ XY surface code › p. 469 — XY surface code can be adapted for a heavy-hexagonal point set [ 3612 ].

HEXAGONAL 𝐶𝑍 CODE [548] hexagonal_cz  

> DESCRIPTION

A hexagonal-lattice realization of the 2 + 1D 𝑙 = 𝑚 =

𝑛 = 1 cubic theory / Type-III Z32 twisted quantum double phase. Its stabilizers are products of Pauli-𝑍 operators and 𝐶𝑍 gates [ 548 ,Fig. 6][ 562 , Fig. 3]. The ground-state subspace of the hexagonal 𝐶𝑍 

code realizes the topological order of the Type-III 𝐺 = Z32 Abelian TQD model [ 548 , 549 ], which is the same topological order as the 

𝐺 = 𝐷 4 non-Abelian quantum double [ 550 ]. The stabilizers include 

𝐶𝑍 operators acting on hexagonal loops, but a reduced version exists where only two 𝐶𝑍 gates act on each loop [562].  

> GATES

⊲ The hexagonal 𝐶𝑍 code can be obtained from two surface codes by gauging [ 216 , 442 – 450 ] their logical 𝐶𝑍 gate [ 562 ]. Gates on the two surface codes in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, such as 𝐶𝑍 gates, can be realized fault-tolerantly by performing this procedure and reversing it [ 545 , 562 ]. ⊲ There is a constant-depth circuit implementing a transversal logical 𝑇 gate via an emergent automorphism symmetry of the underlying D4 topological order [690].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ The hexagonal 𝐶𝑍 code can be obtained from two surface codes by gauging [ 216 , 442 – 450 ] their logical 𝐶𝑍 gate [562 ]. Gates on the two surface codes in the third level of the Clif-ford hierarchy, such as 𝐶𝑍 gates, can be realized fault-tolerantly by performing this procedure and reversing it [545, 562].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Signatures of the phase detected in a 27-qubit trapped-ion device by Quantinuum [ 3617 ]. Preparation of ground states and braiding of anyons has also been performed.

HIERARCHICAL CODE [3507] hierarchical  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer codes resulting from a concatenation of a constant-rate QLDPC code › p. 439 

with a rotated surface code › p. 448 . Concatenation allows for syn-drome extraction to be performed on a 2D geometry while main-taining a threshold at the expense of a logarithmically vanishing rate. The growing syndrome extraction circuit depth allows known bounds in the literature to be weakened [495, 496].  

> RATE

Rate scales › p. 161 as Ω(1/log (𝑛 )2). 

> DECODING

⊲ Decoding is performed as in a standard concatenated code › p. 380 using decoders for the inner and outer codes. The syn-drome extraction circuit depth for the outer code is optimized using a permutation routing algorithm [ 3618 ]. The bilayer architecture allows for logical entangling gates between logical surface-code patches. ⊲ Soft output decoding [3619].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ 2D geometrically local syndrome extraction cir-cuits of depth of order › p. 161 𝑂 (√𝑛 /𝑅 ) that utilize Clifford and SWAP gates of range 𝑅 and that require order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 ) data and ancilla qubits. Such parameters (including a range of one) are possible while maintaining a threshold because of the concatenation step. This reduces the noise that would otherwise accumulate within a growing-depth syndrome extraction circuit. A key idea is that constant-depth syndrome extraction is not a necessary condition for fault-tolerance.  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Threshold exists for the locally decaying error model; see [ 3507 , Thm. 1.3]. However, the logical error rate below thresh-old falls super-polynomially (as opposed to exponentially) with the code distance. The code family possesses a threshold equal to that of surface codes given by tuning the inner code size for any fixed physical error rate.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Concatenated qubit code  

> › p. 380

— Using the concatenation convention of the Zoo, hierarchical codes are concatenations of constant-rate QLDPC (inner) codes with rotated surface (outer) codes. The cited paper [ 3507 ] uses the oppo-site inner/outer terminology. The block length of the outer code is picked to grow logarithmically with the block length of the inner code.  

> COUSIN

⊲ Rotated surface code › p. 448 — Hierarchical codes are con-catenations of constant-rate QLDPC codes with rotated surface codes. 

HIGH-DIMENSIONAL EXPANDER (HDX) CODE [652, 3620]  

> ramanujan_tensor_product
> DESCRIPTION

CSS code obtained by applying the generalized distance-balancing/product construction of Ref. [652 ] to a Ramanujan-complex quantum code and an asymptotically good classical LDPC code. Ramanujan quantum codes are defined using LSV Ramanujan complexes, which are simplicial complexes that generalize Ramanu-jan graphs [ 65 , 66 ]. The auxiliary classical code is viewed as a 1-dimensional chain complex, and the output code is defined on the co-complex of the product of the two co-complexes. Using a 2D LSV complex yields a QLDPC family with 𝐾 = Ω (√︁ 𝑛 /log 𝑛 ) and 𝐷 =Ω(√︁ 𝑛 log 𝑛 ), while using a 3D LSV complex yields 𝐾 = Ω (√𝑛 /log 𝑛 )

and 𝐷 = Ω (√𝑛 log 𝑛 ). 

> PROTECTION

The unbalanced component code from a 2D LSV com-plex can have 𝑑 𝑋 = Ω (log 𝑛 ) and 𝑑 𝑍 = Ω (𝑛 ), while one from a 3D LSV complex can have 𝑑 𝑋 = Ω (log 2 𝑛 ) and 𝑑 𝑍 = Ω (𝑛 ) [652 ]. After distance balancing, the resulting HDX family has minimum distance 𝐷 = Ω (√︁ 𝑛 log 𝑛 ) in the 2D case and 𝐷 = Ω (√𝑛 log 𝑛 ) in the 3D case.  

> RATE

For 2D LSV complexes, the rate is of order › p. 161 Ω(1/√︁ 𝑛 log 𝑛 ),with minimum distance 𝐷 = Ω(√︁ 𝑛 log 𝑛 ). For 3D LSV com-plexes, the rate is Ω(1/( √𝑛 log 𝑛 )) , with minimum distance 𝐷 =Ω(√𝑛 log 𝑛 ). 

> DECODING

⊲ For HDX codes built from 2D LSV complexes, 𝑋 -error decoding reduces to polynomial-time cycle-code decoding on the 1-skeleton together with decoding of the auxiliary classical LDPC code [ 652 ]. ⊲ For the 2D construction, 𝑍 -errors of linear weight admit a local decoder based on coboundary expansion; replacing the component complex by the 2-skeleton of a 3D LSV complex preserves 2D-type asymptotic parameters while giving linear-time 

𝑍 -decoding with unit-weight local corrections [652].  

> NOTES

⊲ Codes were first to break a 20-year record set by the Freedman-Meyer-Luo code › p. 392 for the lower bound on scaling of the minimum distance [3343].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Homological product code › p. 401 — Ramanujan codes re-sult from a tensor product of a classical-code and a quantum-code chain complex. ⊲ Tensor-product HDX code › p. 459 — Ramanujan codes result from a tensor product of a classical-code and a quantum-code chain complex.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Distance-balanced code › p. 490 — Ramanujan tensor-product constructions use distance balancing to increase distance. 

⊲ Hypergraph product (HGP) code › p. 406 — Ramanujan codes utilize the hypergraph product with a twist, which is an automorphism on one of the complexes in the tensor product, in order to increase distance [ 3343 ]. ⊲ Freedman-Meyer-Luo code › p. 392 — Ramanu-jan codes broke 20-year record on minimum code distance set by Freedman-Meyer-Luo codes. 

HIGHER-DIMENSIONAL HOMOLOGICAL PRODUCT CODE [ 644 , 797 ,1565, 2899] multisector_hypergraph  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Higher-dimensional tensor product code 

⊲ Multi-sector homological product code ⊲ Multi-sector tensor product code ⊲ Iterative homological product code ⊲ Iterative tensor product code 400  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit CSS code formulated using a tensor product of two or more chain complexes, each of length one or greater. The number of chain complexes participating in the product is the dimen-sion of the code. When all chain complexes are length-one, meaning that they correspond to classical codes, the code is called a higher-dimensional HGP code (a.k.a. multi-sector HGP code or iterative HGP code). The stabilizer generator matrices of an 𝑚 -dimensional homo-logical product code are the boundary and co-boundary operators of a 2-dimensional chain complex contained within an 𝑚 -complex that is recursively constructed by taking the tensor product of an 

(𝑚 − 1)-complex and a 1-complex. There is freedom in choosing which 2-dimensional chain complex to pick for the code.  

> PROTECTION

The Künneth formula gives code properties in terms of those of the underlying chain complexes. Hypergraph products of multiple classical codes were considered first [ 797 ]. Homological products of CSS-code and classical chain complexes are used as a building block in Hastings’ weight-reduction construction [ 2899 ], while later work studied explicit product-code families built from length-two chain complexes [ 644 ] (which correspond to qubit CSS codes per the qubit CSS-to-homology correspondence › p. 437 ). Ref. [ 1565 ] gives explicit parameter formulas for the tensor prod-uct A × K ( 𝑃 ) of an 𝑚 -complex A with the 1-complex K ( 𝑃 ) built from an 𝑟 × 𝑐 binary matrix 𝑃 .
