HOMOLOGICAL CODE [407, 460, 1257, 3582] higher_dimensional_surface  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Generalized surface code  

> DESCRIPTION

A CSS extension of the Kitaev surface code to arbitrary manifolds. The version on a Euclidean manifold of some fixed di-mension is called the 𝐷 -dimensional "surface" or 𝐷 -dimensional toric 

code. Given a cellulation of a manifold, qubits are put on 𝑝 -dimensional faces, 𝑋 -type stabilizers are associated with ( 𝑝 − 1)-faces, while 𝑍 -type stabilizers are associated with ( 𝑝 + 1)-faces. Here, 𝑝 ranges between 1 and 𝐷 − 1.Lattice surface codes in 𝐷 spatial dimensions can be partially classified by the dimension of their stabilizer generators (and corre-sponding excitations). There are ( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) surface codes for 𝑞 = 𝐷 − 𝑝 401 [548 ]. Applying this construction to the dual lattice of a ( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) sur-face code yields a (𝑞, 𝑝 ) surface code. All lattice surface codes have bosonic 𝑒 and 𝑚 excitations of dimension 𝑝 −1 and 𝑞 −1, respectively. Their logical operators are also of dimension 𝑝 and 𝑞 , respectively. In 2D, there is only the (1, 1) surface code, which is equivalent to the Kitaev surface code and which admits point-like 𝑒 and 𝑚 

excitations. In 3D, there are the (1, 2) and (2, 1) 3D surface codes, which are equivalent by Hadamard gates. Both admit point-like excitations of one type and loop-like excitations of the other. In 4D, there are the (1, 3), (2, 2), and (3, 1) 4D surface codes, with the first and last being equivalent by Hadamard gates. The (1, 3) code admits point-like 𝑒 excitations and 2D membrane 𝑚 excitations, while the 

(2, 2) loop toric code admits loop-like 𝑒 and 𝑚 excitations. Open-boundary hypercubic realizations give a family of (𝑑 1, 𝑑 2)-surface codes whose logical 𝑋 and 𝑍 operators have dimensions 𝑑 1

and 𝑑 2, respectively; the ordinary surface code, the 3D cubic code, and the 4D tesseract code are examples [3082].  

> PROTECTION

The 2D members of the family obey the Bravyi-Terhal no-go theorem: geometrically local stabilizer generators allow dis-tance at most 𝑂 (𝐿 ) and only an 𝑂 (1) energy barrier, ruling out self-correction in two dimensions [ 2910 ]. By contrast, the 4D (2, 2) loop surface code serves as a self-correcting quantum memory, while surface codes in higher dimensions can have distances not possible in lower dimensions.  

> RATE

Rate depends on the underlying cellulation and manifold [ 407 ,460 ]. For general 2D manifolds, 𝑘 𝑑 2 ≤ 𝑐 (log 𝑘 )2𝑛 for some constant 

𝑐 [ 799 ], meaning that (1) 2D surface codes with bounded geometry have distance scaling at most as 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) [ 650 , 1372 ], and (2) surface codes with finite rate can only achieve an asymptotic minimum distance that is logarithmic in 𝑛 . Higher-dimensional manifolds yield distances scaling more favorably. Loewner’s theorem provides an upper bound for any bounded-geometry surface code [3582].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Locality preserving op-erations can be determined for stacks of homological codes in any dimension [706].

HOMOLOGICAL PRODUCT CODE [797, 2486, 2899]  

> homological_product
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Tensor product code  

> DESCRIPTION

CSS code formulated using the tensor product of two chain complexes of length one or greater (see Qubit CSS-to-homology correspondence › p. 437 ). Homological products and ordinary tensor products of chain complexes differ in a way that depends on whether the underlying code is defined by a general or a length-three chain complex [ 797 ,Sec. 3.4.3].  

> PROTECTION

Given two codes ⟦𝑛 𝑖 , 𝑘 𝑖 , 𝑑 𝑖 , 𝑤 𝑖 ⟧ for 𝑖 ∈ { 1, 2}, where 𝑤 𝑖 

denotes the maximum hamming weight of all rows and columns of 𝜕 𝑖 , the homological product code has parameter ⟦𝑛 = 𝑛 1𝑛 2, 𝑘 =

𝑘 1 𝑘 2, 𝑑 ≤ 𝑑 1 𝑑 2, 𝑤 ≤ 𝑤 1 + 𝑤 2⟧. From this formula, and the fact that a randomly selected boundary operator 𝜕 yields a CSS code that is good with high probability, we see that the product code has 

𝑘 = Θ (𝑛 ) and 𝑤 = 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) with high probability. The main result in Ref. [ 3625 ] is to show that the product code has linear distance with high probability as well. To sum up, it is shown that we have a family of ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 = 𝑐 1𝑛, 𝑑 = 𝑐 2𝑛, 𝑤 = 𝑐 3

√𝑛 ⟧ codes given small enough 𝑐 1, 𝑐 2, 𝑐 3.402

HONEYCOMB FLOQUET CODE [509] honeycomb_floquet  

> DESCRIPTION

2D Floquet code based on the Kitaev honeycomb model [510 ] whose logical qubits are generated through a particular se-quence of measurements. A CSS version of the code has been pro-posed which loosens the restriction of which sequences to use [ 511 ]. The code has also been generalized to arbitrary non-chiral, Abelian topological order [512]. The code is defined on a honeycomb tiling with a physical qubit located at each vertex. Edges are labeled 𝑥 , 𝑦 , and 𝑧 , such that one edge of each label meets at every vertex. Check operators are defined as 𝑋 𝑋 acting on any two qubits joined by an 𝑥 edge, and similarly for 𝑦 and 𝑧 . The honeycomb tiling is 3-colorable, so the hexagons may be labeled 0, 1, 2 such that no two neighboring hexagons have the same label. The code-generating measurement pattern consists of measuring the check operators located on all of the 𝑟 -labeled edges in round 

𝑟 mod 3. The code space is the +1 eigenspace of the instantaneous stabilizer group (ISG). The ISG specifies the state of the system as a Pauli stabilizer state at a particular round of measurement, and it evolves into a (potentially) different ISG depending on the check operators measured. When the same check operators are instead regarded as a static subsystem code, there are no logical qubits; the logical qubits are created dynamically by the measurement ordering [509].  

> PROTECTION

Protective features similar to the surface code: on a torus geometry, the code protects two logical qubits with a code distance proportional to the linear size of the torus. After each complete measurement round in the steady state, a depth-one local Clifford circuit maps the ISG to that of a toric code on a hexagonal superlattice, making the logical content explicit [ 509 ]. Properties of the code with open boundaries are discussed in Refs. [ 3646 , 3647 ], and various other generalizations have been proposed [3648].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Initialization can be performed by preparing each pair of qubits on an edge in some particular state independently spec-ified by the effective-one-qubit operators (two-qubit Pauli strings centered on an edge) and then beginning the check measurement sequence. This is analogous to projecting a state into the code space by measuring stabilizers.  

> GATES

⊲ There are two types of logical operators, inner and outer .An inner logical operator is the product of check operators on a homologically nontrivial cycle. They belong to the stabilizer group as a subsystem code. Outer logical operators have an interpreta-tion in terms of magnetic and electric operators of an embedded toric/surface code, and they do not belong to the stabilizer group of the associated subsystem code. ⊲ Fermionic string excitations can be condensed along 1D paths, yielding twist defects [ 3649 ]. Such excitations are created by taking products of plaquette check opera-tors (that are present in all ISGs) over some region, multiplying them to yield a Pauli string on the boundary of said region, and cutting this string. Information is processed by braiding and fusing defects, which are located at the boundaries of the strings. ⊲ Certain gates [ 3648 ] can be performed by considering adiabatic paths in the space of Hamiltonians [ 3648 , 3650 , 3651 ], yielding an instance of holo-nomic quantum computation [ 3652 ]. Fault-tolerant gates should be interpretable as monodromies under a particular notion of parallel transport [773].  

> DECODING

⊲ The ISG has a static subgroup for all time steps 𝑟 ≥ 3 –that is, a subgroup which remains a subgroup of the ISG for all future times – given by so-called plaquette stabilizers . These are stabilizers consisting of products of check operators around homologically trivial paths. The syndrome bits correspond to the eigenvalues of the plaquette stabilizers. Because of the structure of the check op-erators, only one-third of all plaquettes are measured each round. The syndrome bits must therefore be represented by a lattice in spacetime, to reflect when and where the outcome was obtained.  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ One can run a fault-tolerant decoding algorithm by (1) bipartitioning the syndrome lattice into two graphs which are congruent to the Cayley graph of the free Abelian group with three generators (up to boundary conditions) and (2) performing a matching algorithm to deduce errors.  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ 0.2% − 0.3% in a controlled-not circuit model with a correlated minimum-weight perfect-matching decoder [ 3653 ]. 

⊲ 1.5% < 𝑝 < 2.0% in a circuit model with native weight-two measurements and a correlated minimum-weight perfect-matching decoder [ 3653 ]. Here, 𝑝 is the collective error rate of the two-body measurement gate, including both measurement and correlated data depolarization error processes. ⊲ Against circuit-level noise: within 0.2% − 0.3% for SD6 (standard depolarizing 6-step cycle), 

0.1% − 0.15% for SI1000 (superconducting-inspired 1000 ns cycle), and 1.5% − 2.0% for EM3 (entangling-measurement 3-step cycle) [3529, 3654].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Plaquette stabilizer measurement realized on the IBM Falcon superconducting-qubit device [3580]  

> PARENTS

⊲ Hastings-Haah Floquet code › p. 396 — The honeycomb Floquet code is the first 2D Floquet code. ⊲ Modular-qudit honey-comb Floquet code › p. 480 — The modular-qudit honeycomb Floquet code reduces to the Hastings-Haah Floquet code for 𝑞 = 2. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Z(1) 

> 𝑞

subsystem code › p. 474 — The dynamically generated logical qubit of the honeycomb Floquet code is generated by appro-priately scheduling measurements of the gauge generators of the 

Z(1) 

> 𝑞 =2

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — Measurement of each check operator of the honeycomb Floquet code involves two qubits and projects the 404 state of the two qubits to a two-dimensional subspace, which we regard as an effective qubit. These effective qubits form a surface code on an enlarged honeycomb tiling [ 509 , Fig. 2]. Electric and magnetic operators on the embedded surface code correspond to outer logical operators of the Floquet code. In fact, outer logical operators transition back and forth from magnetic to electric sur-face code operators under the measurement dynamics. Inspired by the honeycomb Floquet code, various weight-two measurement schemes have been designed [ 3655 – 3657 ], with the scheme in Ref. [3656 ] being a special case of DWR. Numerical comparisons have been performed [3658].

However, any measurement sequence can be performed on the color code without destroying the logical qubits, while honeycomb codes can be maintained only with specific sequences. Honeycomb codes require a shorter mea-surement cycle and use fewer qubits at the given code distance [509 ]. ⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 — The Honeycomb code admits a convenient representation in terms of Majorana fermions. HSIEH-HALASZ (HH) CODE [3660] hh_fracton  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of one of two families of fracton codes, named HH-I and HH-II, defined on a cubic lattice with two qubits per site. HH-I (HH-II) is a CSS (non-CSS) stabilizer code family, with the former identified as a foliated type-I fracton code that is decompos-able into two separate lattice models [ 436 ]. The sorting analysis of Ref. [ 436 ] leaves HH-II inconclusive, consistent with either a fractal type-I or a type-II fracton phase.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Fracton stabilizer code › p. 476 

— Both HH-I and HH-II are fracton codes; HH-I is identified as foli-ated type-I, while HH-II remains inconclusive between fractal type-I and type-II in the sorting analysis of Ref. [436].

HYBRID QUBIT CODE [2657, 2789] hybrid_qubits_into_qubits  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit code which stores both quantum and classical information. Usually denoted as (( 𝑛, 𝐾 : 𝑀 )) or (( 𝑛, 𝐾 : 𝑀, 𝑑 )) ,where 𝐾 is the dimension of the underlying quantum code, 𝑀 is the size of the classical code, and 𝑑 is the distance.  

> PROTECTION

Any qubit code can be converted into a hybrid qubit code by using some of its logical qubits to store only classical information [2657 ]. An (( 𝑛, 𝐾 : 𝑀 )) hybrid qubit code can detect more errors than an (( 𝑛, 𝐾 𝑀 )) qubit code [ 3664 ]. A hybrid Hamming bound has been constructed [3199]. Quantum weight enumerators › p. 434 , quantum MacWilliams iden-tities, and linear programming bounds have been extended to hybrid qubit codes [641, 2789, 3664].  

> PARENTS

⊲ OA qubit code › p. 420 — An OA qubit code that has no gauge structure (e.g., gauge qubits) but has a block structure that corre-sponds to a classical code is a hybrid qubit code. ⊲ Hybrid QECC

> COUSINS

HYBRID STABILIZER CODE [2657, 2789] hybrid_stabilizer  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit stabilizer code which stores both quantum and classical information. Usually denoted as ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 : 𝑐 ⟧ or ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 : 𝑐, 𝑑 ⟧,where 𝑘 (𝑐 ) is the number of encoded qubits (classical bits), and where 𝑑 is the distance. The algebraic structure of a hybrid stabilizer code is the same as that of a USt code whose cosets are indexed by a linear binary code: both codes utilize codewords of an inner ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code 

C and its cosets 𝑡 C, where the 2𝑐 Pauli strings 𝑡 correspond to the outer [𝑛, 𝑐 ] linear binary code. However, the hybrid stabilizer code 405 does not utilize superpositions of codewords of 𝑡 C and 𝑡 ′C for 𝑡 ≠ 𝑡 ′

since the different coset blocks correspond to classical codewords.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Hybrid qubit code › p. 404 — An ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 : 𝑐, 𝑑 ⟧ hybrid sta-bilizer code is an (( 𝑛, 2𝑘 : 2 𝑐 , 𝑑 )) hybrid qubit code. ⊲ Operator-algebra (OA) qubit stabilizer code › p. 421 — An OA stabilizer code which has no gauge qubits but has a block structure that corresponds to a linear binary code is a hybrid stabilizer code.

HYPERBOLIC COLOR CODE [669, 798, 799] hyperbolic_color  

> DESCRIPTION

An extension of the color code construction to hyper-bolic manifolds. As opposed to there being only three types of uni-form three-valent and three-colorable lattice tilings in the 2D Eu-clidean plane, there is an infinite number of admissible hyperbolic tilings in the 2D hyperbolic plane [ 798 ]. Certain double covers of hyperbolic tilings also yield admissible tilings [ 799 ]. Other admis-sible hyperbolic tilings can be obtained via a fattening procedure [411 ]; see also a construction based on the more general quantum pin codes [669].  

> PROTECTION

The use of hyperbolic surfaces allows one to circumvent bounds on code parameters (such as the BPT bound › p. 551 ) that are valid for lattice geometries. Hyperbolic color codes can have high rate but tend to have small distance. For example, a {4𝑔, 4𝑔 } tiling with periodic boundary conditions (i.e., a 𝑔 -torus) yields a ⟦4𝑔 +

8, 4𝑔, 4⟧ code family [ 798 ]. More examples, such as the ⟦160 , 20 , 8⟧

code on the 4.10.10 tiling, are provided in [669, Sec. V.A].  

> RATE

In the double-cover construction [ 799 ], an {ℓ, 𝑚 } input tiling yields a code family with an asymptotic rate of 1 − 2/ℓ − 2/𝑚 . 

> DECODING

⊲ Two flag-based decoders [3340].  

> NOTES

⊲ A database of 2D hyperbolic color codes is available in QECDB [ 745 ], where the color codes form the subset of self-dual codes.  

> PARENT

⊲ Color code › p. 379  

> CHILD

⊲ ⟦8, 2, 2⟧ hyperbolic color code › p. 357 — The ⟦8, 2, 2⟧ hyper-bolic color code is defined on the projective plane.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Hyperbolic surface code › p. 405 — Hyperbolic color codes and hyperbolic surface codes are both defined on hyperbolic tilings. 

⊲ Small-distance qubit stabilizer code › p. 451 — Many hyperbolic color codes have distance ≤ 5.

HYPERBOLIC FLOQUET CODE [3647, 3665, 3666] hyperbolic_floquet  

> DESCRIPTION

Floquet code whose check-operators correspond to edges of a hyperbolic lattice of degree 3.  

> PROTECTION

Code distance is at most 𝑂 (log 𝑛 ) due to the hyperbolic qubit geometry [ 3647 ], but semi-hyperbolic lattices yield 𝑂 (√𝑛 )

distance [3665]. A useful concept is the embedded distance [3665 ], which is the distance of the stabilizer code lying inside the subspace defined by measurement outcomes of the weight-two parity checks of the code.  

> RATE

Finite encoding rate whose value depends on the hyperbolic lattice. The asymptotic rate is 1/8 for a lattice of octagons [3666].  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndrome structure allows for MWPM decoding.  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ 0.1% under standard circuit-level depolarizing noise [ 3665 ]. ⊲ 0.1% under phenomenological error model including de-polarizing and measurement errors for the octagonal codes [3666].  

> NOTES

⊲ The code may be suitable for distributed storage [3667].  

> PARENT

⊲ Hastings-Haah Floquet code › p. 396 

HYPERBOLIC SURFACE CODE hyperbolic_surface  

> DESCRIPTION

An extension of the Kitaev surface code construction to hyperbolic manifolds. Given a cellulation of a hyperbolic manifold of arbitrary dimension, qubits are put on 𝑖 -dimensional faces, 𝑋 -type stabilizers are associated with (𝑖 − 1)-faces, while 𝑍 -type stabilizers are associated with 𝑖 + 1-faces.  

> PROTECTION

Constructions (see code children below) have yielded distances scaling favorably with the number of qubits. The use of hyperbolic surfaces allows one to circumvent bounds on code parameters (such as the BPT bound › p. 551 ) that are valid for lattice geometries.  

> GATES

⊲ (1, 𝐷 − 1) surface codes on hyperbolic geometries admit a fault-tolerant implementation of 𝐶 𝐷 𝑍 gates [ 3362 ]. ⊲ Higher-dimensional hyperbolic surface codes can admit a cup product struc-ture and can thus have logical gates in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 

implemented by constant-depth Clifford circuits › p. 244 [1470].  

> DECODING

⊲ Hastings decoder [807].  

> PARENT

⊲ Homological code › p. 400 406  

> CHILDREN

⊲ 2D hyperbolic surface code › p. 363 ⊲ Guth-Lubotzky code › p. 394 ⊲ Freedman-Meyer-Luo code › p. 392 ⊲ Hurwitz surface code › p. 404  

> COUSINS

⊲ Holographic tensor-network code › p. 308 — Both holo-graphic tensor-network and hyperbolic surface codes utilize tes-sellations of hyperbolic surfaces. Encodings for the former are hyperbolically tiled tensor networks, while the latter is defined on hyperbolically tiled physical-qubit lattices. ⊲ Single-shot code  

> › p. 320

— A 4D hyperbolic surface code can be decoded with the Hast-ings decoder [ 807 ] in time 𝑂 (𝑛 log 𝑛 ) and with a logical error scaling inverse polynomially with 𝑛 . ⊲ Hyperbolic color code › p. 405 — Hy-perbolic color codes and hyperbolic surface codes are both defined on hyperbolic tilings.

> DESCRIPTION

A member of a family of CSS codes whose stabilizer generator matrix is obtained from a hypergraph product of two classical linear binary codes. More technically, the 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type stabilizer generator matrices of a hypergraph product code are, respectively, the boundary and coboundary operators of the 2-complex obtained from the tensor product of a chain complex and cochain complex corresponding to two classical linear binary seed codes. for 𝑖 ∈ { 1, 2} with parameters [𝑛 𝑖 , 𝑘 𝑖 , 𝑑 𝑖 ], defined as the kernel of

The case when the two seed codes are equal, 𝐶 1 = 𝐶 2, is called a square hypergraph product code . If, in addition, im 𝐻 = im 𝐻 𝑇 , the hyper-graph product code is called a symmetric hypergraph product code 

[707]. In terms of the Qubit CSS-to-homology correspondence › p. 437 , the hypergraph product can be viewed as a homological product of two length-one chain complexes. The resulting code corresponds to the length-two chain complex that is called the total chain complex of the product of the input complexes (see [3668, Sec. II.C]).

⊲ Fault-tolerant state preparation via dimension jump [3669].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Hadamard (up to logical SWAP gates) and control-𝑍 on all logical qubits [ 707 ]. ⊲ Patch-transversal gates inherited from the automorphism group of the un-derlying classical codes [ 708 , Appx. D]. ⊲ Orientation-preserving constant-depth circuits can only implement gates in the Clifford group [ 704 ]. ⊲ Permutation-based gates (automorphism gadgets) can be inherited from the underlying classical codes in the hyper-graph construction [709].  

> GATES

⊲ Code deformation techniques yield Clifford gates › p. 244 

[ 3670 ]. ⊲ Pieceable fault-tolerant circuits, transversal gates, and magic-state injection yield a universal gate set for symmetric hy-pergraph product codes [ 707 ]. ⊲ Targeted logical gates [ 3671 ]. 

⊲ Logical gates via Dehn twists for hypergraph products of cyclic codes [3304].  

> DECODING

⊲ Single-ancilla syndrome extraction circuits do not admit hook errors › p. 435 [3672 ]. ⊲ ReShape decoder that uses minimum weight decoders for the classical codes used in the hypergraph con-struction [ 3673 ]. ⊲ 2D geometrically local syndrome extraction circuits with depth order › p. 161 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) using order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 ) ancilla qubits [ 495 ]. ⊲ BP-OSD decoder [ 1200 ] and an improved BP-OSD decoder [ 3087 ]. ⊲ Erasure correction can be implemented approx-imately with 𝑂 (𝑛 2) operations with quantum generalizations [ 3674 ]of the peeling and pruned peeling decoders [ 87 ], with a probabilistic version running in 𝑂 (𝑛 1.5) operations. Other nearly optimal erasure decoders exist [ 3675 , 3676 ]. Initial hypergraph product codes can be further optimized against the erasure channel using reinforce-ment learning [ 3677 ]. ⊲ Syndrome measurements are distance-preserving › p. 435 because syndrome extraction circuits can be de-signed to avoid hook errors › p. 435 [3678 ]. ⊲ Generalization [ 3679 ]of Viderman’s algorithm for expander codes [ 1291 ]. ⊲ Linear time iterative decoder [3680].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Pieceable fault-tolerant circuits, transversal gates, and magic-state injection yield a universal gate set for symmet-ric hypergraph product codes [ 707 ]. ⊲ Single-ancilla syndrome extraction circuits do not admit hook errors › p. 435 [3672 ]. ⊲ There is a fault-tolerant universal computation scheme for hypergraph-product codes concatenated with the ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ code in which the full syndrome measurement on the lower hypergraph product code is performed only if an error is detected at the upper four-qubit code [3200].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Some thresholds were determined in Ref. [3342 ]. ⊲ Bounds on code capacity thresholds using ML decoding can be obtained by mapping the effect of noise on the code to a statistical mechanical model [ 3339 ]. For example, a threshold of 7% 

was obtained under independent 𝑋 and 𝑍 noise for codes obtained from random (3, 4)-regular Gallager codes.  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Circuit-level noise: 0.1% with all-to-all connected syn-drome extraction circuits [ 495 ] and DiVincenzo-Aliferis syndrome extraction circuits [ 3681 ] combined with non-local gates [ 3682 ]. No threshold observed above physical noise rates at or above 10 −6 using 2D geometrically local syndrome extraction circuits.  

> NOTES

⊲ A database of hypergraph-product codes is available in QECDB [745].

HYPERINVARIANT TENSOR-NETWORK (HTN) CODE [3684]  

> holographic_hyperinvariant
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Evenbly code  

> DESCRIPTION

Holographic tensor-network code constructed out of a hyperinvariant tensor network [ 612 ], i.e., a MERA-like network admitting a hyperbolic geometry. The network is defined using two layers A and B, with constituent tensors satisfying isometry conditions (a.k.a. multitensor constraints). This code produces boundary correlation functions that align with those expected from conformal field theory (CFT) boundary states. HTN codes exhibit state-dependent breakdown of comple-mentary recovery, consistent with quantum gravity corrections in AdS/CFT.  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ 19 .1% under depolarizing noise and 50% 

under erasure noise for a {5, 4} tiling [ 3685 ]. ⊲ 40% under erasure noise for constant-rate version of the code [3685].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 ⊲ Holographic tensor-network code › p. 308 — The encoding of an HTN code is a hyperinvari-ant tensor network.  

> COUSIN

⊲ ⟦4, 2, 2⟧𝐺 four group-qudit code › p. 542 — The explicit 4-ququart encoding tensor 𝐴 ′ used in the HTN code is a ⟦4, 1, 2⟧Z4

JORDAN-WIGNER TRANSFORMATION CODE [531, 3686, 3687] jw  

> DESCRIPTION

A mapping between qubit Pauli strings and Majorana operators that can be thought of as a trivial ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 ⟧ code. The map-ping is best described as converting a chain of 𝑛 qubits into a chain of 2𝑛 Majorana modes (i.e., 𝑛 fermionic modes). It maps Majorana operators into Pauli strings of weight 𝑂 (𝑛 ).The Majorana modes {𝛾 𝑗 } are defined from Pauli strings as fol-lows, 

𝛾 0 = 𝑍 

−𝛾 1 = 𝑌 𝛾 2 = 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑍 

−𝛾 3 = 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑌 𝛾 4 = 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑍 

−𝛾 5 = 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑋 ⊗ 𝑌 ...

(278) The 𝑋 -type Pauli strings ensure that the resulting Majorana oper-ators satisfy the appropriate anti-commutation relations, namely, 

{𝛾 𝑖 , 𝛾 𝑗 } = 2𝛿 𝑖 𝑗 . 

> ENCODING

⊲ Circuit of depth linear in the number of qubits 𝑛 . The depth can be reduced for particle-preserving systems [ 3688 ] and in other contexts [3689].  

> PARENT

⊲ Fermion-into-qubit code › p. 389  

> COUSINS

⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 — A Majorana stabilizer code is a stabilizer code whose stabilizers are composed of Majorana fermion operators, which are in turn realizable using Pauli strings via the Jordan-Wigner mapping. 

⊲ Kitaev chain code › p. 409 — The Kitaev chain code can be thought of as the Majorana stabilizer analogue of the quantum repe-tition code [ 532 ] and is related to that code via the Jordan-Wigner transformation [ 3690 ]. ⊲ Auxiliary qubit mapping (AQM) code  

> › p. 368

— The AQM fermion-into-qubit code reduces to the JW trans-formation code when the outer code is trivial. ⊲ Bravyi-Kitaev transformation (BKT) code › p. 372 — The weight of a Majorana oper-ator in the BKT (JW transformation) code scales logarithmically (linearly) with 𝑛 , with the former demonstrating an exponential improvement [ 3410 ]. ⊲ 2D bosonization code › p. 361 — The exact 2D bosonization code can be converted by a linear-depth Clifford circuit into a Jordan-Wigner ordering path on the 2D lattice [ 387 , Fig. 24]. 

JUMP CODE [129, 130, 3156] jump  

> DESCRIPTION

A CE code designed to detect and correct AD › p. 508 errors. An (( 𝑛, 𝐾 )) jump code is denoted as (( 𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑡 )) 𝑤 (which conflicts with modular-qudit notation), where 𝑡 is the maximum number of qubits that can be corrected after each one has undergone a jump error 

|0⟩⟨ 1|, and where each codeword is a uniform superposition of qubit basis states with Hamming weight 𝑤 . 

> PROTECTION

Various code bounds, including an upper bound on 𝐾 

given the other parameters, are provided in Ref. [ 130 ]. For example, one can apply bit flips to all qubits of an (( 𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑡 )) 𝑤 jump code to obtain an (( 𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑡 )) 𝑛 −𝑤 jump code.  

> RATE

An infinite family of jump codes asymptotically attains an up-per bound on 𝐾 [130, Thm. 27].  

> GATES

⊲ Two-qubit entangling gate [3691].  

> NOTES

⊲ Survey of jump codes [3692].

KIM-PRESKILL-TANG (KPT) CODE [613] kpt  

> DESCRIPTION

An approximate quantum error-correcting code that protects the encoded interior of a black hole from computationally bounded exterior observers. Under the assumption that the Hawk-ing radiation emitted by an old black hole is pseudorandom, there exists a subspace of the radiation system that encodes the black hole interior, entangled with the late outgoing Hawking quanta. The logical operators of this code, called ghost operators in [ 613 ], com-mute with efficient operations acting on the radiation, protecting the interior up to corrections exponentially small in the black hole’s entropy. The construction is state dependent: the encoding depends on the state that collapsed to form the black hole [613]. This code has been tested in various models of gravity [ 613 , 3693 ].  

> PROTECTION

Protection relies on the pseudorandomness of the radi-ation and on restricting noise to efficient quantum computations acting on the radiation alone. Such operations commute with the interior logical algebra up to errors exponentially small in the re-maining black-hole entropy [613].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Holographic code › p. 308 — The ro-bustness of KPT codes does not rely on arguments from holographic duality, but such codes do aim to describe interiors of black holes.  

> COUSIN

⊲ SYK code › p. 459 — The Brownian SYK model can be used to demonstrate the complexity-based error-correction of KPT codes [613]. 

KITAEV CHAIN CODE [531] kitaev_chain  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Majorana repetition code  

> DESCRIPTION

A Majorana stabilizer code obtained from the ground-state subspace of the Kitaev Majorana chain in its fermionic topo-logical phase [ 531 ]. Its codespace is stabilized by nearest-neighbor Majorana bilinears, while two unpaired edge Majoranas furnish one logical fermionic mode. Under parity-preserving noise, it behaves as the Majorana analogue of the repetition code [532]. At the fixed-point limit, the code Hamiltonian is proportional to 

− Í𝑛 −1 

> 𝑗 =1

𝑖𝛾 2 𝑗 𝛾 2 𝑗 +1, so the codespace is the common +1 eigenspace of the stabilizers 𝑆 𝑗 = 𝑖𝛾 2 𝑗 𝛾 2 𝑗 +1. The two unpaired edge operators 

𝛾 1 and 𝛾 2𝑛 are the Majorana zero modes (MZMs) or Majorana edge modes (MEMs) ; they commute with all stabilizers and define a log-ical fermionic mode 𝑓 L = (𝛾 1 + 𝑖𝛾 2𝑛 )/ 2. Via the Jordan-Wigner transformation, the model maps to the 1D quantum Ising chain in its symmetry-breaking phase. The code can be thought of as the Majorana stabilizer analogue of the quantum repetition code: parity-preserving dephasing operators 𝑍 𝑗 = 𝑖𝛾 2 𝑗 −1𝛾 2 𝑗 play the role of repetition-code bit flips, while the logical Majorana operators have odd weight and therefore encode a logical fermion [532]. The two basis states of a single chain have opposite fermionic parity. Therefore, a single chain does not by itself furnish a fixed-parity qubit encoding; coherent superpositions between the two basis states are not directly accessible in an isolated fermionic sys-tem with parity superselection. One can combine two such code blocks to form a Majorana box qubit, which is the fixed-parity sub-space of the combined codespace. Odd numbers of code blocks also contain fixed-parity logical subspaces in their codespace.  

> PROTECTION

In the fixed-point limit, local parity-preserving bilinears such as 𝑍 𝑗 = 𝑖𝛾 2 𝑗 −1𝛾 2 𝑗 anticommute with nearby stabilizers, so the chain behaves as a repetition code against dephasing or phase errors [532 ]. For a finite chain, the splitting between the two code states is exponentially small in the separation between the edge modes [ 531 ]. As a Majorana stabilizer code, however, its distance is 1 because a single MZM is already a logical operator. The code therefore does not protect against single-Majorana, parity-violating errors such as quasiparticle poisoning. Disorder may help with protection [3694].  

> GATES

⊲ Braiding, 𝑆 , and 𝑇 phase gates, fermion 𝐶𝑍 𝑓 , and mixed qubit-fermion 𝐶𝑍 𝑞 𝑓 gates are described for logical fermions en-coded in this repetition code [532].  

> DECODING

⊲ Local automaton decoder based on a self-dual cellular automaton [ 3695 ]. ⊲ Syndrome extraction of the stabilizers 𝑆 𝑗 =

𝑖𝛾 2 𝑗 𝛾 2 𝑗 +1 can be performed by interfacing with a qubit ancilla and mixed qubit-fermion gates [532].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Photonic systems: braiding of topological Majo-rana modes has been simulated in a device that has a differ-ent notion of locality than a bona fide fermionic system [ 3696 ]. 

⊲ Superconducting circuits: preparation [ 3697 ], braiding [ 3698 ], and detection of Majorana edge modes [ 3698 , 3699 ] have been simulated in devices that have a different notion of locality than a bona fide fermionic system.  

> NOTES

⊲ See notes [3690] for a description of this code.

KITAEV HONEYCOMB CODE [395, 510, 567] kitaev_honeycomb  

> DESCRIPTION

Subsystem qubit stabilizer code underlying the Kitaev honeycomb model [ 510 , 567 ]. Its gauge generators are the two-qubit 

𝑋 𝑋 , 𝑌𝑌 , and 𝑍 𝑍 link operators on the three edge types of the hon-eycomb lattice [ 567 , Sec. 3.2]. Its stabilizer group is generated by loop operators, and syndrome extraction can be reduced to ordered measurements of the two-qubit link operators [ 567 , Sec. 3.2]. This is the 𝑞 = 2 instance of the Z(1) 

> 𝑞

subsystem code and does not encode any logical qubits [567][395, Sec. 7.3]. The original Kitaev honeycomb spin model is exactly solvable by mapping spins to Majorana fermions in a static Z2 gauge field, yielding three gapped 𝐴 phases and one gapless 𝐵 phase [ 510 ]. Its ground state lies in the vortex-free sector, and the gapped 𝐴 phases realize Abelian Z2 topological order [510].  

> ENCODING

⊲ The geometric entanglement measure of a ground state 410 of the Kitaev honeycomb model and any state with anomalous one-form symmetry scales as order › p. 161 Ω(𝑛 ) [3700].

KITAEV SURFACE CODE [404, 2065, 3704, 3705] surface  

> DESCRIPTION

A family of Abelian topological CSS stabilizer › p. 544 codes whose generators are few-body 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type Pauli strings as-sociated to the stars and plaquettes, respectively, of a cellulation of a two-dimensional surface (with a qubit located at each edge of the cellulation). Codewords correspond to ground states of the surface code Hamiltonian, and error operators create or annihilate pairs of anyonic charges or vortices. The construction on a torus is called the toric code, while the construction on a planar patch with boundaries is called the planar code [ 3285 , 3705 ]. Boundary segments come in two types, open (a.k.a. rough or primal) and closed (a.k.a. smooth or dual); logical operators on patches with boundary are naturally described by relative homol-ogy classes [ 3705 ]. In the homological formulation, a cellulation of a closed surface 𝑀 encodes 𝑘 = 2 − 𝜒 (𝑀 ) qubits, while a cellulation of a surface with boundary encodes 𝑘 = 1 − 𝜒 (𝑀 ) qubits; cutting handles of closed surfaces yields planar patches with holes [ 61 ]. A 

mixed boundary consists of an interleaving of the two boundary types [407].  

> PROTECTION

The original planar code on a square-lattice patch with different boundary conditions on the vertical and horizontal edges is a ⟦𝐿 2 + ( 𝐿 −1)2, 1, 𝐿 ⟧ CSS code [ 3285 ]. On a closed orientable surface of genus 𝑔 , the codespace has dimension 22𝑔 , i.e., the code encodes 

𝑘 = 2𝑔 logical qubits; such higher-genus surfaces have been investi-gated [ 3705 , 3706 ]. Planar patches with holes or mixed boundaries can encode multiple logical qubits, and mixed-boundary layouts can reduce planar overhead by about a factor of three compared with punctured square-lattice constructions [ 407 ]. The surface code has also been shown to be resilient to burst errors [3707]. 

> Topological order and gauge-theory analogy

When treated as ground states of the code Hamiltonian, the code states realize Z2 topological order, a topological phase of matter that also exists in Z2 lattice gauge theory [ 3427 ]. For sufficiently weak lo-cal perturbations on closed surfaces, the splitting of this topological ground-state degeneracy is exponentially small in the shortest linear lattice size [ 404 ]. This order does not persist at nonzero temperature [3038, 3708]. Pauli noise operators can be organized into anyonic strings of the gauge theory, which cause excitations of the ground-state sub-space. The inability of local errors to distinguish the codewords translates to the "topologically protected" degeneracy of the ground state, rigorously formulated by the TQO-1 condition › p. 326 . The joint 

+1-eigenspace of the 𝑍 -type Paulis corresponds to the subspace that conserves Z2 flux, while the joint +1-eigenspace of 𝑋 -type operators corresponds to the subspace that preserves Z2 gauge symmetry (a one-form symmetry). Logical Pauli operators correspond to non-contractible Wilson loops in the case of closed boundaries, and to paths connecting different types of boundaries in the case of open boundaries. Behavior under Hamiltonian 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type perturbations is related to an anisotropic 3D gauge Higgs model [ 3709 – 3713 ]. In order to corrupt logical states, any local noise must bring the code state out of the topological order [3708]. Alternatively, there is a general correspondence between stabi-lizer codes and gauge theory, with the stabilizer group playing the role of the gauge group [ 1318 ]. In this interpretation, both the 𝑋 and 

𝑍 stabilizers are gauge group elements.  

> RATE

Both the planar and toric codes saturate the BPT bound › p. 551 ,which states that 𝑘 𝑑 2 = 𝑂 (𝐿 2) for codes on a 2D lattice of length 

𝑂 (𝐿 ).

> DECODING

⊲ Using data from multiple syndrome measurements prior to decoding allows for correcting syndrome measurement er-rors. The surface code requires order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑑 ) extraction rounds in order to gain a reliable estimate. Syndrome measurements are distance-preserving › p. 435 because syndrome extraction circuits can be designed to avoid hook errors › p. 435 [ 460 ]. ⊲ Syndrome extrac-tion circuits consist of CNOT gates and ancillary measurements since this is a stabilizer code [ 2449 ]. Measurement schedules can be optimized using spacetime circuit codes to yield what is known as the 3CX surface code [3748 ]. Schedules can also be optimized via ZX calculus [ 3490 , 3491 ]. Inspired by the honeycomb Floquet code, various weight-two measurement schemes have been designed [3655 – 3657 ], with the scheme in Ref. [ 3656 ] being a special case of DWR. ⊲ Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction circuits using three-qubit gates [ 3749 , 3750 ]. ⊲ Expanding diamonds decoder correct-ing errors of some maximum fractal dimension [ 3751 ]. The sub-threshold failure probability scales as ( 𝑝 /𝑝 th )𝑑 𝛽 

, where 𝑝 th is the threshold and 𝛽 = log 3 2. ⊲ Minimum weight perfect-matching (MWPM) [ 460 , 3752 –3754 ] (based on work by Edmonds on finding a matching in a graph [ 3755 , 3756 ]), which takes time up to polynomial in 𝑛 for the surface code. For the case of the surface code, minimum-weight decoding reduces to MWPM [ 460 , 3755 , 3757 ]. MWPM solves the MPE decoding problem exactly for independent 𝑋 and 𝑍 noise. Minimum-weight decoding is 𝑁 𝑃 -hard for more general Pauli noise and for transversal-CNOT decoding with Pauli-𝑍 and measurement bit-flip errors [ 3321 , 3758 ]. PyMatching is a Python software library for implementing MWPM [ 3759 ]. ⊲ The Bravyi-Suchara-Vargo (BSV) tensor network decoder [ 3760 ] exactly solves the ML decod-ing problem under independent 𝑋, 𝑍 noise for the surface code and has complexity of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2); the decoder provides an efficient tensor-network contraction for the partition function re-sulting from the statistical mechanical mapping, which is known to be solvable for an Ising model on a planar graph [ 3761 ]. ML decoding [ 460 ] is #𝑃 -hard in general for the surface code [ 3758 ]. 

⊲ Union-find decoder [ 3762 ] uses the union-find data structure [ 3763 –3765 ], solving the MPE decoding problem exactly for low-weight errors under depolarizing noise. A subsequent modification utilizes the continuous signal obtained in the physical implementation of the stabilizer measurement (as opposed to discretizing the signal into a syndrome bit) [ 3766 ]. Belief union find is a combination of belief-propagation and union-find [3767]. Strictly local (as opposed to partially local) union find [ 3768 ] has a worst-case runtime of or-der › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑑 3) in the distance 𝑑 . ⊲ Modified MWPM decoders: topological code Autotune [ 3769 ]; pipeline MWPM (accounting for correlations between events) [ 3770 , 3771 ]; modification tailored to asymmetric noise [ 3772 ]; parity blossom MWPM and fusion blos-som MWPM [ 3773 ], a modification utilizing the continuous signal obtained in the physical implementation of the stabilizer measure-ment (as opposed to discretizing the signal into a syndrome bit) [ 3766 ]; belief perfect matching (a combination of belief-propagation and MWPM) [ 3767 ]; spanning tree matching (STM) and rapid-fire (RFire) decoders [ 3774 ]; ordered decoding based on MWPM [ 3775 ]; Micro Blossom adapted for a parallelized architecture [ 3776 ]; logi-cal observable MWPM and a windowed version [ 3777 ]. Combining, or harmonizing , various decoders can improve performance [3778]. One such example is the Libra decoder [ 3779 ], a combination of MWPM decoders and matching synthesis. ⊲ Renormalization group (RG) [ 3780 –3782 ]; see Ref. [ 3783 ] for the planar surface code. 

⊲ Linear-time ML erasure decoder [ 3366 ]. ⊲ Linear-time decoder for general noise, including coherent noise and correlated noise [3784 ]. ⊲ Markov-chain Monte Carlo [ 3785 ]. ⊲ Cellular automa-ton decoders [ 2937 , 2938 , 3786 ]; see also [ 2939 ]. ⊲ Neural network [ 3787 –3793 ], reinforcement learning [ 3794 –3797 ], and transformer-based [ 3798 , 3799 ] decoders like the AlphaQubit series [ 3800 , 3801 ]. 

⊲ Lightweight low-latency look-up table (LILLIPUT) decoder for small surface codes [ 3802 ]. ⊲ Decoders can be augmented with a pre-decoder [ 3803 , 3804 ], which can allow for some processing to be done inside the cryogenic environment of the quantum system [3805 ]. ⊲ Sliding-window [ 3806 , 3807 ], parallel-window [ 3806 ], and predictive-window [ 3808 ] parallelizable decoders, designed to overcome the backlog problem, can be combined with many in-ner decoders, such as MWPM or union-find. ⊲ Modifications of BP: generalized belief propagation (GBP) [ 3809 ], based on a classi-cal version [ 3810 ]; AMBP4, a quaternary version [ 3636 ] of the MBP decoder [ 3637 ] of complexity 𝑂 (𝑛 log log 𝑛 ); blockBP, a combina-tion of BP and tensor-network decoders [ 3811 ]; machine-learning inspired modifications [ 3812 ]. See Ref. [ 3813 ] for a review of BP decoders. The min-sum decoder, a simple variant of BP, cannot be used to attain the benefits of codes with distance greater than 9 [ 3814 ]. ⊲ A color-code decoder can be used for the surface code [ 3815 ]. ⊲ Progressive-Proximity Bit-Flipping (PPBF) decoder [3816 ]. ⊲ Collision clustering decoder [ 3188 ]. ⊲ Quasi-local Lindbladian decoder based on the approximate Petz theorem [ 3817 ].

⊲ Framework of fault tolerance utilizing ZX calculus [ 3490 , 3491 ] that is applicable to MBQC, FBQC, and conventional computation ver-sions of the surface code [ 3829 ]. ⊲ Syndrome extraction circuits consisting of CNOT gates and ancillary measurements [ 2449 ]. Mea-surement schedules can be optimized using spacetime circuit codes to yield what is known as the 3CX surface code [ 3748 ]. Schedules can also be optimized via ZX calculus [ 3490 , 3491 ]. Inspired by the honey-comb Floquet code, various weight-two measurement schemes have been designed [ 3655 – 3657 ], with the scheme in Ref. [ 3656 ] being a special case of DWR. ⊲ LUCI framework for syndrome extraction circuits [ 3830 , 3831 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant constant-depth encoder and unencoder using measurements [1389].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Circuit-level noise: 1.8% under correlated CNOT-gate errors and single-qubit depolarizing noise [ 3832 ] with optimal de-coder [ 3833 ], and 0.35% under independent 𝑋, 𝑍 noise with opti-mal decoder [ 3833 ]. Also, 0.57% for depolarizing noise on data and syndrome qubits as well as initialization, gate, and measurement errors under MWPM decoding [ 2449 ]. For this model, a logical qubit with a 10 −14 logical error rate requires between 10 3 to 10 4 physical qubits and a target gate fidelity above 99 .9% . Later work gave a rigorous threshold proof for arbitrarily reliable computation under local stochastic circuit noise with physical error rate 𝑝 < 7.4 × 10 −4

[3834 ]. Thresholds of 0.5 − 2.9% have been observed for various noise models [ 3396 , 3434 , 3833 , 3835 – 3838 ]. A threshold of 0.41% 

when concatenated with the ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ code [ 3194 ]. The union-find decoder has a finite threshold under circuit-level local stochastic noise [ 3839 ]. ⊲ Phenomenological noise: 3.3% for square tiling [3450 ], and 2.93 (2)% using several rounds of syndrome measure-ment [ 3835 ]. ⊲ Fabrication errors [ 3840 ]. ⊲ Quasistatic phase damping and readout noise: 2.85% [3841 ]. ⊲ When used as the underlying code of a surface/Hamming concatenation and bench-marked by a logical CNOT implemented via lattice surgery under circuit-level depolarizing noise, the threshold is 0.31% , and achiev-ing logical CNOT error rate 10 −24 at physical error rate 0.1% requires space overhead 4.5 × 10 3 [3123 ]. ⊲ Thresholds for various mea-surement schedules, including that of the 3CX surface code, have been obtained [3842].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Signatures of the corresponding topological phase of matter detected in superconducting circuits [ 3843 ] and two-dimensional neutral atom arrays [3844]. 

⊲ Measurement schedules associated with the 3CX surface code realized in superconducting qubits on the Willow device by Google Quantum AI [3845].

LADDER FLOQUET CODE [509] ladder  

> DESCRIPTION

1D Floquet code defined on a ladder qubit geometry, with one qubit per vertex. The check operators consist of 𝑍 𝑍 checks on each rung and alternating 𝑋 𝑋 and 𝑌𝑌 checks on the legs. The period-four measurement schedule measures 𝑍 𝑍 , 𝑋 𝑋 , 𝑍 𝑍 , and 𝑌𝑌 

in rounds 0, 1, 2, 3 mod 4, respectively, dynamically generating one logical qubit [509].  

> PROTECTION

For 𝑟 ≥ 4, the ISG is generated by plaquette stabilizers on the ladder squares together with the most recently measured checks. The code has effective distance 2: it detects all single-qubit Pauli errors, and chains of check errors produce syndrome defects only at their endpoints, analogously to a repetition code [509].  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndrome bits are the plaquette-stabilizer eigenvalues, recorded every time they can be inferred from consecutive rounds of measurements [ 509 ]. ⊲ Period-four measurement sequence utilizing two-qubit measurements [509].  

> PARENT

⊲ Hastings-Haah Floquet code › p. 396 — The ladder Floquet code is the first 1D Floquet code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ Four-qubit code › p. 345 — The smallest example of the ladder Floquet code is a dynamical version of the ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ code [3154 , 3196 ]. The ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ code can be Floquetified in various ways [3197 , 3198 ]. ⊲ ⟦6, 2, 2⟧ 𝐶 6 code › p. 350 — The ISG of the ladder code includes 𝑍 -type Pauli products around squares of the qubit ladder. These are also included in the checks of the 𝐶 6 code. 

LAYER CODE [2950] layer  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of qubit QLDPC CSS codes with stabilizer generator weights ≤ 6 that are obtained by coupling lay-ers of 2D surface codes according to the Tanner graph of a QLDPC code (or a more general qubit stabilizer code). Geometric locality is maintained because, instead of being concatenated, each pair of parallel surface-code squares is fused (or quasi-concatenated) with perpendicular surface-code squares via lattice surgery.  

> RATE

Layer codes achieve the 3D BPT bound › p. 551 , with parameters 

⟦𝑛, Θ(𝑛 1/3), Θ(𝑛 1/3)⟧ , when asymptotically good QLDPC codes are used in the construction.  

> DECODING

⊲ Decoders against stochastic and adversarial noise [2951].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 — Layer codes are constructed by coupling layers of 2D surface codes accord-ing to the Tanner graph of a QLDPC code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 — The Layer code realizes 2D layers of Z2 gauge theory coupled along defects. ⊲ Fracton sta-bilizer code › p. 476 — Layer codes are non-translation invariant 3D lat-tice stabilizer codes that can be viewed as fracton topological defect networks [ 2950 ]. ⊲ Good QLDPC code › p. 547 — Layer codes achieve the 3D BPT bound › p. 551 , with parameters ⟦𝑛, Θ(𝑛 1/3), Θ(𝑛 1/3)⟧ ,when asymptotically good QLDPC codes are used in the construc-tion. ⊲ Concatenated qubit code › p. 380 — Each pair of surface-code squares in a layer code is fused (or quasi-concatenated) with perpen-dicular surface-code squares via lattice surgery. ⊲ Self-correcting quantum code › p. 319 — The energy barrier of excitations for layer codes constructed using asymptotically good QLDPC codes scales as order › p. 161 Θ(𝑛 1/3) [2950 ]. Layer codes are partially self-correcting quantum memories [ 2951 , 2952 ]. LOCAL HAAR-RANDOM CIRCUIT QUBIT CODE [2135]  

> local_haar_random
> DESCRIPTION

An 𝑛 -qubit code whose codewords are a pair of approx-imately locally indistinguishable states produced by starting with any two orthogonal 𝑛 -qubit states and acting with a random unitary circuit of depth polynomial in 𝑛 . Two states are locally indistinguish-able if they cannot be distinguished by local measurements. A single layer of the encoding circuit is composed of about 𝑛 /2 two-qubit nearest-neighbor gates run in parallel, with each gate drawn ran-domly from the Haar distribution on two-qubit unitaries. The above circuit elements act on nearest-neighbor qubits ar-ranged in a line, i.e., a 1D geometry ( 𝐷 = 1); codes for higher-dimensional geometries require 𝑂 (𝑛 1/𝐷 )-depth circuits [ 2135 ]. Follow-up work [ 3514 ] showed that, at the erasure threshold, 1D random circuits require 𝑂 (√𝑛 ) depth, whereas dimensions 𝐷 ≥ 2

retain 𝑂 (log 𝑛 )-depth scaling. This result has in turn been extended to other types of Pauli noise [ 3865 ], while the previous result applies to erasure noise.  

> PROTECTION

In a 1D geometry, the local Haar-random circuit qubit code approximately detects any error with support on a segment of length ≤ 𝑛 /4, with deviations exponentially suppressed in 𝑛 . There is a phase transition in error correction power vs error rate 𝑝 , with a critical depth of order › p. 161 𝑂 (1/𝑝 ) [3866].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Random local circuit of depth proportional to 𝑛 𝛼 , with 

𝛼 depending on system geometry.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Random-circuit code › p. 318  

> COUSINS

⊲ Topological code › p. 325 — Local Haar-random codewords, like topological codewords, are locally indistinguishable [ 2135 ]. 

⊲ Unitary 𝑡 -design › p. 251 — Local Haar-random circuits of polyno-mial depth form approximate unitary designs [ 2135 ]. ⊲ 1D lattice stabilizer code › p. 542 — In a 1D geometry, the local Haar-random cir-cuit qubit code approximately detects any error with support on a segment of length ≤ 𝑛 /4, with deviations exponentially suppressed in 𝑛 . There is a phase transition in error correction power vs error rate 𝑝 , with a critical depth of order › p. 161 𝑂 (1/𝑝 ) [ 3866 ]. ⊲ Haar-random qubit code › p. 395 — Approximating the random projections through 𝑡 -designs is necessary in order to make the Haar-random qubit protocol practical. Replacing with random Clifford gates › p. 244 

is especially convenient since the Clifford group › p. 244 forms a unitary 2-design and produces stabilizer codes.

LONG-RANGE ENHANCED SURFACE CODE (LRESC) [708] lresc  

> DESCRIPTION

Code constructed using a hypergraph product of two copies of a concatenated LDPC-repetition seed code. This family interpolates between surface codes and hypergraph codes since the hypergraph product of two repetition codes yields the planar surface code. The construction uses small [3, 2, 2] and [6, 2, 4] LDPC codes concatenated with [4, 1, 4] and [2, 1, 2] repetition codes, respectively. An example using a [5, 2, 3] code is also presented.  

> GATES

⊲ Patch-transversal gates for suitable seed codes [708].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Preparation of GHZ state of four logical qubits with beyond break-even fidelity in a ⟦25 , 4, 3⟧ LRESC [3870].  

> PARENT

⊲ Cyclic Hypergraph Product Code › p. 383 — LRESCs are constructed using a hypergraph product of a concatenated LDPC-repetition code with itself.  

> COUSINS

MAJORANA BOX QUBIT [384, 531, 3871] mbq  

> DESCRIPTION

A family of Majorana stabilizer codes obtained by fix-ing the total fermion parity of 𝑛 fermionic modes, equivalently 2𝑛 

Majorana zero modes, within the ground-state subspace of 𝑛 Ki-taev Majorana chain Hamiltonians. The resulting positive-parity subspace encodes 𝑛 − 1 logical qubits and has Majorana distance 2.The ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 member is called the tetron Majorana code, while an ⟦3, 2, 2⟧ 𝑓 extension using three Kitaev chains and housing two logical qubits of the same parity is called the hexon Majorana code .Similarly, the ⟦4, 3, 2⟧ 𝑓 octon , ⟦5, 4, 2⟧ 𝑓 decon , and ⟦6, 5, 2⟧ 𝑓 dode-con are codes defined by the positive-parity subspace of 4, 5, and 6

fermionic modes, respectively [385].  

> PROTECTION

Fixing total fermion parity detects single-Majorana events as parity violations if that parity is measured. However, these distance-two box-qubit codes do not correct errors: two-Majorana operators act within the fixed-parity sector and can implement log-ical Pauli errors without changing the stabilizer outcome, while treating the parity constraint as a Hamiltonian term turns single-Majorana events into leakage errors [385].  

> GATES

⊲ Braiding and fusion of MZMs, which act as Ising anyons [3872, 3873].  

> DECODING

⊲ Qubit readout can be done by charge sensing [ 384 , 3871 ,3873, 3874].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant computation scheme [3875].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 ⊲ Small-distance qubit stabilizer code › p. 451 ⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 — When treated as ground states of the code Hamiltonian, codewords of a single Kitaev chain realize Z2 fermionic topological order. ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 — The Majorana box qubit is a 1D qubit stabilizer code with respect to the Majorana operator basis. ⊲ 1D lattice sta-bilizer code › p. 542 — The Majorana box qubit is a 1D qubit stabilizer code with respect to the Majorana operator basis.  

> CHILD

⊲ Tetron code › p. 460 — The Majorana box qubit for 𝑛 = 2 is the tetron code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 — A Majorana box qubit forms a fixed-parity subspace of the ground-state subspace of one or more Kitaev Majorana chain Hamiltonians. ⊲ Majorana sur-face code › p. 418 — The 4.8.8, 6.6.6, and 4.6.12 Majorana surface-code families realize logical tetrons and hexons as fault-tolerant versions of these small Majorana blocks, using tetrons, hexons, or dodecons as parity-fixed building blocks [ 385 ]. ⊲ Majorana color code › p. 416

MAJORANA COLOR CODE [ 385 , 1385 , 3119 , 3331 , 3332 ] majorana_color  

> DESCRIPTION

A fermionic analogue of a 2D color code. In the original construction [ 1385 ], Majorana modes occupy the vertices of a trivalent graph embedded on a cylinder, each face operator is the product of the Majoranas around an even-length face, and the graph is only locally 3-colorable. The code encodes one qubit whose two odd logical operators live on the opposite cylinder boundaries, while an even logical operator is supported on a string connecting the boundaries. Later hardware-oriented Majorana color-code constructions re-alize related codes by concatenating Majorana surface codes with small Majorana fermion codes [ 385 , 3119 , 3331 , 3332 ]. Equivalently, they are multiple Majorana-surface-code layers whose stacked build-ing blocks are replaced by an outer ⟦𝑛 𝑓 , 𝑘, 𝑑 𝑚 ⟧ 𝑓 Majorana code; hexon, octon, ⟦8, 3, 4⟧ 𝑓 , and ⟦10 , 4, 4⟧ 𝑓 outer codes give concrete order-2, -3, and -4 examples [385].  

> PROTECTION

For the original cylindrical family with circumference 𝑅 

and length 𝐿 , the code distance scales as 𝑑 = Ω (min (𝑅, 𝐿 )) , while the minimum diameter of an even logical operator obeys 𝑙 even =Ω(𝐿 ) [1385 , Sec. 7]. The code therefore interpolates between Kitaev-chain-like protection by fermion-parity superselection ( 𝑅 = 𝑂 (1),

𝐿 ≫ 1) and distance-based protection when both linear dimensions are macroscopic.  

> RATE

Concatenating a 4.8.8 Majorana surface code with an outer 

⟦𝑛 𝑓 , 𝑘, 𝑑 𝑚 ⟧ 𝑓 code yields a fermionic mode overhead of 2𝑛 𝑓 

> 𝑘𝑑 2
> 𝑚

𝑑 2 per logical qubit of distance 𝑑 [385].  

> GATES

⊲ Color-to-surface-code lattice surgery [ 3332 ]. ⊲ Logical tetrons and hexons can be encoded in Majorana color codes and ma-nipulated by ordinary, twist-based, or surface-to-color-code lattice surgery [385, 3332].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Ordinary and twist-based lattice surgery can be made fault tolerant, and surface-to-color-code surgery reduces ancilla-measurement weight for the 16-Majorana-stabilizer families [385] (see also [3877]).

MAJORANA STABILIZER CODE [1385] majorana_stab  

> DESCRIPTION

A stabilizer code whose stabilizers are products of an even number of Majorana fermion operators, analogous to Pauli strings for a traditional stabilizer code and referred to as Majorana stabilizers . The codespace is the mutual +1 eigenspace of all Majo-rana stabilizers. Codes can be denoted as ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ 𝑓 [ 539 ], where 𝑛 is the number of fermionic modes (equivalently, 2𝑛 Majorana modes). Two copies of an 𝑛 -Majorana mode code may be combined to form a single 

𝑛 -fermion code by using one copy for the real parts of each fermion, and the other copy for the imaginary parts [ 532 ]. Codes that admit a logical operator of even (odd) weight are called even (odd) Majorana codes [ 715 ]. Even Majorana codes encode logical qubits, and odd Majorana codes have at least one logical Majorana fermion. For odd codes, an additional protection parameter is the minimum diameter 

𝑙 even of an even logical operator [1385]. In some cases, Majorana-based stabilizer codes are designed to protect against fermionic noise [ 531 ] and are thus useful for physical platforms based on fermions. In other cases, Majorana-based frame-works are helpful for understanding conventional qubit stabilizer codes designed for qubit-based platforms.  

> PROTECTION

Detects products of Majorana operators with weight up to 𝑑 − 1. Physically, protects against dephasing errors caused by coupling of fermion density to the environment and bit-flip errors caused by quasiparticle poisoning processes. For odd Majorana codes, the physically relevant logical protection is also governed by the minimum diameter 𝑙 even of an even logical operator [1385]. Code bounds have been developed for small codes [ 3119 ]. LP bounds for Majorana codes have been developed based on the iden-tification of Majorana operators with the Clifford algebra [537].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Unitary encoding using fermionic Clifford operations [3878].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Transversal Clifford op-erations are discussed in Ref. [715].  

> GATES

⊲ Some gates can be implemented through braiding of the computational anyons. Circuit-based gates can be converted into braid patterns via quantum compiling algorithms [3879].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Fermion code › p. 389 ⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — A Majorana stabilizer code is a stabilizer code whose stabilizers are composed of Majorana fermion operators, which are in turn re-alizable using Pauli strings via the Jordan-Wigner mapping. Any 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code can be mapped into a ⟦2𝑛, 𝑘, 2𝑑 ⟧ 𝑓 Majo-rana stabilizer code by concatenating with the tetron code [ 510 ][ 1385 ,Lemma 1]. Embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code is useful for exactly solving the Kitaev honeycomb model Hamiltonian [510] and other qubit Hamiltonians on certain graphs [2759 , 2760 ]. Majorana stabilizer groups can be converted into or-dinary qubit stabilizer groups via the parton mapping, while their corresponding states are converted via the Gutzwiller projection [2761].

MAJORANA SURFACE CODE [3884, 3885] majorana_surface  

> DESCRIPTION

Fermionic analogue of the surface code defined on a three-colorable 2D tiling whose face operators are non-overlapping even-Majorana stabilizers. Open patches with four or six alternating colored boundaries encode logical tetrons or hexons. The uniform 4.8.8, 6.6.6, and 4.6.12 tilings yield families with tetron, hexon, or dodecon building blocks and with twist-based lattice surgery sup-porting minimal-overhead logical Clifford gates [385].  

> PROTECTION

Under quasiparticle-poisoning noise, single Majorana operators flip the syndromes of adjacent stabilizers and can be de-coded with surface-code methods. If the shortest logical operator has Majorana weight 𝑑 𝑚 , then the code corrects up to 𝑑 𝑚 /2 − 1

Majorana errors; the corresponding qubit distance is naturally la-beled by 𝑑 = 𝑑 𝑚 /2 because Pauli errors on tetron/hexon hardware involve pairs of Majoranas [ 385 ]. Implementations that treat one color of stabilizers as parity-fixing constraints reduce measured stabilizer weight, at the cost that parity-violating single-Majorana events become leakage unless that color is also measured [385].  

> RATE

For code distance 𝑑 = 𝑑 𝑚 /2, the 4.8.8, 6.6.6, and 4.6.12 fami-lies require 4𝑑 2, 6𝑑 2 + O( 𝑑 ), and 12 𝑑 2 + O( 𝑑 ) Majoranas per log-ical qubit, respectively [ 385 , Table I]. Their maximum stabilizer weights for fault-tolerant lattice surgery can be reduced to 8, 6, and 

6 Majoranas, respectively, compared to 10 Majoranas for bosonic twist-based surface-code surgery [385].  

> GATES

⊲ All logical Clifford gates, including CNOT, can be im-plemented with zero time overhead by classically tracking them and measuring Pauli products via ordinary and twist-based lattice surgery [ 385 ]. ⊲ Surface-code state injection of noisy magic states into logical tetrons [385, Sec. IV.C].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Repeated syndrome rounds make ordinary and twist-based lattice surgery fault tolerant against both data and mea-surement errors [385] (see also [3877]).

MOVASSAGH-OUYANG HAMILTONIAN CODE [1360]  

> movassagh_ouyang
> DESCRIPTION

This is a family of codes derived via an algorithm that takes as input any binary classical code and outputs a quantum code (note that this framework can be extended to 𝑞 -ary codes). The algorithm is probabilistic but succeeds almost surely if the classical code is random. An explicit code construction does exist for linear distance codes encoding one logical qubit using Radon’s theorem [569 , 570 ]. For finite rate codes, there is no rigorous proof that the construction algorithm succeeds, and approximate constructions are described instead. This family strictly generalizes CSS codes (because CSS codes come only from linear or self-orthogonal classical codes). These codes can be shown to be realized as a subspace of the ground space of a (geometrically) local Hamiltonian.  

> PROTECTION

Let 𝐶 ⊂ { 0, 1, . . . , 𝑞 − 1}𝑛 be a classical code with dis-tance 𝑑 𝑥 . Let 𝑑 𝑧 satisfy 𝑞 𝑛 > 2𝑉 𝑞 (𝑑 𝑧 − 1) − 1, where 𝑉 𝑞 (𝑟 ) is the volume of the 𝑞 -ary Hamming ball of radius 𝑟 . Then the algorithm produces a quantum code with distance 𝑑 = min (𝑑 𝑥 , 𝑑 𝑧 ). Asymp-totically, the distance scales linearly with 𝑛 . 

> RATE

The rate depends on the classical code, but distance can scale linearly with 𝑛 . 

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 ⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 —Movassagh-Ouyang codes reside in the ground space of a Hamil-tonian. Justesen codes can be used to build a family of 𝑛 -qubit Movassagh-Ouyang Hamiltonian spin codes encoding one logical qubit with linear distance. These codes form the ground-state sub-space of a frustration-free geometrically local Hamiltonian [1360].  

> CHILD

⊲ (( 𝑛, 2, 2)) Bravyi-Lee-Li-Yoshida PI code › p. 330 — The 

(( 𝑛, 2, 2)) PI code is a Movassagh-Ouyang Hamiltonian code con-structed from a binary code consisting of all codewords of weight 0, 2, or 𝑛 [502, Appx. D].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — Many, but not all, Movassagh-Ouyang codes are stabilizer codes. ⊲ Binary code

NON-ABELIAN KITAEV HONEYCOMB CODE [510]  

> nonabelian_kitaev_honeycomb
> DESCRIPTION

Code whose logical subspace in the gapped non-Abelian phase of the Kitaev honeycomb model with a magnetic field is la-beled by different fusion outcomes of Ising anyons [510]. The original Kitaev honeycomb spin model is exactly solvable by mapping spins to Majorana fermions in a static Z2 gauge field (equivalently, embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code [ 3316 , Sec. 4.1]), yielding three gapped 𝐴 phases and one gapless 𝐵 phase [ 510 ]. A magnetic field opens a gap in phase 

𝐵 of the underlying Kitaev honeycomb code and yields the non-Abelian Ising-anyon phase [ 510 ] (a.k.a. 𝑝 +𝑖 𝑝 superconducting phase [3888 ]). In the honeycomb model with magnetic field, the spectral Chern number is 𝜈 = ±1 depending on the field direction; more generally, gapped free-fermion phases with Z2 vortices are classified by a spectral Chern number 𝜈 , and their anyonic properties depend on 𝜈 mod 16 [510]. Ising anyons also exist in other phases, such as the fractional quantum Hall phase [3889].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Anyon initialization via quantum control [3890].  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford gates › p. 244 can be performed by braiding Majorana operators and Pauli measurements can be performed by measuring certain Majorana operators [ 3316 , 3889 ]. ⊲ CPHASE gate or a 𝜋 /8

rotation with the help of ancilla states completes a universal gate set [3316, 3889].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ One can distill ancilla states to arbitrary preci-sion for sufficiently small noise rates and assuming perfect Clifford operations [3889].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit code › p. 433 — The Kitaev honeycomb model with a magnetic field is a qubit many-body system in the Ising-anyon phase, and the underlying code stores information in the fusion space of its non-Abelian anyonic excitations. ⊲ Topological code › p. 325 —The Kitaev honeycomb model with a magnetic field is a qubit many-body system in the Ising-anyon phase, and the underlying code stores information in the fusion space of its non-Abelian anyonic excitations.

For the symmetric 𝑛 × 𝑛

In the later operator-algebra construction, one instead chooses a nontrivial subset T0 of coset representatives of the normalizer of the Bacon-Shor stabilizer group inside the Pauli group, so that the classical information is carried by distinct normalizer-coset sectors [ 3384 ]. For the symmetric ℓ × ℓ Bacon-Shor code, choosing

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Qubit Kingdom › p. 13 . 

> DESCRIPTION

An OAQECC family that encompasses ordinary (i.e., subspace) qubit codes, subsystem qubit codes, and hybrid qubit codes using an operator-algebraic framework. A simple example encompassing elements of all three subfamilies encodes a single logical qubit and a single classical bit into a direct sum of two subsystem qubit codes. A quantum subsystem code 

A 𝑗 ⊗ B 𝑗 , with A 𝑗 the logical qubit factor, and B 𝑗 the gauge qubit factor, is associated with each of the two classical-bit values, labeled by 𝑗 ∈ { 1, 2}. The corresponding decomposition of the Hilbert space H is 

H = (A1 ⊗ B1) ⊕ ( A2 ⊗ B2) ⊕ C⊥ , (282) where C⊥ is the combined error space of both codes. The above code reduces to a subsystem code when A2 ⊗ B2 is trivial, reduces to a hybrid code when B1,2 are both trivial, and reduces to an ordinary (i.e., subspace) qubit code when B1 and A2 ⊗ B2 are both trivial. 421

PASTAWSKI-YOSHIDA-HARLOW-PRESKILL (HAPPY) CODE [ 1620 ] 

> happy
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Perfect holographic code  

> DESCRIPTION

Holographic code constructed from six-leg five-qubit perfect tensors › p. 312 placed on hyperbolic pentagon and hexagon tilings. The code serves as a minimal model for several aspects of the AdS/CFT holographic duality [ 614 ] and potentially a dS/CFT duality [615]. It has been generalized to higher dimensions [ 3894 ] and to include gauge-like degrees of freedom on the links of the tensor network [448 , 3895 ]. In the lifted version, the bulk symmetry of the HaPPY code can be interpreted as arising from restricting a bulk gauge-like theory to a fixed-flux sector [ 448 ]. All boundary global symmetries must be dual to bulk gauge symmetries, and vice versa [3896]. The construction below is described for qubits, but the underlying five-leg perfect tensor also has modular-qudit and oscillator exten-sions, and a rotor version can be stacked into an approximately error-correcting 𝑈 (1)-covariant holographic code [ 2642 ]. Encod-ing is accomplished using a tensor network of five-qubit encoding isometries, which are six-legged perfect tensors › p. 312 (with five legs corresponding to the physical qubits and one for the encoded logical qubit). To construct the encoding, one first uniformly tiles the hyperbolic AdS/CFT disc using pentagons and hexagons. Then, one places a 6-legged five-qubit encoding tensor at each hexagon and pentagon, contracting legs between neighboring shapes and leaving one leg un-contracted at each pentagon. This construction forms an encoding isometry from the uncontracted legs in the bulk to the uncontracted legs at the boundary. The single-qubit HaPPY code has a central pentagon encoding one bulk operator and hexagons tiling all other layers. The 

pentagon-hexagon HaPPY code has alternating layers of pentagons and hexagons in the tiling. The pentagon HaPPY code (a.k.a. the hy-perbolic pentagon code, or HyPeC) consists of a purely pentagonal tiling.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against erasure errors and Pauli errors on the boundary qubits.  

> RATE

The pentagon HaPPY code has an asymptotic rate 1√5 ≈ 0.447 .The pentagon-hexagon HaPPY code has a rate of 0.299 if the last layer is a pentagon layer and a rate of 0.088 if the last layer is a hexagon layer.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Heisenberg-picture encoding is done through tensor pushing . Each bulk operator (logical) is pushed to an operator sup-ported on a portion of the boundary region (physical). Pushing all the bulk operators through results in reconstruction of the boundary. 

⊲ ZX calculus based encoder for the pentagon HaPPY code [3429].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Any transversal gate of the five-qubit code is a transversal gate of the HaPPY code since the HaPPY code is constructed from five-qubit encoding tensors, which are covariant under such gates. ⊲ For locality-preserving physical gates on the boundary, the set of transversally implementable logical operations in the bulk is strictly contained in the Clifford group › p. 244 

[705].  

> DECODING

⊲ Hierarchical recovery model [ 1620 ]. ⊲ The greedy al-gorithm reconstructs bulk operators by iteratively absorbing tensors for which at least half of the legs are already included; the resulting greedy geodesic gives an explicit boundary reconstruction region [1620].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ 26% for boundary erasure errors on the pentagon-hexagon HaPPY code under the greedy decoder [ 1620 ]. 

⊲ Lower bound of 1/12 ≈ 8.3% for boundary erasure errors on the single-qubit HaPPY code under hierarchical recovery [ 1620 ]. Numerical evidence indicates the threshold may be closer to 50% .

⊲ There is no threshold for the pentagon HaPPY code as a constant 422 number of errors (four) can make bulk recovery impossible [ 1620 ]. 

⊲ 16 .3% for boundary Pauli errors on the single-qubit HaPPY code with 3 layers using integer optimization decoder [ 2868 ]. ⊲ 50% 

against biased Pauli noise for single-qubit HaPPY code under tensor-network decoder [3613].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ A single-qubit HaPPY code has a measurement thresh-old › p. 435 of one [3897].  

> NOTES

⊲ Reference [ 615 ] discusses the HaPPY code for an AdS_3 space and its relation to a dS_2 braneworld with a conformal bound-ary.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — The HaPPY code is a stabi-lizer code because it is defined by a contracted network of stabilizer tensors; see [ 1620 , Thm. 6]. ⊲ Holographic tensor-network code  

> › p. 308

— The encoding of a HaPPY code is a holographic tensor net-work consisting of pentagon and hexagon perfect tensors › p. 312 . 

> CHILD

⊲ ⟦5, 1, 3⟧ Five-qubit perfect code › p. 348 — The five-qubit code is the smallest (i.e., radius-one) single-qubit HaPPY code. The five-qubit encoding isometry tiles various holographic codes because its corresponding encoding isometry tensor is a perfect tensor › p. 312 

[1620].

PHANTOM CODE [489] phantom  

> DESCRIPTION

Qubit CSS code for which, in some logical basis, every ordered-pair logical CNOT 𝑎𝑏 gate between logical qubits in the same code block can be implemented by a physical-qubit permutation [489 ]. The definition has been extended to non-CSS and non-qubit codes [688].  

> PROTECTION

CSS phantom codes obey a Hamming-type constraint: if 

𝑑 = 𝑑 𝜇 for 𝜇 ∈ { 𝑋, 𝑍 }, then 𝜂 (2𝑘 − 1) ≤ 𝐵 (𝑛, 𝑑 ), where 𝜂 counts weight-𝑑 logical operators in a fixed 𝜇 -type logical equivalence class and 𝐵 (𝑛, 𝑑 ) ≤ ␀𝑛 𝑑 

 is the maximum size of a binary length-𝑛 code whose pairwise sums have weight at least 𝑑 [ 489 ]. Any qubit phan-tom code of distance 𝑑 ≥ 2 encoding 𝑘 ≥ 2 logical qubits with 𝑘 ≠ 4

obeys 𝑛 ≥ 2𝑘 − 1, equivalently 𝑘 ≤ log 2 (𝑛 + 1); this parameter bound also holds for non-CSS phantom codes and for qubit subspace or subsystem phantom-LU codes [688].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ For CSS phantom codes, interblock CNOT gates are transversal. Combining transversal in-terblock CNOTs with in-block permutation CNOTs implements any logical CNOT circuit on 2𝑎 phantom-code blocks in physical depth at most 4(2𝑎 − 1), up to a residual logical-qubit permutation; for uni-directional CNOT circuits, the bound is 2(2𝑎 − 1) while preserving logical-qubit order [ 489 ]. ⊲ A stabilizer code supporting a logical gate by qubit permutations cannot admit any strictly transversal logi-cal gate that does not commute with that permutation-implemented logical gate, ruling out strictly transversal implementations of sev-eral gates on phantom codes [ 489 ]. ⊲ Additional logical Clifford and non-Clifford gates can arise from code automorphisms combin-ing local Cliffords and qubit permutations, from fold-diagonal gates using patterned one- and two-qubit diagonal interactions, and from non-uniform diagonal single-qubit rotations [489].  

> GATES

⊲ Certain phantom quantum RM codes admit the full logical Clifford group via fold-𝑆 𝑖 𝑆 𝑗 gates and teleported Hadamards, and admit a distance-two magic-gate scheme by temporarily projecting into hypercube-code subspaces [489].  

> DECODING

⊲ Spatiotemporal sliding-window correlated list and most-likely-error decoders for Steane-style error correction [489].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Preselection-based fault-tolerant state prepara-tion and Steane-style error correction for non-LDPC phantom quan-tum RM codes [489].  

> NOTES

⊲ Ref. [ 489 ] exhaustively enumerates all 2.71 × 10 10 inequiv-alent CSS codes with 𝑛 ≤ 14 , identifying 1.39 × 10 5 CSS phantom codes, and uses SAT-based search to find further examples up to 

𝑛 = 21 .

PI QUBIT CODE qubit_permutation_invariant  

> DESCRIPTION

Block quantum code defined on two-dimensional sub-systems such that any permutation of the subsystems leaves any codeword invariant.  

> Dicke states:

For 𝑛 -qubit block codes, an often used basis for the 

𝑛 + 1-dimensional PI subspace consists of the Dicke states |𝐷 𝑛 𝑤 ⟩ –normalized PI states of 𝑤 excitations, i.e., a normalized sum over all binary-string basis elements with 𝑤 ones and 𝑛 − 𝑤 zeroes. For 423 example, the single-excitation Dicke state, known as a 𝑊 state , on three qubits is 

|𝐷 31 ⟩ = 1

√3 (| 001 ⟩ + | 010 ⟩ + | 100 ⟩) . (285) The 𝑛 + 1-dimensional PI space can be thought of as a standalone spin-𝑛 /2 quantum system, yielding a way to convert between PI qubit codes and 𝑆𝑈 (2) spin codes. A single-spin code for the 𝑆𝑈 (2)

group correcting spherical tensors can be mapped into a PI qubit code with an analogous distance [2731][3389, Thm. 1].  

> PROTECTION

Permutation invariant qubit codes of distance 𝑑 can protect against 𝑑 − 1 deletion errors [ 2579 , 2580 ], i.e., erasures of subsystems at unknown locations. There are also simplified condi-tions on insertion errors [3898].  

> ENCODING

⊲ With quantum harmonic oscillators (superconduct-ing charge qubits in an ultrastrong coupling regime) in 𝑂 (𝑁 ) as in [ 3899 ]. Can be done in 𝑂 (𝑁 2) steps using quantum circuits [3900 ], or using geometric phase gates in 𝑂 (𝑁 ) [3901 ]. ⊲ Finite-depth quantum circuits with LOCC for Dicke states [ 3902 – 3904 ]. 

⊲ Preparation of sparse Dicke states using the combinatorial num-ber system [1953].  

> GATES

⊲ There is a measurement-free code-switching protocol be-tween a qubit stabilizer code and a PI qubit code [692].  

> DECODING

⊲ Schur-Weyl-transform based decoder [ 2683 ]. Here, one first measures nested total angular momenta, i.e., that of the first qubit, the first and second, followed by the first, second, and third, etc. Then, for codes with spacing, one measures the projection of the angular momentum modulo the spacing. Recovery can be performed by applying geometric phase gates [ 3905 ] or the quantum Schur transform. This decoder has been generalized to work with insertion errors [3589].  

> PARENTS

PROJECTIVE-PLANE SURFACE CODE [61, 3285] real_projective_plane  

> DESCRIPTION

A family of Kitaev surface codes on the non-orientable 2-dimensional compact manifold R𝑃 2 (in contrast to a genus-𝑔 sur-face). Whereas genus-𝑔 surface codes require 2𝑔 logical qubits, qubit codes on R𝑃 2 are made from a single logical qubit.  

> PROTECTION

If C is a cellulation of R𝑃 2, then the bit-flip distance 

𝑑 𝑋 is the shortest cycle in C, and the phase-flip distance 𝑑 𝑍 is the shortest cycle in the dual cellulation C∗. 

> RATE

The rate is 1/𝑛 , where 𝑛 is the number of edges of the particular cellulation.  

> GATES

⊲ Fault-tolerant Hadamard gate via constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 [ 3659 ]. ⊲ Complete logical gate set for a stack of projective-plane surface codes [3659].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant Hadamard gate via constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 [3659].  

> PARENT

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — The projective-plane surface code is the surface code on R𝑃 2. 

> CHILD

⊲ ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ Shor code › p. 358 — The Shor code is one of the nine-qubit surface codes defined on the projective plane [ 3285 , Fig. 4][ 61 ,Fig. 20].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Honeycomb Floquet code › p. 403 — Implementing the hon-eycomb Floquet code on a non-orientable cross-cap geometry al-lows for a logical-𝐻𝑍 gate to be implemented via a measurement schedule [ 3659 ]. ⊲ ⟦9, 1, 3⟧Z𝑞 modular-qudit code › p. 473 — The qu-dit Shor code is a small qudit surface code on a Möbius strip with smooth boundary, which is obtained from removing a face of the tessellation of the projective plane R𝑃 2 [3285, Fig. 4].
