QUANTUM CONVOLUTIONAL CODE [3088, 3909–3911]  

> quantum_convolutional
> DESCRIPTION

1D translationally invariant qubit stabilizer code whose stabilizer group can be partitioned into constant-size subsets of con-stant support and of constant overlap between neighboring sets. Initially formulated as a quantum analogue of convolutional codes, which were designed to protect a continuous and never-ending stream of information. Precise formulations sometimes begin with a finite-dimensional lattice, with the intent to take the thermody-namic limit; logical dimension can be infinite as well. Quantum convolutional codes, like their classical counterparts, can also be understood in terms of frames. Let each encoding frame take in 𝑛 qubits, carry 𝑚 qubits of information between frames, and act on them with 𝑛 − 𝑘 Pauli generators. Each generator, count-ably infinite in length, must commute with each 𝑛 register shift of itself, but need not commute with the other generators [ 3912 ]. The 

𝑚 qubits of information carried between each frame are also sta-bilized by additional memory Pauli operators. It is known that the minimal value for 𝑚 is given by dim (𝑀 ) − 12 rank (𝑀 ), with 𝑀 being the matrix containing the required commutation relations of the memory qubits [ 3539 , 3913 , 3914 ]. These operators can be efficiently determined [3915].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Encoding is efficient and uses only Clifford gates › p. 244 .Some encoders yield catastrophic errors, i.e., errors that require a cir-cuit of infinite depth to correct [ 3911 , Def. 4.1]. ⊲ Pearl-necklace encoding [ 3088 , 3911 , 3916 , 3917 ]. ⊲ Quantum shift register encod-ing [ 3918 ]. ⊲ Encoding circuits can be viewed as matrix-product-state tensor networks [383].  

> DECODING

⊲ Quantum Viterbi decoder [ 3088 , 3910 , 3911 ]. ⊲ ML decoder [3088].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Refs. [ 1619 , 3088 , 3916 , 3919 ] for explicit and simple examples. ⊲ See Ref. [ 3920 ] and the book [ 381 ] for an introduction to quantum convolutional codes. ⊲ Quantum convolutional codes are briefly reviewed in [1966, Sec. 27.6].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ 1D lattice stabilizer code  

> › p. 542

— Quantum convolutional codes are lattice stabilizer codes on a semi-infinite or infinite lattice in one dimension [ 3921 ]. Some notions may be extendable to non-stabilizer codes [ 3911 , Sec. 4]. Any prime-qudit code can be converted using a constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 to several copies of the 1D repetition code along with some trivial codes [3859].  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Quantum irregular convolutional code (QIRCC) › p. 426 

⊲ Quantum turbo code › p. 432 ⊲ (5, 1, 2)-convolutional code › p. 331  

> COUSINS

⊲ Tensor-network code › p. 324 — Quantum convolutional encoding circuits can be viewed as matrix-product-state tensor networks [ 383 ]. ⊲ Generalized RS (GRS) code › p. 222 — GRS codes can be used to construct quantum convolutional codes [ 832 , Ch. 12]. ⊲ Generalized RM (GRM) code › p. 222 — GRM codes can be used to construct quantum convolutional codes [ 1782 , 1783 ][ 832 ,Sec. 12.4]. ⊲ Convolutional code › p. 215 — Quantum convolutional codes are quantum analogues of convolutional codes. ⊲ EA quantum convolutional code › p. 386 — EA quantum convolutional codes are entanglement-assisted versions of quantum convolu-tional codes. ⊲ Hybrid convolutional code › p. 404 — Hybrid con-volutional codes are hybrid analogues of quantum convolutional codes. ⊲ Quantum data-syndrome (QDS) code › p. 424 — The QDS code framework has been extended to quantum convolutional codes [ 3922 ]. ⊲ Quantum Reed-Muller (RM) code › p. 428 — Quantum con-volutional codes can be derived from quantum RM codes [3923]. 

QUANTUM DATA-SYNDROME (QDS) CODE [ 1912 , 2830 , 3924 –3926 ] 

> data_syndrome
> DESCRIPTION

Stabilizer code designed to correct both data qubit er-rors and syndrome measurement errors simultaneously due to extra redundancy in its stabilizer generators. The redundancy can be added to any ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 𝑚 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code by expanding its stabilizer generator matrix 𝐻 as 

𝐻 𝐷𝑆 =

𝐻 𝐼 𝑚 00 𝐴 𝑇 𝐼 𝑟 



, (287) where the redundancy is provided by the underlying [𝑚 + 𝑟, 𝑚 ] syn-drome measurement code with generator matrix 𝐺 = (𝐼 𝑚 | 𝐴 ) [2830].  

> PROTECTION

Protects against both physical qubit and syndrome mea-surement errors. An ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 : 𝑟 ⟧ QDS code corrects any combina-tion of 𝑡 D data-qubit errors and 𝑡 S syndrome-bit errors whenever 

𝑡 D + 𝑡 S < 𝑑 /2, and its distance cannot exceed that of the underlying stabilizer code [2830]. Random QDS codes with 𝑟 ≤ 𝑛 − 𝑘 can attain the stabilizer Gilbert-Varshamov bound [ 2830 , Thm. 12]. Quantum Singleton bounds, quantum Hamming bounds, and quantum MacWilliams identities  

> › p. 434

can be extended to QDS codes. Single-error-correcting QDS codes stemming from impure › p. 434 stabilizer codes must satisfy a variant of the quantum Hamming bound [3927].  

> GATES

⊲ Fault-tolerant flag-based non-transversal logical gates [3109].  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndrome errors are decoded using redundant stabi-lizer measurements. ⊲ Syndrome-measurement codes can out-perform repeated syndrome extraction; for the Steane code, a [15 , 3]

syndrome-measurement code uses the same 15 measurements as 425 five-fold repetition of three syndrome bits while achieving lower syndrome-decoding error [2830, Fig. 1].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Shor error correction can be recast as a QDS code whose underlying matrix 𝐴 is the identity matrix 𝐼 𝑚 repeated ℓ times [2830 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant flag-based non-transversal logical gates [3109].  

> NOTES

⊲ QDS codes can be used to estimate physical Pauli noise up to their pure distance › p. 434 [ 3928 ], and logical Pauli noise for any correctable physical noise [3929].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — QDS codes are stabilizer codes whose stabilizer generators encode extra redundancy (via a linear binary code) so as to protect from syndrome measurement errors.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ Steane code › p. 353 — There exists a set of stabi-lizer generators for the Steane code that make it a QDS code; a [15 , 3]

syndrome-measurement code beats five-fold repeated syndrome extraction at the same measurement cost [ 1912 , 2830 ]. ⊲ ⟦23 , 1, 7⟧

Quantum Golay code › p. 341 — There exists a ⟦23 , 1, 7 : 18 ⟧ QDS code based on the qubit Golay code, requiring 18 additional stabilizer measurements instead of 24 from the general cyclic construction [2830, Ex. 15].  

> COUSINS

⊲ ⟦2𝑟 − 1, 2𝑟 − 2𝑟 − 1, 3⟧ quantum Hamming code › p. 339 —Because every stabilizer generator has the same weight 2𝑟 −1, quan-tum Hamming codes admit QDS extensions based on good binary syndrome-measurement codes [ 2830 ]. ⊲ Quantum maximum-distance-separable (MDS) code › p. 317 — The quantum Singleton bound can be extended to QDS codes [ 2830 ]. ⊲ Perfect quantum code › p. 312 — The quantum Hamming bound can be extended to QDS codes [ 2830 ]. ⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — The QDS code construc-tion employs a particular binary linear code to provide protection against syndrome measurement errors. ⊲ Quantum convolutional code › p. 424 — The QDS code framework has been extended to quan-tum convolutional codes [ 3922 ]. ⊲ Single-shot code › p. 320 — QDS codes are closely related to single-shot codes because both use re-dundant syndrome information to suppress measurement errors in a single round of syndrome extraction [ 644 ]. ⊲ Primitive narrow-sense BCH code › p. 233 — Primitive narrow-sense BCH codes can be used as the syndrome measurement codes of a QDS code [ 1911 ]. QUANTUM DIVISIBLE CODE [720, 3930] quantum_divisible  

> DESCRIPTION

A level-𝜈 quantum divisible code is a CSS code whose 

𝑋 -type stabilizers form a 𝜈 -even linear binary code in the symplectic representation › p. 442 and which admits a transversal gate at the 𝜈 th level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 . A CSS code is doubly even (triply even ) if all 𝑋 -type stabilizers have weight divisible by four (eight), i.e., if they form a doubly even (triply even) linear binary code. The definition can be generalized to weakly 𝜈 -divisible (see, e.g., Ref. [ 724 ]), which means that there exist some disjoint qubit subsets 

𝑀 ± such that 

|𝑥 ∩ 𝑀 + | − | 𝑥 ∩ 𝑀 − | ≡ 0 mod 𝜈 (288) for all rows 𝑥 of the code’s 𝑋 -type stabilizer generator matrix. This generalization reduces to the original definition when 𝑀 + is the full set of qubits, and 𝑀 −

the empty set. An alternative definition [ 729 , 730 ], not used here, is a CSS code defined from two linear binary codes 𝐶 1,2 such that it is quantum divisible with 𝜈 > 1, and all weights in each coset of 𝐶 2 in 𝐶 1 are congruent to 𝜈 . For example [ 730 ], if 𝐶 2 is the first-order RM (1, 𝑚 )

QUANTUM EXPANDER CODE [3932] quantum_expander  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Quantum Sipser-Spielman code ⊲ Expander HGP code  

> DESCRIPTION

CSS code constructed from a hypergraph product of bipartite expander graphs [ 64 ] with bounded left and right vertex degrees. For every bipartite graph there is an associated matrix (the parity check matrix) with columns indexed by the left vertices, rows indexed by the right vertices, and 1 entries whenever a left and right vertex are connected. This matrix can serve as the parity check matrix of a classical code. Two bipartite expander graphs can be used to construct a quantum CSS code (the quantum expander code) via the hypergraph product of their parity check matrices.  

> PROTECTION

The code family has distance scaling as order › p. 161 

Ω(𝑛 1/2), and the small-set-flip decoder corrects a constant fraction of that many adversarial Pauli errors [3932].  

> RATE

⟦𝑛, 𝑘 = Θ (𝑛 ), 𝑑 = 𝑂 (√𝑛 )⟧ code with asymptotically constant rate.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Single-shot state preparation with constant space-time overhead [3621].  

> GATES

⊲ Dimensional jump protocols between various quantum expander codes [3621].  

> DECODING

⊲ Small set-flip linear-time decoder, which corrects or-der › p. 161 Ω(𝑛 1/2) adversarial errors [ 3932 ]. The decoder has been generalized to hypergraph products of 3 or more expander codes [3621 ]. ⊲ Log-time decoder [ 809 ]. ⊲ Constant-time decoder [3933 ]. ⊲ 2D geometrically local syndrome extraction circuits act-ing on a patch of 𝑁 physical qubits must have depth of order › p. 161 

Ω(𝑛 /√𝑁 ) or greater. More generally, there is a tradeoff between the depth 𝐷 and width 𝑊 of a syndrome extraction circuit, namely, 

𝐷 ≥ 𝑛 /√𝑊 [495].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerance with constant overhead can be achieved [809].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Locally stochastic noise: 2.7 · 10 −16 [3934 ]. 

⊲ Dimensional jump protocols between various quantum ex-pander codes have a threshold under local stochastic noise [3621].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Hypergraph product (HGP) code › p. 406 ⊲ Galois-qudit expander code › p. 494 ⊲ Single-shot code › p. 320 — Quantum expander codes are single-shot [809].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Expander code › p. 186 — Quantum expander codes are quantum analogues of expander codes. ⊲ Topological code › p. 325 —Quantum expander codes realize topological quantum spin glass or-der [ 3070 ]. ⊲ Higher-dimensional homological product code › p. 399 

— Quantum expander codes have been generalized to hypergraph products of 3 or more expander codes [ 3621 ]. ⊲ Self-correcting quantum code › p. 319 — Constant-rate random (quantum) expander codes are self-correcting (quantum) memories, but have no thermo-dynamic phase transitions [811].

QUANTUM MULTI-DIMENSIONAL PARITY-CHECK (QMDPC) CODE [497] qmdpc  

> DESCRIPTION

High-rate low-distance CSS code whose qubits lie on a 

𝐷 -dimensional rectangle, with 𝑋 -type stabilizer generators defined on each 𝐷 − 1-dimensional rectangle. The 𝑍 -type stabilizer gener-ators are defined via permutations in order to commute with the 

𝑋 -type generators. For example, the 𝐷 = 2 square geometry corresponds to a 

⟦𝑛 2, 𝑛 2 − 4𝑛 + 2, 4⟧ code, with 𝑋 -type stabilizer generators defined on rows and columns.

QUANTUM POLAR CODE [3946] quantum_polar  

> DESCRIPTION

Entanglement-assisted CSS code utilized in a quantum polar coding scheme producing entangled pairs of qubits between sender and receiver. In such a scheme, the amplitude and phase information of a quantum state is handled in complementary fash-ion [ 524 ] using an encoding based on classical polar codes. Variants of the initial scheme have been developed for degradable channels [525] and extended to arbitrary channels [526]. The scheme requires some a priori quantum side information in the general case, making the associated code entanglement-assisted [3946 ]. They require assistance only to determine positions to store information which optimally protect against both bit and phase noise. Without this assistance, they are just CSS codes constructed out of polar codes. The requirement of having quantum side infor-mation vanishes when the sum of the amplitude channel fidelity and the phase channel fidelity is not greater than 1. It is shown to vanish for the case of degradable noise channels [ 526 ]. A more complicated quantum polar-coding scheme that does not require pre-shared entanglement has also been derived [3947].  

> PROTECTION

Protects against Pauli noise and erasures.  

> RATE

The rate approaches the symmetric coherent information of arbitrary quantum channels [525].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Encoding circuits can be viewed as branching-tree ten-sor networks [383]. 428  

> DECODING

⊲ Arikan-style successive-cancellation decoding can be re-cast as a tensor-network contraction [ 383 ]. ⊲ Quantum successive-cancellation list decoder (SCL-E) for quantum polar codes that do not need entanglement assistance [ 3948 ]. ⊲ Numerics for tensor-network-based decoders on depolarizing and erasure channels in-dicate that good performance is possible without entanglement assistance, with channel polarization rapidly suppressing channels that are bad in both quadratures [383].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ State preparation of a single logical qubit [ 3949 ].  

> PARENT

⊲ Branching MERA code › p. 371 — Branching MERA codes gen-eralize quantum polar codes by restoring the branching-MERA dis-entanglers while retaining efficient tensor-network decoding [383].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 — Quantum polar codes are CSS codes used in an entanglement generation scheme that generally requires entanglement assistance. They require assistance only to determine positions to store information which optimally protect against both bit and phase noise. Without this assistance, they are just CSS codes constructed out of polar codes. A variant of quan-tum polar codes exists that does not require entanglement assis-tance [ 3947 ]. ⊲ Polar code › p. 197 — Without entanglement assis-tance, quantum polar codes are CSS codes constructed out of po-lar codes. ⊲ Tensor-network code › p. 324 — Quantum polar encod-ing circuits can be viewed as branching-tree tensor networks [383]. 

⊲ Concatenated GKP code › p. 519 — Concatenation of GKP codes with quantum polar codes achieves a rate against the displacement chan-nel [ 3950 ]. ⊲ ⟦4, 1, 2⟧ Leung-Nielsen-Chuang-Yamamoto (LNCY) code › p. 343 — The ⟦4, 1, 2⟧ LNCY code is a small quantum polar en-coding [ 3173 ]. ⊲ Quantum Reed-Muller (RM) code › p. 428 — There are codes interpolating between quantum RM and quantum polar codes [3951].

QUANTUM REPETITION CODE [3954] quantum_repetition  

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 1 qubit into 𝑛 qubits according to |0⟩ → | 𝜙 0⟩⊗𝑛 

and |1⟩ → | 𝜙 1⟩⊗𝑛 . The code is called a bit-flip code when |𝜙 𝑖 ⟩ =

|𝑖 ⟩, and a phase-flip code when |𝜙 0⟩ = |+⟩ and |𝜙 1⟩ = |−⟩ . This repetition-style encoding does not clone an arbitrary quantum state; instead, it extends the copying of computational-basis states linearly to entangled codewords [381, Ch. 2]. The ±-basis codewords for the bit-flip code are GHZ states [ 3955 –3957 ] (a.k.a. qubit cat states) |0⟩⊗𝑛 ± | 1⟩⊗𝑛 . These are ground states of the 1D classical Ising model Hamiltonian 𝐻 = Í𝑖 𝑍 𝑖 𝑍 𝑖 +1.The ±-basis codewords for the phase-flip code are expanded in the computational basis as 

|+⟩ = 1

√2𝑛 −1∑︁ Í𝑖 𝑣 𝑖 =0

|𝑣 1, · · · , 𝑣 𝑛 ⟩|−⟩ = 1

√2𝑛 −1∑︁ Í𝑖 𝑣 𝑖 =1

|𝑣 1, · · · , 𝑣 𝑛 ⟩ ,

(290) showing that the phase-flip code stores information in the total parity of the qubits. For example, an early code realized in devices is the 2-qubit phase-flip code [ 3936 ], which encodes a logical qubit into Bell states |00 ⟩ + | 11 ⟩ and |01 ⟩ + | 10 ⟩. 

> PROTECTION

Bit-flip code corrects bit-flip errors 𝑋 on ⌊( 𝑛 − 1)/ 2⌋

qubits and does not detect any phase-flip errors 𝑍 . Phase-flip code corrects phase-flip errors 𝑍 on ⌊( 𝑛 − 1)/ 2⌋ qubits and does not de-tect any bit-flip errors 𝑋 .Because they protect against only one type of noise, both codes can be thought of as a classical [𝑛, 1, 𝑛 ] repetition code embedded in a quantum system. Nevertheless, the phase-flip code can offer some degree of protection in particular physical systems based on superconducting circuits [3958, 3959].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Non-deterministic encoders for various specific states of the 2-qubit phase-flip code [ 3960 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant GHZ-state preparation with small qubit registers [ 3961 ]. ⊲ Unitary circuit of depth logarithmic in 𝑛 [3962 ]. Any circuit has to have range 𝑛 be-cause Ghz states are locally indistinguishable [ 3963 ]. ⊲ Adaptive constant-depth circuit with geometrically local gates and measure-ments throughout [ 3141 , 3142 ]. ⊲ Lindbladian-based dissipative encoding and autonomous QEC passively protecting against bit flips [2709 , 3964 ]. ⊲ Error-corrected GHZ state distillation for Steane error correction [ 3965 ]. ⊲ Approximate Hamiltonian-based en-coding of GHZ states [3966].  

> GATES

⊲ Toffoli magic-state preparation protocol [3967].  

> DECODING

⊲ Fault-tolerant syndrome detection [ 3968 ]. 

⊲ Autonomous QEC for the 3-qubit bit-flip code [ 3969 ]. ⊲ Machine learning algorithm to implement autonomous QEC for the three-qubit quantum repetition code [ 3970 ]. ⊲ Quantum cel-lular automata for majority voting and two-line voting [ 3971 ]. 

⊲ Quantum version of the Tsirelson local automaton decoder [ 3819 ]. 

⊲ Planar decoder designed to work under circuit-level noise [ 3972 ]. 

⊲ Single-rule and shearing-rule local automaton decoders [3973].   

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant syndrome detection [ 3968 ]. 

⊲ An 𝑚 -qubit GHZ state, i.e., qubit cat state, can serve as an an-cilla for fault-tolerant measurement of a weight-𝑚 Pauli operator by coupling each ancilla qubit to one data qubit, applying Hadamards to the ancilla, and reading out the parity of the measurement outcomes [381]. ⊲ Toffoli magic-state preparation protocol [3967].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

> THRESHOLD

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ NMR: 2-qubit phase-flip code [ 3974 , 3975 ]; 3-qubit bit-flip code [ 3976 ]; 3-qubit phase-flip code [ 3977 , 3978 ], with up to two rounds of error correction in liquid-state NMR [ 3979 ]. ⊲ Superconducting circuits: 3-qubit phase-flip and bit-flip code by Schoelkopf group [ 3984 , 3985 ]; 3-qubit bit-flip code [ 3986 ]; 3-qubit phase-flip code up to 3 cycles of error correction [ 3987 ]; IBM 15-qubit device [ 3988 ]; IBM Rochester device using 43-qubit code [ 3989 ]; Google system performing up to 8 error-correction cycles on 5 and 9 qubits [ 3990 ]; Google Quantum AI Sycamore utilizing up to 11 physical qubits and running 50 correction rounds [ 3160 ]; Google Quantum AI Sycamore utilizing up to 25 qubits for comparison of logical error scaling with a quantum code [ 3991 ] (see also [ 3992 ]). Google Quantum AI follow-up experiment on codes up to (classical) distance 29, demonstrating exponential suppression to an error floor of 10 −10 [ 3993 ]. Ising-model Nishimori phase transition realized for GHZ states on 54 qubits on a 127 qubit IBM device [ 3994 ]. GHZ state on 75 qubits made on an IBM device [ 3995 ]. GHZ state of 120 qubits realized on IBM device [3997].

QUANTUM SPATIALLY COUPLED (SC-QLDPC) CODE [ 616 , 617 , 4014 ,4015] sc_qldpc  

> DESCRIPTION

QLDPC code whose stabilizer generator matrix resem-bles the parity-check matrix of SC-LDPC codes. There exist CSS [616 ] and stabilizer constructions [ 617 ]. In either case, the stabilizer generator matrix is constructed by "spatially" coupling sub-matrix blocks in chain-like fashion (or, more generally, in grid-like fashion) to yield a band matrix. The sub-matrix blocks have to satisfy certain conditions amongst themselves so that the resulting band matrix is a stabilizer generator matrix. Matrices corresponding to trans-lationally invariant chains are called time-invariant , and otherwise are called time-varying .A finite-length chain is then capped by imposing either open boundary conditions (yielding non-tail-biting SC-QLDPC codes) or periodic boundary conditions (yielding tail-biting SC-QLDPC codes). Both constructions [616, 617] are tail-biting. In the stabilizer construction [ 617 ], the structure of the band ma-trix allows codes to be concisely defined in terms of characteris-tic polynomials , whose coefficients are the sub-matrix blocks and which resemble the Pauli-to-polynomial mapping › p. 551 associated with translationally invariant stabilizer codes. Some CSS code con-structions can be used to define sub-matrix blocks, yielding spatially coupled (i.e., translationally invariant) extensions of such codes. For example, the 3×3 toric code can be expressed as an SC-QLDPC code with stabilizer generator matrix given in Fig. 65 › p. 431 . 

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ Lattice stabilizer code › p. 551 —Stabilizer generator matrices of SC-QLDPC codes on infinite-length chains or grids define a class of lattice stabilizer codes.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Hypergraph product (HGP) code › p. 406 — Hypergraph-product stabilizer generator matrices can be used as sub-matrices to define a 2D SC-QLDPC code [ 617 ]. ⊲ XYZ product code › p. 469 — XYZ product stabilizer generator matrices can be used as sub-matrices to define a 2D SC-QLDPC code [617].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Spatially coupled LDPC (SC-LDPC) code › p. 203 — SC-QLDPC code stabilizer-generator matrices have similar block form as the parity-check matrices of SC-LDPC codes. ⊲ Quasi-cyclic code  

> › p. 168

— Quasi-cyclic binary code parity-check matrices can be used as sub-matrices to define a 1D SC-QLDPC code [616]. ⊲ Generalized bicycle (GB) code › p. 498 — Qubit GB codes can be categorized as 1D SC-QLDPC codes, see [617, Remark 7]. 

QUANTUM SYNCHRONIZABLE CODE [1199] quantum_synchronizable  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit stabilizer code designed to protect against syn-chronization errors (a.k.a. misalignment), which are errors that misalign the code block in a larger block by one or more locations. In such a setting, the qubits are arranged in a line and embedded into a larger block that represents a stream of information coming into the receiver. The receiver may not properly identify the first qubit in the desired code block, leading to a misalignment of the block. A quantum synchronizable code is denoted by (𝑎 𝑙 , 𝑎 𝑟 ) − ⟦ 𝑛 +

𝑎 𝑙 + 𝑎 𝑟 , 𝑘 ⟧, correcting misalignment by up to 𝑎 𝑙 (𝑎 𝑟 ) qubits to the left (right). The initial construction of quantum synchronizable codes was based on the CSS construction [ 1199 ], but later work extended it to non-CSS stabilizer codes [3893].  

> PROTECTION

In the original CSS construction based on cyclic codes 

𝐶 ⊂ 𝐷 with parameters [𝑛, 𝑘 1, 𝑑 1] and [𝑛, 𝑘 2, 𝑑 2], one obtains an 

(𝑎 𝑙 , 𝑎 𝑟 ) − ⟦ 𝑛 + 𝑎 𝑙 + 𝑎 𝑟 , 2𝑘 1 − 𝑛 ⟧ code whenever 𝑎 𝑙 + 𝑎 𝑟 < 𝑘 2 − 𝑘 1,correcting at least ⌊( 𝑑 1 − 1)/ 2⌋ phase errors and ⌊( 𝑑 2 − 1)/ 2⌋ bit errors [1199, Thm. 1].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441  

> COUSINS

⊲ Cyclic linear binary code › p. 184 — The original construc-tion of quantum synchronizable codes is based on pairs of binary cyclic codes satisfying 𝐶 ⊥ ⊆ 𝐶 ⊂ 𝐷 [1199 ]. ⊲ Binary BCH code

QUANTUM TANNER CODE [1367] quantum_tanner  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of QLDPC codes based on two com-patible classical Tanner codes defined on a two-dimensional Cayley complex, a complex constructed from Cayley graphs of groups. For certain choices of codes and complex, the resulting codes have asymptotically good parameters. See Ref. [ 653 ] for explicit instances based on dihedral groups. This construction has been generalized to Schreier graphs [654]. The underlying geometric complex of the code is a left-right Cay-ley complex Cay 2 ( 𝐴, 𝐺, 𝐵 ), where 𝐺 is a finite group and 𝐴 = 𝐴 −1,

𝐵 = 𝐵 −1 are two symmetric generating sets satisfying the total no-conjugacy condition: 𝑎𝑔 ≠ 𝑔𝑏 for any 𝑔 ∈ 𝐺 , 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴 , and 𝑏 ∈ 𝐵 . The vertices of the complex are group elements, i.e., 𝑉 = 𝐺 . If necessary, the double cover of the graph should be taken so that the graph is bipartite, 𝑉 = 𝑉 0 ⊔ 𝑉 1.There are two types of edges in the resulting complex,

QUANTUM TURBO CODE [382, 4019] quantum_turbo  

> DESCRIPTION

A quantum version of the turbo code, obtained from an interleaved serial quantum concatenation [ 382 , Def. 30] of quan-tum convolutional codes. The interleaver induces long-range en-tanglement and can increase the minimum distance relative to the constituent convolutional codes [383].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Encoders of codes with polynomial distance yield catastrophic errors, but codes with bounded distance admit non-catastrophic encoders.  

> DECODING

⊲ Turbo decoder [ 382 , Sec. V]. ⊲ Modified decoder yields improvement over the memoryless depolarizing channel [ 3534 ]. ⊲ Iterative decoding is analogous to a mean-field treatment of two matrix-product-state chains coupled by random non-local interactions [383]. ⊲ EXIT charts [4020].

QUBIT CODE qubits_into_qubits  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Qubit subspace code  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Qubit Kingdom › p. 13 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes 𝐾 -dimensional Hilbert space into a 2𝑛 -dimensional (i.e., 𝑛 -qubit) Hilbert space. Usually denoted as (( 𝑛, 𝐾 )) 

or (( 𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 )) , where 𝑑 is the code’s distance. The qubit codes are equivalent if the codespace of one code can be mapped into that of the other under a tensor product of single-qubit unitary operations and a qubit permutation. Equivalent qubit codes have the same logical dimension and distance, and their de-coding problems have the same computational complexity up to the corresponding relabeling of errors [381, Ch. 2].  

> PROTECTION

An (( 𝑛, 𝐾, 𝑑 )) code with distance 𝑑 detects errors acting on up to 𝑑 − 1 qubits, corrects erasure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 qubits [3175 ], or corrects errors acting on up to ⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋ qubits. Com-binations of errors and erasures can also be corrected [ 4023 ]. The number of correctable errors is often called the decoding radius , and it is upper bounded by half of the code distance. As a result, qubit codes cannot tolerate adversarial errors on more than (1 − 𝑅 )/ 4

registers, where 𝑅 = log 2 𝐾 /𝑛 is the code rate. 

> Pauli-string error basis

A convenient and often considered error set is the Pauli error or 

Pauli string basis.  

> Pauli strings:

For a single qubit, this set consists of products of powers of the Pauli matrices

For multiple qubits, error set elements are tensor products of elements of the single-qubit error set. Tensor products of 𝑋 (𝑍 )Paulis acting on different qubits are called 𝑋 -type (𝑍 -type ) Pauli strings. Combining the 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type strings with 𝑖 forms a group called the Pauli group on 𝑛 qubits, while combining them with 

−1 forms the real Pauli group .The Pauli error set is a unitary and Hermitian basis for linear op-erators on the multi-qubit Hilbert space that is orthonormal under the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product; it is a prototypical nice error basis › p. 309 . The distance associated with this set is often the mini-mum weight of a Pauli string that implements a nontrivial logical operation in the code. 

> Noise channels

A quantum channel that admits a set of Pauli strings as its Kraus operators is called a Pauli channel , and such channels are typically more tractable than the more general, non-Pauli channels. Rele-vant Pauli channels include dephasing noise and depolarizing noise (a.k.a. Werner-Holevo channel [ 4024 ]). A single-qubit dephasing channel has Kraus operators proportional to 𝐼 and 𝑍 , while the single-qubit depolarizing channel has equal probabilities for the 𝑋 ,

𝑌 , and 𝑍 errors; both are Pauli channels [ 381 , Ch. 1]. One can extract a binary memoryless symmetric channel from a Pauli channel that is a classical counterpart to the Pauli channel [4025]. Relevant non-Pauli channels are AD › p. 508 noise, erasure (which maps all qubit states into a third state |𝑒 ⟩ outside of the qubit Hilbert space), and biased erasure [ 4026 ] (in which case only the |1⟩ qubit state is mapped to |𝑒 ⟩). Erasure channels are easier to correct than general channels because one can, in principle, measure whether the state left the qubit Hilbert space and thereby learn which qubits were erased without measuring the stored qubit state [ 381 , Ch. 1]. Noise can be correlated in space or in time, with the latter being an example of a non-Markovian phenomenon [4027, 4028][381, Ch. 1].

> Pure distance:

The distance 𝑑 of a qubit code is the smallest integer 

0 < 𝑗 = 𝑑 at which the quantum weight enumerator › p. 434 is not equal to its dual, 𝐴 𝑗 ≠ 𝐵 𝑗 [4031 ]. A code is called pure if 𝐴 𝑗 = 0

for all 0 < 𝑗 < 𝑑 ; otherwise, the code is called impure . The pure distance [1912 , 3928 ] (a.k.a. diagonal distance [ 3483 , 3484 ]) 𝑑 pure is the smallest integer 1 < 𝑗 = 𝑑 pure at which 𝐴 𝑗 > 0. Codes for which 

𝑑 pure < 𝑑 are impure, otherwise they are pure. For impure codes, there exists a Pauli error of weight less than the 𝑑 that has a nonzero expectation value with respect to a code state. Degenerate qubit codes are impure, but impure codes may not be degenerate [ 381 , 429 ]. There are subtleties with defining degeneracy  

> › p. 304

for non-stabilizer qubit codes with even distance [381]. Other types of quantum weight enumerators are the Rains uni-tary enumerators [ 4032 ] and the Rains shadow enumerators [2587 ](see also [ 1600 ]), and signed weight enumerators taking into account the sign of the expectation value of a Pauli string [ 3615 ]. For qubit codes, the shadow enumerator coefficients are nonnegative and are determined by the Shor-Laflamme enumerator [381, 2587] via

. (298) Rains shadow enumerators are related to Bell sampling [ 3262 ]. These notions can be generalized to qudit codes and other error bases [ 3012 , 4033 – 4035 ]. There are techniques to compute them for general codes [ 3012 ]. Semidefinite programming (SDP) hierar-chies and a quantum Delsarte bound have been developed for qubit codes, with rational infeasibility certificates later yielding rigorous non-existence proofs and improved upper bounds for small code parameters [4036, 4037].  

> RATE

Exact two-way assisted capacities have been obtained for the erasure and dephasing channels [ 4038 ]. There are many bounds on the quantum capacity of the depolarizing channel (e.g., [ 4039 ]); see review [ 4040 ]. The optimal asymptotic error exponent of en-tanglement distillation is given by the reverse relative entropy of entanglement, a single-letter quantity [4041].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ A qubit code is 𝑈 -quasi-transversal if it can realize the logical gate 𝑈 in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 using the physical gate 𝐶𝑇 ⊗𝑛 , where 𝐶 is some Clifford gate [ 718 , Def. 4]. ⊲ If a qubit code 𝑄 of length 𝑛 

has compact subgroups 𝑁 ⊳ 𝐺 ≤ Aut (𝑄 ) such that 𝐺 /𝑁 is finite, non-Abelian, simple, and not 𝐴 5, then 𝑛 is at least the minimal permutation degree 𝜇 (𝐺 /𝑁 ) [688, Thm. 1].  

> GATES

⊲ Computing with Clifford gates › p. 244 , Pauli measurements, and classical feedforward acting on stabilizer states only can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer by tracking stabilizer and logical generators, according to the Gottesman-Knill theorem 435 [2056 , 2057 ]. There is a canonical form for Clifford circuits › p. 244 

[2059 , 2060 ] and many algorithms for simulating them [ 2061 –2063 ]. Universal quantum computing can be achieved using Clifford gates  

> › p. 244

and a single type of non-Clifford › p. 244 gate, such as the 𝑇 gate [2064 ]. More generally, the Solovay-Kitaev theorem [ 1587 , 2065 ] states that any subset of gates that generates a dense subgroup of the full 

𝑛 -qubit gate group can be used to construct any gate to arbitrary accuracy (see [ 2066 ][ 2067 , Appx. 3]). The task of approximating a desired gate by Clifford gates › p. 244 and a fixed set of non-Clifford  

> › p. 244

gates is called gate compilation or circuit synthesis .

⊲ Non-Clifford gates are typically more difficult to implement than Clifford gates › p. 244 and so are treated as a resource. Gate er-rors in circuit synthesis can sometimes add up destructively [ 4042 ]. There is a threshold against depolarizing noise for any single-qubit gate that determines if the gate enables universal quantum com-putation [ 4043 , 4044 ]. ⊲ The most studied set of universal gates is generated by the Clifford+ 𝑇 gate set. Exactly optimizing 𝑇 -gate count in circuit synthesis is 𝑁 𝑃 -hard [ 4045 , 4046 ]. Gate compilation can be done using various heuristic procedures [ 1531 , 4047 – 4055 ], e.g., ZX calculus (a.k.a. Penrose spin calculus) [ 4056 – 4059 ], reinforce-ment learning [ 4060 –4065 ], genetic algorithms [ 4066 ], or Hermitian lattices [ 4067 ]. There is an optimal asymptotic scaling of the number of T gates needed to prepare an arbitrary state [4068, 4069]. 

⊲ Other gate sets for generating universal gates are Clifford + √𝑇 [4070 ], Toffoli and Hadamard [ 4071 , 4072 ], cosine-sine [ 4073 ], and icosahedral super-golden gates [ 4074 – 4077 ]. The 𝑛 -qubit Toffoli gates can be exactly realized using at least 𝑛𝑇 gates [ 4078 ], but this can be relaxed at the expense of some errors [4079]. ⊲ 

> Clifford hierarchy:

The Clifford hierarchy [ 764 , 3126 , 4080 – 4082 ] is a tower of gate sets which includes Pauli and Clifford gates › p. 244 at its first two levels, and non-Clifford › p. 244 gates at higher levels. The 𝑘 th level is defined recursively by 

𝐶 𝑘 = {𝑈 |𝑈𝑃𝑈 † ∈ 𝐶 𝑘 −1 } , (299) where 𝑃 is any Pauli matrix, where 𝐶 1 is the Pauli group › p. 433 , and where 𝐶 2 is the Clifford group › p. 244 . Gates for one qubit have been classified [4083]. 

⊲ Arbitrary 𝑛 -qubit circuits can be implemented fault-tolerantly in a 3D architecture using 𝑂 (𝑛 3/2 log 3 𝑛 ) qubits, and in a 2D architecture using only 𝑂 (𝑛 2 log 3 𝑛 ) qubits [ 4084 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant gates can be done for any code supporting a transversal implementation of Pauli gates using generalized gate teleportation [4085].  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndrome measurements are assumed to be perfect in the code-capacity model . Incorporating faulty syndrome measure-ments can be done using the phenomenological noise model , which simulates errors during syndrome extraction by flipping some of the bits of the measured syndrome bitstring. In the more involved 

circuit-level noise model , every component of the syndrome extrac-tion circuit can be faulty. ⊲ The decoder determining the most likely error given a noise channel is called the maximum probability error (MPE) decoder. For few-qubit codes ( 𝑛 is small), MPE decoding can be based on creating a lookup table. For infinite code families, the size of such a table scales exponentially with 𝑛 , so approximate decoding algorithms scaling polynomially with 𝑛 have to be used. 

⊲ 

> Effective distance and hook errors:

Decoders are characterized by an effective distance (a.k.a. circuit-level distance or fault distance), the minimum number of faulty operations during syndrome measure-ment that is required to make an undetectable error. A code is 

distance-preserving if it admits a decoder whose circuit-level distance is equal to the code distance. A particularly dangerous class of syn-drome measurement circuit faults are hook errors , which are ancilla faults that cause more than one data-qubit error [ 460 ]. Hook errors occur at specific places in a syndrome extraction circuit and can sometimes be removed by re-ordering the gates of the circuit. If not, the use of flag qubits (see [ 381 ]) to detect hook errors may be necessary to yield fault-tolerant decoders.  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ There are lower bounds on the overhead of fault-tolerant QEC in terms of the capacity of the noise channel [ 4086 ]. A more stringent bound applies to geometrically local QEC due to the fact that locality constrains the growth of the entanglement that is needed for protection [ 496 ]. ⊲ Arbitrary 𝑛 -qubit circuits can be im-plemented fault-tolerantly in a 3D architecture using 𝑂 (𝑛 3/2 log 3 𝑛 )

qubits, and in a 2D architecture using only 𝑂 (𝑛 2 log 3 𝑛 ) qubits [ 4084 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant gates can be done for any code supporting a transversal implementation of Pauli gates using generalized gate teleportation [4085].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ 

> Computational threshold:

A fault-tolerant computational threshold is the maximum noise rate in a particular single-parameter noise model below which any logical computation of size 𝑀 can be ex-ecuted on a physical-qubit architecture to arbitrary accuracy and with an overhead of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑀 polylog 𝑀 ). The first methods to achieve a computational threshold use recursively concatenated stabilizer code families [ 490 , 493 , 494 , 788 , 3266 , 3503 – 3505 ]; such a threshold is called a concatenated threshold . Initially proven under lo-cal stochastic noise, the concatenated threshold theorem also holds for various types of non-Markovian noise [ 3504 , 3505 , 4087 , 4088 ]and leakage errors [ 4089 ]. This theorem can be rephrased in terms of Bernoulli site percolation [ 4090 ]. The resulting concatenated code is highly degenerate › p. 304 , with all but an exponentially small fraction of generators having small weights. Circuit and measure-ment designs have to take care of the few stabilizer generators with large weights in order to be fault tolerant, but measurement du-ration may not pose a threat to scalability [ 3681 ]. While generic concatenated methods yield a computational threshold with over-head 𝑂 (𝑀 polylog 𝑀 ), concatenations using quantum Hamming codes can additionally attain constant space overhead with quasi-polylogarithmic time overhead [ 3121 , 3123 ], and concatenations of the Steane code and certain QLDPC codes further improve this time overhead to polylogarithmic while keeping constant space overhead [3506 ]. Subsequently, thresholds were determined for infinite fam-ilies of lattice stabilizer codes, starting with the toric code [ 460 ]; such a threshold is colloquially called a topological threshold . When different classes of circuit locations have different error rates, the single-number threshold generalizes to a threshold surface in the space of error-rate vectors. A one-level crossing where a particular logical location becomes more reliable is then not a full-fledged threshold for the entire circuit; deciding whether a protocol really improves may require following the coupled recurrence relations through additional concatenation levels [ 381 , Sec. 14.7.6]. Fault-tolerant computations with no notion of locality can be made local on a 2D or 3D geometry with minimal overhead [4084]. 

⊲ There is an upper bound on the threshold under local update recovery that is derived via quantum optimal transport [ 4091 ] (see also Ref. [ 4092 ]). ⊲ There is a threshold against depolarizing noise for any single-qubit gate that determines if the gate enables universal quantum computation [4043, 4044]. ⊲436 

Measurement threshold: One can derive conditions quantifying how many random single-qubit measurements can be made without de-stroying the logical information [ 3118 ]. The measurement threshold is the maximum total probability that a single qubit is measured in a random 𝑋 , 𝑌 , or 𝑍 basis at which the logical information is still recoverable. The measurement threshold is at least as large as the erasure threshold [3118, Thm. 4]. 

⊲ There is a dynamical phase transition between a bounded-error and an unbounded-error phase for a model of qubits weakly coupled to a refrigerator [4093].

> CSS-to-homology correspondence
> Qubit CSS-to-homology correspondence:

CSS codes and their properties can be formulated in terms of homology theory, yielding a powerful correspondence between codes and chain complexes, the primary homological structures. There exists a many-to-one mapping from size three chain complexes to CSS codes [ 61 , 2065 , 3625 , 3862 , 4100 ]that allows one to extract code properties from topological features of the complexes. Codes constructed in this manner are sometimes called homological CSS codes , but they are equivalent to CSS codes. This mapping of codes to manifolds allows the application of struc-tures from topology to error correction, yielding various QLDPC codes › p. 546 with favorable properties. A chain complex of size three is given by binary vector spaces 𝐴 2,

𝐴 1, 𝐴 0 and binary matrices 𝜕 𝑖 =1,2 (called boundary operators ) from

𝑑 = min {𝑑 𝑋 , 𝑑 𝑍 } , (307) where 𝑤 𝐻 is the Hamming weight of a codeword. In the homol-ogy correspondence, the code distance is equal to the minimum of the combinatorial ( 𝑑 − 1)-systole of the cellulated 𝑑 -dimensional manifold and its dual. A CSS code has stabilizer weight 𝑤 if the highest weight of any sta-bilizer generator is 𝑤 , i.e., any row of 𝐻 𝑋 and 𝐻 𝑍 has weight at most 

𝑤 . Strong CSS codes are codes for which there exists a set of 𝑋 and 𝑍 

stabilizer generators of equal weight. In the context of comparing weight as well as of determining distances for noise models biased toward 𝑋 - or 𝑍 -type errors, an extended notation for asymmetric qubit CSS codes is ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, (𝑑 𝑋 , 𝑑 𝑍 ), 𝑤 ⟧ or ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 𝑋 /𝑑 𝑍 , 𝑤 ⟧. 

> Steane enlargement:

An ⟦𝑛, 2𝑘 − 𝑛, 𝑑 ⟧ CSS code can be converted to a ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 + 𝑘 ′ − 𝑛, min (𝑑, ⌈3𝑑 ′/2⌉)⟧ code for particular 𝑘 ′ and 𝑑 ′ via the Steane enlargement construction [1966, 4021].  

> RATE

For a depolarizing channel with probability 𝑝 , CSS codes al-lowing for arbitrarily accurate recovery exist with asymptotic rate 

1 − 2ℎ( 𝑝 ), where ℎ is the binary entropy function [460, 4015].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Steane Latin-rectangle encoder [ 4104 , 4105 ]. 

⊲ Stabilizer measurement [ 3722 ]. ⊲ Clusterization, i.e., mea-surement of a particular cluster state [ 3430 ]. ⊲ Entanglement purification [ 4106 ]. ⊲ Reinforcement-learning discovery of logical-state-preparation circuits [ 3108 ]. ⊲ There is a corre-spondence between qubit CSS codes and phase-free ZX calculus diagrams [ 4107 ]. ZX calculus provides a canonical form for the encoding circuit [ 4108 ]. ⊲ Automated fault-tolerant encoding circuit synthesis [4109].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Transversal CNOT gates preserve the logical subspace, up to 𝑋 -type Paulis, iff a qubit stabi-lizer code is CSS [ 381 , 725 ]. The Paulis are necessary for when the code is stabilized by stabilizers with a minus in front of them, e.g., 

−𝑋 𝑋 𝑋 𝑋 and 𝑍 𝑍 𝑍 𝑍 . ⊲ Fold-transversal [403 , 710 , 726 ] Clifford gates › p. 244 are transversal gates combined with qubit permutations. Some of these can be obtained from automorphism groups of the underlying classical codes [ 727 , Thms. 2-3]. ⊲ Necessary and suffi-cient conditions for diagonal physical gates on a CSS code to induce logical gates in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 have been formulated [728 ][ 729 , Thm. 9][ 730 , Thm. 5]. There are routines that can deter-mine what diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 are realized by a code [ 731 , 732 ]. ⊲ CSS code families with asymptotic rate 

> 1/3 and distance at ≥ 3 do not admit logical qubit permutations from physical permutations [ 733 ]. ⊲ Diagonal transversal Clifford gates › p. 244 on ℓ codeblocks of a CSS code form 𝐺 𝐿 (ℓ, F2) for non-self-dual CSS codes, 𝑈 (ℓ, 𝑅 8) for semi-self-dual CSS codes (i.e., CSS codes whose 𝑋 -type stabilizers are contained in the 𝑍 -type stabi-lizers), and 𝑆 𝑝 (2ℓ, F2) for self-dual CSS codes [ 703 ]. ⊲ Diagonal transversal gate groups can be defined using a set of equations [ 734 ].  

> GATES

⊲ LDPC CSS code symmetries called 𝑋 𝑍 -dualities allow for fold-transversal gates, i.e., transversal gates followed by qubit permutations [ 726 ]. ⊲ Generalized lattice surgery [ 4110 ]. 

⊲ Cohomology invariants give rise to logical gates implemented by constant-depth Clifford circuits › p. 244 for codes admitting a cup product structure [ 670 , 1470 , 4111 , 4112 ]. For example, a diagonal 

copy-cup gate in the 𝑚 th level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 can be implemented on a code admitting an 𝑚 -fold cup product [ 1470 ]. 

⊲ Fault-tolerant CNOT gate using generalized lattice surgery [ 4113 ].  

> DECODING

⊲ CSS syndrome decoding splits into two classical decod-ing problems: measuring the 𝑍 -type stabilizers yields the classical syndrome for bit-flip errors with respect to 𝐶 𝑋 , while measuring the 𝑋 -type stabilizers yields the classical syndrome for phase errors with respect to 𝐶 𝑍 . In the Hadamard basis, phase-error decoding 438 is ordinary classical syndrome decoding. ⊲ Coherent decoders allow for measurement-free error correction [ 4114 ]. One method is table/multi-control decoding [ 4115 ], which scales exponentially with the number of ancillas used in syndrome measurement. A fault-tolerant measurement-free scheme for low-distance CSS codes is formulated in Ref. [ 3252 ]. Another method, the Ising-based de-coder, utilizes the mapping of the effect of the noise to a statistical mechanical model [ 460 , 3377 ] such that the decoding problem maps to preparation of the ground state of an Ising model. See [ 3847 , Table 3.2] for a Rosetta stone comparing statistical mechanical models, CSS codes, and chain complexes. Models for bit- and phase-flip noise can be dual to one another [ 4116 ]. ⊲ Transformer-based decoder [4117]. ⊲ MaxSAT decoder [4118].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Steane error correction [ 4119 ], where fault-tolerance is ensured by preparing ancillary encoded states and extracting syndromes via 𝐶𝑁𝑂𝑇 gates. ⊲ Encoded |0⟩ and |+⟩ 

ancillas for Steane error correction can be prepared by hierarchi-cal Steane-style verification; without code-specific optimizations, a two-level procedure uses at least (𝑡 + 1)2 noisy ancillas for a distance-

2𝑡 + 1 CSS code [ 381 , Secs. 13.1.2-13.1.3]. ⊲ Steane’s method also yields non-destructive logical Pauli measurement for CSS codes by coupling the data block transversally to encoded |0⟩ or |+⟩ ancil-las and classically decoding the ancilla measurement results [ 381 ]. 

⊲ Transversal computational-basis measurement followed by classi-cal decoding is a fault-tolerant gadget for logical measurement of all encoded qubits [ 381 , Sec. 11.4]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant error correc-tion and logical measurements using flag qubits for distance-three cyclic CSS codes [ 4120 ]. Parallel syndrome extraction for distance-three codes can be done fault-tolerantly using one flag qubit [ 4121 ]. Distance-preserving › p. 435 flag fault-tolerant error correction can be done using lookup tables for small codes [ 4122 ]. ⊲ Homomorphic gadgets fault-tolerant measurement unify Steane and Shor error correction [ 3823 ]. ⊲ A fault-tolerant error-correction protocol us-ing 𝑂 (𝑑 log 𝑑 ) syndrome measurements can be applied to any CSS code with distance 𝑑 ≥ Ω(𝑛 𝛼 ) for any 𝛼 > 0 [2953 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant measurement-free scheme for low-distance CSS codes [3252 ]. ⊲ Automated fault-tolerant encoding circuit synthesis [4109 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant homological measurement of logical Pauli operators [ 4123 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant CNOT gate using generalized lattice surgery [4113].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Bounds on code capacity thresholds for various noise models exist in terms of stabilizer generator weights [3342, 4124].

> COUSINS

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — Qubit CSS codes are qubit stabilizer codes whose stabilizer groups admit a generating set of pure-𝑋 and pure-𝑍 Pauli strings. Transversal CNOT gates preserve the logical subspace iff a qubit stabilizer code is CSS [ 381 , 725 ]. Any 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code can be mapped onto a ⟦2𝑛, 2𝑘, ≥ 𝑑 ⟧ two-block CSS code › p. 505 via symplectic doubling › p. 485 , which preserves geometric locality of a code up to a constant factor. For any non-CSS qubit stabilizer code C, there exists a CSS code C′ such that 

C = 𝐷𝑄 C′, where 𝐷 is a diagonal Clifford operator, and where 𝑄 

is an element of an XP stabilizer group [ 732 , Prop. B.3.1]. There is a holographic relation between qubit CSS codes describing CFTs and qubit stabilizer codes describing path integrals over certain topologies [3512]. 

⊲ Movassagh-Ouyang Hamiltonian code › p. 419 — Qubit CSS codes encoding one logical qubit are a subset of Movassagh-Ouyang codes. ⊲ Two-block CSS code › p. 505 — Any ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code can be mapped onto a ⟦2𝑛, 2𝑘, ≥ 𝑑 ⟧ two-block CSS code › p. 505 via symplectic doubling › p. 485 , which preserves geometric locality of a code up to a constant factor. ⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — The CSS construction uses two related binary linear codes, 𝐶 𝑋 and 𝐶 𝑍 .

⊲ Alternant code › p. 213 — Alternant codes used in the CSS construc-tion yield quantum codes that asymptotically achieve the quantum GV bound › p. 298 [ 1679 ]. ⊲ Random stabilizer code › p. 557 — Random CSS codes asymptotically achieve linear distance with high prob-ability, achieving the quantum GV bound › p. 298 [3104 ]. ⊲ Binary quantum Goppa code › p. 489 — Quantum Goppa codes can exceed the quantum GV bound › p. 298 [ 4130 ]. ⊲ Subsystem qubit stabilizer code › p. 457 — Qubit CSS "seed" codes can be used to produce subsys-tem qubit stabilizer codes [ 4131 ]. ⊲ Lattice stabilizer code › p. 551 —The mapping of qubit CSS codes to chain complexes › p. 437 allows the application of structures from topology to error correction. Chain complexes describing some QLDPC codes [ 464 , 465 ], and, more gen-erally, CSS codes [ 466 ] can be "lifted" into higher-dimensional mani-folds admitting some notion of geometric locality. Qubit CSS codes admit several dualities [ 449 , 2461 ]. In particular, a CSS code and two dual classical codes can be organized by the same 2-complex, and gauging [ 216 , 442 – 450 ] either classical code yields the same CSS code up to Hadamard [ 449 ]. ⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 —The mapping of qubit CSS codes to chain complexes › p. 437 allows the application of structures from topology to error correction. Chain complexes describing some QLDPC codes [ 464 , 465 ], and, more gen-erally, CSS codes [ 466 ] can be "lifted" into higher-dimensional mani-439 folds admitting some notion of geometric locality. Qubit CSS codes admit several dualities [ 449 , 2461 ]. In particular, a CSS code and two dual classical codes can be organized by the same 2-complex, and gauging [ 216 , 442 – 450 ] either classical code yields the same CSS code up to Hadamard [ 449 ]. ⊲ Conformal-field theory (CFT) code

— There is a holographic relation between qubit CSS codes de-scribing CFTs and qubit stabilizer codes describing path integrals over certain topologies [ 3512 ]. ⊲ Cycle code › p. 184 — Cycle codes, including the Petersen cycle and Hoffman-Singleton cycle codes, feature in magic-state distillation protocols [ 89 , Appx. AD › p. 508 errors [ 3169 ][ 701 , Sec. 8.7]. ⊲ Concatenated cat code › p. 519 

— Stabilizers of CSS codes concatenated with two-component cat codes in their coherent-state basis come directly from the CSS codes via the mapping 𝑋 → (− 1) ˆ𝑛 and 𝑍 → ˆ𝑎 [365 ]. Stabilizers of CSS codes concatenated with two-component cat codes in their cat-state basis come directly from the CSS codes via the mapping 𝑍 → (− 1) ˆ𝑛 

and 𝑋 → ˆ𝑎 . In both cases, one type of noise is handled actively via syndrome extraction and correction, while the other type is handled passively via stabilizing dissipation. ⊲ Error-corrected sensing code › p. 303 — Qubit CSS codes can be used for sensing whenever the HNLS condition is satisfied, with the quantum Fisher information related to the number of weight-two codewords of the dual code [2682 ]. ⊲ Constant-excitation (CE) code › p. 300 — Qubit CE codes are protected from coherent noise in the form of transversal 𝑍 -rotations because such rotations act identically on all codewords [772 , 2631 ]. In the case of qubit CSS codes, all codes oblivious to such rotations are CE codes [ 772 , 2631 ]. Any ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ CSS code can be made into an ⟦𝑚𝑛, 𝑘, > 𝑑 ⟧ CE code [ 2631 ]. Concatenating the dual-rail code with an inner ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code yields a degenerate ⟦2𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ constant-excitation stabilizer code that avoids coherent phase errors and is equivalent to a Pauli-rotated repetition-concatenated stabilizer code [ 2633 ]. CSS structure is preserved when the original code is CSS [498]. 

⊲ Quantum locally testable code (QLTC) › p. 316 — A qubit CSS code defined by 𝐻 𝑍 and 𝐻 𝑋 is locally testable with some soundness iff the constituent codes ker 𝐻 𝑍 and ker 𝐻 𝑋 are locally testable with the same soundness [ 1058 , Fact 17]. ⊲ EA qubit stabilizer code  

> › p. 387

— As opposed to CSS codes, EA qubit stabilizer codes can be constructed from any linear binary code. ⊲ Quantum polar code  

> › p. 427

— Quantum polar codes are CSS codes used in an entanglement generation scheme that generally requires entanglement assistance. They require assistance only to determine positions to store infor-mation which optimally protect against both bit and phase noise. Without this assistance, they are just CSS codes constructed out of polar codes. A variant of quantum polar codes exists that does not require entanglement assistance [ 3947 ]. ⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 — Every ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ 𝑓 Majorana stabilizer code is associated with a ⟦2𝑛, 2𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit CSS code whose 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -check supports coincide [ 1385 , Lemma 2]. An odd-length self-dual CSS code can be converted into a complex-fermion code by replacing qubit 𝑍 -type and 𝑋 -type operators with 𝛾 -type and ˜𝛾 -type Majorana operators, respectively [ 532 ]. ⊲ XP stabilizer code › p. 468 — Each XP-regular code can be mapped to a CSS code with the same diagonal logical op-erators and similar non-diagonal logical operators [ 762 ]. ⊲ Union stabilizer (USt) code › p. 467 — An ⟦𝑛, 2𝑘 − 𝑛, 𝑑 ⟧ CSS code can be con-verted to a ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 + 𝑘 ′ − 𝑛, min (𝑑, ⌈3𝑑 ′/2⌉)⟧ code for particular 𝑘 ′

and 𝑑 ′ via Steane enlargement › p. 437 . This code can be treated as a union stabilizer code [ 1322 ]. ⊲ Hermitian qubit code › p. 397 — A Hermitian qubit code that can be put into CSS form via single-qubit Clifford operations remains Hermitian [ 434 ]. ⊲ Cluster-state code  

> › p. 376

— A resource cluster state can be constructed out of any qubit CSS code via foliation. Conversely, CSS codes can be constructed out of cluster states [ 3430 ]. In the fault-complex formalism, foliation of a CSS code is expressed as a homological product of the code’s chain complex with a repetition-code complex [3084].

QUBIT QLDPC CODE qldpc  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Sparse qubit stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

Member of a family of ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer codes for which the number of sites participating in each stabilizer gen-erator and the number of stabilizer generators that each site par-ticipates in are both bounded by a constant 𝑤 as 𝑛 → ∞ . The code can be denoted by ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑, 𝑤 ⟧. Sometimes, the two parameters are explicitly stated: each site of an (𝑙, 𝑤 )-regular qubit QLDPC code is acted on by ≤ 𝑙 generators of weight ≤ 𝑤 .Qubit QLDPC codes can correct many stochastic errors far be-yond the distance, which may not scale as favorably. Together with more accurate, faster, and easier-to-parallelize measurements than those of general stabilizer codes, this property makes QLDPC codes interesting in practice. A geometrically local qubit stabilizer code is a qubit QLDPC code where the sites involved in any syndrome value are contained in a fixed volume that does not scale with 𝑛 . As opposed to general stabilizer codes, syndrome extraction of the constant-weight check operators of a QLDPC code can be done using a constant-depth circuit.  

> PROTECTION

Detects errors on 𝑑 − 1 sites, corrects errors on 

⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋ sites. Code distance may not be a reliable marker of code performance. Since qubit QLDPC codes are stabilizer QLRCs whose locality 

𝑟 ≤ 𝑤 , their relative distance is bounded by [775, Thm. 35]

> RATE

Asymptotic scaling of 𝑘 and 𝑑 with 𝑛 depends heavily on the code construction. Bounds generalizing the BPT bound › p. 551 to qubit QLDPC codes depend on the separation profile of the code’s under-lying connectivity graph [ 4132 , 4133 ]. A constant relative minimum distance can be achieved only for graphs that contain expanders [ 4132 ]. Conversely, a code with parameters 𝑘 and 𝑑 requires a graph with order › p. 161 Ω(𝑑 ) edges of length of order › p. 161 Ω(𝑑 /𝑛 1/𝐷 ) [ 4134 ]. Random qubit QLDPC codes found by solving certain constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) practically achieve the capacity of the erasure channel [4135]. Qubit QLDPC codes cannot attain the capacity of the erasure channel [ 3344 ], but this capacity can be attained by code families with weight 𝑤 = 𝑂 (polylog 𝑛 ) [4136 ]. There are bounds on their performance against erasure noise [3344].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Fault-tolerant encoders utilizing pre-shared entangle-ment for qubit QLDPC codes [ 3544 ]. ⊲ Any logical state of an 

𝑠 -sparse qubit QLDPC code with 𝑑 > 𝑠 425ℎ has depth-ℎ geomet-ric entanglement Ω(𝑑 ), equivalently exponentially small overlap with any depth-ℎ topologically trivial state, even allowing arbitrary ancillas [ 502 , Thm. 1]. ⊲ For a qubit QLDPC code with parame-ters (𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ), any logical state has depth-ℎ geometric entanglement 440 

Ω␀𝑛𝐻 −1 (𝑘 /𝑛 )/ 24ℎ ; in particular, constant-rate families require 

Ω(𝑛 /24ℎ) entanglement [ 502 , Thm. 3(ii)]. Here, 𝐻 −1 is the inverse of the binary entropy function 𝐻 ( 𝑝 ) = −𝑝 log 2 𝑝 − ( 1 − 𝑝 ) log 2 (1 − 𝑝 ).

⊲ Fault-tolerant state preparation can be done in an overhead that is constant with the number of qubits 𝑛 [4137].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ There are recipes to de-termine transversal gates for asymmetric qubit QLDPC codes [735].  

> GATES

⊲ Fault-tolerant logical measurements by gauging logical op-erators have worst-case qubit overhead 𝑂 (𝑊 log 2 𝑊 ) for a weight-

𝑊 Pauli and improve earlier QLDPC measurement schemes [ 450 ]. This can be used for a generalization of lattice surgery for CSS QLDPC codes [ 4138 ]. There are conditions on when fault-tolerant surgery can be performed with constant-time overhead [ 4139 ]. 

⊲ Repetition-code adapter for logical Pauli measurements and log-ical CNOT gates via Dehn twists [ 4140 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant logical measurements based on an extractor system and allowing for uni-versal computation [ 4141 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant batched gadgets for CSS QLDPC codes with constant spacetime overhead [3392].  

> DECODING

⊲ Iterative error estimation based on the MIN-SUM and SUM-PRODUCT algorithms [ 3414 ]. ⊲ Quantum belief propagation (BP) decoder [ 4142 – 4144 ] is a quantum version of the classical BP decoder, but performance suffers due to degeneracy [ 4145 ]. Vari-ous post-processing algorithms have been proposed (see below and also Refs. [ 4146 , 4147 ]). ⊲ BP-OSD decoder, scaling as 𝑂 (𝑛 3), adds a post-processing step based on ordered statistics decoding (OSD) to the belief propagation (BP) decoder [ 1200 ]. ⊲ Neural network BP decoders [ 4148 , 4149 ] and GNN decoders [ 4150 , 4151 ] for qubit codes. ⊲ Partially and fully decoupled BP decoders, which use the decoupling representation, yield improvements against depolar-izing noise [ 4152 ]. ⊲ Message-passing decoder utilizing stabilizer inactivation (MP-SI a.k.a. BP-SI) for CSS-type QLDPC qubit codes [4153 ]. ⊲ BP localized statistics decoding (BP-LSD) that exploits error clustering [ 4154 ]. ⊲ Syndrome-based linear programming (SB-LP) algorithm can be applied as a post-processing step after syndrome-based min-sum (SM-MS) decoding [ 4155 ]. ⊲ BP guided decimation (BPGD) decoder [ 4156 ]. ⊲ SymBreak decoder, which adaptively modifies the decoding graph to break the degeneracy of the BP decoder [ 4157 ]. ⊲ Ambiguity clustering (AC) decoder, in which measurement data is divided into clusters and decoded inde-pendently [ 3099 ]. ⊲ 2D geometrically local syndrome extraction circuits with bounded depth using order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2) ancilla qubits [495 ]. For CSS codes, syndrome extraction can be implemented in constant depth [ 4158 ]. ⊲ Soft (i.e., analog) syndrome iterative BP for CSS-type QLDPC codes, utilizing the continuous signal ob-tained in the physical implementation of the stabilizer measure-ment (as opposed to discretizing the signal into a syndrome bit) [4159 ]. ⊲ The MWPM decoder for surface codes may be gener-alizable to QLDPC codes [ 4160 ]. ⊲ Extensions of the union-find decoder for qubit QLDPC codes [ 4161 – 4163 ]. ⊲ Sliding-window decoding [ 4164 ]. ⊲ Closed-branch decoder [ 4165 ]. ⊲ BP with guided decimation guessing (GDG) sliding-window decoder for CSS qubit codes [ 3098 ]. ⊲ Performing 𝑑 syndrome extraction rounds obtains an effective distance › p. 435 of 𝑑 for a qubit QLDPC code [ 4166 ]. 

⊲ BP plus ordered Tanner forest (BP+OTF) almost-linear time de-coder [ 4167 ]. ⊲ Cluster decoder [ 3676 ]. ⊲ BP approximate de-generate OSD (BP+ADOSD) decoder [ 4168 ]. ⊲ Decision tree de-coders (DTDs), one that provably finds the minimum-weight cor-rection, and one that is heuristic [ 3639 ]. ⊲ AutDEC decoder for codes with large automorphism groups [ 3110 ]. ⊲ Tesseract ML decoder [ 4169 ]. ⊲ Relay-BP decoder [ 4170 ]. ⊲ HyperBlossom [4171 ]. ⊲ Post-selection strategies for clustering based decoders [4172 ]. ⊲ Decoder switching between soft-output and higher-accuracy decoders [ 4173 ]. ⊲ Graph augmentation and rewiring for interference (GARI) framework for circuit-level noise [4174].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Lattice surgery techniques with ancilla qubits [810 , 3097 , 3399 ]. In one such technique, one first performs a log-ical measurement by code switching › p. 559 into a code whose sta-bilizer group includes the original stabilizers together with the logical Paulis that are to be measured. Then, one can reduce the weight of the output code using weight reduction › p. 490 . ⊲ Fault-tolerance with constant overhead can be performed on certain qubit QLDPC codes [ 4166 ], e.g., quantum expander codes [ 809 ]. ⊲ Error-corrected GHZ state distillation for Steane error correction [ 3965 ]. 

⊲ Fault-tolerant logical measurements by gauging logical opera-tors have worst-case qubit overhead 𝑂 (𝑊 log 2 𝑊 ) for a weight-𝑊 

Pauli and improve earlier QLDPC measurement schemes [ 450 ]. This can be used for a generalization of lattice surgery for CSS QLDPC codes [ 4138 ]. There are conditions on when fault-tolerant surgery can be performed with constant-time overhead [ 4139 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant logical measurements based on an extractor system and al-lowing for universal computation [ 4141 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant batched gadgets for CSS QLDPC codes with constant spacetime overhead [3392 ]. ⊲ High-rate surgery, which yields parallelizable logical Pauli-product measurements [ 4175 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant state prepa-ration can be done in an overhead that is constant with the number of qubits 𝑛 [4137].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ Bounds on code capacity thresholds us-ing ML decoding can be obtained by mapping the effect of noise on the code to a statistical mechanical model [ 460 , 3342 , 4176 ]. In particular, any family of qubit QLDPC codes with superlogarithmic distance achieves a threshold [ 3342 ]. ⊲ Bounds on code capac-ity thresholds for various noise models exist in terms of stabilizer generator weights [4124].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Qubit QLDPC codes with a constant encoding rate can reduce the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation to be constant [4166].

> COUSINS

⊲ Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 — Qubit QLDPC codes are quantum analogues of binary LDPC codes. 

⊲ Commuting-projector Hamiltonian code › p. 298 — Qubit QLDPC codes with check soundness, meaning that every weight-𝑚 stabilizer can be written as a product of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑚 ) stabilizer genera-tors, are robust against few-body perturbations. This means that phases of matter can be defined from certain non-geometrically local QLDPC code Hamiltonians [ 2603 ]. ⊲ Single-shot code › p. 320 

— Qubit QLDPC codes satisfying linear confinement are single shot [806 ]. Any code that admits a local greedy decoder also satisfies linear confinement, and so is single shot [ 810 ]. ⊲ Low-density generator-matrix (LDGM) code › p. 194 — LDGM codes can yield CSS [1395 – 1398 ] and non-CSS [ 1399 , 1400 ] qubit QLDPC codes. Some of the LDGM-based CSS codes have 𝑛 -independent minimum distance and no code capacity threshold [ 1401 , Sec. 4.2]. ⊲ Random sta-bilizer code › p. 557 — Random qubit QLDPC codes found by solving certain constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) practically achieve the capacity of the erasure channel [ 4135 ]. ⊲ Algebraic LDPC code  

> › p. 178

— Algebraic LDPC codes made from Latin squares can be used to make qubit QLDPC codes [ 832 , Ch. 15]. ⊲ Asymmetric quantum code (AQC) › p. 296 — There are recipes to determine transversal gates for asymmetric qubit QLDPC codes [ 735 ]. ⊲ 2D lattice stabilizer code › p. 543 — Chain complexes describing qubit QLDPC codes can be converted to 2D lattice stabilizer codes [ 468 ]. ⊲ Lattice stabi-lizer code › p. 551 — Chain complexes describing some QLDPC codes [464 , 465 ], and, more generally, CSS codes [ 466 ] can be ’lifted’ into higher-dimensional manifolds admitting some notion of geometric locality. In addition, chain complexes describing QLDPC codes can be converted to 2D lattice stabilizer codes [ 468 ]. ⊲ QLDPC subsys-tem code › p. 555 — Any qubit QLDPC code with stabilizer-generator weights 𝑤 𝑖 can be mapped constructively to a sparse subsystem qubit code with the same number of logical qubits and distance, using 

𝑛 = 𝑂 (Í𝑖 𝑤 𝑖 ) physical qubits and constant-weight gauge generators [638 ]. ⊲ Honeycomb Floquet code › p. 403 — The Floquet check oper-ators are weight-two, and each qubit participates in one check each round. ⊲ Dynamical code › p. 385 — Using ZX calculus, an ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧

qubit stabilizer code admitting stabilizer generators of weight no more than 𝑚 can be Floquetified into an ⟦𝑛 + ⌈ 𝑚 /2⌉ + ℓ, 𝑘, 𝑑 ′⟧ dynam-ical code with single- and two-qubit operations, where ℓ ≤ log 2 𝑚 

and 𝑑 ′ ≥ 𝑑 [3198 ] (see also Ref. [ 3197 ]). A more general locality-preserving spacetime concatenation procedure yields a dynamical code out of any qubit stabilizer code by structuring measurement gadgets using low-weight measurements while ensuring the preser-vation of logical information [ 3530 ]. In particular, spacetime con-catenation reformulates the notion of a dynamical code associated with a stabilizer code in terms of code concatenation for every qubit (spatial concatenation) and measurements between these codes (temporal concatenation), leading to a temporal evolution of the stabilizer state [ 3530 ]. A matrix rank condition on the bond opera-tors connecting the gadgets, called the Bond-Kernel-Rank Condition, and a strict locality preservation condition (SLPC), along with preser-vation of the operator algebra of the stabilizer code under the gadget action, preserves fault-tolerance and the spacetime distance of the code [3530]. 

⊲ EA QLDPC code › p. 386 — EA QLDPC codes utilize additional ancillary qubits in a pre-shared entangled state, but reduce to qubit QLDPC codes when said qubits are interpreted as noiseless phys-ical qubits. ⊲ Bicycle code › p. 370 — Bicycle codes are the first QLDPC codes [ 651 ]. ⊲ Concatenated Steane code › p. 381 — The com-bination of the concatenated Steane code and QLDPC codes with non-vanishing rate yields fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant space and polylogarithmic time overheads, even when classical computation time is taken into account [ 3506 ]. ⊲ 𝐷 -dimensional twisted toric code › p. 361 — It is conjectured that appro-priate twisted boundary conditions yield multi-dimensional toric code families with sublinear distance scaling of 𝑁 1− 𝜖 for any 𝜖 > 0

and logarithmic-weight stabilizer generators [ 3311 ]. Assuming this conjecture, Hastings’ weight-reduction construction yields QLDPC families with distance Θ∗ (𝑁 1− 𝜖 ) for any 𝜖 > 0 [2899]. 

QUBIT STABILIZER CODE [701, 3271] qubit_stabilizer  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Binary stabilizer code ⊲ Pauli stabilizer code 

⊲ Symplectic code ⊲ Additive quantum code ⊲ Additive CWS code ⊲ Clifford code  

> DESCRIPTION

An (( 𝑛, 2𝑘 , 𝑑 )) qubit stabilizer code is denoted as ⟦𝑛, 𝑘 ⟧

or ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧, where 𝑘 is the number of logical qubits (code dimen-sion), and where 𝑑 is the code’s distance. The logical subspace is the joint eigenspace of commuting Pauli operators forming the code’s stabilizer group S. Traditionally, the logical subspace is the joint +1

eigenspace of a set of 2𝑛 −𝑘 commuting Pauli operators which do not contain −𝐼 . The distance is the minimum weight of a Pauli string that implements a nontrivial logical operation in the code. Qubit stabilizer codes form the joint +1-eigenspace of a stabilizer group S, i.e., a group of commuting Paulis that does not contain 

−𝐼 and is generated by 𝑟 = 𝑛 − 𝑘 generators. The table below summarizes the relevant groups and their sizes for a qubit stabilizer code. 

purpose symbol size 

stabilizer group S 2𝑛 −𝑘 

code-preserving Paulis N(S) 4 · 2𝑛 +𝑘 

logical Paulis N(S)/ S 4𝑘 

TABLE LXVII: Groups relevant to qubit stabilizer codes. The normalizer N(S)

(technically, the centralizer, but these are equivalent for this case) is the group formed by all elements of the 𝑛 -qubit Pauli group that commute with all elements in S. The normalizer is defined so as to include 𝑖 and its powers as elements, while the stabilizer group is not. 

Two qubit stabilizer codes are equivalent if the codespace of one 442 code can be mapped into that of the other under a tensor prod-uct of elements of the single-qubit Clifford group › p. 244 and a qubit permutation (see Refs. [ 429 , 434 ]). Equivalence under single-qubit Clifford operations is not the same as equivalence under a tensor product of arbitrary single-qubit unitary operations [ 3438 ] (see also Ref. [ 4181 ] about this false LC-LU conjecture). Any qubit stabilizer code is equivalent to a graph quantum code via a single-qubit Clif-ford circuit › p. 244 [ 3461 ] (see also [ 827 ]). At the state level, every qubit stabilizer state is equivalent to a graph state under a single-qubit Clifford circuit › p. 244 , and local-Clifford equivalence between graph states is generated by local complementations of the underlying graph [ 3436 ]. In the binary symplectic representation, local-Clifford equivalence of stabilizer states can be tested by solving a system of 

𝑛 2 linear equations in the 4𝑛 entries of the local Clifford operator [3436] (see also [3463–3465]). A qubit stabilizer code is decomposable if there exists a permu-tation that maps the stabilizer group into a tensor product of two stabilizer groups acting on disjoint sets of qubits. Otherwise, the code is indecomposable. For example, a 2𝑛 -qubit code consisting of two copies of an 𝑛 -qubit indecomposable code is decomposable. 

> Code representations

Qubit stabilizer states are quadratic-phase states on affine sub-spaces of Z𝑛

For any logical state of a distance-𝑑 stabilizer code, the squared overlap with any 𝑛 -qubit product state is at most 21−𝑑 [502, Thm. 2]. Instead of being represented by a basis of codewords, stabilizer codes can be concisely defined and represented by a presentation of the generators of the stabilizer group. A set of generators is not unique, and various stabilizer codes admit generators with certain locality properties. Stabilizer generators can be arranged as rows of a matrix, forming a stabilizer tableau . For example, a stabilizer tableau of the two-qubit Bell state |00 ⟩ + | 11 ⟩ is

> Symplectic representation:

In the symplectic representation, the single-qubit identity, 𝑋 , 𝑌 , and 𝑍 Pauli matrices are represented using two bits as (0|0), (1|0), (1|1), and (0|1), respectively. In other words, the single-qubit Pauli string 𝑋 𝑎 𝑍 𝑏 is converted to the vector 𝑎 |𝑏 . The multi-qubit version follows naturally. Each stabilizer code can be represented by a (𝑛 − 𝑘 ) × 2𝑛 check matrix (a.k.a. stabilizer generator matrix ) 𝐻 = ( 𝐴 |𝐵 ), where each row 

(𝑎 |𝑏 ) is the symplectic representation › p. 442 of an element from a set of generating elements of the stabilizer group. The check matrix can be brought into standard form (a.k.a. canonical form) via Gaussian elimination [2060, 2503]. A pair of 𝑛 -qubit stabilizers with symplectic representation › p. 442 

(𝑎 |𝑏 ) and (𝑎 ′ |𝑏 ′) commute iff their symplectic inner product is zero,
