F4 representation: An 𝑛 -qubit Pauli stabilizer can be represented as a length-𝑛 quaternary vector using the one-to-one correspondence between the four Pauli matrices {𝐼, 𝑋, 𝑌 , 𝑍 } and the four elements 

{0, 1, 𝜔 2, 𝜔 } of the quaternary Galois field › p. 164 F4.The sets of F4-represented vectors for all generators yield a trace-Hermitian self-orthogonal additive quaternary code. In other words, an additive self-orthogonal code 𝐶 ⊆ F𝑛  

> 4

of size 2𝑟 yields an ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 −

𝑟 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code [ 3614 ][ 429 , Thm. 2]. This classical code corresponds to the stabilizer group S while its trace-Hermitian dual corresponds to the normalizer N(S). In the case of stabilizer states, the correspondence is between such states and trace-Hermitian self-dual quaternary codes; such codes, and therefore such states, have been classified up to equivalence for 𝑛 ≤ 12 [1598 , 3616 ]. There is a complete set of invariants characterizing stabilizer states up to equivalence [4184, 4185]. ZX calculus is complete, sound, and universal for qubit stabilizer codes [ 4186 ]. Any stabilizer code can be represented by a ZX canon-ical form (ZXCF) [ 819 ], and there exist two other representations [819, 4187] that utilize ZX calculus.  

> Encoder-respecting form:

In an encoder-respecting form , each qubit sta-bilizer code [ 819 ] (see also Ref. [ 4188 ]) is represented by a semi-bipartite graph with 𝑘 input and 𝑛 output nodes in which the 𝑘 input nodes are not connected to each other. Conversion from stabilizer tableaus to graphs can be done in time of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 3), while the inverse map from graphs to stabilizer codes can be computed in 𝑂 (𝑛 2), both using ZX calculus [ 819 ]. Properties of the underly-ing graph are related to properties of the code; for example, bipar-tite encoder-respecting graphs yield CSS codes, and graph degree controls bounds on code distance, stabilizer weight, and encoding-circuit depth [819]. Alternative representations include the decoupling representation ,in which Pauli strings are represented as vectors over F2 using three bits [4152].  

> PROTECTION

Detects errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 qubits, and corrects era-sure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 qubits. There are algorithms to calcu-late the minimum distance [ 3011 , 4189 – 4191 ]. Computing the dis-tance exactly or approximately is generally 𝑁 𝑃 -complete, and is 

𝑁 𝑃 -hard for non-degenerate › p. 304 codes [ 4192 ]. Distance approxima-tion, minimum-weight stabilizer-generator selection, and decoding are approximately optimal strategies for various quantum lights-out (QLO) games that can be played on the codes’ encoder-respecting form › p. 442 [819]. There is the following analogue of the Knill-Laflamme conditions  

> › p. 304

for qubit stabilizer codes. Define the normalizer N(S) of S to be the set of all Pauli operators that commute with all 𝑆 ∈ S. A stabilizer code can correct a Pauli error set E if and only if 𝐸 † 𝐹 ∉ N(S) \ S

for all 𝐸, 𝐹 ∈ E .There are subtleties with defining degeneracy › p. 304 for non-stabilizer qubit codes with even distance [ 381 ], but they are resolved 443 for stabilizer codes. A stabilizer code is degenerate › p. 304 with re-spect to E if and only if 𝐸 † 𝐹 ∈ S for some Pauli strings 𝐸, 𝐹 ∈ E .As a distance-𝑑 code, a stabilizer code is degenerate if it admits a non-identity stabilizer whose weight is lower than the distance [ 381 ]. Since that stabilizer is in the normalizer, a stabilizer code is degen-erate › p. 304 if and only if it is impure › p. 434 . The pure distance › p. 434 

of a qubit stabilizer code is the minimum weight of a non-identity stabilizer, and a qubit stabilizer code is pure › p. 434 if the weight of the lowest-weight stabilizer is the code distance. There is a toolkit for studying degenerate › p. 304 codes for Pauli channels [ 4193 ]. The quantum GV bound › p. 298 can be extended into a three-way tradeoff between distance, rate, and stabilizer weight of a qubit stabilizer code [819].  

> Cleaning lemma:

If all logical operators act trivially on some subset of qubits in a stabilizer code, then any logical Pauli operator can be represented on the complementary qubit subset via a stabilizer. More technically, given any subset 𝑀 of qubits that is correctable (under erasure), any logical Pauli operator 𝑃 can be cleaned off of 𝑀 

using a stabilizer 𝑆 such that 𝑃𝑆 is supported on 𝑀 ⊥. More generally, for any 𝑀 , we have 𝑔 (𝑀 ) + 𝑔 (𝑀 ⊥) = 2𝑘 , where 𝑔 (𝑀 ) is the number of logical-𝑋 and logical-𝑍 Pauli operators supported fully on 𝑀 (up to stabilizers). The Cleaning Lemma was originally proven [ 2910 ], where an analogous result is stated for subsystem codes; see also Ref. [4194]. Qubit stabilizer codes can be interleaved to protect against burst errors [ 2585 ]. Entropic conditions have been formulated for random projective measurement noise [ 3118 ]. An effective logical channel can be derived for qubit stabilizer codes under Pauli noise [ 4195 ,4196].  

> RATE

The ancilla-added rate is defined as the ratio of logical qubits to the total number of physical qubits including ancillas, 𝑘 /( 𝑛 +

𝑐 ), where 𝑐 is the number of ancilla qubits. The hashing bound 

states that there is a qubit stabilizer code achieving a rate 𝑅 = 1 −

𝐻 (p) for a Pauli noise channel with Pauli error probabilities p =

( 𝑝 𝐼 , 𝑝 𝑋 , 𝑝 𝑌 , 𝑝 𝑍 ), where 𝐻 (p) is the entropy of the argument [ 2699 ,Thm. 23.6.2]. Finite block length bounds and a refinement of the hashing bound have been developed [2060].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Clifford circuits › p. 244 , i.e., those consisting of CNOT, Hadamard, and certain phase gates [ 3272 ], using an algorithm [ 2063 ]based on the Gottesman-Knill theorem [ 2061 ] or using ZX calculus [3490 , 3491 ]. Generic constructions use 𝑂 (𝑛 2) Clifford gates and can be adjusted to realize a chosen set of logical Pauli operators [ 381 ]. Encoding circuits can be done in linear depth, up to logarithmic corrections, for most practical use cases [4197].  

> Destabilizers:

A Clifford encoding circuit maps the first 𝑘 qubits to the logical qubits of the code, and the Pauli 𝑍 operators of the last 

𝑟 = 𝑛 − 𝑘 qubits are mapped into a set of stabilizer generators. The set of Pauli 𝑋 operators of the first 𝑟 qubits that are mapped into a set of generators for the destabilizer group [ 2061 , 4198 ]. Each such generator anticommutes with only one stabilizer generator while commuting with the rest of the stabilizer generators. 

⊲ For a code given in encoder-respecting form › p. 442 with maxi-mum graph degree Δ, there is an efficient construction of an encod-ing circuit of depth at most 2Δ+3 [ 819 ]. ⊲ Circuits obtained by first constructing the CWS form of the code [ 814 , 4199 ]. These consist of 𝑛 

Hadamard gates, a classical encoder which takes at most 𝑛 CX gates for a single-qubit encoding code, and at most 𝑛 (𝑛 − 1)/ 2 CZ gates to create the needed graph state. ⊲ Lindbladian-based dissipative encoding [ 4200 , 4201 ], for which the codespace is the steady-state space of a Lindbladian. This does not give a speedup, in terms of scaling with 𝑛 , over circuit-based encoders [ 4202 ]. A finite-time non-Lindbladian dissipative encoder may always be constructed [4203 ]. ⊲ Algorithm for fault-tolerant magic-state initialization [4204 ]. ⊲ Measurement-based purification protocol yielding ar-bitrary logical states from initial thermal states [ 4205 ]. ⊲ State injection protocols that generalize lattice surgery for the surface code [ 714 ]. ⊲ The overlap with any state prepared by a depth-ℎ

Clifford circuit with a product state is at most 21−𝑑 /2ℎ

[502].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Logical Pauli transfor-mations [ 701 , 736 , 737 ]. ⊲ The four-block transversal gate mapping each 𝑋 → 𝐼 𝑋 𝑋 𝑋 and each 𝑍 → 𝐼 𝑍 𝑍 𝑍 implements the same log-ical gate on all qubits [ 701 ][ 505 , Exam. 1]. More generally, in the 

𝑡 -block setting, the commutant of the 𝑡 -fold action of the 𝑛 -qubit Clifford group contains invertible operators realizing the stochastic orthogonal group 𝑂 𝑡 (2), yielding inter-block symmetries in tensor powers of stabilizer constructions [ 738 ]. ⊲ Transversal logical gates are in a finite level of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 , which is shown using stabilizer disjointness [ 739 ] (see also [ 740 , 741 ]). Transver-sal gates for 𝑛 ∈ { 1, 2} are semi-Clifford [742]. 

⊲ No stabilizer code can implement a classical universal gate set transversally [ 743 ]. ⊲ Fold-transversal gates have been ex-tended from qubit CSS codes to qubit stabilizer codes, and there is an algorithm to determine them from the stabilizer group [ 686 ]. 

⊲ Computation can be sped up substantially for codes that admit transversal measurements of logical 𝑋 and 𝑍 [744 ]. ⊲ Diagonal transversal Clifford gates › p. 244 on multiple code blocks must form one of six families of matrix groups: 𝑂 (ℓ, F2) generically, 𝑈 (ℓ, F4)

for Hermitian qubit codes, 𝐺 𝐿 (ℓ, F2) for non-self-dual CSS codes, 

𝑂 (ℓ, F2 [𝑥 ]/( 𝑥 2)) for self-dual non-CSS codes, 𝑈 (ℓ, 𝑅 8) for interme-diate semi-self-dual CSS or self-dual semi-CSS cases, and 𝑆 𝑝 (2ℓ, F2)

for self-dual CSS codes [ 703 ]. There are two ⟦8, 1, 3⟧ self-dual non-CSS codes; see QECDB [ 745 ]. ⊲ An entangling diagonal transversal two-qubit Clifford gate › p. 244 exists only for codes equivalent to CSS or self-dual codes; canonical representatives are the inter-block CNOT in the CSS case and a 𝑌 -controlled-𝑌 gate, locally Clifford equivalent to 𝐶𝑍 , in the self-dual case [ 703 ]. ⊲ Implementing the full Clif-ford group on 𝑘 logical qubits requires 𝑘 -fold transversal gates; in particular, stabilizer codes cannot admit a transversal (1-fold) imple-mentation of the full Clifford group › p. 244 on more than one logical qubit, a fold-transversal (2-fold) implementation on more than two logical qubits, or a code-automorphism implementation on more than one logical qubit [ 746 ]. These bounds are tight: 𝑘 copies of the ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ Steane code form a ⟦7𝑘, 𝑘, 3⟧ code admitting a 𝑘 -fold transversal Clifford group › p. 244 [746].  

> GATES

⊲ Logical Clifford gates › p. 244 can be performed by physi-cal Clifford circuits › p. 244 that permute logical Pauli operators [ 737 ]. 

⊲ With pieceable fault-tolerance, any non-degenerate › p. 304 stabi-lizer code with a complete set of fault-tolerant single-qubit gates in the Clifford group › p. 244 has a universal set of non-transversal fault-tolerant gates [ 770 ]. ⊲ Non-Clifford gates can be done using gate teleportation , in which a gate can be obtained from a particular magic state (a.k.a. resource state) [ 684 , 3126 ]. Such protocols can be made fault tolerant with the help of magic-state distillation [ 658 ] as well as state-injection and purification schemes based on concatenated error-detecting codes [ 428 ]. There exist various performance met-rics for magic-state distillation [ 4078 , 4206 – 4208 ] focusing mostly on distilling 𝑇 gates. This Clifford+T gate set is self-testable [ 4209 ]. Gate errors in magic-state distillation protocols can sometimes add up destructively [ 4042 ]. The Hadamard gate cannot be obtained from a magic state [ 4210 ]. A magic state arising from a general-ized controlled 𝑍 gate is a type of hypergraph state [ 3471 –3473 ] (see [670 , 723 ]). The Toffoli gate can be distilled from a particular two-444 qubit state [ 4211 ]. Magic-state protocol fidelity is upper bounded by the fidelity of protocols that have undergone stabilizer reduction, and there exist non-distillable states outside of the stabilizer octa-hedron [ 4212 , 4213 ]. ⊲ Certain operations can be implemented in a fault-tolerant version [ 4214 –4217 ] of holonomic quantum compu-tation [ 3652 ]. ⊲ Magic-state distillation and circuit compilation based on the SWAP test [4218]. ⊲ Logical Clifford synthesis (LCS) taking in a code and a logical Clifford operation and producing a circuit acting on the physical qubits [ 3235 ]. ⊲ Clifford stabilizer circuits can be compiled using stabilizer tableau manipulation [ 4219 ]. 

⊲ A teleported version of the CPC construction, the Clifford noise reduction (CliNR) scheme, can reduce noise in Clifford circuits › p. 244 

with Pauli measurements with at most a three-fold overhead in the number of qubits and gates [ 3492 , 3493 ]. There is a simple formula for the probability that a Clifford circuit › p. 244 contains a logical error [3489 ]. ⊲ Logical Trotter circuits for any stabilizer code can be implemented via symplectic transvections [ 3273 ]. ⊲ Hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits › p. 244 [3176 ]. ⊲ The Bravyi-Koenig bound › p. 552 can be generalized to arbitrary qubit stabilizer codes [704 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant flag-based non-transversal logical gates [3109].  

> DECODING

⊲ The size of the circuit extracting the syndrome depends on the weight of its corresponding stabilizer generator. Syndrome extraction circuits can be simulated efficiently using dedicated soft-ware (e.g., STIM [ 3860 ]) and there are many general schemes for generating them [ 4220 ] (see also [ 3080 ]). Noise can be characterized without interrupting syndrome extraction [ 4221 ]. Decoding of qubit stabilizer codes is an approximately optimal strategy for various quantum lights-out (QLO) games that can be played on the codes’ encoder-respecting form › p. 442 [819 ]. ⊲ Instead of applying the Pauli recovery from a fault-tolerant syndrome-extraction gadget, one can usually track it classically as a Pauli frame ; Clifford opera-tions update the frame by conjugation, while measurement-based non-Clifford gadgets must be interpreted relative to the current frame [ 381 ]. ⊲ A greedy graph decoder for encoder-respecting forms › p. 442 corrects all recoverable errors for sufficiently sparse graphs, including graphs with girth at least 13 and some lower-girth families with additional spacing constraints [ 819 ]. ⊲ DiVincenzo-Aliferis syndrome extraction circuits [ 3681 ]. ⊲ Greedy syndrome measurement schedule [ 3340 ]. ⊲ Dynamical weight reduction (DWR) scheme in which measurements of smaller-weight Paulis yield the outcome of a larger-weight Pauli via the use of ZX cal-culus and ancillary qubits [ 4222 ]. ⊲ Ancilla modes can be used for syndrome extraction instead of ancilla qubits [ 4223 ], and using two-component cat codes [ 4224 ] yields fault-tolerant syndrome ex-traction circuits. ⊲ Autonomous QEC protocol [ 4225 ]. ⊲ MPE decoding, i.e., the process of finding the most likely error, is 𝑁 𝑃 -complete in the worst case [ 4226 , 4227 ]. If the noise model is such that the most likely error is the lowest-weight error, then ML decod-ing is called minimum-weight decoding. Maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding (a.k.a. degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding), i.e., the process of finding the most likely error class (up to degeneracy of errors), is #𝑃 -complete in the worst case [ 4228 ]. Decoding a random qubit stabilizer code (i.e., the learning stabilizers with noise, or LSN, problem [ 4229 ]) is at least as hard as decoding a random classical code at constant rate [ 4230 ]. ⊲ Incorporating faulty syndrome measurements can be done by performing spacetime decoding, i.e., using data from past rounds for decoding syndromes in any given round. If a decoder does not process syndrome data sufficiently quickly, it can lead to the backlog problem [2878 ], slowing down the computation. ⊲ Splitting decoders [ 4231 ]. ⊲ Trellis decoder, which builds a compact representation of the algebraic structure of the normalizer N(S) [ 4019 ]. ⊲ Quantum extension of GRAND decoder [ 4232 ]. ⊲ Deep neural-network probabilistic decoder [4233 ]. ⊲ Generalized belief propagation (GBP) [ 3809 ] based on a classical version [ 3810 ]. ⊲ Integer optimization decoder [ 2868 ]. 

⊲ Autonomous Lindbladian based decoders for codes encoding a single logical qubit [ 4234 ]. ⊲ For codes encoding a single logical qubit, logical information can be extracted by single-qubit opera-tions and classical communication [ 4235 ]. ⊲ Correlated decoding can improve performance of Clifford and non-Clifford › p. 244 entan-gling gates [ 4236 ]. ⊲ Detector graphs [ 3860 , 4237 ] and detector er-ror models [ 3632 ] can be used to design syndrome extraction circuits and logical measurements. ⊲ Fault-tolerant constant-depth unen-coder transforming logical states into physical states using single-qubit measurements [ 1389 ]. ⊲ Degenerate erasure decoder show-ing near ML decoding for various codes [ 4238 ]. ⊲ Tensor-network decoder for non-Markovian noise [ 4239 ]. ⊲ Delayed-erasure con-version decoder [ 4240 ]. ⊲ Trickle-down dissipative correction [4241].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Shor error correction [ 725 , 3204 ] (see also Steane’s ancilla factory [ 1076 ]), in which fault tolerance against syn-drome extraction errors is ensured by simply repeating syndrome measurements. A modification uses adaptive measurements [ 4242 ]. 

⊲ Gates in the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 can be done using gate tele-portation , in which a gate can be obtained from a particular magic state [ 684 , 3126 ]. Such protocols can be made fault tolerant with the help of magic-state distillation [ 658 ]. See review on magic-state distillation [ 4243 ]. ⊲ Logical Bell measurements can be done transversally, and thus fault tolerantly, by performing bitwise Bell measurements for each pair of qubits (with each member of the pair taken from one of the two code blocks) and processing the result. ⊲ With pieceable fault-tolerance, any non-degenerate

stabilizer code with a complete set of fault-tolerant single-qubit gates in the Clifford group › p. 244 has a universal set of non-transversal fault-tolerant gates [ 770 ]. ⊲ Generalization of Steane error correction for stabilizer codes [ 3373 , Sec. 3.6]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant error correction scheme by Knill (a.k.a. telecorrection [3093 ]), which is based on teleportation [ 428 , 4244 ]. A variant of it has been termed the Fibonacci scheme [ 4245 ]. ⊲ For a non-CSS stabilizer code, the logical Bell-state ancilla needed for Knill error correction can be prepared by treating two code blocks as one larger stabilizer state and verifying the combined stabilizer via the Shor-style preparation procedure [ 381 , Sec. 13.1.3]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant error correction using flag qubits for codes satisfying certain con-ditions [ 3127 ]. ⊲ GHZ state distillation for Steane error correc-tion [ 4246 ]. ⊲ Syndrome extraction using flag qubits and classical codes [ 4247 ]. ⊲ Fault-tolerant constant-depth unencoder trans-forming logical states into physical states using single-qubit mea-surements [ 1389 ]. ⊲ Post-selection based algorithm preparing magic state corresponding to arbitrary rotations [ 4248 ]. ⊲ Code switching › p. 559 can be done using only transversal gates for qubit sta-bilizer codes [ 4249 ]. ⊲ Flag-Proxy Networks (FPNs) [ 3340 ]. ⊲ Alogical Pauli can be gauged out › p. 485 to yield a fault-tolerant measure-ment with worst-case qubit overhead 𝑂 (𝑊 log 2 𝑊 ) for a weight-𝑊

> PARENTS

⊲ Union stabilizer (USt) code › p. 467 — A stabilizer code with stabilizer group S can be thought of as a USt with only the identity coset representative. Conversely, if the set of coset representatives of a USt form a linear binary code, then they can be absorbed into a stabilizer group that defines the USt. 

⊲ XP stabilizer code › p. 468 — XP stabilizer codes reduce to qubit stabilizer codes for 𝑁 = 2. ⊲ Operator-algebra (OA) qubit sta-bilizer code › p. 421 — An OA qubit stabilizer code storing no classi-cal information and admitting no gauge qubits is a qubit stabilizer code. ⊲ Modular-qudit stabilizer code › p. 481 — Modular-qudit stabi-lizer codes for 𝑞 = 2 correspond to qubit stabilizer codes. Modular-qudit stabilizer codes for prime-dimensional qudits 𝑞 = 𝑝 inherit most of the features of qubit stabilizer codes, including encoding an integer number of qudits and a modular-qudit Pauli group › p. 478 with a unique number of generators. Conversely, qubit codes can be ex-tended to modular-qudit codes by decorating appropriate generators with powers. For example, ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ qubit code generators can be adjusted to 𝑍 𝑍 𝑍 𝑍 and 𝑋 𝑋 −1 𝑋 𝑋 −1. A systematic procedure extend-ing a qubit code to prime-qudit codes involves putting its generator matrix into local-dimension-invariant (LDI) form [ 4267 ]. Various bounds exist on the distance of the resulting codes [782, 4268]. 

⊲ True Galois-qudit stabilizer code › p. 504 — True Galois-qudit stabilizer codes for 𝑞 = 2 correspond to qubit stabilizer codes.

⊲ Codeword stabilized (CWS) code › p. 378 — CWS codes whose underlying classical code is a linear binary code are qubit stabilizer codes containing a cluster-state codeword [ 814 , 3172 ]. Con-versely, stabilizer codes admit a CWS standard form [ 814 ]; at the state level, the underlying stabilizer state can be mapped to a cluster state by a single-qubit Clifford circuit › p. 244 [3436][3462, Appx. A]. 

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — Qubit stabilizer codes are the clos-est quantum analogues of binary linear codes because addition mod-ulo two corresponds to multiplication of stabilizers in the quantum case. Any binary linear code can be thought of as a qubit stabilizer code with 𝑍 -type stabilizer generators [ 1386 ][ 1387 , Table I]. The stabilizer generators are extracted from rows of the parity-check matrix, while logical 𝑋 Paulis correspond to rows of the generator matrix. States close to the equal superposition of all bitstrings within Hamming distance 𝑏 of a binary linear code can be prepared effi-ciently [ 1388 ]. Binary linear codes can be used for error-corrected entanglement distillation protocols [1389].

> DESCRIPTION

Extension of the GNU PI codes to those encoding logical qudits into physical qubits. Codewords can be expressed as super-positions of Dicke states › p. 422 with coefficients given by square roots of polynomial coefficients, with the case of binomial coefficients reducing to the GNU PI codes.

RAUSSENDORF-BRAVYI-HARRINGTON (RBH) CLUSTER-STATE CODE [3433, 3434, 4271] rbh  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal (RHG) cluster-state code  

> DESCRIPTION

A three-dimensional cluster-state code defined on the bcc lattice (i.e., a cubic lattice with qubits on edges and faces). The MBQC version of the code is defined as the unique ground state of a certain code Hamiltonian. This state is the resource state used in the first MBQC scheme [ 3433 , 3434 ]. It encodes the temporal gate operations on the surface code into a third spatial dimension. Addition of certain boundary Hamiltonians yields a degener-ate ground-state space that serves as an example of a symmetry-protected self-correcting memory [2969].  

> PROTECTION

Exhibits symmetry-protected self-correction [ 2969 ]. The energy barrier for symmetry-preserving excitations outside of the code space grows linearly with the lattice width. When the system is coupled locally to a thermal bath respecting the symmetry and below a critical temperature, the memory time grows exponentially with the lattice width.  

> GATES

⊲ The computation is encoded in a pre-determined fashion via topological features of the lattice, such as boundaries, defects, or twists. For example, qubits may be encoded in 2D defects along slices of the surface code, and Clifford gates › p. 244 are encoded by spatially braiding the defects along the 3rd dimension. Non-Clifford gates are performed by inserting non-Clifford › p. 244 states into par-ticular singular qubits. To perform the computation, qubits along the extra dimension are measured, e.g., along one two-dimensional slice per time step. This effectively teleports the logical information into the remaining unmeasured portion of the cluster state.  

> DECODING

⊲ MBQC syndrome extraction consists of single-qubit measurements and classical post-processing. The six 

𝑋 -measurements of qubits on the faces of a cube of the bcc lattice multiply to the product of the six cluster-state stabilizers whose vertices are on the faces of the cube. Such measurements, if done on a 2D slice, also yield 𝑍 -type syndromes on the next slice. 

⊲ Minimum weight perfect-matching (MWPM) [ 460 , 3754 ] (based on work by Edmonds on finding a matching in a graph [ 3755 , 3756 ]).  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ For the topological 3D cluster-state scheme of Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal, the reported threshold is 1.4% for lo-cal depolarizing noise and 0.11% per location in a circuit-level model with preparation, gate, storage, and measurement errors [ 3433 ]. 

⊲ Various thresholds for optical quantum computing schemes with RBH codes [ 4272 , 4273 ]. ⊲ 0.75% for preparation, gate, storage, and measurement errors [ 3434 ]. ⊲ 24 .9% under erasure noise [4274 ]. ⊲ Concatenation of the RBH code with small codes such as the ⟦2, 1⟧ repetition code, ⟦4, 1, 1, 2⟧ subsystem code, or Steane code can improve thresholds [3155].  

> NOTES

⊲ Introduction to MBQC protocols with the RBH state [ 3847 ]. 

⊲ Blind quantum computation is possible with the RBH state [ 4275 ].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Cluster-state code › p. 376 ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439

ROTATED SURFACE CODE [406, 1269, 3287, 3328] rotated_surface  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Checkerboard code ⊲ Medial surface code 

⊲ Rectified surface code  

> DESCRIPTION

Variant of the surface code obtained by taking the me-dial graph of the surface code lattice (treated as a graph) and applying a procedure to construct the check operators [ 406 , 407 ][ 408 , Fig. 8]. On a square lattice, this amounts to a rotation by 45 degrees such that qubits are on vertices, and both 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type check operators occupy plaquettes in an alternating checkerboard pattern. Stabilizer generators for this code on a square lattice are shown in Fig. 67 › p. 448 . 

> PROTECTION

The ⟦𝐿 2, 1, 𝐿 ⟧ planar rotated surface code variant [ 406 ]includes the ⟦9, 1, 3⟧ surface-17 › p. 359 code, named as such because 8 ancilla qubits are used for check operator measurements alongside the 9 physical qubits. The ⟦𝐿 2, 2, 𝐿 ⟧ periodic variant is a rotated toric or checkerboard code, whose smallest example is the ⟦4, 2, 2⟧

code. Non-bipartite rotated toric codes with odd distance include the family ⟦𝑡 2 + ( 𝑡 + 1)2, 1, 2𝑡 + 1⟧ [1269, Exam. 4].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Unitary encoder based on code conversion between rotated and regular surface codes [4281]. XXZZXXXZ ZXZZ

RUBY FLOQUET CODE [506, 515] floquet_xyz_ruby  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Floquet color code ⊲ Ruby Floquet color code  

> DESCRIPTION

2D Floquet code whose qubits are placed on vertices of a ruby tiling, with weight-two Pauli check operators on 𝑥 -, 𝑦 -, and 

𝑧 -labeled edges [ 515 ]. The code admits two different measurement schedules, the XYZ ruby schedule and the color-code schedule. One third of the time during the XYZ ruby measurement schedule, its ISG is that of the 6.6.6 color code concatenated with a three-qubit repetition code. Together, all ISGs generate the gauge group of the 3F subsystem code. A different three-round color-code schedule [ 506 ] admits ISGs are FDLQC-equivalent to the 2D color code; in one round, the ISG is ex-actly the color code concatenated with a three-qubit repetition code. The color-code schedule has a Z3 automorphism of the dynamically generated logical operators, while the rewinding schedule 012102 

and another six-round schedule both trivialize that automorphism. A parent stabilizer code for this schedule is FDLQC-equivalent to two copies of the 2D color code [506].  

> RATE

On a torus, the color-code schedule encodes four logical qubits, two of which are dynamically generated relative to the underlying subsystem code [506].  

> GATES

⊲ In the round whose ISG is the 2D color code concatenated with a three-qubit repetition code, the usual transversal logical Clif-ford gates of the color code remain available [506].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Pairs of consecutive ISGs of the color-code sched-ule are locally reversible, and the paper argues that this suggests a non-zero fault-tolerant threshold [506].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Circuit-level noise: ≈ 0.18% using BP-OSD decoder [515].

SELF-DUAL CSS CODE self_dual_css  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Weakly self-dual CSS code ⊲ Symmetric CSS code ⊲ Self-orthogonal CSS code ⊲ Homogeneous CSS code  

> DESCRIPTION

A qubit CSS code for which transversal Hadamard is a logical operation. Equivalently, the stabilizer group is preserved by exchanging 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type Pauli operators. Specializing the CSS construction to the case when 𝐶 𝑍 = [𝑛, 𝑘 ] is dual-containing and 𝐶 𝑋 = 𝐶 𝑍 yields an ⟦𝑛, 2𝑘 − 𝑛 ⟧ self-dual qubit CSS code (a.k.a. weakly self-dual, symmetric [ 752 ], self-orthogonal, or homogeneous [ 4289 ] qubit CSS code). Its 𝑋 -type and 𝑍 -type sta-bilizers are identically supported, and transversal Hadamard pre-serves the stabilizer group. Self-dual CSS codes split into normal and hyperbolic classes depend-ing on whether transversal Hadamard acts as logical Hadamards or as pairwise logical swaps in a suitable logical basis [ 89 , Sec. III]. Hyperbolic codes necessarily encode an even number of logical qubits and have even blocklength and distance [89, Sec. III].  

> MAGIC

Normal and hyperbolic self-dual CSS codes yield magic-state distillation protocols with asymptotically constant space overhead and yield parameter 𝛾 → 1+ [672][89, Thms. 4.1 and 4.2].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Self-dual CSS codes ad-mit a transversal Hadamard gate. There are criteria for when such codes realize logical gates from tensor products of 𝑆 and 𝑆 † gates [748 ]. ⊲ Diagonal transversal Clifford gates › p. 244 on ℓ codeblocks of a CSS code form 𝑆 𝑝 (2ℓ, F2) for self-dual CSS codes [ 703 ]. ⊲ Aself-dual weakly doubly even ⟦𝑛, 1, 𝑑 ⟧ CSS code admits a partitioned transversal physical 𝑆 gate that realizes 𝑆 𝑚 , where 𝑚 = |𝑀 + | − | 𝑀 − |(mod 4); for odd 𝑚 , together with transversal Hadamard and CNOT, this yields the full logical Clifford group transversally [ 696 ][ 724 ,Lemma 4]. 450  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Any self-dual CSS code with bounded-weight stabilizer generators admits flag fault-tolerant syndrome extraction [3127 ]. ⊲ Triorthogonal codes realizing logical 𝑇 gates using only physical 𝑇 gates can be paired up with self-dual CSS codes to yield a transversal CNOT gate and universal fault-tolerant gates using Steane error correction [752].  

> PARENT

⊲ Qubit CSS code › p. 436 — Self-dual CSS codes are qubit CSS codes whose stabilizer group is preserved by transversal Hadamard.

SIX-QUBIT-TENSOR HOLOGRAPHIC CODE [2775] holographic_6_1_3  

> DESCRIPTION

Holographic tensor-network code constructed out of a network of encoding isometries of the ⟦6, 1, 3⟧ six-qubit stabilizer code. The structure of the isometry is similar to that of the heptagon holographic code since both isometries are rank-six tensors, but the isometry in this case is neither a perfect tensor › p. 312 nor a planar-perfect tensor › p. 314 . 

> RATE

SPACETIME CIRCUIT CODE [637, 638, 4292] spacetime_circuit  

> DESCRIPTION

Qubit stabilizer code constructed from a Clifford circuit 

> › p. 244

, i.e., a circuit made up of Clifford gates › p. 244 and Pauli measure-ments, in order to detect and correct circuit faults. The code utilizes redundancy in the measurement outcomes of a circuit to correct circuit faults, which correspond to Pauli errors of the code. The structure of the Clifford circuit › p. 244 yields correlations be-tween the circuit’s possible measurement outcomes. The set of outcomes can be made into a classical binary linear code called the 

outcome code [637 , Corr. 2]. The spacetime circuit code is defined such that its error syndromes can be backpropagated to obtain the parity checks of the outcome code. In other words, both codes have the same set of parity check outcomes. More technically, given an [𝑚, 𝑘 ] outcome code associated with an 𝑛 -qubit circuit of depth Δ with 𝑚 measurements and 2𝑘 outcomes, the corresponding spacetime circuit code is an ⟦𝑛 (Δ + 1), 𝑛 (Δ + 1) − (𝑚 − 𝑘 )⟧ code [637, Thm. 2]. The spacetime circuit code is the stabilizer-code counterpart of earlier subsystem constructions [ 638 , 4292 ], which dealt with re-stricted families of Clifford circuits › p. 244 . A more general construc-tion includes circuits with intermediate and multi-qubit measure-ments [637]. Many features of the spacetime circuit formalism can be under-stood through ZX calculus [ 515 ]. Two circuits are fault-equivalent if all undetectable faults on one circuit have a corresponding fault on the other [4293].  

> DECODING

⊲ A most-likely error decoder for the spacetime code can be converted into a most-likely fault decoder for the underlying circuit [ 637 ]. ⊲ Efficient decoders can be constructed for some circuits, especially when the resulting outcome and spacetime codes are LDPC [637]. 452  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ The outcome-code distance is a lower bound on the circuit-level distance › p. 435 , and the bound need not be tight be-cause some undetectable fault configurations are logically trivial. The circuit-level distance corresponds to the minimum-weight out-come codeword that is not in the kernel of the logical effect matrix [4294].  

> NOTES

⊲ See [ 3639 , Sec. 2] for a brief overview of spacetime circuits.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 — Spacetime circuit codes are useful for constructing fault-tolerant syndrome extraction circuits for qubit QLDPC codes. General spacetime circuit codes can be spar-sified to yield QLDPC spacetime circuit codes [ 637 ]. ⊲ Dynamically generated QECC › p. 302  

> COUSINS

⊲ Linear binary code › p. 193 — The set of measurement out-comes of a Clifford circuit › p. 244 can be made into a classical binary linear code. Error syndromes of the spacetime circuit code can be used to obtain the parity checks of the outcome code. 

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — Stabilizer generators of a space-time code are called detectors in Refs. [ 637 , 3860 ]. ⊲ Subsystem qubit stabilizer code › p. 457 — Spacetime circuit codes can be upgraded to subsystem codes by gauging out › p. 485 a subgroup of the logical Pauli group › p. 433 which causes trivial faults in the corresponding Clif-ford circuit › p. 244 . ⊲ Low-density parity-check (LDPC) code › p. 194 

— There is an equivalence between Clifford circuits › p. 244 and LDPC codes with bit-check symmetry [ 1440 ]. ⊲ Subsystem spacetime circuit code › p. 458 — Spacetime circuit codes can yield subsystem spacetime circuit codes by gauging out › p. 485 a subgroup of the logi-cal Pauli group › p. 433 which causes trivial faults in the corresponding Clifford circuit › p. 244 . This construction is used to show the exis-tence of geometrically local subsystem codes that nearly saturate the subsystem BT bound › p. 553 [638].

SQUARE-LATTICE CLUSTER-STATE CODE [409, 410, 3428]  

> square_lattice_cluster
> DESCRIPTION

A code based on the cluster state on a square lattice that was used in the first proposal for MBQC [ 409 , 410 ]. In the one-way model, the pre-entangled square-lattice cluster is a universal resource, and the computation is carried out entirely by adaptive single-qubit measurements.  

> PROTECTION

Random measurement outcomes induce Pauli byprod-uct operators that are tracked classically and propagated to later measurements or the final readout [ 410 ]. For computations longer than the available lattice extent, the original paper proposed split-ting the computation into consecutive segments and stabilizing each segment using standard error-correction techniques [410].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Initialization of each qubit in the |+⟩ state followed by nearest-neighbor Ising-type entangling evolution, equivalently controlled-phase gates on the edges of the square lattice, prepares the resource state [410].  

> GATES

⊲ Measurements in the 𝑍 basis remove qubits from the lattice to carve out the computation network. 𝑋 -basis measurements prop-agate quantum information along a wire, adaptive equatorial-basis measurements on a five-qubit chain implement arbitrary single-qubit 𝑆𝑈 (2) rotations, and a four-qubit pattern implements CNOT between neighboring wires. Later measurement bases can depend on earlier outcomes because of the tracked Pauli byproducts [ 410 ]. 

⊲ Universal MBQC remains possible on irregular occupied sublat-tices above the percolation threshold because wires and gates can be bent and stretched without changing circuit topology [410].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Encoding on 72 qubits of the Zuchongzhi 3.1 quan-tum processor [4295].  

> NOTES

⊲ The original proposal discussed implementations using neutral atoms in optical lattices with controlled collisions and ca-pacitively coupled quantum dots [410].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Cluster-state code › p. 376 ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 

⊲ 2D lattice stabilizer code › p. 543  

> COUSIN

⊲ Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) code › p. 323 — The square-lattice cluster state, which is the prototypical resource for universal MBQC [ 409 , 410 ], and other 2D cluster states [ 2992 – 2994 ]have SPT order protected by subsystem symmetries [ 2992 , 2995 ,2996]. 

SQUARE-OCTAGON (4.8.8) COLOR CODE [677] 488_color  

> DESCRIPTION

2D color code defined on a patch of the 4.8.8 (square-octagon) tiling, which itself is obtained by applying a fattening pro-cedure to the square lattice [ 411 ]. An equivalent description uses the Tetrakis square tiling (a.k.a. the Union Jack lattice), which is dual to the 4.8.8 lattice [ 412 ]. Among the three semiregular triangular 2D color-code families, the 4.8.8 family uses the fewest physical qubits for a given distance and is the only one of the three with transversal implementations of the full Clifford group [413]. Stabilizer generators are shown in Fig. 68 › p. 453 .Different boundaries affect the logical dimension [4296].

SUBSET-SUM-LINEAR-PROGRAMMING (SS-LP) CODE [501] sslp  

> DESCRIPTION

Qubit block quantum code that encodes a logical qubit and that is constructed using the Subset-Sum-Linear-Programming (SS-LP) numerical construction. SS-LP codes are optimized to admit diagonal gates transversally and include (( 7, 2, 3)) codes that realize the BD 16 and BD 32 groups transversally, yielding 𝑇 and √𝑇 gates, re-spectively. Larger codes include an (( 8, 2, 3)) code that transversally realizes BD 64 .

SUBSYSTEM COLOR CODE [455, 577] subsystem_color  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Gauge color code  

> DESCRIPTION

A subsystem version of the color code. Subsystem color codes form a (𝑑, 𝑒 ) family on punctured 𝐷 -colexes, or equivalently on suitably colored simplicial 𝐷 -balls, en-coding one logical qubit and interpolating between conventional and subsystem color codes via gauge fixing [ 455 ]. Examples include 2D subsystem color codes obtained by expanding the vertices of a two-colex embedded in a surface of genus 𝑔 , where each vertex is split into a triangle and each edge into a pair of edges. The stabilizer group may contain generators of unbounded weight, distinguishing these codes from stabilizer codes with bounded-weight generators for which some logical qubits were re-assigned to be gauge qubits. Gauge fixing between subsystem color codes defined on the same lattice can be implemented using local measurements and classical processing analogous to error correction [455].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ For a 𝐷 -dimensional 

(𝑑, 𝑒 ) gauge color code, 𝐶𝑁𝑂𝑇 is transversal, Hadamard is transver-sal when 𝑑 = 𝑒 , and 𝑅 𝑛 = diag (1, 𝑒 2 𝜋𝑖 /2𝑛 

) is transversal whenever 

𝐷 ≥ 𝑛 (𝐷 − 𝑒 ) [455].  

> DECODING

⊲ Clustering decoder [ 794 ]. ⊲ Erasure decoder [ 3348 ]. 

⊲ Gauge-fixing decoders [3347, 3348].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Subsystem qubit CSS code › p. 456 ⊲ Modular-qudit sub-system color code › p. 482 — Modular-qudit subsystem color codes re-duce to subsystem color codes for 𝑞 = 2. 

> CHILDREN

⊲ 2D subsystem color code › p. 363 ⊲ 3D subsystem color code › p. 365 ⊲ Capped color code (CCC) › p. 373  

> COUSINS

⊲ Color code › p. 379 — Gauge fixing relates subsystem color codes to conventional color codes defined on the same lattice [ 455 ]. 

⊲ EAOA qubit stabilizer code › p. 388 — The 15-qubit subsystem color code yields several EAOA qubit stabilizer constructions, including 

⟦13 , 1, 3; 6 , 2, 3⟧, ⟦15 , 1, 3; 5 , 1, 2⟧, and ⟦15 , 1, 3; 4 , 1, 4⟧ examples ob-tained via clean-qubits and entanglement-assisted gauge-fixing con-structions [ 818 ]. ⊲ Honeycomb Floquet code › p. 403 — Both hon-eycomb and subsystem color codes are generated via periodic se-quences of measurements. However, any measurement sequence can be performed on the color code without destroying the logical qubits, while honeycomb codes can be maintained only with specific sequences. Honeycomb codes require a shorter measurement cycle and use fewer qubits at the given code distance [ 509 ]. ⊲ Majorana subsystem stabilizer code › p. 418 — A particular self-dual stabilizer Hamiltonian within the 3D subsystem color code admits a Majorana variant whose boundaries support 2D Majorana color codes [ 446 ]. 

⊲ Quantum pin code › p. 427 — Quantum pin codes have a subsystem version that can be viewed as a generalization of subsystem color codes [669].

SUBSYSTEM HOMOLOGICAL CODE subsystem_higher_dimensional_surface  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Subsystem generalized surface code  

> DESCRIPTION

A subsystem CSS code that is a subsystem version of the homological code, defined on cellulations of manifolds in arbitrary dimensions. Gauge-group generators are of lower weight than the stabilizers of the corresponding surface code, enabling fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with simpler circuits. The stabilizer group may contain generators of unbounded weight, distinguishing these codes from stabilizer codes with bounded-weight generators for which some logical qubits were re-assigned to be gauge qubits.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Subsystem qubit CSS code › p. 456 ⊲ QLDPC subsystem code › p. 555  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Subsystem surface code › p. 458  

> COUSIN

⊲ Homological code › p. 400 — Subsystem homological codes are subsystem versions of homological codes, with gauge-group generators of lower weight than the corresponding surface-code stabilizers. 455

> subsystem_quantum_parity
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Subsystem generalized Shor code ⊲ Bacon-Casaccino subsystem code  

> DESCRIPTION

A CSS subsystem version of the generalized Shor code that has the same parameters as the subspace version, but requires fewer stabilizer measurements, resulting in a simpler error recovery routine. The code can also be thought of as a subsystem version of an HGP code because two such codes reduce to an HGP code upon gauge fixing [ 636 , Sec. III]. The code can be obtained from a generalized Shor code by removing certain stabilizers that do not affect the code distance. The 𝑋 - and 𝑍 -type gauge generators of this CSS 

⟦𝑛 1𝑛 2, 𝑘 1 𝑘 2, min (𝑑 1, 𝑑 2)⟧ code correspond to rows of the fol-lowing two respective matrices, 

𝐺 𝑋 = 𝐻 1 ⊗ 𝐼 𝑛 2

𝐺 𝑍 = 𝐼 𝑛 1 ⊗ 𝐻 2 , (316) where 𝐻 1,2 are the parity-check matrices of two binary linear codes, 

𝐶 1 = [𝑛 1, 𝑘 1, 𝑑 1] and 𝐶 2 = [𝑛 2, 𝑘 2, 𝑑 2] [636].

SUBSYSTEM HYPERGRAPH PRODUCT SIMPLEX (SHYPS) CODE [749] shyps  

> DESCRIPTION

Family of quantum LDPC codes obtained by combin-ing the subsystem hypergraph product code › p. 455 construction with classical simplex codes › p. 172 . The results are CSS subsystem codes 456 with weight-three gauge generators and code parameters ⟦𝑛 =

(2𝑟 − 1)2, 𝑘 = 𝑟 2, 𝑑 = 2𝑟 −1⟧ for 𝑟 ≥ 3.Due to their symmetric structure, SHYPS codes inherit the large automorphism group of the underlying classical simplex codes. More precisely, | 𝐴𝑢𝑡 (𝑆𝐻𝑌 𝑃𝑆 (𝑟 ))| ≥ | 𝐺 𝐿 (𝑟, F2)| 2, which is expo-nential in the number of logical qubits. This large automorphism group can be leveraged to obtain a depth-one fault-tolerant imple-mentation for a large set of logical Clifford operators. This set of depth-one Clifford generators is sufficiently large to allow for effi-cient compilation, i.e., any 𝑚 -qubit Clifford operator can be exe-cuted in depth of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑚 ). SHYPS codes exhibit practical single-shot features, so only order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑚 ) rounds of syndrome ex-traction are required to fault-tolerantly execute any logical 𝑚 -qubit Clifford circuit › p. 244 . 

> PROTECTION

Memory simulations of the ⟦49 , 9, 4⟧ and ⟦225 , 16 , 8⟧

SHYPS codes under circuit-level noise, using a sliding-window BPLSD decoder, yield pseudo-thresholds of approximately 0.32% 

and 0.35% , respectively [ 749 ]. Depth-126 logical Clifford-circuit › p. 244 

simulations on two blocks of the ⟦49 , 9, 4⟧ SHYPS code were also performed in [749].  

> RATE

The exact encoding rate is 𝑘 /𝑛 = 𝑟 2/( 2𝑟 − 1)2, i.e., asymptoti-cally › p. 161 as Θ(( log 𝑛 )2/𝑛 ) [749].

SUBSYSTEM QUBIT CSS CODE [1691, 2800, 4303] qubit_subsystem_css  

> DESCRIPTION

Subsystem qubit stabilizer code which admits a set of gauge-group generators which consist of either all-𝑍 or all-𝑋 Pauli strings. This ensures that the code’s stabilizer group is also CSS. The gauge-group generators can be expressed as a matrix using the symplectic representation. This matrix is of the form

and an [𝑛, 𝑘 𝑍 , 𝑑 𝑍 ] code 𝐶 𝑍 , respectively. Code parameters can be expressed in terms of only data associated with these two classical codes [ 1691 , 2800 ]. Explicit basis-state constructions are given in Ref. [4304].

SUBSYSTEM QUBIT STABILIZER CODE [ 3286 ] qubit_subsystem_stabilizer  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Gauge qubit stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

A stabilizer code with some of its logical qubits denoted as gauge qubits and not used for storage of logical information. Note that this doesn’t lead to new codes but does lead to new error correc-tion and fault tolerance procedures. Subsystem codes are denoted by 

⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑔, 𝑑 ⟧, similar to stabilizer codes, but with an extra parameter 

𝑔 denoting the number of gauge qubits. Subsystem qubit stabilizer codes are defined by a gauge group 

G, together with a stabilizer subgroup S of the center of G. The table below summarizes the relevant groups and their sizes for a subsystem qubit stabilizer code.

TABLE LXVIII: Groups relevant to subsystem qubit stabilizer codes. The central-izer N(S) is the group formed by all elements of the 𝑛 -qubit Pauli group that commute with all elements in S. The notation N is used because the centralizer of a stabilizer group S is the same as the group’s normalizer, the group formed by all elements of the 𝑛 -qubit Pauli group that conjugate S to itself. This equivalence is no longer the case for non-stabilizer Pauli groups, e.g., the normalizer of the Pauli group is the group itself, while its centralizer is just ⟨𝑖 ⟩. The gauge group and centralizer are defined so as to include 𝑖 and its powers as elements, while the stabilizer group is not. 

To create these codes proceed as follows. Choose 2𝑛 operators 

{ ˜𝑋 𝑗 , ˜𝑍 𝑗 }𝑛 𝑗 =1 from P𝑛 , the Pauli group › p. 433 on 𝑛 qubits, such that they obey the same commutation relations as the regular 𝑛 -qubit Pauli generators {𝑋 𝑗 , 𝑍 𝑗 }𝑛 𝑗 =1 (the subscript on these latter operators indicates the single qubit the Pauli matrix acts on). The tilde oper-ators might act on more than one physical (or bare ) qubit but they behave as if they acted only on a single qubit. WLOG we can choose a stabilizer group as S = ⟨ ˜𝑍 1, . . . , ˜𝑍 𝑠 ⟩. It follows that the normal-izer of S is N(S) = ⟨𝑖, ˜𝑍 1, . . . , ˜𝑍 𝑛 , ˜𝑋 𝑠 +1, . . . , ˜𝑋 𝑛 ⟩. We now choose a gauge group as G = ⟨𝑖, ˜𝑍 1, . . . , ˜𝑍 𝑠 , ˜𝑋 𝑠 +1, ˜𝑍 𝑠 +1, . . . , ˜𝑋 𝑠 +𝑔 , ˜𝑍 𝑠 +𝑔 ⟩

with 𝑠 + 𝑔 ≤ 𝑛 . The logical group is chosen as L = N(S)/ G ≃⟨ ˜𝑋 𝑠 +𝑔 +1, ˜𝑍 𝑠 +𝑔 +1, . . . , ˜𝑋 𝑛 , ˜𝑍 𝑛 ⟩. Now the codespace 𝐶 is as usual the +1

eigenspace of the stabilizer S. But the gauge and logical groups have further decomposed this space into 𝐶 = 𝐴 ⊗ 𝐵 ≃ ( C2)⊗𝑘 ⊗ ( C2)⊗𝑔 .Thus the Hilbert space is partitioned into 3 sets; 𝑘 logical qubits, 𝑔 

gauge qubits, and 𝑠 error-syndrome qubits, with 𝑠 + 𝑔 + 𝑘 = 𝑛 . 

> PROTECTION

Detects errors on 𝑑 − 1 qubits, corrects errors on 

⌊( 𝑑 − 1)/ 2⌋ qubits. There is the following analogue of the Knill-Laflamme conditions  

> › p. 304

for subsystem qubit stabilizer codes. A set of errors {𝐸 𝑎 } is correctable iff 𝐸 𝑎 𝐸 𝑏 ∉ N(S) \ G for all pairs 𝑎, 𝑏 . The distance of the code is the minimal weight of operators in N(S) \ G.Pure › p. 434 ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑔, 𝑑 ⟧ subsystem stabilizer codes codes satisfy 

𝑘 + 𝑔 ≤ 𝑛 − 2𝑑 + 2, and there are no ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 2𝑑 + 2, 𝑔 > 0, 𝑑 ⟧ codes [1691, Cor. 12; Thm. 20]. Entropic conditions have been formulated for random projective measurement noise [3118].  

> ENCODING

⊲ A subsystem codeword can be encoded with the Clif-ford circuits › p. 244 of the stabilizer code corresponding to treating all gauge qubits as logical qubits. One can use the standard-form or the conjugation method [4033, 4306].  

> GATES

⊲ Logical Clifford gates › p. 244 can be implemented fault-tolerantly for subsystem codes of distance at least three [3112].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Logical Clifford gates › p. 244 can be implemented fault-tolerantly for subsystem codes of distance at least three [ 3112 ].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ For correlated Pauli noise, bounds can be obtained by mapping the effect of noise on the code to a statistical mechanical model [4252].

SUBSYSTEM SPACETIME CIRCUIT CODE [638, 4292]  

> subsystem_spacetime_circuit
> DESCRIPTION

Subsystem stabilizer code obtained from a spacetime circuit code by gauging out › p. 485 logical operators that correspond to circuit faults with trivial effect [ 637 , Sec. 5.4]. In the original circuit-to-code construction, each circuit element is replaced by low-weight gauge generators enforcing its input-output relations, yielding sub-system codes from restricted Clifford postselection circuits [638]. An ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code can be mapped into a sparse sub-system code with the same 𝑘 and 𝑑 as follows. One can take the fault-tolerant syndrome extraction circuit associated with the stabi-lizer code, construct its spacetime circuit code, and then gauge out  

> › p. 485

qubits corresponding to trivial faults. The subsystem code can be made geometrically local at the cost of more ancilla qubits [ 638 ].  

> PROTECTION

When derived from a fault-tolerant error-detecting cir-cuit for an ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code, the resulting subsystem space-time circuit code has parameters ⟦𝑂 (| 𝑉 |) , 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧, so the base-code distance is preserved [638].  

> RATE

The spacetime circuit code construction is used to show the existence of spatially local subsystem codes that nearly saturate the subsystem BT bound › p. 553 [638].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant measurement gadget that is a mod-ification based on the DiVincenzo-Shor cat-state method [ 725 , 3204 ]. 

⊲ The original construction uses |+⟩ -state vertex qubits together with expander-graph parity checks to obtain 𝑂 (𝑤 )-size postselec-tion gadgets for measuring weight-𝑤 stabilizers, with gates acting on at most ten wires [638].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Subsystem qubit stabilizer code › p. 457 ⊲ QLDPC subsys-tem code › p. 555  

> COUSIN

⊲ Spacetime circuit code › p. 451 — Spacetime circuit codes can yield subsystem spacetime circuit codes by gauging out › p. 485 asubgroup of the logical Pauli group › p. 433 which causes trivial faults in the corresponding Clifford circuit › p. 244 . This construction is used to show the existence of geometrically local subsystem codes that nearly saturate the subsystem BT bound › p. 553 [638].

SUPER-COMPACT FERMION-TO-QUBIT CODE [387] super_compact  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Super-compact encoding  

> DESCRIPTION

A 2D fermion-into-qubit encoding on the square lattice obtained from exact 2D bosonization by a finite-depth generalized local unitary Clifford circuit, followed by re-pairing of Majorana modes and a slight lattice deformation. The code uses 1.25 qubits per fermion, improving on the square-lattice compact encoding with ratio 𝑟 = 1.5. Its fermion-parity, hopping, and stabilizer operators have weights 1-2, 2-6, and 12 , respectively [387, Table I].  

> PARENT

compact/DK construction to a qubit-to-fermion ratio of 1.25 [387].

TENSOR-PRODUCT HDX CODE [4313] iterated_ramanujan  

> DESCRIPTION

A code constructed in a similar way as the HDX code, but utilizing iterated homological products of multiple Ramanujan complexes and then applying distance balancing. For any fixed tensor-power parameter 𝑐 , these yield explicit QLDPC codes with distance scaling as √𝑛 log 𝑐 𝑛 , improving on the original HDX con-struction by replacing a single logarithmic enhancement with arbi-trarily high fixed polylogarithmic enhancement. The utility of such tensor products comes from the fact that one of the Ramanujan com-plexes is a collective cosystolic expander as opposed to just a cosystolic expander.  

> PROTECTION

Construction yields explicit QLDPC codes with distance 

√𝑛 log 𝑐 𝑛 for any fixed 𝑐 , using the 𝑐 -fold tensor product of Ramanu-jan complexes followed by distance balancing [4313].  

> PARENT

> CHILD

TETRON CODE [384, 510, 1385, 4316] tetron  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Kitaev-Wen Majorana mapping ⊲ Kitaev hon-eycomb mapping ⊲ Bravyi-Leemhuis-Terhal (BLT) Majorana map-ping ⊲ Majorana representation ⊲ Parton construction  

> DESCRIPTION

A ⟦2, 1, 2⟧ 𝑓 Majorana box qubit encoding a logical qubit into four Majorana modes, equivalently into the fixed-total-parity sector of two physical fermionic modes. Four Majorana zero modes are the smallest aggregate that supports a qubit in a fixed fermion-parity sector [ 384 ]. This code can be concatenated with various qubit codes such as surface codes and color codes. Four-boundary Majo-rana surface-code patches are logical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance analogues of this physical tetron block [385]. Embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code is useful for exactly solving the Kitaev honeycomb model Hamiltonian [510] and other qubit Hamiltonians on certain graphs [2759 , 2760 ]. It has been used throughout condensed matter physics under the name of the Majorana representation [ 4317 , 4318 ] or par-ton construction [ 4319 ], allowing for a mean-field treatment of many models that are otherwise not amenable. Majorana stabilizer groups can be converted into ordinary qubit stabilizer groups via the parton mapping, while their corresponding states are converted via the Gutzwiller projection [2761].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Majorana box qubit › p. 416 — The Majorana box qubit for 

𝑛 = 2 is the tetron code. ⊲ Quantum repetition code › p. 429 — The tetron code is a special case of the quantum repetition code with 

𝑛 = 2. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Hamiltonian-based code › p. 306 — Embedding each physi-cal qubit into two fermions via the tetron code is useful for exactly solving the Kitaev honeycomb model Hamiltonian [ 510 ] and other qubit Hamiltonians on certain graphs [ 2759 , 2760 ]. Majorana stabi-lizer groups can be converted into ordinary qubit stabilizer groups via the parton mapping, while their corresponding states are con-verted via the Gutzwiller projection [ 2761 ]. ⊲ Majorana surface code › p. 418 — Four-boundary Majorana surface-code patches are log-ical tetrons, i.e., higher-distance versions of the tetron code [ 385 ]. 

⊲ Qubit stabilizer code › p. 441 — Any ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ stabilizer code can be mapped into a ⟦2𝑛, 𝑘, 2𝑑 ⟧ 𝑓 Majorana stabilizer code by concate-nating with the tetron code [ 510 ][ 1385 , Lemma 1]. Embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code is useful for exactly solving the Kitaev honeycomb model Hamiltonian [ 510 ] and other qubit Hamiltonians on certain graphs [ 2759 , 2760 ]. Majorana stabilizer groups can be converted into ordinary qubit stabilizer groups via the parton mapping, while their corresponding states are converted via the Gutzwiller projection [2761]. 

⊲ Majorana subsystem stabilizer code › p. 418 — The B ↦ →F map-ping yields Majorana subsystem codes from qubit stabilizer codes such that their gauge groups contain tetrons [ 3882 ][ 3883 , Sec. IV]. The output Majorana subsystem codes can correct odd-weight er-rors. ⊲ Non-Abelian Kitaev honeycomb code › p. 419 — Embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code allows the logical subspace of the Kitaev honeycomb model to be formulated as a joint eigenspace of certain Majorana operators [ 3316 , Sec. 4.1], which admit braiding-based gates due to their non-Abelian statis-tics and which can be used for topological quantum computation. When done in reverse, this embedding can be thought of as a 2D bosonization fermion-into-qubit encoding by converting to a rela-beled square lattice and performing single-qubit rotations [ 386 ][ 387 ,Sec. IV.B]. 

⊲ Self-dual CSS code › p. 449 — Any ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧ qubit stabilizer code maps to a ⟦4𝑛, 2𝑘, 2𝑑 ⟧ self-dual CSS code by applying the BLT map-ping and concatenating each qubit pair with the ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ code [ 759 ,Corr. 2][ 1385 , Corr. 1]. The BLT mapping proceeds by first concate-nating each qubit with the tetron code › p. 460 to obtain an interme-diate ⟦2𝑛, 𝑘, 2𝑑 ⟧ 𝑓 Majorana stabilizer code. ⊲ Toric code › p. 461 —Coherent physical errors in the toric code are expected to become incoherent logical errors under syndrome measurement; see corrob-orating numerical studies performed by embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code [ 4320 ] as well as deriving analytical bounds [ 4321 ]. ⊲ Kitaev honeycomb code › p. 409 — Em-bedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code is useful for exactly solving the Kitaev honeycomb model Hamiltonian [510] and other qubit Hamiltonians on certain graphs [2759, 2760]. 

THREE-FERMION (3F) SUBSYSTEM CODE [395, 575]  

> subsystem_three_fermion
> DESCRIPTION

2D subsystem stabilizer code whose low-energy excita-tions realize the three-fermion anyon theory [ 574 –576 ]. One version uses two qubits at each site [ 395 ], while other manifestations utilize a single qubit per site and only weight-two (two-body) interactions [ 575 , 577 ]. All are expected to be equivalent to each other via a local constant-depth Clifford circuit › p. 244 .461  

> PARENTS

⊲ Subsystem qubit stabilizer code › p. 457 ⊲ Lattice subsys-tem code › p. 552 ⊲ Abelian topological code › p. 292 — The 3F code is a 2D subsystem code characterized by 3F topological order [ 395 ], which is chiral and modular.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Kitaev surface code › p. 410 — One version of the 3F sub-system code can be obtained from two copies of the square-lattice surface code by gauging out › p. 485 the anyons 𝑒 1𝑚 1𝑒 2 and 𝑒 2𝑚 2 [395 ,Sec. 7.4]. ⊲ Three-fermion (3F) Walker-Wang model code › p. 461 —The (three-dimensional) 3F Walker-Wang model cluster-like state encodes the temporal gate operations on the (two-dimensional) 3F subsystem code into a third spatial dimension [ 458 ]. ⊲ 2D color code › p. 362 — The 2D color code is equivalent to two decoupled copies of the 3F code in the sense that the same anyon theory describes the low-energy excitations of both codes [ 3334 ][ 425 , Appx. B]. ⊲ Ruby Floquet code › p. 449 — Together, all ISGs of the ruby Floquet code generate the gauge group of the 3F subsystem code. 

THREE-FERMION (3F) WALKER-WANG MODEL CODE [457, 458]  

> three_fermion
> DESCRIPTION

A 3D lattice stabilizer code whose bulk realizes a 3D time-reversal SPT order [ 457 ] and whose gapped boundary supports the 2D three-fermion (3F) topological order. The code can be used as a resource state for fault-tolerant MBQC [458].  

> ENCODING

⊲ 3F QCA encoder [ 2978 , 2979 ], which can be simplified using bosonization [ 3353 ] and can be extended to SPTs in higher dimensions based on an exact bosonization duality [2975].  

> GATES

TORIC CODE [404, 2065, 3704] toric  

> DESCRIPTION

Version of the Kitaev surface code on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions, encoding two logical qubits. Being the first manifestation of the surface code, "toric code" is of-ten an alternative name for the general construction. Twisted toric code [ 415 , Fig. 8] refers to the construction on a torus with twisted (a.k.a. shifted) boundary conditions. In the original Hamiltonian construction, open Pauli-𝑍 and Pauli-𝑋 strings create pairs of elec-tric charges and magnetic vortices, and braiding one type around the other yields the nontrivial Abelian anyonic phase [404]. The stabilizers of the toric code are generated by star operators 

𝐴 𝑣 and plaquette operators 𝐵 𝑝 . Each star operator is a product of four Pauli-𝑋 operators on the edges adjacent to a vertex 𝑣 of the lattice; each plaquette operator is a product of four Pauli-𝑍 operators applied to the edges adjacent to a face, or plaquette, 𝑝 of the lattice (Fig. 69 › p. 461 ). We denote by 𝑋 𝑖 , 𝑍 𝑖 the logical Pauli-𝑋 and Pauli-𝑍 operator of the 𝑖 -th logical qubit (with 𝑖 ∈ { 1, 2}). They are represented by strings of Pauli-𝑋 operators or Pauli-𝑍 operators that wrap around the torus, as shown in Fig. 69 › p. 461 . 

> PROTECTION

Toric code on an 𝐿 × 𝐿 torus is a ⟦2𝐿 2, 2, 𝐿 ⟧ CSS code. The number of error patterns can be used to bound the ground-state energy of a ±𝐽 Ising model [ 4324 ]. Coherent physical errors in the toric code are expected to become incoherent logical errors under syndrome measurement; see corroborating numerical studies performed by embedding each physical qubit into two fermions via the tetron code [ 4320 ] as well as deriving analytical bounds [ 4321 ]. More generally, there is a tensor-network routine that calculates the effective logical channel [4325]  

> ENCODING

⊲ Lindbladian-based dissipative encoding for the toric code [ 4201 ] that does not give a speedup relative to circuit-based 462 encoders [4202].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Transversal logical Pauli gates correspond to Pauli strings on non-trivial loops of the torus.  

> GATES

⊲ Logical 𝐶 𝑋 gate for the ⟦12 , 2, 3⟧ twisted toric code [ 3176 ].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

The model for the case of the toric code has been thoroughly investigated [ 4330 , 4331 ]. The Bravyi-Suchara-Vargo (BSV) tensor network decoder [ 3760 ] exactly solves the ML decoding problem under independent 𝑋, 𝑍 noise for the surface code and has complexity of order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝑛 2); the decoder provides an efficient tensor-network contraction for the partition function resulting from the statistical mechanical map-ping, which is known to be solvable for an Ising model on a planar graph [ 3761 ]. TRANSVERSE-FIELD ISING MODEL (TFIM) CODE [4347] tfim  

> DESCRIPTION

A 1D translationally invariant stabilizer code whose encoding is a constant-depth circuit of nearest-neighbor gates on alternating even and odd bonds that consist of transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian interactions. The code allows for perfect state transfer of arbitrary distance using local operations and classical communi-cations (LOCC).  

> PROTECTION

Code distance is 1 for open boundary conditions similar to a repetition code, and 3 for periodic boundary conditions with an encoding circuit depth of 4.  

> ENCODING

⊲ 1D geometrically local constant-depth brickwork cir-cuit of nearest-neighbor gates on alternating even and odd bonds. Gates are generated by interaction terms of the transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Small-distance qubit stabilizer code › p. 451 ⊲ Qubit QLDPC code › p. 439 ⊲ 1D lattice stabilizer code › p. 542 463  

> COUSINS

⊲ Majorana stabilizer code › p. 417 — The TFIM code stabiliz-ers can be expressed in terms of Majorana operators. ⊲ Quantum repetition code › p. 429 — When written in the computational basis, the phase-flip and TFIM codewords are superpositions of qubit states of fixed total parity. The superposition is equal for the phase-flip code, whereas some states appear with a −1 coefficient for the TFIM code. However, the TFIM code can be encoded in constant depth. 

TRAPEZOID SUBSYSTEM CODE [3152, 3238] trapezoid  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of a family of BBS codes with weight-two (two-body) gauge generators designed to suppress errors in adiabatic quantum computation. The family consists of odd-𝑚 codes with 𝑚 = 2𝑘 + 1 and parame-ters ⟦4𝑘 + 2𝑙, 2𝑘, 2𝑘 + 2𝑙 − 2, 2⟧, together with even-𝑚 codes with 

𝑚 = 2𝑘 and parameters ⟦4𝑘 + 2𝑙 − 2, 2𝑘 − 1, 2𝑘 + 2𝑙 − 3, 2⟧, where 

1 ≤ 𝑙 ≤ 𝑘 [3152].  

> PROTECTION

These are distance-two subsystem codes, so they detect arbitrary single-qubit errors. In the energy-penalty setting of Hamil-tonian quantum computation, the 𝑙 = 1 subfamily maximizes the code rate and has the largest penalty gap within the trapezoid family [3152].  

> GATES

⊲ Single-qubit dressed logical operators are two-local, and products of two dressed logical operators of the same Pauli type can also be implemented using two-local physical interactions up to gauge operators [3152, 3238].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bravyi-Bacon-Shor (BBS) code › p. 372 ⊲ Lattice subsys-tem code › p. 552  

> CHILD

⊲ ⟦6, 2, 3, 2⟧ BBS code › p. 351 — The even-logical-qubit trape-zoid family at 𝑙 = 𝑘 = 1 reduces to the ⟦6, 2, 3, 2⟧ BBS code.  

> COUSINS

⊲ ⟦2𝑚, 2𝑚 − 2, 2⟧ error-detecting code › p. 342 — The trape-zoid code family can be obtained from the ⟦2𝑚, 2𝑚 − 2, 2⟧ error-detecting code by using some logical qubits as gauge qubits and imposing a two-dimensional qubit geometry [ 3152 ]. ⊲ ⟦6𝑟, 2𝑟, 2⟧

TRIANGULAR SURFACE CODE [414] triangle_surface  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Triangle surface code  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of a twist-defect surface code family with a single central twist whose planar layout fits within a triangle. Tri-angle codes can be viewed as three conjoined surface-code patches projected into two dimensions, with weight-four plaquette stabi-lizers and weight-two edge stabilizers [ 414 ]. Symmetric distance-𝑑 

triangle codes use 3𝑑 2/4 + 1/4 data qubits, i.e., about 25% fewer than the rotated surface code for a given odd distance. Logical 𝑋 , 𝑌 ,and 𝑍 operators can be supported on the three sides of the triangle, enabling initialization and measurement in any Pauli basis. The size of the triangular patches and which patch encodes data versus acts as ancillas for gates depends on the initialization and measurement procedures. See Ref. [414] for tables and figures.  

> RATE

Symmetric distance-𝑑 triangle codes use 3𝑑 2/4+1/4 data qubits per logical qubit. Including ancillas needed for planar Clifford computation, the CC, BC, and CS architectures use 3𝑑 2 + 𝑂 (𝑑 ),

9𝑑 2/4 + 𝑂 (𝑑 ), and 6𝑑 2/4 + 𝑂 (𝑑 ) physical qubits per logical qubit, respectively [414, Table 2].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Code conversion (CC) initialization and measurement method, in which the surface code is used to hold data between gates in patches. ⊲ Basis-state conversion (BC) initialization and measurement method in which one initializes and then measures a logical Pauli eigenstate. To do this, triangle ancilla qubits are required outside of the triangle patches that hold the data. That is, the ancilla patches must be empty of data and be adjacent to the side that contains the logical Pauli that needs to be measured or initialized. ⊲ The CAT states (CS) initialization and measurement method uses a row of 𝑑 ancilla qubits along some edge of a triangle code with distance 𝑑 to create and verify a GHZ state that is used to measure the logical operator along the same edge. Creating this GHZ state takes 𝑂 (𝑑 ) time steps. To reliably measure the logical state, the GHZ state must be measured 𝑂 (𝑑 ) times, resulting in 𝑂 (𝑑 2)

time for logical measurement. Initialization is a similar procedure that requires 𝑂 (𝑑 2) time for logical-operator measurements that occur 𝑂 (𝑑 ) times as well as 𝑂 (𝑑 2) time to project the code onto a logical state [414].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Triangle codes admit transversal order-three single-qubit gates in the Clifford group › p. 244 ,e.g., ¯𝑆𝐻 [414].  

> GATES

⊲ Triangle codes admit a distillation-free implementation of the full Clifford group using lattice surgery, 1-bit teleportation, and patch reorientation [ 414 ]. ⊲ Performing single-qubit gates in the Clifford group › p. 244 using the CC procedure requires surface code patches to be embedded in triangle patches. This procedure requires 𝑂 (𝑑 ) Clifford gate times for 𝐻, 𝑆, 𝐶𝑁𝑂𝑇 [414 ]. ⊲ The BC procedure requires 𝑂 (1) time to perform 𝐻, 𝑆 gates and 𝑂 (𝑑 )

time to perform 𝐶𝑁𝑂𝑇 . Sometimes reorientation of the sides is required, and that takes 𝑂 (𝑑 ) to perform [414].  

> DECODING

⊲ The decoding uses a single decoding graph since the triangle code is not a CSS code. Nodes of the graph are located at each stabilizer (center of the triangle graph) and have red or blue edges, where red associates with 𝑋 errors and blue with 𝑍 errors. To take into account any errors from measuring the error syndrome, a three-dimensional stack of decoding graphs is laid on top of the code with vertical edges connecting qubits between layers [414].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ The symmetry of triangle codes allows for fault-tolerant measurement and encoding in any Pauli basis [ 414 ]. ⊲ Anon-fault-tolerant circuit initializes the triangle code. To guarantee fault-tolerance, post-selection is performed on trivial measurements of the syndrome and of the logical Pauli, depending on the basis of the logical states [ 414 ]. ⊲ Making syndrome extraction fault 464 tolerant requires a specific ordering of syndrome measurements so as to avoid hook errors › p. 435 [414].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ 10% under either bit-flip or bit-phase noise for ideal syndrome measurements. The decoder used is a decoding graph with the same weight assigned to each edge, and Dijkstra’s algorithm is used to compute the total weight of any path [414].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ 3.2% bit-flip error-correction threshold for noisy syn-drome measurements and 2.6% for bit-phase flip noise. The decoder used is a decoding graph as described above [ 414 ]. ⊲ In general, the triangular surface code has a threshold of similar magnitude to the toric code for uncorrelated 𝑋 and 𝑍 errors. For correlated errors, the triangle code has a lower threshold by a factor of about 

36 [414].  

> PARENT

⊲ Stellated surface code › p. 453 — The triangular surface code is the 𝑠 = 3 member of the stellated surface-code family [ 425 , Appx. D].  

> CHILD

⊲ ⟦7, 1, 3⟧ twist-defect surface code › p. 355  

> COUSINS

⊲ Tensor-network code › p. 324 — Triangle surface codes can be reproduced by inserting a defect tensor and Hadamard-modified tensors into the surface-code tensor network [ 2785 ]. ⊲ Stellated color code › p. 453 — Stellated color codes are color-code analogues of triangle surface codes in that both encode logical information in lattices with a single twist defect. Instances of the former can be obtained by fattening [411] the vertices of the latter [425]. 

TRIORTHOGONAL CODE [659, Secs. III-IV] quantum_triorthogonal  

> DESCRIPTION

Qubit CSS code whose 𝑋 -type logicals and stabilizer generators form a triorthogonal matrix (defined below) in the sym-plectic representation › p. 442 .An 𝑚 × 𝑛 binary matrix is triorthogonal if its rows 𝑟 1, . . . , 𝑟 𝑚 

satisfy |𝑟 𝑖 · 𝑟 𝑗 | = 0 and |𝑟 𝑖 · 𝑟 𝑗 · 𝑟 𝑘 | = 0 modulo 2, with binary addition and multiplication. The triorthogonal CSS code associated with the matrix is constructed by mapping nonzero entries in even-weight rows to 𝑋 -type stabilizer generators, odd-weight rows to 𝑋 -type logical operators, and 𝑍 operators for each row in the orthogonal complement. Generalized versions of triorthogonality allow odd pair and triple overlaps inside the logical-row block 𝐾 while keeping every overlap involving an 𝑆 -row even, which yields quasitransversal logical gates beyond a single logical 𝑇 gate [718, Appx. D][720, Sec. 2.3].  

> PROTECTION

Weight 𝑡 Pauli errors, where 𝑡 depends on the family. For example, Ref. [ 659 , Sec. VII] provides a family of distance 2

codes.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Encoder for magic states for the code constructed in [659].  

> TRANSVERSAL AND PERMUTATION-BASED GATES

⊲ Transversal action of 𝑇 

gates on all qubits, followed by a particular pattern of 𝐶𝑍 and 𝑆 gates, will realize a logical 𝑇 gate [ 659 , Lemma 2][ 724 , Rem. 3]. When an ad-ditional condition on logical-𝑋 operators is satisfied, the 𝐶𝑍 and 𝑆 

gates are no longer necessary [ 689 , Thm. 14]. ⊲ Triorthogonality is necessary but not sufficient for physical transversal 𝑇 gates on each qubit to realize the identity logical gate [ 689 , Thm. 12]. ⊲ Certain codes realize controlled-controlled-𝑍 gates [ 751 ], realized via phys-ical 𝐶𝐶𝑍 gates on three code blocks. ⊲ Triorthogonal codes re-alizing logical 𝑇 gates using only physical 𝑇 gates can be paired up with self-dual CSS codes to yield a transversal CNOT gate [752].  

> DECODING

⊲ Steane error correction [752].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Universal fault-tolerant gates can be performed without magic-state distillation [ 751 , 3112 ]. ⊲ Universal fault-tolerant gates can be achieved by pairing with a self-dual CSS code and using Steane error correction [752].  

> NOTES

⊲ Reference [ 3115 ] presents a classification of triorthogonal codes up to 𝑛 + 𝑘 ≤ 38 by associating each triorthogonal code with a RM code polynomial. ⊲ A database of triorthogonal codes is available in QECDB [745].  

> PARENTS

⊲ 𝑘 -orthogonal code › p. 361 — 𝑘 -orthogonal codes reduce to triorthogonal codes for 𝑘 = 3. ⊲ Prime-qudit triorthogonal code › p. 484 — Prime-qudit triorthogonal codes reduce to triorthogo-nal codes when 𝑝 = 2.

> › p. 343

> COUSINS

⊲ Quantum Reed-Muller (RM) code › p. 428 — Classification of triorthogonal codes yields a connection to RM code polynomials [3115 ]. ⊲ Self-dual linear code › p. 239 — Self-dual binary codes can be used to construct triorthogonal codes [ 1983 ]. ⊲ CSS-T code  

> › p. 383

— Triorthogonal and CSS-T codes overlap, but neither is a sub-set of the other [ 724 ]. CSS-T codes reduce to triorthogonal codes when the logical action of the physical transversal 𝑇 gate is a logi-cal 𝑇 gate on all encoded qubits. Triorthogonality is necessary for physical transversal 𝑇 gates on each qubit to realize the identity logical gate [ 689 , Thm. 12]. The 𝑋 -type stabilizer generator matrix for a CSS-T code is always triorthogonal [ 1268 , Corr. 5]. ⊲ Binary dihedral PI code › p. 370 — There exist binary dihedral PI codes that have distance 5 (7, 9, 11, 13) and encode in 27 (49, 73, 107, 147) qubits, all realizing transversal 𝑇 gates. ⊲ ⟦5, 1, 3⟧ Five-qubit perfect code › p. 348 — A fault-tolerant logical 𝑇 gate can be obtained by en-coding the five-qubit code’s five physical qubits into the five logical qubits of a ⟦31 , 5, 3⟧ outer quantum divisible CSS code preserved by transversal 𝑇 †; this layered construction can be viewed as a fac-torization of a ⟦31 , 1, 3⟧ triorthogonal code and does not require magic-state distillation [ 730 ]. ⊲ ⟦6𝑘 + 2, 3𝑘, 2⟧ Campbell-Howard code › p. 352 — Campbell-Howard codes arise from the generalized-triorthogonal/quasitransversal 𝐺 -matrix framework, which extends Bravyi-Haah triorthogonal matrices by allowing odd pair and triple overlaps entirely within the logical-row block 𝐾 [ 718 , Appx. D].

triorthogonal code family satisfying the necessary conditions for the magic-state yield parameter 𝛾 to become arbitrarily small [ 671 ]. 

⊲ ⟦23 , 1, 7⟧ Quantum Golay code › p. 341 — A ⟦95 , 1, 7⟧ triorthogonal code with a transversal 𝑇 gate can be obtained from the qubit Go-lay code via the doubling transformation [ 3137 ]. ⊲ Self-dual CSS code › p. 449 — Triorthogonal codes realizing logical 𝑇 gates using only physical 𝑇 gates can be paired up with self-dual CSS codes to yield a transversal CNOT gate and universal fault-tolerant gates using Steane error correction [ 752 ]. ⊲ Quantum quadratic-residue (QR) code › p. 502 — Qubit quantum QR codes are doubly even and admit transversal implementations of the single-qubit Clifford group › p. 244

TWIST-DEFECT COLOR CODE [422, 679, 4353] twist_defect_color  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Color code with a twist  

> DESCRIPTION

A non-CSS extension of the 2D color code whose non-CSS stabilizer generators are associated with twist defects of the associated lattice. These twists terminate domain walls that permute color labels, Pauli labels, or interchange the two. For lattices with dislocations and rotational disclinations, twist-defect stabilizer generators are placed at the location of the dis-locations. Logical dimension is determined by the genus of the underlying surface (for closed surfaces), types of boundaries (for open surfaces), and any twist defects present.  

> PROTECTION

Code properties depend on the number and size of the twist defects. There are 72 types of twist defects in the 2D color code, organized by the 𝑆 3 ≀ Z2 symmetry of the anyons [425].  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford gates › p. 244 can be implemented via twist-based lattice surgery [3730] or braiding twist defects [4354]. 

⊲ Domino twists [4355].

𝑧 -type Pauli boundaries, which make the code non-CSS [ 425 , Fig. 7].

TWIST-DEFECT SURFACE CODE [ 408 , 414 , 416 , 422 , 425 , 3068 ,4356][510, Sec. 12, pt. 2] twist_defect_surface  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Surface code with a twist ⊲ Genon surface code  

> DESCRIPTION

A non-CSS extension of the 2D surface-code construc-tion whose non-CSS stabilizer generators are associated with twist defects of the associated lattice. A related construction [ 416 ] doubles the number of qubits in the lattice via symplectic doubling › p. 485 .For lattices with dislocations and rotational disclinations, twist-defect stabilizer generators are placed at the location of the disloca-tions to yield a stabilizer code whose logical dimension depends on the defects. Logical dimension is determined by the genus of the underlying surface (for closed surfaces), types of boundaries (for open surfaces), and any twist defects present. A simple example is a surface code on a lattice with a single lattice dislocation which hosts a weight-five non-CSS twist-defect stabilizer generator [ 422 , Fig. 2]. More generally, given a graph embedded in a 2D manifold, qubits are placed on vertices, stabilizers on faces, and twist defects are associated to odd-degree vertices.  

> PROTECTION

Code properties depend on the number and size of the twist defects. 466  

> RATE

Twist-defect surface codes have negative curvature around their defects, and thus circumvent the BPT bound › p. 551 for codes on Euclidean lattices.  

> GATES

⊲ Clifford gates › p. 244 can be implemented via twist-based lattice surgery [ 4357 ] or braiding twist defects [ 422 , 2448 –2452 , 4358 ]. 

⊲ State injection protocols yield arbitrary logical rotations [ 4356 ]. ⊲ Symplectic doubles of codes yield fault-tolerant Clifford gates › p. 244 performed via Dehn twists [416].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant measurement of defects [ 4356 ]. 

⊲ Twisted double covers of codes yield fault-tolerant Clifford gates  

> › p. 244

performed via Dehn twists [416].

⟦8, 2, 2⟧ and ⟦10 , 2, 3⟧ double covers, were realized on a trapped-ion device by Quantinuum [416].
