QUANTUM TAMO-BARG (QTB) CODE [775] quantum_tamo_barg  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of a family of Galois-qudit CSS codes whose underlying classical codes consist of Tamo-Barg codes together with specific low-weight codewords. Folded versions of QTB codes, or 

FQTB codes , defined on qudits whose dimension depends on 𝑛 , yield explicit examples of QLRCs of arbitrary locality 𝑟 [775, Cor. 64].  

> PROTECTION

A family of QTBs can be defined for every prime 𝑟 , rate 

𝑅 ∈ ( 0, 1), and qudit dimension 𝑞 = 𝑛 + 1 such that their relative distance is 𝛿 ≥ 1 −√︁ (1 + 𝑅 )/ 2 − 𝑂 (1/𝑟 ) [775, Thm. 62]. 

Folding these codes by combining qudits into larger qudits yields FQTB codes with relative distance 𝛿 ≥ ( 1 − 𝑅 )/ 2 − 𝑂 (1/√𝑟 ) [775 ,Cor. 64] and qudit dimension 𝑞 = 𝑛 𝑂 (𝑟 2 ) . This relative distance is of order › p. 161 𝑂 (1/√𝑟 ) below the Singleton-like QLRC bound.  

> DECODING

⊲ Polynomially efficient decoder for QTB codes against errors acting on a number of subsystems that can go up to half of the distance bound proved for the family [ 775 , Thm. 69]. The decoder is based on decoding RS codes, and its runtime is independent of the locality 𝑟 . ⊲ Polynomially efficient decoder for FQTB codes against errors acting on a number of subsystems that can go up to half of the distance bound proved for the family [ 775 , Cor. 72]. The runtime depends on the locality 𝑟 . 

> PARENTS

⊲ Galois-qudit CSS code › p. 493 ⊲ Quantum locally recov-erable code (QLRC) › p. 316 — Folded quantum Tamo-Barg codes yield explicit QLRCs of arbitrary prime locality 𝑟 , rate at least 𝑅 , relative distance 𝛿 ≥ ( 1 − 𝑅 )/ 2 − 𝑂 (1/√𝑟 ), and qudit dimension 𝑞 = 𝑛 𝑂 (𝑟 2 )

[775, Cor. 64].  

> COUSIN

⊲ Tamo-Barg code › p. 240 — QTB codes are CSS codes con-structed from Tamo-Barg codes.

SINGLETON-BOUND APPROACHING AQECC [472] quantum_singleton  

> DESCRIPTION

A member of an approximate quantum code family of rate 𝑅 that can tolerate adversarial errors nearly saturating the quantum Singleton bound of (1 − 𝑅 )/ 2. The formulation of such codes relies on a notion of quantum list decoding [472, 777]. One construction first builds constant-alphabet quantum list-decodable CSS codes from folded quantum Reed-Solomon outer codes, random CSS inner codes, and quantum Alon-Edmonds-Luby distance amplification/alphabet reduction, and then compiles them  

> 73 https://web.archive.org/web/19991106022224/http://www.mathi.uni-heidelberg.de/~yves/Matritzen/QTBCH/QTBCHIndex.html

into AQECCs using purity-testing codes and robust secret sharing [472 ]. The resulting codes are efficiently encodable and decodable, and descriptions of the codes can be sampled by an efficient ran-domized algorithm with 2−Ω(𝑛 ) failure probability.  

> PROTECTION

For any 𝛾 > 0 and rate 0 < 𝑅 < 1, these approximate quantum ⟦𝑛, 𝑅 · 𝑛 ⟧𝑞 codes have constant Galois-qudit dimension 

𝑞 = 2𝑂 (1/𝛾 5 ) and correct errors acting on (1 − 𝑅 − 𝛾 ) · 𝑛 /2 registers, up to a recovery error of 2−Ω(𝑛 ) [472].  

> RATE

For any target rate 𝑅 ∈ ( 0, 1), codes can tolerate adversarial errors on nearly a (1 − 𝑅 )/ 2 fraction of registers while keeping constant alphabet size [472].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Efficient encoding.  

> DECODING

⊲ Efficient decoder based on quantum list decoding to-gether with purity-testing and robust-secret-sharing post-processing [472].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Galois-qudit CSS code › p. 493 ⊲ Approximate quantum error-correcting code (AQECC) › p. 294  

> COUSINS

⊲ Quantum maximum-distance-separable (MDS) code › p. 317 

— Singleton-bound approaching AQECCs asymptotically approach the quantum Singleton bound, rather than exactly saturating it at finite blocklength. ⊲ Folded quantum RS (FQRS) code › p. 492 

— Singleton-bound approaching AQECCs are built using folded quan-tum Reed-Solomon (FQRS) codes [ 472 ]. ⊲ Approximate secret-sharing code › p. 488 — Quantum secret-sharing codes have asymptoti-cally decaying rate and require qudit dimension to increase expo-nentially with 𝑛 , while Singleton-bound approaching AQECCs have constant rate and qudit dimension. ⊲ Good QLDPC code › p. 547 

— AEL distance amplification [ 470 , 471 ] can be used to construct constant-alphabet QLDPC CSS codes of any target rate 𝑅 and relative distance (1 − 𝑅 − 𝛾 )/ 2 that are decodable in linear time up to half that distance [ 472 , Corr. 5.3]. The AEL distance-amplification frame-work also yields constant-alphabet approximate quantum codes that decode nearly up to the quantum Singleton bound [472].

TRUE GALOIS-QUDIT STABILIZER CODE [381 , 663 ] 

> galois_true_stabilizer
> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Linear stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

A ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧𝑞 stabilizer code whose stabilizer’s Galois symplectic representation › p. 497 forms a linear subspace. In other words, the set of 𝑞 -ary vectors representing the stabilizer group is closed under both addition and multiplication by elements of F𝑞 . In contrast, Galois-qudit stabilizer codes admit sets of vectors that are closed under addition only. The number of generators 𝑟 for a true stabilizer code is a multiple of 𝑚 (recall that 𝑞 = 𝑝 𝑚 for Galois qudits). As a result, the number 

𝑘 = 𝑛 − 𝑟 /𝑚 of logical qudits is an integer. Each code can be represented by a stabilizer generator matrix 𝐻 =

( 𝐴 |𝐵 ), where each row (𝑎 |𝑏 ) is the Galois symplectic representation  

> › p. 497

of a stabilizer generator.  

> PROTECTION

Detects errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 qudits, and corrects erasure errors on up to 𝑑 − 1 qudits.

⊲ See Ref. [ 1966 , 2906 ] for introductions to various stabilizer code constructions.

𝜒 (2) CODE [4515] chi2  

> DESCRIPTION

A 3𝑛 -mode bosonic Fock-state code that requires only linear optics and the 𝜒 (2) optical nonlinear interaction for encoding, decoding, and logical gates. Codewords lie in Fock-state subspaces that are invariant under Hermitian combinations of the 𝜒 (2) nonlin-earities 𝑎𝑏𝑐 † and 𝑖𝑎𝑏𝑐 †, where 𝑎 , 𝑏 , and 𝑐 are lowering operators acting on one of the 𝑛 triples of modes on which the codes are de-fined. Codewords are also +1 eigenstates of stabilizer-like symmetry operators , and photon parities are error syndromes.  

> PROTECTION

Codes protect against loss, gain, and dephasing errors conditional on the knowledge of the total number of photons lost.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Linear optics and 𝜒 (2) interactions.  

> GATES

⊲ Linear optics and 𝜒 (2) interactions yield a universal set of gates.  

> DECODING

⊲ Linear optics and 𝜒 (2) interactions.  

> PARENT

⊲ Fock-state bosonic code › p. 521

AMPLITUDE-DAMPING (AD) CODE [820, 2524] ampdamp  

> DESCRIPTION

Block quantum code on either qubits or bosonic modes that is designed to detect and correct qubit or bosonic AD › p. 508 errors, respectively. 

> PROTECTION

Amplitude damping noise: The amplitude damping (AD) channel is a bosonic channel that models loss of particles in a bosonic mode 

FIG. 72: Projection of the 4{3}4 polytope with logical constellations marked in different colours. 

(a.k.a. photon loss, pure loss, or fiber attenuation). Its Kraus opera-tors are proportional to powers of a mode’s annihilation operator 𝑎 ,with the power signifying the number of particles lost during the error, 

𝐸 ℓ =

 𝛾 

1 − 𝛾 

ℓ/2 𝑎 ℓ

√ℓ! (1 − 𝛾 ) ˆ𝑛 /2 , (369) where 𝛾 ∈ [ 0, 1) is the noise rate [ 473 , 4519 ]. For multiple modes, error set elements are tensor products of elements of the single-mode error set. The fixed point of this channel for any truncation of Fock space is unique [4520]. Restricting the channel to the first two Fock states {| 0⟩, |1⟩} yields the non-Pauli qubit AD channel, which requires protecting against the loss error 𝐸 1 ∝ 𝑋 + 𝑖𝑌 (instead of 𝑋 and 𝑌 Pauli errors indi-vidually). Both channels are called AD since the context makes clear which one is being referred to. In this restriction, the qubit AD channel has Kraus operators 𝐴 0 = |0⟩ ⟨ 0| + √1 − 𝑝 |1⟩ ⟨ 1| and 

𝐴 1 = √𝑝 |0⟩ ⟨ 1|; 𝐴 1 is the decay event and 𝐴 0 is the no-jump operator whose action still changes the relative amplitudes [ 381 , Ch. 1]. Other extensions to qudits are also known [4521]. Protection against AD › p. 508 noise is typically approximate because the tensor product of Kraus operators with all ℓ = 0 is typically corrected only up to some order in 𝛾 [ 820 , 2524 ]. For example, a qubit code that corrects a single AD › p. 508 error is one for which all tensor products 𝐸 ℓ1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝐸 ℓ𝑛 with ℓ1 + · · · + ℓ𝑛 ≤ 1 are correctable (per the Knill-Laflamme conditions › p. 304 ) up to order › p. 161 𝑂 (𝛾 2).Certain codes also have intrinsic protection against AD › p. 508 , such as constant-excitation codes (CE), QSCs, or self-complementary codes. Amplitude damping can be thought of as a quantum ana-logue to asymmetric noise [1139].

ANALOG CLUSTER-STATE CODE [4528–4530] cv_cluster_state  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ CV cluster-state code ⊲ CV graph-state code 

⊲ Bosonic cluster-state code  

> DESCRIPTION

A code based on a continuous-variable (CV), or analog, cluster state. Such a state can be used to perform MBQC of logical modes, which substitutes the temporal dimension necessary for decoding a conventional code with a spatial dimension. The exact analog cluster state is non-normalizable, so approximate construc-tions have to be considered. Analog cluster states are analog stabilizer states defined on a graph. There is one nullifier ˆ𝜂 𝑗 per graph vertex 𝑗 of the form 

ˆ𝜂 𝑗 = ˆ𝑝 𝑗 −∑︁      

> 𝑘 ∈𝑁 (𝑗 )

𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 , (370) where the neighborhood 𝑁 ( 𝑗 ) is the set of vertices which share an edge with 𝑗 , and where 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 is a weighted (real-valued) adjacency matrix of a graph [4531]. Analog cluster states, like cluster states, can be defined on various geometries. Analog cluster states defined on a 1D array of modes are called quantum wires [ 4532 , 4533 ], not to be confused with the Kitaev quantum wire, a fermion code. Analog cluster states defined on a 1D ladder are sometimes called dual-rail, not to be confused with the dual-rail code.  

> PROTECTION

Protection is related to the analog stabilizer code under-lying the analog cluster state.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Initialization of all modes in momentum eigenstates and action of gates of the form exp (𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 ). The normalizable version substitutes momentum eigenstates with finitely squeezed states. ⊲ Squeezers and beam-splitters [4534].  

> GATES

⊲ Combination of linear-optical gates and homodyne mea-surements on subsets of vertices [ 4529 , 4530 ]. ⊲ Gaussian oper-ations can be realized as operations acting on graphs underlying a cluster state. They can be done in any order, demonstrating par-allelism [ 4529 , 4530 ]. ⊲ Magic-state distillation is required for universal computation [4529, 4530].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Analog cluster states on a number of modes ranging from tens to millions [ 4535 –4537 ] have been synthesized in photonic degrees of freedom. A 12 × 𝑁 mode cluster state, where 𝑁 is the number of clock cycles of the experiment, has been realized in a photonic device by Xanadu [ 4538 ]. ⊲ Required primitives for Gaussian gates have been realized [4539].  

> NOTES

⊲ See Ref. [ 3457 ] for a review of analog cluster states and their applications.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Analog stabilizer code › p. 510 — Analog cluster-state codes are particular analog stabilizer codes. Any analog stabilizer state is equivalent to an analog cluster state under a single-mode Gaussian circuit [ 482 ]. Relaxing the real weighted adjacency matrix of an analog cluster state to be complex yields a description of a general analog (i.e., Gaussian) stabilizer state [ 4540 ]. Pure Gaussian states, which are normalizable approximate versions of analog stabilizer states, are not equivalent to finitely squeezed analog cluster states via Gaussian local unitaries [ 4531 ]. ⊲ Graph quantum code › p. 547 

— Graph quantum codes for 𝐺 = R reduce to analog cluster-state codes.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Perfect-tensor code › p. 312 — Analog cluster states are generically CV AME [ 2838 ], and explicit constructions exist for any number of modes [ 482 ]. ⊲ 1D lattice stabilizer code › p. 542 — Analog cluster states defined on a 1D array of modes are called quantum wires [ 4532 , 4533 ], not to be confused with the Kitaev quantum wire, a fermion code. Analog cluster states defined on a 1D ladder are sometimes called dual-rail, not to be confused with the dual-rail code. ⊲ GKP CV-cluster-state code › p. 521 — GKP CV-cluster-state 510 codes reduce to analog-cluster-state codes when all physical modes are initialized in momentum states.

ANALOG STABILIZER CODE [482, 3274] analog_stabilizer  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Gaussian stabilizer code ⊲ Linear stabi-lizer code ⊲ Symplectic stabilizer code ⊲ Wavepacket code 

⊲ Infinitely squeezed state code  

> DESCRIPTION

An oscillator-into-oscillator stabilizer code encoding logical oscillator modes into 𝑛 physical modes. If the code is defined by 𝑟 independent nullifiers, then it is denoted by ⟦𝑛, 𝑛 − 𝑟 ⟧R and encodes 𝑘 = 𝑛 − 𝑟 logical modes [ 482 ]. Any analog stabilizer state can be thought of as a pure Gaussian state that has been infinitely squeezed on all modes [482]. Analog stabilizer codes admit a continuous stabilizer group of dis-placements. This group can equivalently be defined in terms of its Lie algebra. The codespace is equivalently the common 0-eigenvalue eigenspace of the Lie algebra generators, which are mutually com-muting linear combinations of oscillator position and momentum operators called nullifiers [ 4530 ] or annihilators . An analog stabilizer code admitting a set of nullifiers such that each nullifier consists of either position or momentum operators is called an analog CSS code . 

> PROTECTION

Protects against erasures of, or any errors on, at most 𝑑 −

1 modes. If an error operator does not commute with a nullifier, then that error is detectable. There are conditions on the encoding circuit which guarantee that the code can correct errors [ 4511 ]. The code can be further optimized to increase resolution between syndrome spaces for certain noise [4511]. Protection of logical modes against small displacements or other errors acting in every physical mode cannot be done using only Gaussian resources [ 4548 ]. For Gaussian displacement noise, linear oscillator encodings can at best squeeze the logical noise between conjugate quadratures rather than suppressing it in both simulta-neously [ 397 , Sec. VI] (see also [ 4549 , 4550 ]). There are no such restrictions for non-Gaussian noise [4511, 4551].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Gaussian circuit applied to 𝑘 modes storing logical in-formation and 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes initialized in a position state.  

> DECODING

⊲ Homodyne measurement of nullifiers yields real-valued syndromes, and recovery can be performed by displacements con-ditional on the syndromes.  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ One-sided device-independent QKD [4552].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bosonic stabilizer code › p. 515 — Analog stabilizer codes are bosonic stabilizer codes with a continuous stabilizer group, corresponding to linear constraints on positions and momenta. 

⊲ Oscillator-into-oscillator code › p. 527

⊲ Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP code › p. 527 — Analog stabi-lizer codes protect logical modes against arbitrarily large displace-ments on a few modes, while oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes protect an infinite-dimensional logical space against sufficiently small displacements in any number of modes. Encoding in analog-stabilizer (oscillator-into-oscillator GKP) codes can be done by a Gaussian operation acting on a tensor product of an arbitrary state in the first mode and position states (GKP states) on the remaining modes. For Gaussian displacement noise, linear oscillator encod-ings only squeeze the logical noise between conjugate quadratures [ 397 , Sec. The codespace of an analog stabilizer code with pure distance › p. 434 𝑑 pure is a (𝑑 pure − 1)-uniform space [ 482 ]. Normalizable finitely squeezed versions of infinitely squeezed Gaus-sian states are locally thermal, up to corrections in the squeezing parameter [ 2836 , 2854 ]. ⊲ Real block code › p. 261 — Analog stabi-lizer codes are quantum counterparts of real block codes. ⊲ EA analog stabilizer code › p. 521 — EA analog stabilizer codes utilize addi-tional ancillary modes in a pre-shared entangled state, but reduce to ordinary analog stabilizer codes when said modes are interpreted as noiseless physical modes. ⊲ Qudit cubic code › p. 484 — The qudit cubic code can be generalized to oscillators [2458].

BOSONIC CODE oscillators  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Continuous-variable (CV) quantum code 

⊲ Oscillator code ⊲ Quantum modulation scheme  

> KINGDOM ROOT CODE

for the Bosonic Kingdom › p. 13 . 

> DESCRIPTION

Encodes logical Hilbert space, finite- or infinite-dimensional, into a physical Hilbert space that contains at least one oscillator (a.k.a. bosonic mode or qumode ). States of a single oscillator correspond to 𝐿 2-normalizable func-tions on R that have finite energy, finite variance, and finite val-ues of all other moments (where the energy operator is defined to be the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian); such functions form 

Schwartz space (a.k.a. nuclear space [ 4573 ]), a subspace of Hilbert space [ 4574 ]. Ideal codewords may not be normalizable because the space is infinite-dimensional, so approximate versions have to be constructed in practice. States can be represented by a series via a basis expansion, such as that in the countable basis of Fock states |𝑛 ⟩ with 𝑛 ≥ 0 for a single oscillator. Alternatively, states can be represented as functions over the reals by expanding in a continuous "basis" (more technically, set of tempered distributions in the space dual to Schwartz space), such as the position "basis" |𝑦 ⟩ with 𝑦 ∈ R or the momentum "basis" 

| 𝑝 ⟩ with 𝑝 ∈ R. A third option is to use coherent states |𝛼 ⟩ with 

𝛼 ∈ C, which are eigenstates of the annihilation operator, which correspond to classical electromagnetic signals, and which resolve the identity [ 3559 , 4575 – 4577 ]. States can further be represented as functions over the joint position-momentum phase space in the Wigner function formalism [ 4578 , 4579 ]. GKP states have negative Wigner functions, but the alternative Zak-Gross Wigner function represents them positively [4580]. An important subset of states is formed by the Gaussian states ,which are in one-to-one correspondence with a (displacement) vec-tor and covariance matrix [ 3555 , 3556 , 4581 – 4587 ]. Pure Gaussian states correspond to the pure states with positive Wigner functions, a result known as Hudson’s theorem [ 4588 , 4589 ]. Pure Gaussian states can be obtained from the vacuum Fock state |𝑛 = 0⟩ via a Gaus-sian unitary transformation (defined below). Any coherent state can be obtained from the vacuum Fock state, itself a coherent state, by a displacement. There is a de Finetti theorem for Gaussian states [4590]. 

> PROTECTION
> Displacement error basis

An error set relevant to bosonic stabilizer › p. 515 codes is the set of displacement operators (a.k.a. Weyl operators [ 4399 ]), a bosonic analogue of the Pauli string basis for qubit › p. 433 codes.  

> Displacement operators:

For a single mode, its elements are products of exponentials of the mode’s position and momentum operators, acting on the mode’s position states |𝑦 ⟩ for 𝑦 ∈ R as 

𝑒 −𝑖𝑞 ˆ𝑝 |𝑦 ⟩ = |𝑦 + 𝑞 ⟩ and 𝑒 𝑖𝑞 ˆ𝑥 |𝑦 ⟩ = 𝑒 𝑖𝑞𝑦 |𝑦 ⟩ , (381) 513 where 𝑞 ∈ R. The former is also called a translation, while the latter is called a modulation in signal processing. For multiple modes, error set elements are tensor products of elements of the single-oscillator error set, characterized by the vector of coefficients 𝜉 ∈

R2𝑛 .The displacement error set is a unitary basis for bounded opera-tors on the 𝑛 -mode Hilbert space that is Dirac-orthonormal under the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product. Expanding a bounded operator in terms of displacements is called the Fourier-Weyl transform (a.k.a. Fourier-Weyl relation) [ 4591 ][ 4592 , Eq. (4.11)]. For the expansion of Gaussian unitary operations in terms of displacements, see [ 4593 ,Eq. (7.62)]. There are two definitions of code distance associated with dis-placements. The definition inherited from qubit codes is the mini-mum weight of a displacement operator (i.e., number of nonzero entries in 𝜉 ) that implements a nontrivial logical operation in the code. The second definition is the minimum Euclidean distance (i.e., ℓ2-norm of 𝜉 ) such that the corresponding displacement imple-ments a nontrivial logical operation in the code. Quantum weight enumerators › p. 434 and the Cohn-Elkies bound have been extended to the case of displacement noise [4594]. 

> Loss and gain operators

An error set relevant to Fock-state bosonic › p. 521 codes is the set of loss operators associated with the AD › p. 508 channel, a common form of physical noise in bosonic systems. For a single mode, loss opera-tors are proportional to powers of the mode’s annihilation operator 

𝑎 = ( ˆ𝑥 + 𝑖 ˆ𝑝 )/ √2, where ˆ𝑥 ( ˆ𝑝 ) is the mode’s position (momentum) operator, and with the power signifying the number of particles lost during the error. For multiple modes, error set elements are tensor products of elements of the single-mode error set. Quantum Hamming bounds have been extended to the case of loss noise [ 4515 ]

> Number-phase operators

A related error set is the set of powers of the Susskind–Glogower phase operator 1√𝑎𝑎 † 𝑎 and its adjoint [ 4595 –4597 ] along with Fock-space rotations generated by the occupation number operator 𝑎 †𝑎 .These can also be obtained from qudit Pauli matrices through a limiting procedure [ 4597 ] and allow one to expand trace-class opera-tors despite not forming an orthonormal set [ 4574 ]. These operators correspond to the number-phase interpretation , a polar-like decom-position of a single mode, complementing the cartesian-like decom-position in terms of position and momentum displacements. This decomposition can be called a number-phase rotor, which differs from the ordinary 𝑈 (1) rotor in the absence of states of negative angular momentum. Mathematically, the restriction of an ordinary rotor to states of non-negative momentum is a projection onto Hardy space, and the phase operator is an example of a Toeplitz operator on that space [4598]. 

> Noise channels

Gaussian channels are quantum channels that map Gaussian states to Gaussian states [ 4599 – 4605 ]; their Kraus representation is calcu-lated in Ref. [ 4606 ]. These include the AD › p. 508 channel and the displacement noise channel. The algebraic structure of the Lie alge-bra of Gaussian channels is the same as that of the super-Poincare algebra in three-dimensional spacetime [4607]. An important non-Gaussian noise channel is the dephasing noise channel, which applies a random rotation in phase space about the origin.  

> RATE

The quantum capacity of the AD › p. 508 channel [ 4522 ] and the dephasing noise channel [ 4608 ] are both known. The capacity of the displacement noise channel, the quantum analogue of AWGN, has been bounded using GKP codes [ 2532 , 4609 ]. Exact two-way assisted capacities have been obtained for the AD › p. 508 channels and quantum limited amplifiers in what is known as the PLOB bound [4038 ]. Bounds exist on the two-way quantum and secret-key capac-ities for some prominent Gaussian channels [ 4610 – 4619 ] and non-Markovian channels, i.e., channels with memory effects [ 4620 ]. The continuous-variable erasure channel has a known quantum capacity [4621 , 4622 ]. Non-Gaussian channel capacities can be bounded for single [ 4623 ] and multiple [ 4517 , Lemma 14] modes. Non-asymptotic bounds exist for memoryless channels [ 4624 ] as well as for those with memory effects [ 4625 ]. The optimal asymptotic error exponent of entanglement distillation is given by the reverse relative entropy of entanglement, a single-letter quantity [4626].  

> GATES

⊲ Displacement operations form a group called the Heisenberg-Weyl group, the oscillator analogue to the Pauli group 

> › p. 433

. Analogues of (non-Pauli) Clifford-group transformations are the Gaussian unitary transformations (a.k.a. symplectic, Bogoliubov-Valatin, or linear canonical transformations) [ 3558 , 4586 , 4627 , 4628 ], which are unitaries generated by quadratic polynomials in posi-tions and momenta. The Gaussian unitary transformation group permutes displacement operators amongst themselves, and, up to any phases, is equivalent to the symplectic group 𝑆 𝑝 (2𝑛, R). Ev-ery Gaussian unitary can be decomposed into single-mode squeez-ing gates sandwiched by passive linear-optical transformations in what is known as the Bloch-Messiah (a.k.a. Euler) decomposition [4592 , 4629 ]. ⊲ Computing using Gaussian states and Gaussian unitaries only can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer [ 4630 –4632 ], and there are efficient algorithms to do so [ 4583 , 4633 ]. This remains true even if superpositions of Gaussian states are con-sidered [ 4634 , 4635 ], but is no longer the case when the number of modes scales exponentially [ 4636 ]. ⊲ A gate generated by a cubic or higher-degree polynomial is required to make a universal gate set on the oscillator (an infinite-dimensional version of the Solovay-Kitaev theorem) [ 4582 , 4637 , 4638 ]. The cubic phase gate [488 ] is a common gate used in tandem with Gaussian gates for uni-versality, and Fock-state matrix elements of the cubic and quartic phase gates have been derived [ 4639 ] (see also Refs. [ 4640 , 4641 ]). Arbitrary-degree polynomial gates are well defined, but cubic or higher versions of squeezing admit subtle mathematical proper-ties [ 4642 – 4645 ]. Unitaries generated by polynomials of position and momentum can exactly realize any finite-dimensional unitary evolution, and any physical bosonic unitary evolution can be approx-imated by a finite-dimensional unitary evolution [ 4638 , 4646 , 4647 ]. Certain non-quadratic Hamiltonians yield infinite-energy states in finite time [ 4648 ]. See Ref. [ 4649 ] for bosonic computational com-plexity classes. The stellar rank [ 4650 ] and symplectic rank [ 4651 ]quantify the degree of non-Gaussianity of bosonic states. Functional MPS can be used to simulate evolution of non-Gaussian states [ 4652 ]. Universal bosonic quantum computations can be simulated in expo-nential time on a classical computer [4653]. 

⊲ There is a bosonic analogue of the Clifford hierarchy › p. 435 

[4654 , 4655 ]. ⊲ Controllability of bosonic states has been proven when the normalizable state space is restricted to Schwartz space [4656 ] and using polynomials in position and momentum [ 4638 ]. 

⊲ Measurements can be performed by homodyne, heterodyne, and generalized homodyne measurements [ 4657 ]. ⊲ The number-phase interpretation allows for the mapping of rotor Clifford gates into the oscillator, some of which become non-unitary (e.g., con-ditional occupation number addition) [ 2621 ]. ⊲ ZX calculus has been extended to bosonic codes for both Gaussian operators [ 4658 ], 514 Fock-state based operators [ 4659 ], and passive linear-optical trans-formations [ 4660 ]. An earlier graphical calculus exists for Gaussian pure states [ 4540 ]. ⊲ Circuits can be decomposed into a series of primitives such as quantum lattice gates, which are exponentials of cosines and sines of position and momentum [ 4661 ]. ⊲ Number-phase teleportation can be done using a two-mode squeezed state [4662].

The code admits the following basis of codewords for complex 

𝛼 > 0, up to normalization:

BOSONIC ROTATION CODE [4569] bosonic_rotation  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Rotationally symmetric bosonic (RSB) code  

> DESCRIPTION

A single-mode Fock-state bosonic code whose codespace is preserved by a phase-space rotation by a multiple of 

2𝜋 /𝑁 for some 𝑁 . The rotation symmetry ensures that encoded states have support only on every 𝑁 th Fock state. For example, single-mode Fock-state codes for 𝑁 = 2 encoding a qubit admit 515 basis states that are, respectively, supported on Fock state sets 

{| 0⟩, |4⟩, |8⟩, · · · } and {| 2⟩, |6⟩, |10 ⟩, · · · } .Codewords can be uniquely specified by choosing a primitive state 

|Θ⟩. To ensure valid (orthogonal and nonzero) codewords, |Θ⟩ must satisfy the following requirement: for each 𝑗 ∈ Z𝑞 , |Θ⟩ must have support on at least one Fock state |( 𝑘 𝑗 𝑞 + 𝑗 )𝑁 ⟩ for some 𝑘 𝑗 ∈ N0.A set of logical codewords is then obtained by projecting |Θ⟩ onto the 𝑞 eigenspaces of the discrete rotation operator, equivalently by summing the 𝑞𝑁 rotated copies of |Θ⟩ with appropriate phases.  

> PROTECTION

Losses or gains less than 𝑁 are detectable. Dephasing rotations exp (i𝜃 ˆ𝑛 ) can be detected whenever 𝜃 is roughly less than 

𝜋 /𝑁 . To get precise bounds on 𝜃 , one needs to analyze the particular bosonic rotation code.  

> ENCODING

⊲ The optimal way to prepare codewords depends on the exact rotation code in question [4569].

> 𝑛 =0

|𝑛 ⟩ ⟨ 𝑛 + 𝑁 |. ⊲ For qubit codes, a logical phase gate is 𝑆 = e𝜋 i ˆ 𝑛 2 /2𝑁 2

. ⊲ The 𝑇 =

diag (1, exp (i𝜋 /4)) gate can be done via gate teleportation and a re-source state |0𝑁 ⟩ + exp (i𝜋 /4)| 1𝑁 ⟩. ⊲ A controlled-rotation gate between an order 𝑁 rotation code and an order 𝑀 rotation code is 

CROT 𝑁 𝑀 = e(2 𝜋 i/𝑞 𝑁 𝑀 ) ˆ𝑛 ⊗ ˆ𝑛 . 

> DECODING

⊲ For qubit rotation codes, one can distinguish the computational-basis codewords destructively by performing a Fock-state number measurement. If a Fock state |𝑛 ⟩ is measured, then one rounds to the nearest multiple of 𝑁 and infers the logical value from the parity of that multiple [ 4569 ]. ⊲ One can distinguish states in the dual basis by performing phase estimation on ei 𝜃 ˆ𝑛 .One then rounds the resulting 𝜃 to the nearest number 2𝜋 𝑗 /𝑞𝑁

BOSONIC STABILIZER CODE oscillator_stabilizer  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ CV stabilizer code ⊲ Oscillator stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

Bosonic code whose codespace is defined as the com-mon +1 eigenspace of a group of mutually commuting displacement operators. Displacements form the stabilizers of the code, and have continuous eigenvalues, in contrast with the discrete set of eigen-values of qubit stabilizers. As a result, exact codewords are non-normalizable, so approximate constructions have to be considered. Stabilizer groups are any locally compact Abelian subgroups of R𝑛 ,can themselves contain discrete or continuous subgroups, and can admit logical qudit and/or oscillator logical subspaces. Stabilizer codewords encoding a finite-dimensional codespace admit a discrete infinite stabilizer group and encode quantum infor-mation in a lattice. Such qudit-into-oscillator › p. 530 stabilizer codes are GKP › p. 530 and multimode GKP › p. 522 codes. Stabilizer codewords encoding a logical oscillator (i.e., CV quan-tum information) admit either a discrete or a continuous stabilizer group. The former, called oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes, are obtained from multimode GKP codes by removing stabilizer gen-erators for some of the modes. The latter encode information in hyperplanes and can be defined in terms of the continuous group’s Lie algebra, i.e., as the common 0-eigenvalue eigenspace of mutually commuting linear combinations of oscillator position and momen-tum operators called nullifiers [4530 ] or annihilators . An oscillator-into-oscillator › p. 527 stabilizer code encoding 𝑘 logical modes into 

𝑛 physical modes is denoted as ⟦𝑛, 𝑘, 𝑑 ⟧R, where 𝑑 is the code’s distance.  

> PROTECTION

Protective properties can be delineated in terms of the nullifiers or displacements, and the most natural noise model for such codes is displacement noise. If an error operator does not com-mute with a stabilizer group element, then that error is detectable. Oscillator-into-oscillator stabilizer codes protect against erasures of a subset of modes, while GKP codes protect against sufficiently small displacements in any number of modes.  

> GATES

⊲ General gates can be done using the bosonic analogue of gate teleportation [4654].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bosonic code › p. 512 ⊲ Stabilizer code › p. 559  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Analog stabilizer code › p. 510 — Analog stabilizer codes are bosonic stabilizer codes with a continuous stabilizer group, corresponding to linear constraints on positions and momenta. 

⊲ Quantum lattice code › p. 529 — Quantum lattice codes are bosonic stabilizer codes with a countably infinite stabilizer group, cor-responding to modular constraints on positions and momenta. 

⊲ Bosonic CSS code › p. 514  

> COUSINS

⊲ Number-phase code › p. 526 — Number-phase codewords span the joint right eigenspace of the 𝑁 th power of the Susskind-Glogower phase operator and the bosonic rotation operator [ 4569 ]. These operators no longer form a group since the phase operator is not unitary. ⊲ Homological number-phase code › p. 524 — Homo-logical number-phase codewords span the joint right eigenspace of powers of the non-unitary Susskind–Glogower phase operators and unitary bosonic rotation operators. 

CAT CODE [4684] cat  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Superposition of coherent states (SCS) 516  

> DESCRIPTION

Rotation-symmetric bosonic Fock-state code encoding a 

𝑞 -dimensional qudit into one oscillator which utilizes a constellation of 𝑞 (𝑆 + 1) coherent states distributed equidistantly around a circle in phase space of radius 𝛼 .Codewords for a qubit code ( 𝑞 = 2) consist of a coherent state |𝛼 ⟩

projected onto a subspace of Fock state number modulo 2(𝑆 +1). The logical state |0⟩ is in the {| 0⟩, |2(𝑆 +1)⟩ , |4(𝑆 +1)⟩ · · · } Fock-state sub-space, while |1⟩ is in the {|( 𝑆 +1)⟩ , |3(𝑆 +1)⟩ , |5(𝑆 +1)⟩ , |7(𝑆 +1)⟩ · · · } 

subspace. These projected coherent states make up generalized cat states [4685, 4686].  

> PROTECTION

Due to the spacing between sets of Fock states, the dis-tance between two distinct logical states is 𝑑 = 𝑆 + 1. Hence, this code is able to detect up to 𝑆 photon-loss › p. 508 errors.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Lindbladian-based dissipative encoding and au-tonomous QEC utilizing multi-photon generalization of two-photon absorption [ 4687 – 4690 ]. Encoding passively protects against modal dephasing, suppressing dephasing noise exponentially with |𝛼 |2

[4691 ]. ⊲ Approximate cat states can be prepared using Gaussian operations and photon detectors [4692].  

> GATES

⊲ Holonomic gates utilizing the Berry phase of coherent states are universal [ 4693 ]. ⊲ Universal gates for the 𝑆 = 1 code can be performed using squeezing operators and quantum Zeno effect and a rotation based on the Kerr nonlinearity [ 4691 ]. ⊲ Error-detecting 𝐶𝐶𝑍 and 𝑐𝑆𝑊 𝐴𝑃 gates for four-component cat code using three-level ancilla [ 4557 ]. ⊲ Universal set of error-corrected oper-ations tolerating a single photon loss › p. 508 and an arbitrary ancilla fault [4694].  

> DECODING

⊲ Measuring the Fock-state number modulo 𝑆 + 1 can be used to determine if photon-loss › p. 508 or excitation errors occurred. For 𝑆 = 1, this is the occupation number parity [4569].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Universal set of error-corrected operations toler-ating a single photon loss › p. 508 and an arbitrary ancilla fault [ 4694 ]. 

⊲ Linear-optical noise suppression and mitigation scheme [4695].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Parity-syndrome measurement tested [ 4696 ] and implemented for the four-component ( 𝑆 = 1) cat code [ 4697 ] in a mi-crowave cavity coupled to a superconducting circuit. The latter work [4697 ] is the first to reach break-even error-correction, where the life-time of a logical qubit is on par with the cavity lifetime, despite pro-tection against dephasing not being implemented. A fault-tolerant version of parity measurement has also been realized [4698].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bosonic rotation code › p. 514 — The cat code is a bosonic rotation code whose primitive state is the coherent state |𝛼 ⟩ [4569 ]. 

⊲ Cat-repetition code › p. 516 — The cat-repetition code for 𝑛 = 1 re-duces to the cat code.  

> CHILD

⊲ Two-component cat code › p. 534 — The cat code reduces to its two-component version for 𝑆 = 0. 

> COUSINS

⊲ Number-phase code › p. 526 — In the limit as 𝑁, 𝑆 → ∞ ,phase measurement in the cat code has vanishing variance, just like in a number-phase code [ 4569 ]. Conversely, a cat code can be thought of as an appropriately regularized number-phase code. 

⊲ Group-representation code › p. 306 — Cat codes are not group rep-resentation codes with 𝐺 being a cyclic group since their repre-sentation is reducible [ 2728 ]. ⊲ Phase-shift keying (PSK) modu-lation format › p. 273 — PSK (cat) codes are used to transmit classical (quantum) information using (superpositions of) single-mode coher-ent states distributed on a circle over classical (quantum) channels. 

⊲ Polygon code › p. 273 — The 𝑞 (𝑆 + 1)-component cat coherent-state constellation forms the vertices of a 𝑞 (𝑆 + 1)-gon. ⊲ PSK c-q modulation format › p. 573 — PSK c-q (cat) codes are used to transmit classical (quantum) information using (superpositions of) single-mode coherent states distributed on a circle over quantum channels. 

⊲ Hybrid cat code › p. 551 — Hybrid cat codewords consist of a bosonic mode in either coherent or cat states. ⊲ Pair-cat code › p. 528 — Cat (pair-cat) codewords are superpositions of coherent (pair-coherent) states. CAT-REPETITION CODE [2540, 2570, 4699] cat_repetition  

> DESCRIPTION

A concatenated qubit-into-𝑛 -mode code obtained by encoding each qubit of a quantum repetition code into a two-component cat code in its cat-state basis. A basis of codewords for the two-component case is 

|±⟩ ∝ (| 𝛼 ⟩ ± |− 𝛼 ⟩) ⊗𝑛 (383) for any complex 𝛼 . 

> PROTECTION

The code can detect arbitrary losses in up to 𝑛 /2 modes. The cat-repetition code on a 2D mode lattice is a candidate for a memory that may be self-correcting, but only in the limit of infinite energy per mode [2949].  

> GATES

⊲ Fault-tolerant logical 𝑋 , CNOT, and Toffoli gates and a logi-cal Hadamard synthesized from state preparation and measurement in the dual basis, without magic-state preparation or distillation [2540 ]. ⊲ Using a physical bias-preserving CX between cat qubits, the logical CX gadget can be implemented transversally between repetition-code blocks; magic-state preparation using transversal 

𝑍 𝑍 (𝜃 ) gates was also analyzed [2570].  

> DECODING

⊲ A measurement-code decoder for the repetition layer yields a CX -gadget threshold of about 6 × 10 −3 for 𝑛 = 5; reaching a comparable threshold with naive repeated-syndrome decoding requires 𝑛 = 11 and 𝑟 = 5 [2570].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant logical 𝑋 , CNOT, and Toffoli gates and a logical Hadamard synthesized from state preparation and measurement in the dual basis, without magic-state preparation or distillation [2540].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ For dephasing bias 𝜂 = 10 4, the cat-based logical CX 

gadget has threshold 7.5 × 10 −3, compared with 3.55 × 10 −3 for an earlier scheme; at 𝜀 = 2.5 × 10 −3, its circuit volume is about five times smaller [2570].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Superconducting circuit devices: a repetition code out of two-component cat qubits has been realized for distances 3 and 5 [4700].  

> PARENT

CHUANG-LEUNG-YAMAMOTO (CLY) CODE [2524]  

> chuang-leung-yamamoto
> DESCRIPTION

Bosonic Fock-state code that encodes 𝑘 qubits into 𝑛 

oscillators, with each oscillator restricted to having at most 𝑁 ex-citations. Codewords are superpositions of oscillator Fock states which have exactly 𝑁 total excitations, and are either uniform (i.e., balanced) superpositions or unbalanced superpositions. Codes can be denoted as ⟦𝑁, 𝑛, 2𝑘 , 𝑑 ⟧, which conflicts with stabi-lizer code › p. 559 notation.  

> PROTECTION

Protects against AD › p. 508 for up to 𝑡 = 𝑑 − 1 excitation losses. Defining the spacing between two Fock states |𝑢 1 · · · 𝑢 𝑛 ⟩ and 

|𝑣 1 · · · 𝑣 𝑛 ⟩,Spacing (𝑢, 𝑣 ) = 12

> 𝑛

∑︁ 

> 𝑖 =1

|𝑢 𝑖 − 𝑣 𝑖 |, (385) the code distance 𝑑 can be defined as the minimal spacing between Fock states making up the codewords.  

> RATE

Code rate is 𝑘 𝑛 log 2 ( 𝑁 +1) . To correct the loss of up to 𝑡 excitations with 𝐾 + 1 codewords, a code exists with scaling 𝑁 ∼ 𝑡 3𝐾 /2. 

> ENCODING

⊲ Photon Fock state input into a network of beamsplitters, phase shifters, and Kerr media. These operations all preserve total photon number. Beamsplitters and phase shifters take annihilation operators to linear combinations of annihilation operators, and the transformation matrix is unitary. The operations corresponding to Kerr nonlinear media are diagonal in the Fock basis, but they im-plement phases that in general depend nonlinearly on the number of photons in each mode. State preparation may require ancillary modes and be conditioned on photon-number measurement results.  

> DECODING

⊲ Destructive decoding with a photon number measure-ment on each mode. ⊲ State can be decoded with a network of beamsplitters, phase shifters, and Kerr media.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Fock-state bosonic code › p. 521 — Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto codes are multi-mode Fock-state codes. ⊲ Constant-excitation (CE) code › p. 300 — Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto codewords are constructed out of Fock states with the same total excitation number.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ One-hot quantum code › p. 527 ⊲ Two-mode binomial code › p. 535  

> COUSIN

⊲ Jump code › p. 408 — Jump codes can be thought of as qubit analogues of uniform CLY codes. 

CLIFFORD GROUP-REPRESENTATION QSC [2728] clifford_qsc  

> DESCRIPTION

Non-uniform QSC whose projection is onto a copy of an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Clifford group › p. 244 ,taken as the binary octahedral subgroup of the group 𝑆𝑈 (2) of Gaus-sian rotations. Its codewords consist of non-uniform superpositions of 40 coherent states drawn from a 48-element Clifford-group orbit.  

> GATES

⊲ The single-qubit Clifford group › p. 244 can be realized via Gaussian rotations. The 𝑇 and 𝐶𝑍 gates can be realized using quartic Kerr operations [2728].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Quantum spherical code (QSC) › p. 529 — The Clifford group-representation QSC has non-uniform coefficients. ⊲ Group-representation code › p. 306 — The Clifford group-representation QSC is a group-representation code with 𝐺 being single-qubit Clifford group › p. 244 , taken as the binary octahedral subgroup of the group 

𝑆𝑈 (2) of Gaussian rotations.

COHERENT-STATE CONSTELLATION CODE coherent_constellation  

> DESCRIPTION

Qudit-into-oscillator code whose codewords can suc-cinctly be expressed as superpositions of a countable set of coherent states that is called a constellation . Some useful constellations form a group (see gkp › p. 530 , cat › p. 515 or 2𝑇 -qutrit › p. 508 codes) while others make up a Gaussian quadrature rule [889, 890].  

> RATE

Coherent-state constellation codes consisting of points from a Gaussian quadrature rule can be concatenated with quantum polar codes to achieve the Gaussian coherent information of the thermal noise channel [889, 890].

CONCATENATED GKP CODE [3195] gkp_concatenated  

> DESCRIPTION

A concatenated code whose outer code is a GKP code. In other words, a bosonic code that can be thought of as a concatenation of an arbitrary inner code and another bosonic outer code. Most examples encode physical qubits of an inner stabilizer code into the square-lattice GKP code.  

> PROTECTION

The analog syndrome information of the outer GKP code can improve protection of the inner code. As an example, concate-nating a three-qubit quantum repetition code with GKP codes can correct some two-bit-flip errors [3195].  

> RATE

Recursively concatenating the 𝐶 6 and ⟦4, 2, 2⟧ codes with GKP codes achieves the hashing bound of the displacement channel [3195 ]. Concatenating Abelian LP codes with GKP codes can sur-pass the CSS Hamming bound [ 1509 ]. Particular families of GKP codes achieve the capacity of AD › p. 508 and amplification channels for some loss rates [ 4703 ]. Concatenations of square-lattice GKP codes with Hermitian Galois-qudit codes achieve the capacity for all loss rates [ 3950 ]. Concatenation of GKP codes with quantum polar codes achieves a rate against the displacement channel [3950].  

> GATES

⊲ Linear-optical computation [4704].  

> DECODING

⊲ Circuit-level soft information decoder [4705].  

> CODE CAPACITY THRESHOLD

⊲ 0.599 threshold displacement standard deviation for GKP-repetition code [ 4011 ]. ⊲ 0.59 threshold dis-placement standard deviation for GKP-color code [ 4301 ]. ⊲ A con-catenated threshold › p. 435 with GKP codes on the lowest level exists for general Markovian noise [ 4706 ]. ⊲ There is an upper bound on the threshold under local update recovery that is derived via quantum optimal transport [4092].  

> NOTES

⊲ Bosonic Pauli+ model is a numerical simulation tool for concatenated GKP codes [4707].

DUAL-RAIL QUANTUM CODE [4709–4711] dual_rail  

> DESCRIPTION

Two-mode bosonic code encoding a logical qubit in Fock states with one excitation. The logical-zero state is represented by 

|10 ⟩, while the logical-one state is represented by |01 ⟩. This encoding is often realized in temporal or spatial modes, corresponding to a 

time-bin or frequency-bin encoding. Two different types of photon polarization can also be used. This code is a DFS [ 2634 – 2637 ] with respect to phase errors [ 4712 ].  

> PROTECTION

This is an error-detecting code against one photon loss  

> › p. 508

event; it is often used in photonic quantum devices because of its ease of realization. A single loss event can be detected be-cause, after the loss occurs, the output state |00 ⟩ is orthogonal to the codespace. Recovery is not possible, so a successful run of a quantum circuit is conditioned on not losing a photon during the circuit. Photon loss from a dual-rail or polarization encoding maps the qubit outside its two-dimensional codespace into a vacuum state, so it is naturally modeled as an erasure rather than as a qubit amplitude-damping channel [381, Ch. 1]. For Deutsch”s problem specifically, this code protects against errors resulting in states that have the correct photon number, but in the wrong modes [4709].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Optimal control pulses [4713]  

> GATES

⊲ General gates are performed using two-body Hamilto-nian rotations [ 4712 ]. ⊲ Bosonic gates include beamsplitters [4714 ] and Kerr nonlinearities. In particular, a cross Kerr rota-tion at angle 𝜋 induces a 𝐶𝑍 gate. Universal quantum comput-ing can be achieved using the KLM protocol [ 3268 ] with only lin-ear optical elements and photon detectors. ⊲ Photon-number-conserving universal quantum logic can be implemented using continuous-time quantum walks on dual-rail transmon arrays [ 4715 ]. 

⊲ Dynamical-decoupling protocols [ 4712 , 4716 ]. ⊲ A probabilistic CZ gate via a non-linear sign-shift gate, which transforms the Fock states 𝛼 |0⟩ + 𝛽 |1⟩ + 𝛾 |2⟩ into 𝛼 |0⟩ + 𝛽 |1⟩ − 𝛾 |2⟩, followed by mea-surement [ 4717 ]. ⊲ Error-detecting 𝐶𝐶𝑍 and 𝑐𝑆𝑊 𝐴𝑃 gates using three-level ancilla [ 4557 ]. ⊲ Cavity-assisted bias-preserving CNOT gate [4718].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Dual-rail qubits can be used to convert leakage and AD › p. 508 noise into erasure noise [1140, 4527].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ The dual-rail code is ubiquitous in linear-optical quantum devices and is behind the KLM protocol, one of the first proposals for fault-tolerant computation. See reviews [ 3480 , 4719 ,4720 ] for more details. ⊲ Superconducting circuit devices: Gates have been demonstrated in the Schoelkopf group at Yale University [ 4714 ]. Error detection has been demonstrated in 3D cavities in the Devoret group at Yale University [ 4713 ] and Amazon Web Services [ 4721 ] using transmon qubits, following earlier theoretical proposals [4527 , 4722 ]. GHZ and Bell states as well as universal gates have been implemented on a four-qubit dual-rail code by the Yu group [3263 ]. Logical readout in 3D cavities has been demonstrated by Quantum Circuits Inc. [ 4723 ]. Cavity-assisted bias-preserving CNOT gate has been demonstrated [ 4718 ]. ⊲ Photonic platforms: state preparation and measurement fidelity of 99 .98% in the C telecom band by PsiQuantum [4724].

FOCK-STATE BOSONIC CODE fock_state  

> DESCRIPTION

Qudit-into-oscillator code whose protection against AD  

> › p. 508

noise (i.e., photon loss) stems from the use of disjoint sets of Fock states for the construction of each code basis state. The sim-plest example is the dual-rail code, which has codewords consisting of single Fock states |10 ⟩ and |01 ⟩. This code can detect a single loss error since a loss operator in either mode maps one of the codewords to a different Fock state |00 ⟩. More involved codewords consist of several well-separated Fock states such that multiple loss events can be detected and corrected.  

> PROTECTION

Code distance 𝑑 is the minimum distance (assuming some metric) between any two labels of Fock states corresponding to different code basis states. For a single mode, 𝑑 is the minimum absolute value of the difference between any two Fock-state labels; such codes can detect up to 𝑑 − 1 loss events. Multimode distances can be defined analogously; see, e.g., Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto codes › p. 517 . There are tradeoffs in how well a Fock-state code pro-tects against loss/gain errors and dephasing noise [4726].  

> RATE

For every 𝐾, 𝑡 ≥ 2, there are explicitly constructible 𝐾 -dimensional Fock-state codes with 𝑞 = 𝑁 = (𝐾 − 1)𝑡 (𝑡 + 1) modes, total excitation 𝑁 , and bosonic distance 𝑡 + 1; there also exist fami-lies with logical dimension 𝐾 = 𝑜 (2𝑁 ) and distance of order › p. 161 

𝑜 (𝑁 /log 𝑁 ) [475].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Qudit-into-oscillator code › p. 530 ⊲ Amplitude-damping (AD) code › p. 508 — Fock-state codes are designed to protect against bosonic AD › p. 508 noise.  

> CHILDREN

⊲ Bosonic 𝑞 -ary expansion › p. 512 — The bosonic 𝑞 -ary expansion allows one to map between prime-dimensional qudit states and a Fock subspace of a single mode. ⊲ 𝜒 (2) code › p. 507 

⊲ Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto (CLY) code › p. 517 — Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto codes are multi-mode Fock-state codes. ⊲ Ouyang-Chao constant-excitation PI code › p. 528 ⊲ Icosahedral Fock-state code › p. 525 ⊲ Very small logical qubit (VSLQ) code › p. 535 ⊲ Matrix-model code › p. 525 — Matrix-model logical states lie in a low-energy Fock-state subspace. ⊲ Pair-cat code › p. 528 ⊲ Bosonic rotation code › p. 514 — Single-mode Fock-state codes are typically rotationally invariant.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Binary code › p. 179 — Fock-state code distance is a natural extension of Hamming distance between binary strings. ⊲ Fock-state OOK c-q modulation format › p. 572 — Fock-state OOK transmits classical information using Fock states, while Fock-state bosonic codes store quantum information in subspaces built from Fock states. ⊲ Tiger code › p. 533 — Tiger codes encoding logical qudits are Fock-state codes. ⊲ Permutation-invariant (PI) code › p. 313 —Modular-qudit PI codes can be converted to constant-excitation Fock-state codes via the simplex mapping › p. 313 [475 , Prop. V.2]. Any transversal gates are mapped to Gaussian gates on the Fock-state codes [ 475 ]. ⊲ Twisted 1-group code › p. 541 — Twisted 1-group codes can be converted to constant-excitation Fock-state codes via the simplex mapping › p. 313 [475 , Prop. GKP CV-CLUSTER-STATE CODE [483] gkp-cluster-state  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ Hybrid cluster-state code  

> DESCRIPTION

A cluster-state code that utilizes a generalized analog cluster state with some of its physical modes initialized in GKP (re-source) states. Alternatively, it can be thought of as a multimode GKP code whose encoding consists of initializing 𝑘 modes in mo-mentum states (or, in the normalizable case, squeezed vacua), 𝑛 − 𝑘 

modes in (normalizable) GKP states, and applying a Gaussian circuit consisting of two-body gates 𝑒 𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 for some angles 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 . The code provides a way to perform fault-tolerant MBQC, with the required number 𝑛 − 𝑘 of GKP-encoded physical modes determined by the particular protocol [396, 483–485].  

> ENCODING

⊲ Initializing 𝑘 modes in momentum states (or, in the normalizable case, squeezed vacua), 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes in (normalizable) GKP states, and applying a Gaussian circuit consisting of two-body gates 𝑒 𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 for some angles 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 . 

> GATES

⊲ Logical Clifford gates are performed on the cluster state via a combination of linear-optical gates and homodyne measurements on subsets of vertices [ 4529 , 4530 ]. Magic-state distillation is re-quired for universal computation. ⊲ Single-mode logical Clifford gates can be performed using Gaussian operations and measure-ments on a 1D GKP cluster state, while two-mode logical Clifford gates require a 2D cluster state. Magic-state distillation using photon-counting can be used for a non-Clifford logical 𝜋 /8 gate. ⊲ Gate teleportation and error correction can be performed without active squeezing [4727]. 522  

> DECODING

⊲ GKP error correction can be naturally combined with CV MBQC protocols since the performance of both is quantified by a squeezing parameter [483].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ A lower bound on the squeezing required to obtain a particular error rate can be formulated in terms of the displacement noise strength. This in turn determines how much squeezing is required in order to be below threshold › p. 435 for a particular con-catenated code. For a qubit-level fault-tolerance threshold of 10 −6,the required squeezing is above 20.5 dB [ 483 ]. Anti-squeezing does not affect this threshold estimate [ 4728 ]. ⊲ For topologically pro-tected MBQC on 3D cluster states built from finitely squeezed GKP qubits, analog QEC together with postselected measurements dur-ing cluster-state construction reduces the required squeezing to 9.8

dB [396].  

> REALIZATIONS

GOTTESMAN-KITAEV-PRESKILL (GKP) CODE [ 488 , 4609 ] 

> multimodegkp
> DESCRIPTION

Quantum lattice code for a non-degenerate lattice, thereby admitting a finite-dimensional logical subspace. Codes on 𝑛 modes can be constructed from lattices with 2𝑛 -dimensional full-rank Gram matrices 𝐴 . Any GKP code can be generated from a Gram matrix in standard form via a Gaussian unitary transformation [486, Corr. 1]. The centralizer for the stabilizer group within the displacement operators case can be identified with the symplectic dual lattice L⊥

(i.e. all points in R2𝑛 that have integer symplectic inner product with all points in L ), such that logical operations are identified with the dual quotients L⊥/L . The size of this dual quotient is the determinant of the Gram matrix, yielding the logical dimension 

𝑑 =√︁ ∥ det 𝐴 ∥ [488 ]. Stabilizer generator matrices equivalent un-der symplectic transformations are classified by distinct Hermite normal forms [4729]. The space of all single-mode GKP codes is the moduli space of elliptic curves, i.e., the three sphere with a trefoil knot removed [4730].  

> PROTECTION

The level of protection against displacement errors is quantified by the Euclidean code distance Δ = min 𝑥 ∈ L ⊥\L ∥𝑥 ∥2

[4729]. There are upper bounds on this distance [4729, 4731].  

> RATE

Transmission schemes with multimode GKP codes achieve a lower bound on displacement noise and a lower bound on the thermal-noise Gaussian channel capacities [ 2532 , 4609 , 4732 , 4733 ]. Particular random lattice families of multimode GKP codes achieve the hashing bound of the displacement noise channel [ 4609 ]. Par-ticular families of GKP codes achieve the capacity of AD › p. 508 and amplification channels for some loss rates [4703].  

> ENCODING

⊲ GKP codes with fixed 𝑛 and prime-dimensional logical Hilbert space are symplectically related to a disjoint product of single-mode GKP codes on 𝑛 modes, such that encoding via Gaussian unitaries is possible. ⊲ Dissipative stabilization of finite-energy 523 GKP states using stabilizers conjugated by cooling ([ 483 ], Appx. B) or 

damping operator, i.e., a damped exponential of the total occupation number [ 462 , 4734 ]. ⊲ Logical Bell state can be created from two canonical GKP states by applying a beamsplitter [4727].  

> GATES

⊲ Gaussian operations and homodyne measurements on non-magic GKP states are classically simulable [ 4735 ], and there is a sufficient condition for an additional element to achieve universal quantum computation [ 4736 ]. There is an algorithm for GKP circuit simulation whose runtime scales with the amount of negativity of the Zak-Gross Wigner function [ 4737 ]. ⊲ There is a relation between magic (i.e., how far away a state is from being a stabilizer state) and non-Gaussianity for GKP codewords [ 4735 , 4738 ]. In particular, implementing a non-Clifford logical gate requires a higher degree of non-Gaussianity than that expressed by ideal non-normalizable GKP states [ 4735 ]. ⊲ By applying GKP error correction to Gaussian input states, computational universality can be achieved without additional non-Gaussian elements [ 4739 ]. This procedure can be alternatively described as performing heterodyne detection on one half of a GKP encoded Bell pair. The cubic phase gate is not a suit-able gate [ 4740 ]. ⊲ Logical shadow tomography protocol [ 4741 ]. 

⊲ Some gates have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing [4742].  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndrome extraction is performed by measuring stabi-lizers and correcting. Issues arising from the use of finite-energy approximate states can be mitigated [ 4743 ]. ⊲ The MLD decoder for Gaussian displacement errors is realized by evaluating a lattice theta function, and in general the decision can be approximated by either solving (approximating) the closest vector problem (CVP) [4744 ] (a.k.a. closest lattice point problem) or by using other effective iterative schemes when, e.g., the lattice represents a concatenated GKP code [ 397 , 398 , 1509 , 4729 ]. While the decoder time scales ex-ponentially with number of modes 𝑛 generically, the time can be polynomial in 𝑛 for certain codes [ 401 ]. ⊲ Babai’s nearest plane algorithm [ 4745 ] can be used for bounded-distance decoding [ 401 ]. 

⊲ Combining AD › p. 508 noise with amplification yields displacement noise, the noise that GKP codes are designed to correct [ 2532 , 4746 ]. 

⊲ ML decoder for correcting shift errors in GKP two-qubit gates [400].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Logical Clifford operations are given by Gaussian unitaries, which map bounded-size errors to bounded-size errors [488 ]. For single-mode GKP codes, these operations correspond to non-trivial loops in the space of all single-mode GKP codes (the moduli space of elliptic curves, i.e., the three sphere with a trefoil knot removed) [ 4730 ]. Such gates provide another example of mon-odromy under the particular notion of parallel transport introduced in Ref. [ 773 ]. ⊲ The 4D square-lattice GKP code admits the isth-mus property, which allows certain ancilla errors to be detectable [462].

HEXAGONAL GKP CODE [488, Sec. VI] hexagonal_gkp  

> DESCRIPTION

Single-mode GKP qudit-into-oscillator code based on the triangular lattice. Offers the best error correction against dis-placement noise in a single mode due to the optimal packing of the underlying lattice [488, Sec. VI].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Microwave cavity coupled to superconducting cir-cuits: reduced form of GKP error correction, where displacement error syndromes are measured to one bit of precision using an an-cillary transmon [4751].  

> NOTES

⊲ Hexagonal GKP codes were obtained after iterative numer-ical optimization of encoding and recovery against photon loss › p. 508 ,starting with Haar-random states [2532].

HOMOLOGICAL NUMBER-PHASE CODE [ 2621 ] 

> homological_number-phase
> DESCRIPTION

A homological 𝑛 -rotor code › p. 550 mapped into the Fock-state space of 𝑛 oscillators by identifying non-negative rotor angular-momentum states with oscillator Fock states. The resulting oscilla-tor code can encode logical rotors or qudits due to the presence of torsion in the chain complex defining the original rotor code. These codes are tailored to settings in which photon loss is present but ran-dom rotations, i.e., dephasing, are the dominant noise mechanism [2621]. Due to the absence of negative Fock states, a given homological rotor code first has to be rotated such that it has non-trivial support in the all-positive momentum orthant. This can be done by flipping the signs of the angular momenta of some of the rotors [ 2621 , Prop. 1]. Ideal codewords are not normalizable, and approximate versions have to be constructed. Since homological rotor codes use an extension of the qubit CSS-to-homology correspondence › p. 437 to rotors, the mapping into oscil-lators makes such homological encodings possible for oscillators.  

> PROTECTION

The homology group of the logical operators has a tor-sion component because the chain complexes are defined over the ring of integers, which yields codes with finite logical dimension. Products of chain complexes can also yield rotor codes. The distances of the original homological rotor code are pre-served, although the resulting number-phase code is approximately error-correcting due to the non-orthogonality of Pegg-Barnett phase states [ 476 ], which act as the angular position states in the number-phase interpretation of the oscillator.  

> PARENT

⊲ Bosonic code › p. 512 — Homological number-phase codes are bosonic codes encoding logical qudits and/or logical rotors.  

> COUSINS

⊲ Homological rotor code › p. 550 — Homological number-phase codes can be thought of as homological rotor codes but whose underlying rotors consist of the number and phase degrees of free-dom of physical modes. ⊲ Bosonic stabilizer code › p. 515 — Homo-logical number-phase codewords span the joint right eigenspace of powers of the non-unitary Susskind–Glogower phase operators and unitary bosonic rotation operators. ⊲ Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP code › p. 527 — Homological number-phase codes are finite-dimensional cousins of number-phase-rotor GKP-stabilizer codes: both use number-phase resource states and Clifford-semigroup en-coders to protect oscillator information against photon loss and dephasing [ 2621 , Secs. 6-7]. ⊲ Number-phase code › p. 526 — Ho-mological number-phase codes are multi-mode generalizations of number-phase codes, obtained by projecting suitably parity-flipped homological rotor codes onto the non-negative angular-momentum orthant [ 2621 , Prop. 1]. ⊲ Generalized homological-product CSS code › p. 546 — Homological number-phase codes are non-stabilizer codes constructed from chain complexes over the integers. The homology group of the logical operators has a torsion component 525 because the chain complexes are defined over the ring of integers, which yields codes with finite logical dimension. ⊲ Four-rotor code › p. 546 — After suitable rotor-parity flips and projection onto the non-negative angular-momentum orthant, the four-rotor current-mirror code yields a homological number-phase code [2621, Ex. 4]. 

⊲ Tiger code › p. 533 — Tiger codes of infinite Fock-state support can be thought of as appropriately regularized homological number-phase codes [4516].

INTEGER-HOMOLOGY BOSONIC CSS CODE [392] homological_cv  

> DESCRIPTION

A bosonic stabilizer code whose physical modes have been restricted, via a single GKP stabilizer, from the space of func-tions on the real line to the space of periodic functions. This restric-tion effectively realizes a rotor on each physical mode, allowing one to construct homological rotor codes out of displacement stabilizer groups. The stabilizer group is continuous, but contains discrete components in the form of the single-mode GKP stabilizers. The homology group of the logical operators has a torsion component because the chain complexes are defined over the ring of integers, which yields codes with finite logical dimension.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Bosonic CSS code › p. 514 — Integer-homology bosonic CSS codes are constructed from chain complexes over the integers and realize homological rotor codes out of continuous displacement stabilizer groups. The stabilizer group is continuous, but contains discrete components in the form of the single-mode GKP stabiliz-ers. ⊲ Generalized homological-product CSS code › p. 546 — Integer-homology bosonic CSS codes are constructed from chain complexes over the integers and realize homological rotor codes out of con-tinuous displacement stabilizer groups. The homology group of the logical operators has a torsion component because the chain complexes are defined over the ring of integers, which yields codes with finite logical dimension.  

> CHILD

⊲ Compactified R gauge theory code › p. 518 — The compactified 

R gauge theory code realizes 𝑈 (1) gauge theory on bosonic modes.  

> COUSIN

⊲ Homological rotor code › p. 550 — Integer-homology bosonic CSS codes are constructed from chain complexes over the integers and realize homological rotor codes out of continuous displacement stabilizer groups [392].

> DESCRIPTION

The model’s degrees of freedom are matrix-valued bosons 𝑎 , each consisting of 𝑁 2 harmonic oscillator modes and subject to an 𝑆𝑈 (𝑁 ) gauge symmetry. A simple matrix-model code [ 2768 ] consists of two spatially sepa-rated bosons with codewords

> DESCRIPTION

> PROTECTION

Number-phase codes detect up to 𝑁 photon loss › p. 508 

or gain errors, and approximately correct rotations up to 𝜃 = 𝜋 /𝑁 .However, the code is only approximately error-correcting due to the non-orthogonality of Pegg-Barnett phase states [ 476 ], which act as the angular position states in the number-phase interpretation of the oscillator.  

> DECODING

⊲ Modular phase measurement done in the logical 𝑋 ,or dual, basis has zero uncertainty in the case of ideal number-phase codes. This is equivalent to a quantum measurement of the spectrum of the Susskind-Glogower phase operator [ 4569 ]. Approx-imate number-phase codes are characterized by vanishing phase uncertainty [ 4569 ]. Such measurements can be utilized for Knill error correction (a.k.a. telecorrection [ 3093 ]), which is based on teleportation [ 428 , 4244 ]. This type of error correction avoids the complicated correction procedures typical in Fock-state codes, but requires a supply of clean codewords [ 4569 ]. Performance of this method was analyzed in Ref. [ 4754 ], and it was extended in Ref. [4755 ]. ⊲ Number measurement can be done by extracting modu-lar number information using a CROT gate e(2 𝜋 i/𝑁 𝑀 ) ˆ𝑛 ⊗ ˆ𝑛 and per-forming phase measurements [ 4756 , 4757 ] on an ancillary mode [4569].  

> FAULT TOLERANCE

⊲ Fault-tolerant computation schemes with number-phase codes have been proposed based on concatenation with Bacon-Shor subsystem codes [4569].  

> REALIZATIONS

⊲ Motional degree of freedom of a trapped ion: state initialization [4758].  

> PARENT

⊲ Bosonic rotation code › p. 514 — Number-phase codes are bosonic rotation codes whose primitive state is a Pegg-Barnett phase state [476].  

> COUSINS

⊲ Rotor GKP code › p. 558 — Number-phase codes are ob-tained by projecting planar-rotor GKP codes onto the non-negative angular-momentum subspace and identifying that subspace with os-cillator Fock space [ 2621 , Ex. 3]. ⊲ Bosonic stabilizer code › p. 515 —Number-phase codewords span the joint right eigenspace of the 𝑁 th power of the Susskind-Glogower phase operator and the bosonic ro-tation operator [ 4569 ]. These operators no longer form a group since the phase operator is not unitary. ⊲ Square-lattice GKP code › p. 530 

— Square-lattice GKP codes utilize translational symmetry in phase space, while number-phase codes utilize rotational symmetry. OSCILLATOR-INTO-OSCILLATOR GKP CODE [4623] gkp-stabilizer  

> ALTERNATIVE NAMES

⊲ GKP-stabilizer code  

> DESCRIPTION

Multimode GKP code with an infinite-dimensional log-ical space. Can be obtained by considering an 𝑛 -mode GKP code with a finite-dimensional logical space, removing stabilizers such that the logical space becomes infinite dimensional, and applying a Gaussian circuit. Simple oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes include GKP-repetition codes and GKP two-mode-squeezing (TMS) codes [ 4623 ]. Arbitrary oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes can be reduced to a standard form consisting of a direct sum of GKP TMS codes, up to symplectic transformations [ 4517 ]. The optimal code design problem of determining the squeezing parameters can be efficiently solved [4517].  

> PROTECTION

Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes to protect one or more modes against displacement noise using GKP resource states.  

> ENCODING

⊲ Gaussian circuit applied to 𝑘 modes storing logical in-formation and 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes initialized in a fixed GKP state.  

> DECODING

⊲ Syndromes can be read off using ancilla modes, yielding partial information about noise in the logical modes that can then be used in an efficient ML decoding procedure [4708].  

> THRESHOLD

⊲ Thresholds against displacement noise cannot be ob-tained without ideal (i.e., non-normalizable) codewords [4764].  

> NOTES

⊲ Introduction to and examples of oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes [4574].  

> PARENTS

⊲ Quantum lattice code › p. 529 — Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes are 𝑛 -mode quantum lattice codes with less than 2𝑛 sta-bilizers, i.e., constructed using a degenerate lattice (see Appx. A of Ref. [4729]). ⊲ Oscillator-into-oscillator code › p. 527  

> CHILD

⊲ GKP CV-cluster-state code › p. 521 — A GKP CV-cluster-state code can be created by initializing 𝑘 modes in momentum states (or, in the normalizable case, squeezed vacua), 𝑛 − 𝑘 modes in (nor-malizable) GKP states, and applying a Gaussian circuit consisting of two-body 𝑒 𝑖𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 ˆ𝑥 𝑗 ˆ𝑥 𝑘 for some angles 𝑉 𝑗 𝑘 . 

> COUSINS

⊲ Concatenated GKP code › p. 519 — Oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes concatenated with qubit-into-oscillator GKP codes can outperform more conventional concatenations of qubit-into-oscillator GKP codes with qubit stabilizer codes [ 4708 ]. ⊲ 𝐷 4

hyper-diamond GKP code › p. 507 — 𝐷 4 hyper-diamond GKP codes may be optimal for oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes utilizing two ancilla modes [ 4517 ]. ⊲ Hexagonal GKP code › p. 524 — Hexag-onal GKP codes may be optimal for oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes utilizing one ancilla mode [ 4517 ]. ⊲ Number-phase code  

> › p. 526

— Number-phase codes can serve as resource states for number-phase-rotor GKP-stabilizer codes, a polar analogue of oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes that protects against photon loss and de-phasing [ 2621 , Sec. 7]. ⊲ Analog stabilizer code › p. 510 — Analog stabilizer codes protect logical modes against arbitrarily large dis-placements on a few modes, while oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes protect an infinite-dimensional logical space against suffi-ciently small displacements in any number of modes. Encoding in analog-stabilizer (oscillator-into-oscillator GKP) codes can be done by a Gaussian operation acting on a tensor product of an ar-bitrary state in the first mode and position states (GKP states) on the remaining modes. For Gaussian displacement noise, linear os-cillator encodings only squeeze the logical noise between conju-gate quadratures [ 397 , Sec. VI], and protection of logical modes against small displacements cannot be done using only Gaussian resources [ 4548 , 4549 ], so oscillator-into-oscillator GKP codes can 528 be thought of as analog stabilizer encodings utilizing non-Gaussian GKP resource states. ⊲ Homological number-phase code › p. 524 —Homological number-phase codes are finite-dimensional cousins of number-phase-rotor GKP-stabilizer codes: both use number-phase resource states and Clifford-semigroup encoders to protect oscillator information against photon loss and dephasing [2621, Secs. 6-7].

PAIR-CAT CODE [4765] paircat  

> DESCRIPTION

Two- or higher-mode extension of cat codes whose code-words are right eigenstates of powers of products of the modes’ low-ering operators. Many gadgets for cat codes have two-mode pair-cat analogues, with the advantage being that such gates can be done in parallel with a dissipative error-correction process. Two-mode codewords are supported by Fock states with oc-cupation number ˆ𝑛 2 − ˆ𝑛 1 fixed to some integer Δ. The occupation-number differences form the syn-dromes, as opposed to the photon-number parity for the single-mode cat code. Any loss event or combination of losses that changes the relative occupation-number differences between modes is de-tectable.

PAULI TESSELLATION QSC [2729] pauli_qsc  

> DESCRIPTION

Two-mode non-uniform QSC whose projection is onto a copy of an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Pauli group › p. 433 , realized geometrically by the {2, 2, 4} tessellation of the sphere [ 2729 ]. RENORMALIZATION GROUP (RG) CAT CODE [ 2471 , 4775 , 4776 ] 

> rg_cat
> DESCRIPTION

Code whose codespace is spanned by 𝑞 field-theoretic coherent states which are flowing under the renormalization group (RG) flow of massive free fields. The code approximately protects against displacements that represent local (i.e., short-distance, ultra-violet, or UV) operators. Intuitively, this is because RG cat codewords represent non-local (i.e., long-distance) degrees of freedom, which should only be excitable by acting on a macroscopically large num-ber of short-distance degrees of freedom.  

> PROTECTION

Approximately protects against displacements that rep-resent ultraviolet coherent operators, i.e., short-distance degrees of freedom of the field theory.  

> PARENTS

⊲ Coherent-state constellation code › p. 518 ⊲ Holographic code › p. 308 — The RG cat code encoder has coarse-graining features reminiscent of holography [ 2471 ]. ⊲ Approximate quantum error-correcting code (AQECC) › p. 294 — RG cat codes approximately protect against displacements that represent ultraviolet coherent operators.
